docs.title: C++ from Zero to Advanced
docs.text:
A friendly, intuition-first C++ course — from your first main() to lock-free queues, coroutines, and embedded-style containers. 16 weeks, short video-sized lessons, quizzes, labs, and programming assignments. Every code example on this site is a real file that is compiled and run automatically.

The idea behind this course

You don't need to memorize the standard. You need good intuition for what the machine is doing, a handful of reliable habits, and lots of small, successful steps. We'll build all three — one idea at a time.

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text:
• You've programmed before (any language) and want to learn C++ properly.
  • You already write some C++ (maybe through Android NDK, game engines, or embedded work) and want real depth: value categories, move semantics, the memory model, templates and concepts, and how professionals build, test, and profile C++.

docs.title: Course structure
docs.text:
Each week has 5–7 lessons. Each lesson is sized like a 6–12 minute video and follows the same rhythm:

  1. Why this matters — a concrete problem that motivates the idea.
  2. The idea, built up from a tiny example, often showing the wrong way first, then the fix.
  3. Key takeaways — a short recap.
  4. Quiz — 3–5 questions with hidden answers.
  5. Practice lab (optional) — starter code and a full solution.

Each week ends with a week quiz and a programming assignment. The course ends with two capstone projects.

Start with How to take this course, then Setup, then Week 1. And keep the Feature checklist handy.

docs.title: How to take this course
docs.text: Welcome! Here's how to get the most out of this course.

docs.title: Pace
docs.text: There are 16 weeks. At roughly 5–7 hours per week (lessons + labs + assignment) you'll finish in about four months. If you already know some C++, you can move faster through Weeks 1–3 — but do take the quizzes. If you get a quiz question wrong, that's the lesson to revisit.

docs.title: Type the code
docs.text: Reading code feels like understanding. Typing it, changing it, and breaking it is understanding. For each lesson, open the example in your editor (they're all in the repository under examples/weekNN/), run it, then change one thing and predict what will happen before you run it again.

docs.title: What's optional
docs.text:
Not everything is equally important on a first pass. Lessons and sections marked optional or advanced can be skipped and revisited later:

  • Week 6.4 (multiple and virtual inheritance) — good to know, rarely needed.
  • Week 7.5 (SFINAE) — mostly historical; concepts replaced it. Learn to read it.
  • Week 14 (memory orderings, lock-free) — genuinely hard. Don't worry if it takes two passes. Most professionals use mutexes and stay happy.
  • Week 16.5 (C++26 preview) — the future, not yet in your compiler.

docs.title: Be honest with yourself about difficulty
docs.text: C++ is a large language. Some topics (value categories, the memory model, template error messages) are confusing for everyone at first. If something doesn't click, that's normal. Move on, come back after a week, and it'll usually make much more sense.

docs.title: How the code is verified
docs.text: Every example is a real .cpp file in the repository, included verbatim into the pages. A script (scripts/check_examples.sh) compiles each one with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic and the right -std=, runs it, and compares the output with what's shown on the page. Examples meant to show a compile error are checked to actually fail. Concurrency examples are also run under ThreadSanitizer and UB examples under AddressSanitizer/UBSan in CI. Short snippets inside the prose (marked as fragments, like int x; // WRONG) are illustrations, not full programs.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
You need a C++20 compiler (C++23 for a few lessons), CMake, and an editor.

Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)macOSWindows 
sudo apt install g++-14 clang cmake ninja-build gdb
g++-14 --version

xcode-select --install        # Apple clang
brew install llvm cmake ninja # newer clang with more C++23 support

Install Visual Studio 2022 (Desktop development with C++), or use WSL2 with the Linux instructions.

Recommended editors: VS Code with the clangd extension, CLion, or Visual Studio.

docs.title: Compiler support
docs.text: C++20 is well supported by GCC ≥ 13, Clang ≥ 17 and MSVC 19.3x. C++23 library features vary: std::print, std::expected work in GCC 14 and recent Clang/libc++; std::flat_map needs GCC 15 or libc++ 20+; std::generator is in GCC 14 but not yet in libc++. Lessons tell you when a feature needs a recent compiler. Check cppreference's compiler support table.

docs.title: Capstones
docs.text:
Two projects pull the course together. Each comes with a complete reference implementation (a header-only library), a test program, and a demo — all compiled and run by the same checker as every lesson example, on GCC 14 and Clang, with sanitizers in CI.

Capstone Builds on You'll practise A: Concurrent task library + CLI Weeks 4–5, 9, 13–14 RAII, futures, condition variables, back-pressure, shutdown, testing under TSan B: Embedded ring buffer Weeks 3, 7–8, 10, 14, 16 templates, constexpr, no-heap design, iterators, lock-free SPSC

docs.title: How to approach them (Andrew Ng-style)
docs.text:
1. Read the spec and write the tests first — or at least list the cases.
  2. Build the simplest version that passes one test. Then the next.
  3. Run under sanitizers early (-fsanitize=address,undefined, and separately -fsanitize=thread).
  4. Only then compare with the reference implementation. It's fine — expected, even — if yours differs.

Honest note: Capstone A's concurrency is the hardest thing in this course. If a test hangs or TSan complains, that's not failure; it's the learning.

docs.title: Capstone B: An embedded fixed-capacity ring buffer
The problem
docs.text: A microcontroller samples a sensor in an interrupt at 8 kHz; the main loop filters and transmits the data. You need a buffer that: never allocates, has bounded and predictable timing, can be used in constexpr code and tests, supports an overwrite-oldest policy for "latest N readings" use cases, and has a lock-free variant for the ISR→main-loop hand-off.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. RingBuffer<T, N>: push / pop / peek / indexing (0 = oldest) / iteration, full, empty, clear; overflow policy reject or overwrite oldest (with a counter).
  2. All operations noexcept for trivially copyable T, and usable in constant expressions.
  3. SpscRing<T, N>: lock-free single-producer/single-consumer, power-of-two capacity, drop counter.
  4. No heap allocation anywhere; static_asserts for misuse (zero capacity, non-power-of-two, non-trivial ISR payloads, non-lock-free atomics).
  5. Tests run under ASan/UBSan; the SPSC test runs under TSan.

docs.title: The library
Tests
Demo: a simulated sensor ISR
docs.text:
A thread stands in for the interrupt; the main loop drains the SPSC ring and keeps a moving average of the last 8 readings in an overwrite-oldest RingBuffer.

examples/capstone/ringbuffer_demo.cpp
#include "ring_buffer.hpp"

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

struct Sample { std::uint32_t seq; std::int16_t value; };

int main() {
    embedded::SpscRing<Sample, 64> isr_to_main;
    std::atomic<bool> sensor_done{false};
    constexpr std::uint32_t total = 5000;

    std::thread isr{[&] {                                    // stands in for the 8 kHz sampling interrupt
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < total; ++i) {
            Sample s{i, static_cast<std::int16_t>((i % 100) - 50)};
            while (!isr_to_main.push(s)) std::this_thread::yield();   // a real ISR would drop instead
        }
        sensor_done.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
    }};

    embedded::RingBuffer<std::int16_t, 8> window{embedded::RingBuffer<std::int16_t, 8>::Overflow::overwrite_oldest};
    std::uint32_t received = 0, expected_seq = 0;
    bool in_order = true;
    for (;;) {
        if (auto s = isr_to_main.pop()) {
            in_order = in_order && s->seq == expected_seq++;
            (void)window.push(s->value);
            ++received;
        } else if (sensor_done.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {
            if (auto last = isr_to_main.pop()) { in_order = in_order && last->seq == expected_seq++; (void)window.push(last->value); ++received; continue; }
            break;
        } else {
            std::this_thread::yield();
        }
    }
    isr.join();
    int sum = 0;
    for (auto v : window) sum += v;
    std::cout << "received " << received << " samples, in order: " << std::boolalpha << in_order << '\n';
    std::cout << "last 8 readings average: " << static_cast<double>(sum) / static_cast<double>(window.size()) << '\n';
    std::cout << "window overwrote " << window.overwritten() << " older readings; no heap used\n";
}

Output:

received 5000 samples, in order: true
last 8 readings average: 45.5
window overwrote 4992 older readings; no heap used

docs.text:

  • Port to a real board (e.g. an STM32 with arm-none-eabi-g++ -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti) and measure cycles per push.

docs.title: Capstone A: A concurrent task library with a CLI
The problem
docs.text: You have a batch of jobs — say, checksumming files or rendering audio stems. You want a reusable library that runs them on N threads, returns results through futures, propagates exceptions, applies back-pressure (a bounded queue, so a fast producer can't exhaust memory), reports statistics, and shuts down cleanly. Then a small command-line tool on top.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. ThreadPool(threads, max_queue) — validates arguments.
  2. submit(f, args...) → std::future<R>; blocks while the queue is full; throws after shutdown.
  3. try_submit(...) → std::optional<std::future<R>>; never blocks.
  4. Exceptions inside tasks reach the caller via future::get(); the pool keeps running.
  5. wait_idle() waits until all submitted work is done.
  6. shutdown(drain) finishes queued work; shutdown(discard) drops it (futures report broken_promise).
  7. stats() returns submitted / completed / failed / rejected counts.
  8. Tests pass under ThreadSanitizer.

docs.title: The library
Tests
The CLI
docs.text:
taskrun [--threads N] [--jobs M] [--queue Q] computes a CPU-bound job set and prints a summary. With no arguments it uses defaults (which is how the checker runs it).

examples/capstone/threadpool_cli.cpp
#include "threadpool.hpp"

#include <charconv>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

struct Options { unsigned threads = 4; int jobs = 32; std::size_t queue = 8; };

bool parse_uint(std::string_view s, auto& out) {
    auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), out);
    return ec == std::errc{} && p == s.data() + s.size() && out > 0;
}

bool parse_args(int argc, char** argv, Options& o) {
    for (int i = 1; i < argc; ++i) {
        std::string_view a = argv[i];
        if (i + 1 >= argc) { std::cerr << "missing value for " << a << '\n'; return false; }
        std::string_view v = argv[++i];
        bool ok = a == "--threads" ? parse_uint(v, o.threads)
                : a == "--jobs"    ? parse_uint(v, o.jobs)
                : a == "--queue"   ? parse_uint(v, o.queue) : false;
        if (!ok) { std::cerr << "bad option " << a << ' ' << v << '\n'; return false; }
    }
    return true;
}

std::uint64_t collatz_steps(std::uint64_t n) {
    std::uint64_t steps = 0;
    while (n != 1) { n = (n % 2) ? 3 * n + 1 : n / 2; ++steps; }
    return steps;
}

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    Options opt;
    if (!parse_args(argc, argv, opt)) {
        std::cerr << "usage: taskrun [--threads N] [--jobs M] [--queue Q]\n";
        return 2;
    }
    tasklib::ThreadPool pool{opt.threads, opt.queue};
    std::vector<std::future<std::uint64_t>> results;
    for (int j = 0; j < opt.jobs; ++j)
        results.push_back(pool.submit([j] {                  // blocks when the queue is full
            std::uint64_t best = 0;
            for (std::uint64_t n = 1 + static_cast<std::uint64_t>(j) * 1000; n <= static_cast<std::uint64_t>(j + 1) * 1000; ++n)
                best = std::max(best, collatz_steps(n));
            return best;
        }));
    std::uint64_t overall = 0;
    for (auto& f : results) overall = std::max(overall, f.get());
    pool.wait_idle();
    auto s = pool.stats();
    std::cout << "threads=" << pool.thread_count() << " jobs=" << opt.jobs << " queue=" << opt.queue << '\n';
    std::cout << "longest Collatz chain below " << opt.jobs * 1000 << ": " << overall << " steps\n";
    std::cout << "stats: submitted=" << s.submitted << " completed=" << s.completed
              << " failed=" << s.failed << " rejected=" << s.rejected << '\n';
}

Output:

threads=4 jobs=32 queue=8
longest Collatz chain below 32000: 307 steps
stats: submitted=32 completed=32 failed=0 rejected=0

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Work stealing with per-worker deques.
  • Task priorities, or cancellation with std::stop_token.
  • Replace std::function with std::move_only_function (C++23) to avoid the shared_ptr.
  • Expose the pool as a std::execution scheduler (C++26, via stdexec).

docs.title: Feature checklist
docs.text:
This page lists the important C++ language features and standard library topics, each mapped to the lesson that teaches it and tagged with the standard that introduced it (or made it usable in its modern form). It is generated from the lesson sources, so if a row is here, the lesson really covers it.

Tags: C++98/03 (classic), C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23, C++26 (preview). A "—" tag means a tool or practice rather than a language feature.

Use it as a checklist: tick off what you can explain to a colleague without notes.

docs.title: Week 1: Getting started: toolchain, compilation, types
docs.text:
Welcome to Week 1! This week is about getting comfortable. We'll install a compiler, write a program, and then — this is the part most courses skip — understand what actually happens between your .cpp file and a running program. Then we'll meet C++'s basic types, how variables get initialized, and the operators you'll use every day.

If you already write some C++, don't skip the compilation-model lesson. Many "mysterious" linker errors you've seen in Android NDK builds will suddenly make sense.

# Lesson Standard Length 1.1 Hello, toolchain: compilers, CMake and Compiler Explorer C++20 10 min 1.2 The compilation model: preprocessor, translation units, linking, ODR C++20 12 min 1.3 Fundamental types, literals, and fixed-width integers C++20 11 min 1.4 Variables and initialization: auto, const, constexpr C++20 10 min 1.5 Operators, integer promotion and narrowing C++20 11 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 1 programming assignment: A WAV header inspector
docs.text:
Let's put the week together. A WAV file starts with a 44-byte header. You'll write a program that builds a header for given parameters into a byte array and then parses it back, printing the fields.

Requirements:

  1. Use fixed-width types (std::uint16_t, std::uint32_t) for every field.
  2. Write little-endian values byte-by-byte with shifts (don't memcpy structs — padding and endianness make that non-portable).
  3. Compute byte_rate = sample_rate * channels * bits/8 using constexpr where possible.
  4. Compile warning-free with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic.

Don't worry if the shifting feels unfamiliar: we cover bit operations properly in Week 3. Peek at the solution if you get stuck — that's part of learning.

Starter code examples/week01/assignment_starter.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

void put_u32(std::array<std::uint8_t, 44>& h, int pos, std::uint32_t v) {
    // TODO: write 4 bytes, least significant first
}

int main() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 44> header{};
    put_u32(header, 24, 48000);  // sample rate lives at offset 24
    std::cout << "TODO\n";
}
Reference solution examples/week01/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

using Header = std::array<std::uint8_t, 44>;

void put_u16(Header& h, std::size_t pos, std::uint16_t v) {
    h[pos] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(v & 0xFF);
    h[pos + 1] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(v >> 8);
}
void put_u32(Header& h, std::size_t pos, std::uint32_t v) {
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 4; ++i) h[pos + i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(v >> (8 * i));
}
std::uint16_t get_u16(const Header& h, std::size_t pos) {
    return static_cast<std::uint16_t>(h[pos] | (h[pos + 1] << 8));
}
std::uint32_t get_u32(const Header& h, std::size_t pos) {
    std::uint32_t v = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 4; ++i) v |= std::uint32_t{h[pos + i]} << (8 * i);
    return v;
}

int main() {
    constexpr std::uint32_t sample_rate = 48'000;
    constexpr std::uint16_t channels = 2, bits = 16;
    constexpr std::uint32_t byte_rate = sample_rate * channels * bits / 8;
    constexpr std::uint32_t data_size = byte_rate * 1;  // one second of audio

    Header h{};
    const char* tags[] = {"RIFF", "WAVE", "fmt ", "data"};
    const std::size_t tag_pos[] = {0, 8, 12, 36};
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 4; ++i) h[tag_pos[t] + i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(tags[t][i]);
    put_u32(h, 4, 36 + data_size);
    put_u32(h, 16, 16);      // fmt chunk size
    put_u16(h, 20, 1);       // PCM
    put_u16(h, 22, channels);
    put_u32(h, 24, sample_rate);
    put_u32(h, 28, byte_rate);
    put_u16(h, 32, static_cast<std::uint16_t>(channels * bits / 8));  // block align
    put_u16(h, 34, bits);
    put_u32(h, 40, data_size);

    std::cout << "format=" << get_u16(h, 20) << " channels=" << get_u16(h, 22)
              << " rate=" << get_u32(h, 24) << " byte_rate=" << get_u32(h, 28)
              << " bits=" << get_u16(h, 34) << " data=" << get_u32(h, 40) << '\n';
}

Output:

format=1 channels=2 rate=48000 byte_rate=192000 bits=16 data=192000

docs.title: Lesson 1.1: Hello, toolchain: compilers, CMake and Compiler Explorer
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Before we can learn a language, we need a way to run it. In Python you type python file.py and you're done. C++ is different: it is a compiled language, so a tool called a compiler turns your text into machine code ahead of time. That's a big part of why C++ is fast — and also why there are a few more moving parts. Let's set those up once, properly, so they never get in your way again.

docs.title: Your first program
docs.text:
Let's start with the smallest useful C++ program.

examples/week01/lesson01.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "Hello, C++!\n";
    return 0;  // 0 tells the OS "success"; you may omit this line in main only
}

Output:

Hello, C++!

Let's go through it line by line:

  • #include <iostream> pulls in the declarations for input/output streams. (We'll see exactly what "pulls in" means in the next lesson.)
  • int main() is where every hosted C++ program starts. It returns an int to the operating system: 0 means success.
  • std::cout << "..." writes text to standard output. std:: means "from the standard library namespace".
  • '\n' is a newline character.

docs.title: Compiling it by hand
docs.text:
On Linux or macOS, with GCC or Clang installed:

g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic hello.cpp -o hello
./hello

Each flag matters:

Flag What it does -std=c++20 Which version of the language to use. C++ evolves every 3 years: 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26. -Wall -Wextra Turn on lots of useful warnings. Despite the name, -Wall is not all of them. -Wpedantic Warn about non-standard compiler extensions. -o hello Name the output file.

Pro tip: treat warnings as bugs

A warning is the compiler saying "this is legal, but you probably didn't mean it." In this course every example compiles warning-free with these flags; that's checked automatically. On real projects, add -Werror in CI so warnings can't creep in.

clang++ accepts the same flags. On Windows, MSVC uses /std:c++20 /W4. Throughout the course we test with both GCC and Clang.

docs.title: Compiler Explorer: your new best friend
docs.text: Compiler Explorer lets you paste code and instantly see the assembly produced by dozens of compilers. You don't need to read assembly fluently. But when we talk about "zero-cost abstractions" later, you'll be able to see that the abstraction really did disappear. Bookmark it.

docs.title: CMake: building more than one file
docs.text:
For anything beyond one file, you'll want a build system. The de-facto standard is CMake. A minimal CMakeLists.txt looks like this:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(hello LANGUAGES CXX)

add_executable(hello hello.cpp)
target_compile_features(hello PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
target_compile_options(hello PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)

And you build it with:

cmake -S . -B build        # configure: generate build files into ./build
cmake --build build        # build
./build/hello

Notice the pattern: targets (here hello) and properties attached to targets. That's "modern CMake", and we'll go much deeper in Week 15. Coming from Android? Good news: the NDK uses exactly this CMake, so this skill transfers directly.

docs.title: A slightly bigger example
docs.text:
Here's a program that reads from the user. Don't worry about every detail yet.

examples/week01/lesson01_input.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::cout << "What's your name? ";
    std::string name;
    if (!(std::cin >> name)) {   // reading can fail (e.g. end of input)
        name = "friend";
    }
    std::cout << "\nNice to meet you, " << name << "!\n";
}

Output:

What's your name? 
Nice to meet you, friend!

When there's no input (as in our automated test run), std::cin >> name fails, and we fall back to a default. Checking whether input succeeded is a habit worth building on day one.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • C++ is compiled ahead of time; the compiler turns source text into a native executable.
  • Always compile with a fixed standard and warnings on: -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic.
  • Compiler Explorer shows you what the compiler generates — use it to build intuition.
  • CMake describes targets and their properties; the NDK uses the same CMake.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does return 0; from main mean?

Show answer

It reports success to the operating system. Non-zero means failure. In main (and only main) you may omit it, and it behaves as return 0;.

Q2. Does -Wall enable all warnings?

Show answer

No. Despite its name it enables a common set. -Wextra adds more, and there are still others (like -Wconversion) that you turn on separately.

Q3. In CMake, what is a target?

Show answer

Something the build produces (an executable or library) that properties like compile features, options and include paths are attached to, e.g. add_executable(hello ...) creates target hello.

docs.title: Practice lab (optional)
docs.text:
Write a program that asks for two integers and prints their sum and product. If reading fails, print invalid input and return 1. Build it once by hand with g++ and once with CMake.

Starter code examples/week01/lesson01_lab_starter.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0, b = 0;
    // TODO: read a and b; on failure print "invalid input" and return 1
    std::cout << "sum=" << a + b << '\n';
}
Full solution examples/week01/lesson01_lab_solution.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0, b = 0;
    if (!(std::cin >> a >> b)) {
        std::cout << "invalid input\n";
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "sum=" << a + b << " product=" << a * b << '\n';
}

docs.title: Lesson 1.2: The compilation model: preprocessor, translation units, linking, ODR
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Here's a problem you've probably hit: your code compiles, but then the build fails with undefined reference to 'foo()'. Or the opposite: multiple definition of 'foo'. These errors aren't from the compiler at all — they're from the linker. Understanding the three stages of a build makes these errors go from mysterious to obvious. Let's see how this works.

docs.title: Three stages
docs.text:
When you run g++ main.cpp util.cpp -o app, three things happen:

flowchart LR
  A[main.cpp] -->|preprocess| B[translation unit]
  B -->|compile| C[main.o]
  D[util.cpp] -->|preprocess| E[translation unit]
  E -->|compile| F[util.o]
  C --> L{link}
  F --> L
  L --> G[app]
  1. Preprocessing. Text substitution. #include "util.h" literally pastes the contents of util.h in place. #define and #if are also handled here. The result is a translation unit (TU).
  2. Compilation. Each TU is compiled independently into an object file (.o). The compiler only knows what it can see in that one TU.
  3. Linking. The linker stitches object files and libraries together, matching each use of a function with its single definition.

That word "independently" is the key to everything. When compiling main.cpp, the compiler has never seen util.cpp. So how can main call a function defined there? Through a declaration.

docs.title: Declarations vs definitions
docs.text:
• A declaration says "this thing exists, and here is its type": int add(int, int);
  • A definition provides the thing itself: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

You can declare something many times, but (for most things) define it exactly once in the whole program. That's the One Definition Rule (ODR).

So the classic layout is: declarations in a header (util.h), definitions in a source file (util.cpp), and every file that needs them includes the header.

// util.h
#pragma once            // include guard: paste this file at most once per TU
int add(int a, int b);  // declaration only

// util.cpp
#include "util.h"
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }  // the one definition

// main.cpp
#include "util.h"
int main() { return add(2, 3); }

Now the two classic errors become easy to explain:

  • undefined reference to add(int, int): you declared it, used it, but the linker never got an object file containing the definition. (Forgot to compile/link util.cpp, or the signatures differ.)
  • multiple definition of add: you put the definition in the header, and two .cpp files included it. Now two object files both define add.

docs.title: The wrong way, then the fix
docs.text:
Putting a definition in a header is the most common mistake:

// config.h  -- WRONG if included from two .cpp files
int max_users = 100;          // a definition! each TU gets its own -> link error

There are two good fixes. The C++17 way is an inline variable: inline tells the linker "there may be identical copies in many TUs; keep one".

// config.h  -- OK
inline int max_users = 100;          // C++17 inline variable
constexpr int max_sessions = 8;      // constexpr at namespace scope: internal linkage, also fine

Functions defined in headers need inline for the same reason (member functions defined inside a class body and templates are implicitly OK).

docs.title: Internal linkage: keeping helpers private
docs.text:
Sometimes a helper should be visible only inside one .cpp file. Put it in an anonymous namespace (or mark it static). It then has internal linkage: two files can each have their own helper() with no conflict.

Here's a single-file program that demonstrates these ideas — we can't show multiple files in one example, but we can show the declaration/definition split and internal linkage:

examples/week01/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>

// A declaration: tells the compiler the function exists.
int add(int a, int b);

namespace {                 // anonymous namespace => internal linkage
int helper(int x) { return x * 10; }
}

inline int global_counter = 0;   // C++17 inline variable: safe to put in a header

constexpr int square(int x) { return x * x; }  // instead of #define SQUARE(x)

int main() {
    ++global_counter;
    std::cout << add(2, 3) << ' ' << helper(4) << ' ' << square(1 + 2)
              << ' ' << global_counter << '\n';
}

// The definition can come later in the file (or in another file entirely).
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

Output:

5 40 9 1

docs.title: The preprocessor: useful, but keep it small
docs.text:
The preprocessor knows nothing about C++ — it's text substitution. That's exactly why macros are risky. The classic bug:

#define SQUARE(x) x * x
int y = SQUARE(1 + 2);   // expands to 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 == 5, not 9!

In modern C++, use constexpr functions instead of function-like macros. Keep the preprocessor for #include, include guards, and conditional compilation (#if defined(__ANDROID__)), which is still genuinely useful.

Common pitfall: ODR violations that don't error

If two TUs define the same inline function or class differently (say, different #defines changed a struct's layout), the linker usually picks one silently. That's undefined behaviour and a nightmare to debug. Keep headers self-contained and avoid configuration macros that change layouts. In C++20, modules (Week 15) fix much of this.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Build = preprocess → compile each translation unit independently → link.
  • Headers hold declarations; one .cpp holds each definition (the ODR).
  • undefined reference = missing definition at link time; multiple definition = defined in a header without inline.
  • Use inline (C++17) variables / functions or constexpr for things defined in headers.
  • Prefer constexpr functions over function-like macros.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. You get undefined reference to 'foo()'. Is this a compiler or linker error, and what are two likely causes?

Show answer

A linker error. Either the .cpp defining foo wasn't compiled/linked into the program, or the declaration and definition don't match (different parameter types, namespace, or extern "C" mismatch).

Q2. Why does int x = 5; in a header cause trouble, but inline int x = 5; doesn't?

Show answer

Each TU that includes the header gets its own definition of x, violating the ODR (multiple definitions at link time). inline allows identical definitions in multiple TUs; the linker merges them.

Q3. What does SQUARE(1+2) evaluate to with #define SQUARE(x) x * x?

Show answer

5, because it expands textually to 1 + 2 * 1 + 2. Use a constexpr function instead.

Q4. What does an anonymous namespace do?

Show answer

Gives everything inside it internal linkage, so it is private to that translation unit and can't clash with names in other files.

docs.title: Lesson 1.3: Fundamental types, literals, and fixed-width integers
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Suppose you're decoding an audio stream: 16-bit signed samples, a 32-bit sample-rate field, an 8-bit channel count. If you pick int for everything and the code runs on a platform where int isn't the size you assumed, the file is garbage. C++ gives you precise control over representation — but you have to know what the types actually guarantee. Let's look.

docs.title: The basic types
docs.text:
Type Typical size (64-bit Linux/Android) Guaranteed by the standard bool 1 byte holds true/false char 1 byte sizeof(char) == 1; signedness is implementation-defined! short 2 at least 16 bits int 4 at least 16 bits long 8 (4 on Windows) at least 32 bits long long 8 at least 64 bits float / double 4 / 8 usually IEEE-754 single/double

Notice "at least". The standard deliberately leaves exact sizes to the platform. On Windows, long is 32 bits; on 64-bit Linux it's 64. That has broken plenty of portable code.

docs.title: When size matters, say so: <cstdint>
docs.text:
For file formats, network protocols and hardware registers, use the fixed-width types: std::int8_t, std::uint16_t, std::int32_t, std::uint64_t. For sizes and indexes use std::size_t (what sizeof and .size() return).

examples/week01/lesson03.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>

int main() {
    std::cout << "sizeof(int)=" << sizeof(int)
              << " sizeof(long long)=" << sizeof(long long)
              << " sizeof(double)=" << sizeof(double) << '\n';

    std::cout << "int range: " << std::numeric_limits<int>::min() << " .. "
              << std::numeric_limits<int>::max() << '\n';
    std::cout << "uint16_t max: " << std::numeric_limits<std::uint16_t>::max() << '\n';

    int bin = 0b1111'1111;  // binary literal with digit separator
    std::cout << "0b1111'1111 = " << bin << ", 0xFF = " << 0xFF << '\n';

    double x = 0.1 + 0.2;
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << "0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ? " << (x == 0.3) << '\n';
    std::cout.precision(17);
    std::cout << "0.1 + 0.2 = " << x << '\n';

    std::uint8_t channels = 65;
    std::cout << "uint8_t printed directly: " << channels
              << ", as int: " << static_cast<int>(channels) << '\n';
}

Output:

sizeof(int)=4 sizeof(long long)=8 sizeof(double)=8
int range: -2147483648 .. 2147483647
uint16_t max: 65535
0b1111'1111 = 255, 0xFF = 255
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ? false
0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
uint8_t printed directly: A, as int: 65

A few things to notice in that output:

  • std::numeric_limits<T> (from <limits>) tells you a type's range, precision and more at compile time.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Floating point stores binary fractions; 0.1 has no exact binary representation. Never compare floats with == unless you know why it's safe.
  • uint8_t printed via std::cout shows up as a character because it's (usually) a typedef for unsigned char. Cast to int to print the number. This one bites every multimedia developer at least once.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
Literals are how you write values in code:

int dec = 255, hex = 0xFF, oct = 0377, bin = 0b1111'1111;  // all 255; ' is a digit separator (C++14)
unsigned u = 42u;  long l = 42L;  long long ll = 42LL;  std::size_t n = 42uz; // uz: C++23
double d = 1.5e3;  float f = 1.5f;
char c = 'A';  char8_t c8 = u8'A';  char16_t c16 = u'A';  char32_t c32 = U'A';
const char* s = "text";  bool b = true;  int* p = nullptr;   // nullptr: C++11

nullptr (C++11) replaced the old NULL/0 for null pointers — it has its own type, so overloads can't mistake it for an integer.

docs.title: Common mistake: assuming char is signed
docs.text:
char c = '\xFF';
if (c < 0) { /* true on x86 Linux, FALSE on ARM Linux/Android! */ }

On x86, plain char is signed; on ARM (most Android devices), it's unsigned. If you mean "a byte", use unsigned char, std::uint8_t, or std::byte (Week 3).

Pro tip

static_assert(sizeof(Header) == 12); (Week 9) lets you lock down assumptions about layout at compile time, so a port to a new platform fails loudly instead of silently corrupting data.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • The standard guarantees minimum sizes, not exact ones; long differs between Windows and Linux.
  • Use <cstdint> fixed-width types for formats/protocols, std::size_t for sizes.
  • Floating point is approximate: don't compare with == casually.
  • Plain char signedness differs between x86 and ARM; use unsigned char/std::byte for bytes.
  • uint8_t prints as a character with iostreams; cast to int.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Is sizeof(long) always 8 on 64-bit systems?

Show answer

No. It's 8 on 64-bit Linux/macOS/Android (LP64) but 4 on 64-bit Windows (LLP64).

Q2. Why does std::cout << std::uint8_t{65} print A?

Show answer

std::uint8_t is typically an alias for unsigned char, and the stream prints character types as characters. Cast to int first, or use std::format/std::print (Week 12), which format unsigned char as a number.

Q3. What's the value of 0b1010'0000?

Show answer

160 (binary 10100000). The ' is just a digit separator.

Q4. Why prefer nullptr over NULL?

Show answer

nullptr has type std::nullptr_t and converts only to pointer types, so overload resolution can't confuse it with an integer like NULL (often 0) could.

docs.title: Lesson 1.4: Variables and initialization: auto, const, constexpr
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Here's a bug that has shipped in real products: int volume; if (muted) volume = 0; play(volume);. When not muted, volume is uninitialized — reading it is undefined behaviour. C++ won't stop you, so you need habits that make the mistake impossible. This lesson is about those habits.

docs.title: Always initialize
docs.text:
A local variable of fundamental type without an initializer has an indeterminate value. Reading it is undefined behaviour (UB) — the program may print garbage, or the optimizer may do something truly strange.

int x;            // WRONG (if you read it before assigning)
int y = 0;        // OK

docs.title: Three ways to initialize (and which to prefer)
docs.text:
int a = 3;      // copy-initialization
int b(3);       // direct-initialization
int c{3};       // list-initialization (brace init), C++11

All three give 3 here. The braces have one superpower: they reject narrowing conversions.

double ratio = 2.7;
int n1 = ratio;   // compiles, silently truncates to 2 (warning with -Wconversion)
int n2{ratio};    // ERROR: narrowing conversion from double to int

That's why many style guides say "prefer {}". There are a few pitfalls with braces and constructors that take std::initializer_list (we'll meet them in Week 4), but for plain variables, braces are a great default.

docs.title: auto: let the compiler figure out the type
docs.text:
auto deduces the type from the initializer:

auto count = 10;        // int
auto ratio = 0.5;       // double
auto name = std::string{"Ada"};  // std::string

Use auto when the type is obvious from the right-hand side or long and noisy (iterators). It also forces you to initialize — auto x; doesn't compile. One gotcha: auto drops top-level const and references; we'll see that in Lesson 2.3.

docs.title: const and constexpr
docs.text:
• const means "I won't modify this after initialization." The value may be computed at run time.
  • constexpr means "this is known at compile time" — the compiler must be able to evaluate it.
examples/week01/lesson04.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

constexpr int kSampleRate = 48'000;          // compile-time constant
constexpr int kFrameMs = 20;
constexpr int kSamplesPerFrame = kSampleRate * kFrameMs / 1000;

int main() {
    int buffer[kSamplesPerFrame]{};          // OK: size is a constant expression; {} zero-fills
    const auto user = std::string{"Arun"};   // const: computed at runtime, never modified
    auto volume = 0.8;                       // double
    int level{static_cast<int>(volume * 10)};  // explicit conversion; {} would reject implicit narrowing

    decltype(level) copy = level;            // int
    std::cout << user << ": " << kSamplesPerFrame << " samples/frame, level "
              << copy << ", buffer[0]=" << buffer[0] << '\n';
}

Output:

Arun: 960 samples/frame, level 8, buffer[0]=0

constexpr values can be used where the language needs a compile-time constant, like array sizes and template arguments. We'll go much deeper (constexpr functions, consteval, constinit) in Week 8.

Pro tip: make const the default

Mark everything const that doesn't need to change. It documents intent, prevents accidents, and makes code easier to reason about. Many experienced C++ programmers find most of their local variables end up const.

docs.title: decltype: the type of an expression
docs.text: decltype(expr) gives you the declared type of an expression without evaluating it. You'll mostly see it in generic code, e.g. decltype(a + b). Don't worry about it much yet.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Always initialize variables; reading an uninitialized int is undefined behaviour.
  • Brace initialization {} rejects narrowing conversions.
  • auto deduces from the initializer and forces you to initialize.
  • const = won't change; constexpr = known at compile time.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Does int n{3.5}; compile?

Show answer

No. List-initialization forbids narrowing from double to int. int n = 3.5; compiles (truncating to 3), typically with a warning under -Wconversion.

Q2. What's the difference between const int a = f(); and constexpr int b = f();?

Show answer

a can be initialized at run time; it just can't be modified afterwards. b requires f() to be evaluable at compile time (a constexpr function with constant arguments), otherwise it's a compile error.

Q3. What type is auto x = 5u;?

Show answer

unsigned int.

docs.title: Lesson 1.5: Operators, integer promotion and narrowing
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Quick puzzle: what does this print?

std::vector<int> v;   // empty
if (-1 < v.size()) std::cout << "less"; else std::cout << "not less";

It prints not less. -1 gets converted to an unsigned 64-bit number (a huge value) before the comparison. This lesson explains the conversion rules that cause surprises like this, and the modern tools to avoid them.

docs.title: The everyday operators
docs.text:
You know most of these from other languages: + - * / %, comparisons == != < <= > >=, logical && || !, assignment = += -= and friends, increment ++/--. Two C++-specific notes:

  • Integer division truncates toward zero: -7 / 2 == -3, and -7 % 2 == -1.
  • && and || short-circuit: in p && p->ok(), the right side isn't evaluated if p is null.

When precedence isn't obvious, add parentheses. Nobody remembers that & binds weaker than ==.

docs.title: Integer promotion: small types become int
docs.text: Before arithmetic, types smaller than int (char, short, uint8_t, bool) are promoted to int. So uint8_t a = 200, b = 100; auto c = a + b; gives c == 300 with type int — no overflow.

docs.title: Usual arithmetic conversions: the signed/unsigned trap
docs.text:
When you mix two different types, they're converted to a common type. The surprising rule: if one operand is unsigned and at least as wide as the other, the signed one is converted to unsigned. That's the -1 < v.size() puzzle: -1 becomes 18446744073709551615.

The fix, in C++20: std::cmp_less, std::cmp_greater etc. from <utility> compare integers by value, regardless of signedness. Or just keep your types consistent (use std::ssize(v) for a signed size).

examples/week01/lesson05.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;  // size() == 0, type std::size_t (unsigned)

    // The trap: -1 is converted to a huge unsigned value.
    // (We cast explicitly here so the example compiles warning-free; the implicit
    //  comparison `-1 < v.size()` would trigger -Wsign-compare.)
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;
    std::cout << "-1 < v.size() (as unsigned): " << (static_cast<std::size_t>(-1) < v.size()) << '\n';
    std::cout << "std::cmp_less(-1, v.size()): " << std::cmp_less(-1, v.size()) << '\n';

    std::uint8_t a = 200, b = 100;
    auto c = a + b;  // promoted to int
    std::cout << "200 + 100 with uint8_t operands = " << c << '\n';

    unsigned int u = 0;
    --u;  // well-defined wrap-around
    std::cout << "0u - 1 = " << u << '\n';

    std::cout << "-7 / 2 = " << -7 / 2 << ", -7 % 2 = " << -7 % 2 << '\n';
    double avg = 7.9;
    std::cout << "static_cast<int>(7.9) = " << static_cast<int>(avg) << '\n';
}

Output:

-1 < v.size() (as unsigned): false
std::cmp_less(-1, v.size()): true
200 + 100 with uint8_t operands = 300
0u - 1 = 4294967295
-7 / 2 = -3, -7 % 2 = -1
static_cast<int>(7.9) = 7

docs.title: Overflow: signed is UB, unsigned wraps
docs.text:
Unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 2ⁿ — that's well-defined. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour. The optimizer is allowed to assume it never happens, which can delete your "overflow checks":

bool will_overflow(int x) { return x + 1 < x; }   // WRONG: compiler may fold this to `false`

Check before the operation instead: x == std::numeric_limits<int>::max(), or use compiler builtins like __builtin_add_overflow (GCC/Clang) — and in C++26, <stdckdint.h>'s ckd_add is coming from C23.

docs.title: Casts: say what you mean
docs.text:
C++ has named casts so each one is searchable and limited:

Cast Use for static_cast<T>(x) Normal, checked-at-compile-time conversions (double→int, base→derived pointers you know are right) const_cast<T>(x) Removing const (rarely legitimate) reinterpret_cast<T>(x) Reinterpreting bits/pointers (low-level, dangerous) dynamic_cast<T>(x) Checked downcasts in class hierarchies (Week 6)

Avoid C-style (int)x casts — they silently pick the most dangerous cast that works.

docs.title: Order of evaluation
docs.text:
In f(a(), b()), the order in which a() and b() run is unspecified. C++17 did fix some cases: in a << b, a = b, a[b] and a.b, the left side is now evaluated first. So std::cout << i++ << i; is defined since C++17 (but still confusing — don't write it).

Common pitfall

Turn on -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion for code that does a lot of arithmetic (DSP, codecs). They are noisy at first, but they catch exactly the bugs in this lesson.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Small integer types are promoted to int before arithmetic.
  • Mixing signed and unsigned converts the signed value to unsigned — use std::cmp_less & co. (C++20).
  • Signed overflow is UB (the optimizer exploits it); unsigned wraps.
  • Use named casts (static_cast), never C-style casts.
  • C++17 fixed evaluation order for <<, =, [], but function-argument order is still unspecified.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is x + 1 < x a bad overflow check for int x?

Show answer

Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may assume it never happens and simplify the expression to false. Check against INT_MAX before adding instead.

Q2. What type and value does std::uint8_t{250} + std::uint8_t{10} have?

Show answer

int with value 260, because of integer promotion.

Q3. What does std::cmp_less(-1, 0u) return?

Show answer

true. It compares mathematical values regardless of signedness.

Q4. Which cast would you use to convert a double to an int deliberately?

Show answer

static_cast<int>(d).

docs.title: Practice lab (optional)
docs.text:
Write int clamp_add(int a, int b) that returns a + b, but saturates at INT_MAX/INT_MIN instead of overflowing — without ever performing an overflowing signed addition.

Full solution examples/week01/lesson05_lab_solution.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>

int clamp_add(int a, int b) {
    constexpr int hi = std::numeric_limits<int>::max();
    constexpr int lo = std::numeric_limits<int>::min();
    if (b > 0 && a > hi - b) return hi;   // a + b would exceed hi
    if (b < 0 && a < lo - b) return lo;   // a + b would go below lo
    return a + b;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << clamp_add(2, 3) << ' '
              << clamp_add(std::numeric_limits<int>::max(), 1) << ' '
              << clamp_add(std::numeric_limits<int>::min(), -5) << '\n';
}

Output:

5 2147483647 -2147483648

docs.title: Week 1 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 1.1) What does return 0; from main mean?

Show answer

It reports success to the operating system. Non-zero means failure. In main (and only main) you may omit it, and it behaves as return 0;.

Q2. (from 1.1) Does -Wall enable all warnings?

Show answer

No. Despite its name it enables a common set. -Wextra adds more, and there are still others (like -Wconversion) that you turn on separately.

Q3. (from 1.2) You get undefined reference to 'foo()'. Is this a compiler or linker error, and what are two likely causes?

Show answer

A linker error. Either the .cpp defining foo wasn't compiled/linked into the program, or the declaration and definition don't match (different parameter types, namespace, or extern "C" mismatch).

Q4. (from 1.2) Why does int x = 5; in a header cause trouble, but inline int x = 5; doesn't?

Show answer

Each TU that includes the header gets its own definition of x, violating the ODR (multiple definitions at link time). inline allows identical definitions in multiple TUs; the linker merges them.

Q5. (from 1.3) Is sizeof(long) always 8 on 64-bit systems?

Show answer

No. It's 8 on 64-bit Linux/macOS/Android (LP64) but 4 on 64-bit Windows (LLP64).

Q6. (from 1.3) Why does std::cout << std::uint8_t{65} print A?

Show answer

std::uint8_t is typically an alias for unsigned char, and the stream prints character types as characters. Cast to int first, or use std::format/std::print (Week 12), which format unsigned char as a number.

Q7. (from 1.4) Does int n{3.5}; compile?

Show answer

No. List-initialization forbids narrowing from double to int. int n = 3.5; compiles (truncating to 3), typically with a warning under -Wconversion.

Q8. (from 1.4) What's the difference between const int a = f(); and constexpr int b = f();?

Show answer

a can be initialized at run time; it just can't be modified afterwards. b requires f() to be evaluable at compile time (a constexpr function with constant arguments), otherwise it's a compile error.

Q9. (from 1.5) Why is x + 1 < x a bad overflow check for int x?

Show answer

Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may assume it never happens and simplify the expression to false. Check against INT_MAX before adding instead.

Q10. (from 1.5) What type and value does std::uint8_t{250} + std::uint8_t{10} have?

Show answer

int with value 260, because of integer promotion.

docs.title: Week 2: Control flow, functions, references, scope
docs.text:
This week we learn to structure programs: making decisions, looping, splitting work into functions, and passing data around efficiently with references. We'll finish with how long objects live and how namespaces, enums and structs help organize code.

By Friday you'll be able to write small but real programs — and you'll understand where each object lives in memory and when it dies, which is the single most important mental model in C++.

# Lesson Standard Length 2.1 Control flow: if, switch, loops, and range-for C++20 9 min 2.2 Functions, overloading and default arguments C++20 10 min 2.3 References, const, and how to pass parameters C++20 11 min 2.4 Scope, lifetime, storage duration and namespaces C++20 12 min 2.5 Enums, structs and attributes C++23 10 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 2 programming assignment: A tiny command-line unit converter
docs.text:
Write a program that converts between units of audio level and time:

  • enum class Unit { ms, samples, seconds } with a [[nodiscard]] double convert(double value, Unit from, Unit to, int sample_rate = 48000) function.
  • Overload a print function for double and for a struct Result { double value; Unit unit; }.
  • Use const& parameters for anything that isn't a cheap scalar.
  • Process a fixed list of test conversions in main with a range-for loop and print the results.

Compile warning-free. Bonus: use a switch with using enum Unit;.

Reference solution examples/week02/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

enum class Unit { ms, samples, seconds };

std::string_view suffix(Unit u) {
    switch (u) {
        using enum Unit;
        case ms:      return "ms";
        case samples: return "samples";
        case seconds: return "s";
    }
    return "?";
}

[[nodiscard]] double to_seconds(double v, Unit u, int rate) {
    switch (u) {
        using enum Unit;
        case ms:      return v / 1000.0;
        case samples: return v / rate;
        case seconds: return v;
    }
    return 0.0;
}

[[nodiscard]] double convert(double value, Unit from, Unit to, int sample_rate = 48000) {
    const double s = to_seconds(value, from, sample_rate);
    switch (to) {
        using enum Unit;
        case ms:      return s * 1000.0;
        case samples: return s * sample_rate;
        case seconds: return s;
    }
    return 0.0;
}

struct Result { double value; Unit unit; };

void print(double v) { std::cout << v; }
void print(const Result& r) { print(r.value); std::cout << ' ' << suffix(r.unit) << '\n'; }

struct Job { double value; Unit from; Unit to; };

int main() {
    const std::vector<Job> jobs{{20, Unit::ms, Unit::samples},
                                {44100, Unit::samples, Unit::seconds},
                                {1.5, Unit::seconds, Unit::ms}};
    for (const auto& j : jobs) {
        print(j.value);
        std::cout << ' ' << suffix(j.from) << " -> ";
        print(Result{convert(j.value, j.from, j.to), j.to});
    }
    std::cout << "at 44.1kHz, 20 ms = " << convert(20, Unit::ms, Unit::samples, 44100) << " samples\n";
}

Output:

20 ms -> 960 samples
44100 samples -> 0.91875 s
1.5 s -> 1500 ms
at 44.1kHz, 20 ms = 882 samples

docs.title: Lesson 2.1: Control flow: if, switch, loops, and range-for
docs.text: C++20 · about 9 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Imagine scanning a buffer of audio samples looking for the first one that clips. You need to loop, test each value, and stop early. That's control flow, and C++ has a few modern touches — like declaring a variable right inside an if — that make such code tighter and safer. Let's go through them quickly.

docs.title: if and the if-with-initializer
docs.text:
You've seen if (cond) { ... } else { ... }. Since C++17 you can put a declaration inside the if:

if (auto it = settings.find("volume"); it != settings.end()) {
    use(it->second);
}   // `it` is out of scope here: it can't be misused later

The variable lives only as long as the if/else. Small scopes are a great habit: fewer names in play, fewer chances to use a stale one.

docs.title: switch
docs.text: switch works on integers and enums. Each case falls through to the next unless you break. Accidental fallthrough is a classic bug, so compilers warn (-Wimplicit-fallthrough). When you mean it, say so with [[fallthrough]];.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { ... }   // classic counted loop
while (cond) { ... }                  // test first
do { ... } while (cond);              // run at least once
for (const auto& x : container) { ... }   // range-based for (C++11)

Range-based for is the default for "do something with each element". Use const auto& to avoid copying each element; use auto& if you want to modify them.

C++20 added an initializer to range-for too: for (auto v = make(); auto x : v).

Here's everything together, finding the first clipped sample:

examples/week02/lesson01.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

enum class Level { quiet, normal, loud, clipping };

Level classify(float s) {
    const float a = s < 0 ? -s : s;   // conditional operator
    if (a >= 1.0f) return Level::clipping;
    if (a > 0.7f) return Level::loud;
    if (a > 0.1f) return Level::normal;
    return Level::quiet;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<float> samples{0.05f, 0.4f, -0.8f, 1.2f, 0.3f};

    int index = 0;
    for (const auto& s : samples) {
        if (const Level l = classify(s); l == Level::clipping) {   // if with initializer
            std::cout << "first clip at index " << index << '\n';
            break;
        }
        ++index;
    }

    for (auto& s : samples) s *= 0.5f;   // auto& modifies the elements

    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < samples.size(); ++i) {
        switch (classify(samples[i])) {
        case Level::clipping:
            std::cout << "C";
            [[fallthrough]];          // deliberate: clipping is also "loud"
        case Level::loud:   std::cout << "L "; break;
        case Level::normal: std::cout << "n "; break;
        case Level::quiet:  std::cout << ". "; break;
        }
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

first clip at index 3
. n n n n

docs.title: A common mistake: modifying a copy
docs.text:
for (auto s : samples) s *= 0.5f;   // WRONG: halves a copy; samples unchanged
for (auto& s : samples) s *= 0.5f;  // right

Pro tip

Before writing a loop, ask: "is there an algorithm for this?" Finding the first matching element is std::ranges::find_if. We'll do a full tour of algorithms in Week 11 — loops are still fine for now.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Use if (init; cond) to keep helper variables scoped to the if.
  • switch cases fall through without break; mark intentional fallthrough with [[fallthrough]].
  • Range-for with const auto& reads without copying; auto& modifies in place.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's wrong with for (auto x : v) x = 0;?

Show answer

x is a copy of each element, so the vector is unchanged. Use auto& x.

Q2. Where is it visible in if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()) {...} else {...}?

Show answer

In the condition, the if body and the else body, but not after the whole statement.

Q3. Why does the compiler warn about a case without break?

Show answer

Implicit fallthrough is a common bug. [[fallthrough]]; documents that it's intentional and silences the warning.

docs.title: Lesson 2.2: Functions, overloading and default arguments
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: As soon as a program does more than one thing, you want to name each thing. Functions are names for behaviour. C++ adds two conveniences you may not have in C: overloading (several functions with the same name but different parameters) and default arguments. They're handy — and they have a couple of sharp corners we'll walk through.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }       // classic
auto add(double a, double b) -> double;        // trailing return type (C++11), same meaning
auto twice(int x) { return 2 * x; }            // return type deduced (C++14): int

Most of the time, write the return type explicitly for public functions (it's documentation) and use deduced auto for short local helpers.

docs.title: Overloading
docs.text:
You can have several functions with the same name if their parameter lists differ. The compiler picks the best match for each call — that's overload resolution. Roughly: an exact match beats a promotion, which beats a conversion.

examples/week02/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

void describe(int x)                { std::cout << "int " << x << '\n'; }
void describe(double x)             { std::cout << "double " << x << '\n'; }
void describe(const std::string& s) { std::cout << "string \"" << s << "\"\n"; }

// Default argument
std::string pad(const std::string& s, std::size_t width = 8, char fill = '.') {
    if (s.size() >= width) return s;
    return s + std::string(width - s.size(), fill);
}

// Deduced return type and an abbreviated function template (C++20)
auto square(int x) { return x * x; }
auto largest(auto a, auto b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

// Recursion
long long factorial(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1); }

int main() {
    describe(42);
    describe(2.5f);                  // float -> double is a promotion
    describe('x');                   // char -> int is a promotion
    describe(std::string{"hello"});
    std::cout << '[' << pad("abc") << "] [" << pad("abc", 5, '-') << "]\n";
    std::cout << square(7) << ' ' << largest(3, 9) << ' ' << largest(2.5, 1.5) << '\n';
    std::cout << "20! = " << factorial(20) << '\n';
}

Output:

int 42
double 2.5
int 120
string "hello"
[abc.....] [abc--]
49 9 2.5
20! = 2432902008176640000

Notice describe(2.5f): there's no float overload, but float → double is a promotion, which beats float → int (a conversion). And describe('x'): char → int is a promotion, so it calls describe(int).

docs.title: The ambiguous call (the wrong way)
docs.text:
void f(long);
void f(double);
f(42);   // ERROR: ambiguous. int->long and int->double are both conversions

When this happens, either add an exact overload or make the call explicit (f(42L)).

docs.title: Default arguments
docs.text:
void log(const std::string& msg, int level = 1);
log("hi");        // level = 1
log("oops", 3);

Defaults go in the declaration (usually the header), not repeated in the definition. They're substituted at the call site — so changing a default in a header requires recompiling the callers, a subtle point if you ship shared libraries.

Common pitfall: defaults + overloads

void f(int x, int y = 0); and void f(int x); together make f(1) ambiguous. Pick one tool.

docs.title: Generic functions with auto parameters (C++20)
docs.text:
auto largest(auto a, auto b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

This is an abbreviated function template: a template in disguise. We'll unpack templates in Week 7; for now just know it works for any types that support >.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Overload resolution prefers exact matches, then promotions, then conversions; ties are errors.
  • Put default arguments in the declaration; they're filled in at the call site.
  • auto return types are deduced; auto parameters (C++20) make a function template.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Given void f(int); void f(double);, which is called by f('a')? By f(1.0f)?

Show answer

f(int) (char→int is an integral promotion) and f(double) (float→double is a floating-point promotion).

Q2. Why might changing a default argument in a library header not affect an already-compiled app?

Show answer

Defaults are inserted at each call site at compile time, so the app keeps the old value until recompiled.

Q3. What does auto f(auto x) declare?

Show answer

An abbreviated function template (C++20): equivalent to template<class T> auto f(T x).

docs.title: Lesson 2.3: References, const, and how to pass parameters
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Suppose a function processes a 10 MB video frame stored in a std::vector<std::uint8_t>. If you write void process(std::vector<std::uint8_t> frame), every call copies 10 MB. Change one character — const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& frame — and the copy disappears. References are how C++ lets you refer to an existing object without copying it. Let's build the intuition.

docs.title: A reference is another name for an existing object
docs.text:
int volume = 5;
int& v = volume;   // v *is* volume, under another name
v = 7;             // volume is now 7

A reference must be initialized, and it can never be "re-seated" to refer to something else. Assigning to it assigns to the object it refers to.

docs.title: Three ways to pass a parameter
const T& binds to temporaries
docs.text: print_twice(std::string{"temp"}) works even though the argument is a temporary: a const reference may bind to a temporary, and the temporary lives until the end of the full expression. A non-const reference can't bind to a temporary — that would let you modify a value that's about to disappear.

docs.title: auto and references
docs.text:
auto deduces a value type: it strips references and top-level const.

const std::string& name = get_name();
auto a = name;          // std::string — a copy!
const auto& b = name;   // const std::string& — no copy

So when you want a reference, ask for one: auto& or const auto&.

docs.title: The big danger: dangling references
docs.text:
A reference doesn't keep its object alive. Returning a reference to a local is the classic mistake:

const std::string& make_label() {
    std::string s = "label";
    return s;          // WRONG: s is destroyed when the function returns
}                      // the caller gets a dangling reference -> UB

Compilers warn about this simple case (-Wreturn-local-addr / -Wreturn-stack-address), but subtler versions — references into a vector that later reallocates, for example — need you to think about lifetime. That's next lesson.

Pro tip

Return by value. Thanks to copy elision and move semantics (Week 5), returning a std::string or std::vector by value is cheap. Return references only to things that clearly outlive the call (like a member of *this).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A reference is an alias for an existing object; it must be initialized and can't be re-seated.
  • Pass cheap types by value, expensive ones by const&, and use & only to modify the caller's object.
  • auto deduces a value type; write const auto& when you want a reference.
  • References don't extend lifetimes (except a const& bound directly to a temporary) — beware dangling.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't void f(std::string& s) be called as f(std::string{"x"})?

Show answer

A non-const lvalue reference can't bind to a temporary (an rvalue). Use const std::string& (or std::string&& / by value if you want to consume it).

Q2. Given const std::vector<int>& r = v;, what is the type of auto x = r;?

Show answer

std::vector<int> — a full copy, because auto drops the reference and top-level const.

Q3. Is it fine to pass an int by const int&?

Show answer

It works, but by value is simpler and usually faster: an int fits in a register; a reference may force it into memory and introduces aliasing questions.

docs.title: Lesson 2.4: Scope, lifetime, storage duration and namespaces
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Every bug involving a dangling pointer or a use-after-free comes down to one question: when does this object die? In garbage-collected languages you rarely ask it. In C++ you get to decide — which is where the performance (and the deterministic cleanup!) comes from. This lesson gives you the rules.

docs.title: Scope vs lifetime
docs.text:
• Scope is where a name is visible in the source code.
  • Lifetime is when an object exists at run time.

They often coincide for local variables, but not always (a reference's name can outlive the object it refers to — that's a dangling reference).

docs.title: The four storage durations
Function-local statics
docs.text: Since C++11, initializing a function-local static is thread-safe: if two threads call the function at once, one initializes and the other waits. This makes "construct on first use" a safe singleton pattern and is the cure for the static initialization order fiasco: globals in different translation units are initialized in an unspecified order, so one global constructor must never depend on another TU's global.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Namespaces prevent name clashes between libraries:

namespace media::audio {        // nested namespace definition, C++17
    int sample_rate();
}
media::audio::sample_rate();

using media::audio::sample_rate; brings in one name. using namespace std; brings in everything; fine in a small .cpp, but never in a header — you'd be forcing it on everyone who includes you.

Inline namespaces are a versioning tool: namespace lib { inline namespace v2 { ... } } makes lib::f refer to lib::v2::f, while the mangled symbol includes v2. The standard library uses this for ABI versioning (e.g. libc++'s std::__1).

Common pitfall: shadowing

An inner variable with the same name hides the outer one. -Wshadow warns about it. A renamed loop counter that silently shadows a member variable can take hours to find.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Scope is about names; lifetime is about objects.
  • Automatic objects die at the end of their block, in reverse order of construction.
  • Function-local statics are initialized on first use, thread-safely (C++11).
  • Never put using namespace in a header; use nested namespaces a::b (C++17).

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. In what order are three local objects a, b, c destroyed?

Show answer

c, b, a — reverse order of construction.

Q2. What is the static initialization order fiasco and one fix?

Show answer

Globals in different translation units are initialized in unspecified order, so one global's constructor may use another before it's initialized. Fix: replace the global with a function returning a reference to a function-local static (construct on first use), or use constinit/constexpr for constant initialization.

Q3. Why is using namespace std; in a header bad?

Show answer

Every file including the header gets all of std dumped into the global namespace, which can cause ambiguities and silently change overload resolution.

docs.title: Lesson 2.5: Enums, structs and attributes
docs.text: C++23 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Here's a function signature from a real codebase: open_stream(int, int, bool, bool). What does open_stream(2, 1, true, false) mean? Nobody knows without reading the docs. Enums and structs let you give meaning to values, and the compiler then checks that meaning for you. Attributes let you tell the compiler (and readers) even more. Let's make that call readable.

docs.title: Old enums leak and convert
docs.text:
enum Color { red, green };       // unscoped: `red` is a global name
enum Fruit { apple, orange };
int x = red + apple;             // compiles! nonsense, but legal (and warns)

docs.title: enum class: scoped and strongly typed (C++11)
docs.text:
enum class Codec : std::uint8_t { aac, opus, flac };   // explicit underlying type
Codec c = Codec::opus;          // must qualify
// int n = c;                   // ERROR: no implicit conversion
auto n = std::to_underlying(c); // C++23; or static_cast<std::uint8_t>(c)

Always prefer enum class. In C++20, using enum Codec; inside a switch saves you typing Codec:: on every case.

docs.title: Structs group data
docs.text:
struct StreamConfig {
    Codec codec = Codec::aac;   // default member initializers (C++11)
    int sample_rate = 48'000;
    int channels = 2;
    bool low_latency = false;
};

Now open_stream(StreamConfig{.codec = Codec::opus, .low_latency = true}) reads like documentation. (Those .name = designated initializers are C++20; Week 5 covers them in detail.)

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes are annotations in [[double brackets]]:

Attribute Meaning [[nodiscard]] (C++17; with reason C++20) warn if the caller ignores the return value [[maybe_unused]] silence unused warnings [[deprecated("use X")]] (C++14) warn on use [[noreturn]] (C++11) function never returns (e.g. calls std::abort) [[fallthrough]] (C++17) intentional switch fallthrough [[likely]] / [[unlikely]] (C++20) branch hints for the optimizer [[no_unique_address]] (C++20) an empty member may take no space [[assume(expr)]] (C++23) the optimizer may assume expr is true — UB if it isn't! examples/week02/lesson05.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>

enum class Codec : std::uint8_t { aac, opus, flac };

struct StreamConfig {
    Codec codec = Codec::aac;
    int sample_rate = 48'000;
    int channels = 2;
    bool low_latency = false;
};

std::string_view name(Codec c) {
    switch (c) {
        using enum Codec;            // C++20: no need to write Codec:: below
        case aac:  return "AAC";
        case opus: return "Opus";
        case flac: return "FLAC";
    }
    return "?";
}

[[nodiscard]] bool open_stream(const StreamConfig& cfg) {
    if (cfg.channels <= 0) [[unlikely]] return false;
    std::cout << "open " << name(cfg.codec) << " @" << cfg.sample_rate << "Hz x"
              << cfg.channels << (cfg.low_latency ? " low-latency" : "") << '\n';
    return true;
}

struct Empty {};
struct WithTag {
    int value;
    [[no_unique_address]] Empty tag;   // takes no extra space
};

int main() {
    const bool ok = open_stream({.codec = Codec::opus, .low_latency = true});
    [[maybe_unused]] const bool ignored = open_stream(StreamConfig{});
    std::cout << "ok=" << ok << " underlying(flac)=" << int{std::to_underlying(Codec::flac)}
              << " sizeof(WithTag)=" << sizeof(WithTag) << '\n';
}

Output:

open Opus @48000Hz x2 low-latency
open AAC @48000Hz x2
ok=1 underlying(flac)=2 sizeof(WithTag)=4

[[nodiscard]] is the one to adopt immediately. Put it on functions where ignoring the result is almost certainly a bug: error codes, empty()-style queries, factory functions.

Be careful with [[likely]] and [[assume]]

Measure before adding branch hints; the compiler and CPU predictor are usually good already. [[assume]] is a promise: if it's ever false, you have undefined behaviour.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Prefer enum class (scoped, no implicit conversions, explicit underlying type).
  • Use structs with default member initializers to replace long lists of int/bool parameters.
  • [[nodiscard]] turns ignored error results into compiler warnings — use it generously.
  • [[assume]] and [[likely]] are optimization hints; [[assume]] is UB if false.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Name two problems with unscoped enums that enum class fixes.

Show answer

Unscoped enumerators leak into the enclosing scope (name clashes), and they implicitly convert to int (allowing nonsense arithmetic/comparisons between unrelated enums).

Q2. How do you get the integer value of an enum class in C++23?

Show answer

std::to_underlying(e) from <utility> (or static_cast<std::underlying_type_t<E>>(e) before C++23).

Q3. What happens if the condition in [[assume(x > 0)]] is false at run time?

Show answer

Undefined behaviour. The optimizer was allowed to rely on it.

docs.title: Week 2 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 2.1) What's wrong with for (auto x : v) x = 0;?

Show answer

x is a copy of each element, so the vector is unchanged. Use auto& x.

Q2. (from 2.1) Where is it visible in if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()) {...} else {...}?

Show answer

In the condition, the if body and the else body, but not after the whole statement.

Q3. (from 2.2) Given void f(int); void f(double);, which is called by f('a')? By f(1.0f)?

Show answer

f(int) (char→int is an integral promotion) and f(double) (float→double is a floating-point promotion).

Q4. (from 2.2) Why might changing a default argument in a library header not affect an already-compiled app?

Show answer

Defaults are inserted at each call site at compile time, so the app keeps the old value until recompiled.

Q5. (from 2.3) Why can't void f(std::string& s) be called as f(std::string{"x"})?

Show answer

A non-const lvalue reference can't bind to a temporary (an rvalue). Use const std::string& (or std::string&& / by value if you want to consume it).

Q6. (from 2.3) Given const std::vector<int>& r = v;, what is the type of auto x = r;?

Show answer

std::vector<int> — a full copy, because auto drops the reference and top-level const.

Q7. (from 2.4) In what order are three local objects a, b, c destroyed?

Show answer

c, b, a — reverse order of construction.

Q8. (from 2.4) What is the static initialization order fiasco and one fix?

Show answer

Globals in different translation units are initialized in unspecified order, so one global's constructor may use another before it's initialized. Fix: replace the global with a function returning a reference to a function-local static (construct on first use), or use constinit/constexpr for constant initialization.

Q9. (from 2.5) Name two problems with unscoped enums that enum class fixes.

Show answer

Unscoped enumerators leak into the enclosing scope (name clashes), and they implicitly convert to int (allowing nonsense arithmetic/comparisons between unrelated enums).

Q10. (from 2.5) How do you get the integer value of an enum class in C++23?

Show answer

std::to_underlying(e) from <utility> (or static_cast<std::underlying_type_t<E>>(e) before C++23).

docs.title: Week 3: Memory: arrays, pointers, strings, bits
docs.text:
This is the week where C++ shows its systems-language roots. We'll look at how objects sit in memory, how pointers work, what goes wrong with manual memory management (and why modern C++ rarely does it), how text is stored, and how to manipulate individual bits.

It's also the week where we meet undefined behaviour properly. Don't worry — the goal isn't to scare you, it's to give you a clear map of where the cliffs are, so you can walk confidently everywhere else.

# Lesson Standard Length 3.1 Arrays: C arrays, std::array, and a first look at std::span C++20 10 min 3.2 Pointers: addresses, arithmetic, and const C++20 12 min 3.3 Dynamic memory and a first map of undefined behaviour C++20 12 min 3.4 Strings: C strings, std::string, and std::string_view C++23 12 min 3.5 Bits and bytes: bitwise operators, std::byte, and C++23 11 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 3 programming assignment: A bit-packed sensor record
docs.text:
A sensor sends 32-bit records: bits 0–11 are a temperature reading (unsigned, 0.1°C steps with an offset of -40°C), bits 12–19 humidity (percent), bits 20–27 a sensor id, bits 28–31 flags.

  1. Write constexpr std::uint32_t pack(...) and Record unpack(std::uint32_t).
  2. Take a std::span<const std::uint32_t> of records and print each one.
  3. Report how many records have flag bit 0 set, using std::popcount or masks.
  4. No raw new, no C strings, no reinterpret_cast.
Reference solution examples/week03/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <array>
#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

struct Record { double temp_c; unsigned humidity, id, flags; };

constexpr std::uint32_t pack(double temp_c, unsigned humidity, unsigned id, unsigned flags) {
    const auto raw_t = static_cast<std::uint32_t>((temp_c + 40.0) * 10.0 + 0.5) & 0xFFFu;
    return raw_t | (std::uint32_t{humidity & 0xFFu} << 12) | (std::uint32_t{id & 0xFFu} << 20)
           | (std::uint32_t{flags & 0xFu} << 28);
}

Record unpack(std::uint32_t r) {
    return {static_cast<double>(r & 0xFFFu) / 10.0 - 40.0, (r >> 12) & 0xFFu, (r >> 20) & 0xFFu, (r >> 28) & 0xFu};
}

int count_flag0(std::span<const std::uint32_t> recs) {
    int n = 0;
    for (auto r : recs) n += static_cast<int>((r >> 28) & 1u);
    return n;
}

int main() {
    constexpr std::array<std::uint32_t, 3> recs{pack(21.5, 40, 7, 0b0001), pack(-5.0, 85, 8, 0b0010),
                                                pack(36.6, 55, 9, 0b1001)};
    static_assert(pack(0.0, 0, 0, 0) == 400);   // checked at compile time
    for (auto r : recs) {
        const auto x = unpack(r);
        std::cout << "id=" << x.id << " temp=" << x.temp_c << "C hum=" << x.humidity
                  << "% flags=" << x.flags << " (" << std::popcount(x.flags) << " set)\n";
    }
    std::cout << "flag0 set in " << count_flag0(recs) << " records\n";
}

Output:

id=7 temp=21.5C hum=40% flags=1 (1 set)
id=8 temp=-5C hum=85% flags=2 (1 set)
id=9 temp=36.6C hum=55% flags=9 (2 set)
flag0 set in 2 records

docs.title: Lesson 3.1: Arrays: C arrays, std::array, and a first look at std::span
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Audio and video code is full of fixed-size buffers: a 1024-sample FFT window, a 16-entry lookup table, a 4×4 matrix. Arrays are the simplest container there is — but C-style arrays have a nasty habit of forgetting their own size the moment you pass them to a function. Let's see the problem and the modern fixes.

docs.title: C arrays, and how they forget their size
docs.text:
int window[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
std::cout << sizeof(window);     // 16: the whole array (4 * sizeof(int))

void f(int a[4]) {               // looks like an array parameter...
    std::cout << sizeof(a);      // 8: it's really `int* a`!
}

When you pass a C array to a function, it decays to a pointer to its first element. The size is gone — the [4] in the parameter is ignored. This is where countless buffer overflows begin.

docs.title: std::array: an array that behaves like a value
