docs.text: std::array<int, 4> is a thin wrapper around a C array with zero overhead. It knows its size, can be copied and compared, and can be returned from functions.

docs.title: std::span: "a view of some contiguous elements" (C++20)
docs.text:
When a function just needs to look at a sequence of elements, take a std::span<const T>. A span is a pointer plus a length; it doesn't own anything. It accepts C arrays, std::array, and std::vector alike — and it can't forget its size.

examples/week03/lesson01.cpp
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

// One function works for C arrays, std::array and std::vector.
double mean(std::span<const float> xs) {
    if (xs.empty()) return 0.0;
    return std::accumulate(xs.begin(), xs.end(), 0.0) / static_cast<double>(xs.size());
}

void apply_gain(std::span<float> xs, float g) {
    for (auto& x : xs) x *= g;
}

int main() {
    float c_array[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    std::array<float, 4> arr{1, 2, 3, 4};
    std::vector<float> vec{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};

    std::cout << "sizeof(c_array)=" << sizeof(c_array) << " std::size(c_array)=" << std::size(c_array) << '\n';
    std::cout << mean(c_array) << ' ' << mean(arr) << ' ' << mean(vec) << '\n';

    apply_gain(std::span(vec).subspan(2, 2), 10.0f);   // only elements 2 and 3
    for (float x : vec) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::array<float, 4> copy = arr;   // std::array copies like a value
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << (copy == arr) << '\n';
    try {
        std::cout << arr.at(10) << '\n';
    } catch (const std::out_of_range&) {
        std::cout << "at(10) threw out_of_range\n";
    }
}

Output:

sizeof(c_array)=16 std::size(c_array)=4
2.5 2.5 3.5
1 2 30 40 5 6 
true
at(10) threw out_of_range

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
a[i] with i out of range is undefined behaviour — no exception, no guaranteed crash. std::array and std::vector offer .at(i) which throws std::out_of_range. In debug builds you can also turn on library assertions (-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS for libstdc++, hardening modes in libc++) to catch bad operator[] indexes; many distributions enable that by default now.

Pro tip

Rule of thumb: own data with std::array / std::vector; pass it to functions as std::span<const T> (read) or std::span<T> (write). We'll revisit spans and mdspan in Week 10.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • C arrays decay to pointers when passed to functions and lose their size.
  • std::array<T, N> is a zero-overhead fixed array with value semantics.
  • Pass contiguous data as std::span<const T> / std::span<T> — one signature for all containers.
  • Out-of-bounds [] is UB; .at() throws; library hardening catches it in debug builds.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Inside void f(int a[10]), what is sizeof(a) on a 64-bit system?

Show answer

8 — the parameter is actually int*; the 10 is ignored.

Q2. Does std::span own its elements?

Show answer

No. It is a non-owning view (pointer + size). The underlying storage must outlive the span.

Q3. What's the difference between arr[10] and arr.at(10) for a std::array<int, 4>?

Show answer

arr[10] is undefined behaviour; arr.at(10) throws std::out_of_range.

docs.title: Lesson 3.2: Pointers: addresses, arithmetic, and const
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Pointers have a scary reputation, but the idea is simple: a pointer is a variable that holds the address of another object. Android's NDK APIs, every C library, and hardware registers all speak in pointers, so you need to be fluent. Let's build the picture step by step.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
int level = 42;
int* p = &level;   // p holds the address of level
*p = 7;            // dereference: "the object p points to" -> level is now 7

Draw it as a box (level, containing 42) and an arrow (p) pointing at it. Unlike a reference, a pointer can be null (point at nothing) and can be re-pointed to another object.

Reference T& Pointer T* can be null no yes (nullptr) can be re-seated no yes syntax to use like the object *p, p->member use when always refers to something "optional" object, or re-pointing, or C APIs

docs.title: Pointer arithmetic
docs.text: If p points into an array, p + 1 points to the next element (not the next byte). p[i] is exactly *(p + i). Arithmetic is only valid within the same array (and one-past-the-end); going outside is UB.

docs.title: const and pointers: read right to left
docs.text:
const int* a;        // pointer to const int: can't modify *a, can re-point a
int* const b = &x;   // const pointer to int: can modify *b, can't re-point b
const int* const c = &x;  // neither

Trick: read the declaration right-to-left. int* const b = "b is a const pointer to int".

examples/week03/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>

struct Frame { int width; int height; };

void describe(const Frame* f) {       // pointer: may be null
    if (f == nullptr) { std::cout << "no frame\n"; return; }
    std::cout << f->width << 'x' << f->height << '\n';   // f->width == (*f).width
}

int main() {
    int level = 42;
    int* p = &level;
    *p = 7;
    std::cout << "level=" << level << '\n';

    int samples[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    int* first = samples;              // array decays to pointer to first element
    int* last = samples + 4;
    std::cout << "*(first+2)=" << *(first + 2) << " first[3]=" << first[3]
              << " distance=" << (last - first) << '\n';

    for (const int* it = samples; it != samples + 5; ++it)   // one-past-the-end is OK to form
        std::cout << *it << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    const int* ro = &level;   // can't write through ro
    ro = &samples[0];         // but can re-point it
    int* const fixed = &level;
    *fixed = 99;              // can write, can't re-point
    std::cout << *ro << ' ' << level << '\n';

    Frame hd{1280, 720};
    describe(&hd);
    describe(nullptr);
}

Output:

level=7
*(first+2)=30 first[3]=40 distance=4
10 20 30 40 50 
10 99
1280x720
no frame

docs.title: The wrong way: dereferencing null or dangling pointers
docs.text:
int* p = nullptr;
*p = 1;              // UB: often a crash (SIGSEGV), but not guaranteed

int* q;
{ int local = 5; q = &local; }
*q = 6;              // UB: local is dead, q dangles

The fix is mostly design: prefer references when null isn't meaningful, keep pointers non-owning (owning pointers are smart pointers — Week 12), and don't let a pointer outlive what it points to.

About void*

void* can hold any object address but has no type. C APIs (like pthread_create or JNI) use it for "user data". In C++ code, prefer templates or std::function, and when you must use void*, static_cast it back to the exact original type.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A pointer stores an address; *p is the object, &x is the address of x.
  • Pointer arithmetic moves by whole elements and is only valid within one array (plus one-past-the-end).
  • Read pointer declarations right to left: const int* vs int* const.
  • Use references when there's always an object; raw pointers for optional, non-owning access.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. If int a[4] starts at address 1000 and sizeof(int)==4, what address is a + 3?

Show answer

1012 — arithmetic is in units of elements.

Q2. Which of these can you do with const char* s: s = other; / *s = 'x';?

Show answer

s = other; is fine (re-pointing). *s = 'x'; is an error (the pointee is const).

Q3. When would you choose a pointer parameter over a reference?

Show answer

When "no object" is a legitimate input (null), or for C interop. Otherwise a reference documents that an object is required.

Q4. Is forming the pointer a + 4 for int a[4] UB? Dereferencing it?

Show answer

Forming one-past-the-end is allowed (used as an end marker); dereferencing it is UB.

docs.title: Lesson 3.3: Dynamic memory and a first map of undefined behaviour
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Sometimes you don't know until run time how much memory you need — a frame whose size comes from a video header, say. That memory comes from the heap. C++ lets you manage it by hand with new and delete... and this lesson is mostly about why you almost never should. Seeing the failure modes once will make you appreciate RAII and smart pointers in the coming weeks.

docs.title: Stack vs heap
docs.text:
• Stack (automatic storage): local variables. Allocation is just moving a pointer — extremely fast — and cleanup is automatic at the end of scope. But it's limited (often 1–8 MB per thread) and sizes are fixed at compile time.
  • Heap (dynamic storage): new asks the allocator for memory at run time. You decide when it's freed.
int* one = new int{5};        // allocate one int
delete one;                   // free it

int* many = new int[n]{};     // allocate n ints, zeroed
delete[] many;                // arrays need delete[]

docs.title: Four ways manual memory goes wrong
docs.text:
1. Leak: forget to delete (or an early return/exception skips it).
  2. Double free: delete the same pointer twice.
  3. Use-after-free: use memory after deleting it.
  4. Mismatch: new[] with delete (or malloc with delete).

The last three are undefined behaviour.

docs.title: What "undefined behaviour" really means
docs.text:
UB doesn't mean "crashes" or "gives a random value". It means the standard places no requirements on the program at all. The optimizer assumes UB never happens and transforms code accordingly. So a single out-of-bounds read can make an unrelated if vanish. Common sources you've met so far:

  • signed integer overflow, out-of-bounds access, null/dangling dereference,
  • reading uninitialized variables, data races (Week 13), violating aliasing rules (Week 16).

We keep a full catalogue in Lesson 9.5.

docs.title: The fix: let objects own memory
docs.text:
Here's the modern answer. You rarely write new at all:

examples/week03/lesson03.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Frame {
    int w, h;
    std::vector<unsigned char> pixels;
    Frame(int w_, int h_) : w(w_), h(h_), pixels(static_cast<std::size_t>(w_ * h_)) {}
};

int main() {
    // Manual (the old way): works, but every exit path must remember delete[].
    int n = 4;
    int* raw = new int[n]{};
    raw[0] = 1;
    delete[] raw;

    // Modern: containers and smart pointers own memory.
    std::vector<int> v(static_cast<std::size_t>(n));   // n zeroed ints, freed automatically
    v[0] = 1;
    auto frame = std::make_unique<Frame>(640, 480);    // heap object, freed automatically
    std::cout << "frame " << frame->w << 'x' << frame->h << " bytes=" << frame->pixels.size()
              << " v[0]=" << v[0] << '\n';
}   // frame and v cleaned up here, in reverse order

Output:

frame 640x480 bytes=307200 v[0]=1

std::vector and std::unique_ptr free their memory automatically when they go out of scope — even if an exception is thrown. That's RAII, the heart of Week 4.

docs.title: Tools that catch memory bugs
docs.text:
Compile with AddressSanitizer while developing:

g++ -std=c++20 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined bug.cpp && ./a.out

ASan reports use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds and leaks with a stack trace. Here's a program with a deliberate use-after-free. Our checker runs it under ASan in CI to make sure ASan really catches it:

Deliberately buggy

CI runs this under -fsanitize=address and checks the sanitizer reports the bug.

examples/week03/lesson03_uaf.cpp
// Deliberately broken: use-after-free. Compile with -fsanitize=address to see the report.
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int* p = new int{42};
    delete p;
    std::cout << *p << '\n';   // UB: heap-use-after-free
}

ASan prints something like ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4. Android supports ASan and HWASan too (HWASan is the recommended one on arm64).

Honest note

Valgrind and sanitizers find bugs in the code paths you execute. They're not proofs. Combine them with tests (Week 15) and with designs where ownership is obvious.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Stack allocation is fast and automatic; heap allocation is flexible but must be freed.
  • Manual new/delete invites leaks, double frees, use-after-free and mismatched delete[].
  • UB means no requirements at all; the optimizer assumes it never happens.
  • Let std::vector / std::unique_ptr own memory, and develop with -fsanitize=address,undefined.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's wrong with int* p = new int[10]; delete p;?

Show answer

Memory from new[] must be released with delete[]; using delete is undefined behaviour.

Q2. Why can't you rely on UB 'just crashing'?

Show answer

The standard imposes no requirements; the optimizer may assume UB is impossible and transform surrounding code, so the effect can be anything, including silently wrong results.

Q3. Which tool reports heap-use-after-free with a stack trace?

Show answer

AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address), or HWASan on arm64 Android; also Valgrind's memcheck.

docs.title: Lesson 3.4: Strings: C strings, std::string, and std::string_view
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Text is everywhere: file paths, log messages, codec names, JSON. C++ inherited C's strings — arrays of char ending in a zero byte — and they've caused more security bugs than almost anything else. Modern C++ gives you std::string to own text and std::string_view to look at it cheaply. Let's see when to use which.

docs.title: C strings: an array and a promise
docs.text:
"hello" is an array of 6 const chars: h e l l o \0. Every C string function (strlen, strcpy, strcat) walks until it finds that \0. If it's missing, or the destination buffer is too small, you overflow memory. strlen is also O(n) every time you call it.

char buf[8];
std::strcpy(buf, "much too long");   // WRONG: buffer overflow, UB

docs.title: std::string: owns its characters
docs.text: std::string stores its length, grows as needed, and frees its memory automatically. Short strings (typically up to 15 characters in libstdc++, 22 in libc++) are stored inside the string object with no heap allocation: the small string optimization (SSO).

docs.title: std::string_view: a window onto characters (C++17)
docs.text:
A string_view is just a pointer + length. It doesn't own anything, never allocates, and can view a std::string, a C string literal, or part of either. It's the ideal type for read-only string parameters:

bool is_audio(std::string_view mime) { return mime.starts_with("audio/"); }
is_audio("audio/opus");          // no std::string created
is_audio(some_std_string);       // no copy
examples/week03/lesson04.cpp
#include <cstring>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

using namespace std::literals;   // for "..."s and "..."sv

bool is_audio(std::string_view mime) { return mime.starts_with("audio/"); }

std::string_view extension(std::string_view path) {   // returns a view INTO path: caller keeps path alive
    const auto dot = path.rfind('.');
    return dot == std::string_view::npos ? std::string_view{} : path.substr(dot + 1);
}

int main() {
    const char* c = "hello";
    std::cout << "strlen=" << std::strlen(c) << " sizeof(\"hello\")=" << sizeof("hello") << '\n';

    std::string s = "track";
    s += "-01";                       // grows as needed
    s.insert(0, "my-");
    std::cout << s << " size=" << s.size() << '\n';

    std::cout << std::boolalpha << is_audio("audio/opus") << ' ' << is_audio(std::string{"video/h264"}) << '\n';

    const std::string path = "/sdcard/Music/song.flac";
    std::cout << "ext=" << extension(path) << '\n';

    auto owned = "literal"s;        // std::string
    auto view = "literal"sv;        // std::string_view
    std::cout << owned.size() << ' ' << view.size() << ' ' << (owned == view) << '\n';
    std::cout << "contains 'song'? " << path.contains("song") << '\n';   // C++23
}

Output:

strlen=5 sizeof("hello")=6
my-track-01 size=11
true false
ext=flac
7 7 true
contains 'song'? true

docs.title: The big pitfall: string_view doesn't keep anything alive
docs.text:
std::string_view codec_name() {
    std::string s = "opus";
    return s;                    // WRONG: view into a destroyed string
}
std::string_view v = std::string("tmp") + "x";   // WRONG: the temporary dies at the ';'

Rule: use string_view for parameters and short-lived local views; return and store std::string unless you're returning a view into something that clearly outlives the caller (like a string literal or a member).

Also: a string_view isn't NUL-terminated

sv.data() isn't guaranteed to end in \0, so don't pass it to C functions expecting a C string. Convert with std::string(sv).c_str() when calling C APIs.

We'll cover text formatting (std::format, std::print) and the hard truth about Unicode in Week 12.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • C strings rely on a terminating \0; strcpy-style functions easily overflow.
  • std::string owns and manages text; short strings avoid heap allocation (SSO).
  • Take read-only text parameters as std::string_view.
  • Never return or store a string_view to something that may die first.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What is sizeof("abc")?

Show answer

4: three characters plus the terminating \0.

Q2. Why is std::string_view a good parameter type but a risky member/return type?

Show answer

As a parameter it avoids copies and accepts any string type, and the argument outlives the call. As a return/member it may outlive the characters it views, producing a dangling view.

Q3. Can you pass sv.data() to fopen?

Show answer

Not safely: a string_view's data isn't guaranteed to be NUL-terminated. Make a std::string first.

docs.title:
Lesson 3.5: Bits and bytes: bitwise operators, std::byte, and

C++23 · about 11 minutes
Why this matters
docs.text: An H.264 NAL unit header packs three fields into a single byte: 1 bit, 2 bits and 5 bits. Hardware registers, flags, compression, hashing — all of it is bit twiddling. C++ gives you direct access to bits, and C++20 finally added a proper <bit> header so you no longer need compiler-specific builtins. Let's decode that header.

docs.title: The operators
docs.text:
Op Meaning Typical use a & b AND test/clear bits with a mask a \| b OR set bits a ^ b XOR toggle bits ~a NOT invert (build "clear" masks) a << n, a >> n shift move fields into place

Extracting a field = shift it down, then mask it: (byte >> 5) & 0b11 gives bits 5–6.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Shifting by a count >= the width of the (promoted) type is UB: 1u << 32 on a 32-bit unsigned.
  • 1 << 31 on int: before C++20 this was UB; since C++20 signed integers are defined to be two's complement and left shift is well-defined — but stick to unsigned types for bit manipulation anyway.
  • Remember integer promotion: ~std::uint8_t{0x0F} is an int 0xFFFFFFF0, not 0xF0.

docs.title: std::byte (C++17)
docs.text: std::byte is "a byte of raw memory", not a character and not a number. It only supports bitwise ops, so you can't accidentally do arithmetic on it. Use std::to_integer<int>(b) to read it.

docs.title: <bit> (C++20)
docs.text:
Portable versions of things you used to need intrinsics for: std::popcount, std::countl_zero, std::countr_zero, std::rotl/rotr, std::has_single_bit (power of two?), std::bit_ceil, std::bit_width, and std::bit_cast — the safe way to reinterpret an object's bits as another type of the same size. C++23 added std::byteswap, and std::endian (C++20) tells you the platform byte order.

examples/week03/lesson05.cpp
#include <bit>
#include <bitset>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

struct NalHeader { unsigned forbidden, ref_idc, type; };

NalHeader parse(std::uint8_t b) {
    return {static_cast<unsigned>(b >> 7) & 0x1u,
            static_cast<unsigned>(b >> 5) & 0x3u,
            static_cast<unsigned>(b) & 0x1Fu};
}

int main() {
    const std::uint8_t nal = 0x67;   // a typical H.264 SPS header byte
    const auto h = parse(nal);
    std::cout << "bits=" << std::bitset<8>(nal) << " forbidden=" << h.forbidden
              << " ref_idc=" << h.ref_idc << " type=" << h.type << '\n';

    unsigned flags = 0;
    flags |= 1u << 3;        // set bit 3
    flags |= 1u << 0;        // set bit 0
    flags &= ~(1u << 0);     // clear bit 0
    flags ^= 1u << 5;        // toggle bit 5
    std::cout << "flags=" << std::bitset<8>(flags) << " popcount=" << std::popcount(flags) << '\n';

    std::cout << "bit_ceil(600)=" << std::bit_ceil(600u) << " has_single_bit(512)=" << std::has_single_bit(512u)
              << " countr_zero(40)=" << std::countr_zero(40u) << '\n';

    std::cout << std::hex << "bits of 1.0f = 0x" << std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(1.0f)
              << " byteswap(0x11223344)=0x" << std::byteswap(0x11223344u) << std::dec << '\n';
    std::cout << "little endian? " << (std::endian::native == std::endian::little) << '\n';

    std::byte b{0b1010'0000};
    b |= std::byte{0x01};
    std::cout << "std::byte as int: " << std::to_integer<int>(b) << '\n';
}

Output:

bits=01100111 forbidden=0 ref_idc=3 type=7
flags=00101000 popcount=2
bit_ceil(600)=1024 has_single_bit(512)=1 countr_zero(40)=3
bits of 1.0f = 0x3f800000 byteswap(0x11223344)=0x44332211
little endian? 1
std::byte as int: 161

docs.title: The wrong way to reinterpret bits
docs.text:
float f = 1.0f;
std::uint32_t u = *reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&f);   // WRONG: violates strict aliasing (UB)
std::uint32_t ok = std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f);          // right (C++20); or std::memcpy

Pro tip: ring buffers love powers of two

If a buffer's capacity is a power of two, index & (capacity - 1) replaces the slower index % capacity. You'll use exactly this in the embedded capstone.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Extract a bit field with shift-then-mask; use unsigned types for bit manipulation.
  • Shifting by >= the type width is UB; watch integer promotion with ~ on small types.
  • std::byte is raw memory, not a number; <bit> gives portable popcount, rotations, bit_cast etc.
  • Use std::bit_cast or memcpy, never reinterpret_cast, to reinterpret an object's bits.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. How do you extract bits 2..4 (3 bits) of x?

Show answer

(x >> 2) & 0b111.

Q2. What is the type and value of ~std::uint8_t{0}?

Show answer

int, value -1 (all bits set), due to integer promotion before ~.

Q3. Why is *reinterpret_cast<int*>(&some_float) wrong?

Show answer

It violates the strict aliasing rule (accessing a float object through an int glvalue), which is UB. Use std::bit_cast<int>(f) or std::memcpy.

Q4. What does std::has_single_bit(x) tell you?

Show answer

Whether x is a power of two.

docs.title: Week 3 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 3.1) Inside void f(int a[10]), what is sizeof(a) on a 64-bit system?

Show answer

8 — the parameter is actually int*; the 10 is ignored.

Q2. (from 3.1) Does std::span own its elements?

Show answer

No. It is a non-owning view (pointer + size). The underlying storage must outlive the span.

Q3. (from 3.2) If int a[4] starts at address 1000 and sizeof(int)==4, what address is a + 3?

Show answer

1012 — arithmetic is in units of elements.

Q4. (from 3.2) Which of these can you do with const char* s: s = other; / *s = 'x';?

Show answer

s = other; is fine (re-pointing). *s = 'x'; is an error (the pointee is const).

Q5. (from 3.3) What's wrong with int* p = new int[10]; delete p;?

Show answer

Memory from new[] must be released with delete[]; using delete is undefined behaviour.

Q6. (from 3.3) Why can't you rely on UB 'just crashing'?

Show answer

The standard imposes no requirements; the optimizer may assume UB is impossible and transform surrounding code, so the effect can be anything, including silently wrong results.

Q7. (from 3.4) What is sizeof("abc")?

Show answer

4: three characters plus the terminating \0.

Q8. (from 3.4) Why is std::string_view a good parameter type but a risky member/return type?

Show answer

As a parameter it avoids copies and accepts any string type, and the argument outlives the call. As a return/member it may outlive the characters it views, producing a dangling view.

Q9. (from 3.5) How do you extract bits 2..4 (3 bits) of x?

Show answer

(x >> 2) & 0b111.

Q10. (from 3.5) What is the type and value of ~std::uint8_t{0}?

Show answer

int, value -1 (all bits set), due to integer promotion before ~.

docs.title: Week 4: Classes and RAII
docs.text:
This week we design our own types. A class bundles data with the operations that keep that data valid. We'll see constructors and destructors, the (many!) ways C++ initializes objects, and then the single most important idiom in the language: RAII, which ties resource cleanup to object lifetime.

If you only remember one thing from this course, make it RAII. It's why well-written C++ rarely leaks, even without a garbage collector.

# Lesson Standard Length 4.1 Classes, encapsulation, and const member functions C++20 10 min 4.2 Constructors, destructors, and every way to initialize C++20 12 min 4.3 RAII: tying resources to object lifetime C++20 12 min 4.4 explicit, conversions, static members, friends, nested classes C++20 11 min 4.5 Operator overloading and the spaceship operator <=> C++23 12 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 4 programming assignment: A Rational number type
docs.text:
Implement class Rational (numerator/denominator, long long):

  1. Invariant: denominator > 0 and the fraction is always reduced (use std::gcd from <numeric>). The constructor throws std::invalid_argument on a zero denominator.
  2. + - * / via the compound-assignment pattern; explicit operator double().
  3. Comparisons with <=> — careful: a defaulted <=> would compare numerators first, which is wrong for fractions! Write a custom operator<=> that cross-multiplies, plus a defaulted operator== (correct because fractions are always reduced).
  4. operator<< printing 3/4.
Reference solution examples/week04/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <compare>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <stdexcept>

class Rational {
public:
    Rational(long long n = 0, long long d = 1) : num_{n}, den_{d} {   // implicit from integers is natural here
        if (den_ == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("zero denominator");
        normalize();
    }
    long long num() const { return num_; }
    long long den() const { return den_; }

    Rational& operator+=(const Rational& o) { num_ = num_ * o.den_ + o.num_ * den_; den_ *= o.den_; normalize(); return *this; }
    Rational& operator-=(const Rational& o) { return *this += Rational{-o.num_, o.den_}; }
    Rational& operator*=(const Rational& o) { num_ *= o.num_; den_ *= o.den_; normalize(); return *this; }
    Rational& operator/=(const Rational& o) { return *this *= Rational{o.den_, o.num_}; }

    friend Rational operator+(Rational a, const Rational& b) { return a += b; }
    friend Rational operator-(Rational a, const Rational& b) { return a -= b; }
    friend Rational operator*(Rational a, const Rational& b) { return a *= b; }
    friend Rational operator/(Rational a, const Rational& b) { return a /= b; }

    bool operator==(const Rational&) const = default;   // OK: always reduced
    std::strong_ordering operator<=>(const Rational& o) const { return num_ * o.den_ <=> o.num_ * den_; }

    explicit operator double() const { return static_cast<double>(num_) / static_cast<double>(den_); }
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Rational& r) { return os << r.num_ << '/' << r.den_; }

private:
    void normalize() {
        if (den_ < 0) { num_ = -num_; den_ = -den_; }
        const long long g = std::gcd(num_, den_);
        if (g > 1) { num_ /= g; den_ /= g; }
    }
    long long num_, den_;
};

int main() {
    Rational a{1, 2}, b{3, -4};
    std::cout << a << " + " << b << " = " << a + b << '\n';
    std::cout << a << " * " << b << " = " << a * b << '\n';
    std::cout << a << " / " << b << " = " << a / b << '\n';
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << (Rational{2, 4} == a) << ' ' << (b < a) << ' ' << (a + 1 > Rational{3, 2}) << '\n';
    std::cout << static_cast<double>(Rational{1, 3}) << '\n';
    try { Rational bad{1, 0}; } catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) { std::cout << "error: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
}

Output:

1/2 + -3/4 = -1/4
1/2 * -3/4 = -3/8
1/2 / -3/4 = -2/3
true true false
0.333333
error: zero denominator

docs.title: Lesson 4.1: Classes, encapsulation, and const member functions
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Imagine a Volume type whose value must always be between 0 and 100. If it's a plain struct with a public int, any line of code anywhere can set it to -7, and you'll find out three weeks later in a bug report. A class lets you make the data private and only allow changes through functions that keep the rule — the invariant — true. That's encapsulation, and it's what makes large programs manageable.

docs.title: class and struct are almost the same
docs.text: The only difference: members of a struct are public by default; members of a class are private by default. Convention: use struct for plain bundles of data with no invariants, and class when there's an invariant to protect.

docs.title: Protecting an invariant
mutable: the escape hatch
docs.text: Sometimes a const function legitimately needs to change something that isn't part of the observable state — a cache, or a mutex. Mark that member mutable. Use it sparingly: it's for implementation details only.

docs.title: The wrong way: getters and setters for everything
docs.text:
class Volume {
    int level_;
public:
    int  getLevel() const { return level_; }
    void setLevel(int l)  { level_ = l; }     // no checking: this is a struct with extra steps
};

A setter that doesn't enforce anything adds ceremony without protection. Either there's an invariant (then enforce it) or there isn't (then use a plain struct).

docs.title: Ref-qualifiers (advanced, optional)
docs.text: You can overload a member function on whether *this is an lvalue or an rvalue: get() & vs get() &&. This lets a temporary give away its internals cheaply. You'll appreciate it after Week 5; C++23's deducing this (Week 8) makes it much easier to write.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • class and struct differ only in default access; use class when you have an invariant.
  • Make data private and enforce invariants in constructors and member functions.
  • Mark every member function that doesn't modify the object const.
  • mutable is for caches/mutexes — not for avoiding thinking about const.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't you call a non-const member function through a const Volume&?

Show answer

A const reference only allows operations that promise not to modify the object, i.e. const member functions.

Q2. What's the type of this inside a const member function of Volume?

Show answer

const Volume*.

Q3. When is a plain struct with public members the right choice?

Show answer

When the members are independent and any combination of values is valid — there's no invariant to protect.

docs.title: Lesson 4.2: Constructors, destructors, and every way to initialize
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: C++ has a famously large number of ways to initialize an object — T x;, T x{};, T x();, T x = y;, T x(a, b);, T x{a, b}; — and some of them do surprisingly different things. This lesson doesn't try to list every rule. Instead it gives you a small set of habits that are always right, and shows you the three traps that catch everyone.

docs.title: Constructors and the member initializer list
docs.text:
A constructor runs when an object is created. Members should be initialized in the member initializer list (after the :), not assigned in the body:

class Track {
    std::string title_;
    int length_s_;
public:
    Track(std::string t, int len) : title_{std::move(t)}, length_s_{len} {}   // initialize
    // Track(std::string t, int len) { title_ = t; length_s_ = len; }        // default-construct, then assign
};

The second version first default-constructs title_ and then assigns — wasted work, and impossible for const members, references, or types with no default constructor.

docs.title: Default member initializers, delegation, = default and = delete
Trap 1: members are initialized in declaration order
docs.text:
class Buffer {
    std::size_t size_;
    std::vector<int> data_;
public:
    Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_(n), size_(data_.size()) {}  // looks fine...
};

This works by luck. But swap the declarations of size_ and data_ and data_(size_) would read an uninitialized size_. Members are always initialized in the order they're declared, regardless of the order in the initializer list. -Wall warns (-Wreorder) when the orders differ — listen to it.

docs.title: Trap 2: braces prefer std::initializer_list
docs.text:
std::vector<int> a(3, 7);   // three elements: 7 7 7
std::vector<int> b{3, 7};   // two elements: 3 7  (initializer_list constructor wins)

If a class has an initializer_list constructor, brace-init strongly prefers it. Use parentheses when you mean "call the size constructor".

docs.title: Trap 3: the most vexing parse
docs.text:
Stream s();      // NOT an object! Declares a function named s returning Stream.
Stream s{};      // value-initialized object. Use braces.

docs.title: Habits that are always right
docs.text:
1. Give every member a default member initializer or initialize it in every constructor.
  2. Use T x{...}; for objects, but ( ) when you need a specific non-list constructor of a container.
  3. Use {} to value-initialize (int x{}; is 0; T t{}; runs the default constructor or zero-fills).
  4. Mark single-argument constructors explicit (next lesson).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Initialize members in the member initializer list (or with default member initializers), don't assign in the body.
  • Members are initialized in declaration order, whatever order you write the list in.
  • Brace-init prefers initializer_list constructors: vector<int>{3,7} has two elements.
  • T x(); declares a function; write T x{};.
  • = default and = delete control which special operations exist.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. How many elements does std::vector<int> v{5}; have? And std::vector<int> v(5);?

Show answer

{5}: one element with value 5 (initializer_list). (5): five zero-valued elements.

Q2. A class declares int a_; int b_; and the constructor writes : b_{1}, a_{b_}. What's a_?

Show answer

Indeterminate (UB to read): a_ is initialized first, from the not-yet-initialized b_. Initialization follows declaration order.

Q3. Why might you = delete a constructor taking bool?

Show answer

To stop accidental implicit conversions (e.g. a pointer or bool converting to int) from silently selecting another constructor.

docs.title: Lesson 4.3: RAII: tying resources to object lifetime
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Suppose you open a file, lock a mutex, or grab a hardware codec. Then something goes wrong halfway through — an early return, an exception. Who releases the resource? In C you write goto cleanup and hope you covered every path. In C++ the answer is beautiful: the destructor does, automatically, on every path. This idea is called RAII, and it's the most important idiom in C++.

docs.title: The wrong way: manual cleanup
docs.text:
bool save(const char* path, const Data& d) {
    std::FILE* f = std::fopen(path, "wb");
    if (!f) return false;
    if (!write_header(f, d)) return false;       // LEAK: forgot fclose
    write_body(f, d);                            // if this throws: LEAK
    std::fclose(f);
    return true;
}

Every new exit path is a chance to forget cleanup.

docs.title: RAII: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor
docs.text:
The trick is to wrap the resource in a small class whose destructor releases it. Because destructors of local objects run whenever a scope is left — normal flow, return, break, or an exception unwinding the stack — cleanup happens on every path, with no extra code at the call site.

examples/week04/lesson03.cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class File {
public:
    File(const char* path, const char* mode) : f_{std::fopen(path, mode)} {
        if (!f_) throw std::runtime_error(std::string{"cannot open "} + path);
        std::cout << "  opened " << path << '\n';
    }
    ~File() { std::fclose(f_); std::cout << "  closed\n"; }
    File(const File&) = delete;              // one owner only
    File& operator=(const File&) = delete;

    void write(const std::string& s) { std::fputs(s.c_str(), f_); }

private:
    std::FILE* f_;
};

template <class F>
class ScopeGuard {                           // runs an action when the scope ends
public:
    explicit ScopeGuard(F f) : f_{std::move(f)} {}
    ~ScopeGuard() { f_(); }
    ScopeGuard(const ScopeGuard&) = delete;
    ScopeGuard& operator=(const ScopeGuard&) = delete;
private:
    F f_;
};

void process(bool fail) {
    File out{"/tmp/raii_demo.txt", "w"};
    ScopeGuard guard{[] { std::cout << "  guard: cleanup step\n"; }};
    out.write("hello\n");
    if (fail) throw std::runtime_error("encoding failed");
    std::cout << "  done\n";
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "normal run:\n";
    process(false);
    std::cout << "failing run:\n";
    try {
        process(true);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "  caught: " << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

normal run:
  opened /tmp/raii_demo.txt
  done
  guard: cleanup step
  closed
failing run:
  opened /tmp/raii_demo.txt
  guard: cleanup step
  closed
  caught: encoding failed

Look at the output: when the exception propagates out of process, the File destructor still runs before the catch block. That's stack unwinding.

A few design points in that File class:

  • The copy operations are = deleted. Two File objects owning the same FILE* would both call fclose — a double close. (In Week 5 we'll make it movable so ownership can be transferred.)
  • The constructor throws if it can't acquire the resource. That way, a File object that exists is always a valid, open file: a class invariant.

docs.title: RAII is everywhere in the standard library
docs.text:
Resource RAII type heap memory std::vector, std::string, std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr mutex lock std::lock_guard, std::scoped_lock, std::unique_lock thread std::jthread (joins in its destructor) file std::fstream

You can also make a general scope guard — an object that runs a lambda in its destructor — for one-off cleanup actions. The example includes a tiny one.

Pro tip: Android & C APIs

NDK APIs are C APIs: AMediaCodec_delete, AAsset_close, ANativeWindow_release... Wrap each in an RAII type (or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter, Week 12) once, and your JNI code stops leaking.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • RAII: acquire a resource in a constructor, release it in the destructor.
  • Destructors run on every exit path, including exceptions (stack unwinding).
  • A resource-owning class must decide its copy behaviour; often = delete copies (and allow moves).
  • The standard library is RAII all the way down; wrap C handles the same way.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why does RAII make code exception-safe without try/catch at every call site?

Show answer

Destructors of local objects run during stack unwinding, so resources are released whatever path leaves the scope.

Q2. What goes wrong if a File RAII class is copyable with the default copy constructor?

Show answer

Both copies hold the same FILE* and both destructors call fclose on it — a double close (UB).

Q3. Name three RAII types from the standard library.

Show answer

For example std::vector, std::unique_ptr, std::lock_guard, std::jthread, std::fstream.

docs.title: Practice lab (optional)
docs.text:
Write an RAII class Timer that records std::chrono::steady_clock::now() in its constructor and prints the elapsed milliseconds (with a label) in its destructor. Use it to time a loop. Make it non-copyable.

Full solution examples/week04/lesson03_lab_solution.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class Timer {
public:
    explicit Timer(std::string label) : label_{std::move(label)}, start_{std::chrono::steady_clock::now()} {}
    ~Timer() {
        const auto ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - start_);
        std::cout << label_ << ": " << ms.count() << " ms\n";
    }
    Timer(const Timer&) = delete;
    Timer& operator=(const Timer&) = delete;
private:
    std::string label_;
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point start_;
};

int main() {
    volatile double sink = 0;   // volatile so the loop isn't optimized away
    {
        Timer t{"sum loop"};
        for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i) sink = sink + i * 0.5;
    }
}

Output:

sum loop: 2.70348 ms

docs.title: Lesson 4.4: explicit, conversions, static members, friends, nested classes
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Here's a real surprise: void play(Duration d); ... play(5); compiles, and plays for 5 what? If Duration has a constructor taking an int, C++ will quietly convert. Implicit conversions are sometimes great (std::string s = "hi";) and sometimes a bug factory. This lesson is about controlling them, plus a few other class features you'll meet constantly.

docs.title: explicit: no surprise conversions
docs.text:
A constructor that can be called with one argument is a converting constructor: the compiler may use it implicitly. Mark it explicit unless the conversion is truly natural and lossless.

struct Millis { explicit Millis(long v) : value{v} {} long value; };
void sleep_for(Millis);
sleep_for(5);           // ERROR (good!) — what unit is 5?
sleep_for(Millis{5});   // clear

C++20 added explicit(condition) for generic code, e.g. "explicit only if the conversion is narrowing".

docs.title: Conversion operators
docs.text: The reverse direction: operator T() const lets your type convert to T. The most common one is explicit operator bool() — it works in if (x) and !x (contextual conversion) but won't let your object silently become 1 in arithmetic.

docs.title: static members: belong to the class, not an object
docs.text: A static data member has one instance shared by all objects; a static member function has no this. Since C++17 you can define it inline: inline static int count = 0;.

docs.title: friend
docs.text: A friend declaration grants a function or class access to private members. It's not a hack — it's the right tool for operators that are naturally non-members (like operator<<) and for tightly coupled helper classes. Keep friends few and close.

docs.title: Nested and local classes
docs.text:
A class defined inside another (Playlist::Iterator) is a nested class: it's scoped by the outer class and can access its private members. A class defined inside a function is a local class — handy for one-off helpers, though lambdas usually do the job.

examples/week04/lesson04.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Millis {
public:
    explicit Millis(long v) : value_{v} {}
    long count() const { return value_; }
private:
    long value_;
};

class Codec {
public:
    explicit Codec(std::string name) : name_{std::move(name)} { ++instances; }
    ~Codec() { --instances; }
    Codec(const Codec&) = delete;
    Codec& operator=(const Codec&) = delete;

    explicit operator bool() const { return !name_.empty(); }   // "is valid?"
    inline static int instances = 0;                              // shared by all Codecs

    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Codec& c) {   // friend: sees name_
        return os << "Codec(" << c.name_ << ")";
    }

    struct Stats { int frames = 0; };                              // nested class
    Stats stats;
private:
    std::string name_;
};

void wait(Millis m) { std::cout << "wait " << m.count() << " ms\n"; }

int main() {
    wait(Millis{20});
    // wait(20);   // would not compile: constructor is explicit

    Codec opus{"opus"}, none{""};
    std::cout << opus << " valid=" << static_cast<bool>(opus) << ", none valid=" << (none ? "yes" : "no")
              << ", instances=" << Codec::instances << '\n';

    struct Counter { int n = 0; void hit() { ++n; } };             // local class
    Counter c;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) c.hit();
    opus.stats.frames = c.n;
    std::cout << "frames=" << opus.stats.frames << '\n';
}

Output:

wait 20 ms
Codec(opus) valid=1, none valid=no, instances=2
frames=3

Common pitfall: implicit operator bool

Pre-C++11 code used operator void*() or non-explicit operator bool() hacks, which allowed nonsense like stream1 + stream2. Always write explicit operator bool() const.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Mark single-argument constructors explicit unless the conversion is obviously safe.
  • Write explicit operator bool(); it still works in if and !.
  • static members belong to the class; inline static (C++17) defines them in the class body.
  • friend is the normal way to write non-member operators that need private access.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why does if (codec) compile with an explicit operator bool, but int n = codec; doesn't?

Show answer

if performs a contextual conversion to bool, which is allowed to use explicit conversion operators. Copy-initialization of int would need an implicit conversion.

Q2. Does a static member function have a this pointer?

Show answer

No; it isn't called on an object. It can access only static members (or objects passed to it).

Q3. When is friend appropriate?

Show answer

For non-member functions that are part of a class's interface and need private access (e.g. operator<<, symmetric binary operators), or tightly coupled helper classes.

docs.title: Lesson 4.5: Operator overloading and the spaceship operator <=>
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Suppose you have a Version{major, minor, patch} and want to sort a list of them, or check if (v >= Version{2, 1, 0}). Before C++20 that meant writing six comparison operators by hand, carefully keeping them consistent. Now it's one line. Operator overloading lets your types feel like built-in ones — let's see how to do it well, and what not to do.

docs.title: The basic idea
docs.text:
An operator is just a function with a special name: a + b calls operator+(a, b) (or a.operator+(b)). The rules of thumb, from the C++ Core Guidelines and decades of experience:

  • Do what the built-in operator would do. + adds, == compares. No clever surprises.
  • Binary operators that treat both sides symmetrically should be non-members (often friends), so conversions apply to both operands.
  • Implement + in terms of +=.

docs.title: Comparisons in C++20: <=> and = default
docs.text:
struct Version {
    int major, minor, patch;
    auto operator<=>(const Version&) const = default;   // gives <, <=, >, >=
    bool operator==(const Version&) const = default;    // gives ==, != (implied by <=> = default too)
};

That defaulted <=> compares members in declaration order (lexicographically), exactly what you want for versions. The result is a comparison category:

Category Meaning Example std::strong_ordering equal values are indistinguishable int std::weak_ordering equivalent values may differ case-insensitive strings std::partial_ordering some values are unordered double (NaN)

C++20 also rewrites expressions: a != b becomes !(a == b), and a < b can use (a <=> b) < 0, including with the arguments reversed. So you write two functions and get all six operators.

examples/week04/lesson05.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <compare>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Version {
    int major = 0, minor = 0, patch = 0;
    auto operator<=>(const Version&) const = default;   // all six comparisons
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Version& v) {
        return os << v.major << '.' << v.minor << '.' << v.patch;
    }
};

struct Vec2 {
    double x = 0, y = 0;
    Vec2& operator+=(const Vec2& o) { x += o.x; y += o.y; return *this; }
    friend Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, const Vec2& b) { return a += b; }   // a is a copy
    friend Vec2 operator*(double k, Vec2 v) { v.x *= k; v.y *= k; return v; }
    bool operator==(const Vec2&) const = default;
};

class Grid {
public:
    int& operator[](int r, int c) { return cells_[static_cast<std::size_t>(r * 3 + c)]; }   // C++23 multi-arg []
private:
    std::vector<int> cells_ = std::vector<int>(9);
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Version> vs{{2, 1, 0}, {1, 9, 9}, {2, 0, 5}, {2, 1, 0}};
    std::ranges::sort(vs);
    for (const auto& v : vs) std::cout << v << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n' << std::boolalpha
              << (Version{2, 1, 0} >= Version{2, 0, 5}) << ' ' << (vs[2] == vs[3]) << ' '
              << (vs[0] != vs[1]) << '\n';

    auto r = (1.5 <=> 2.0);
    std::cout << "1.5 <=> 2.0 is less? " << (r < 0) << '\n';

    Vec2 a{1, 2}, b{3, 4};
    Vec2 c = a + b;
    Vec2 d = 2.0 * c;
    std::cout << c.x << ',' << c.y << ' ' << d.x << ',' << d.y << ' ' << (c == Vec2{4, 6}) << '\n';

    Grid g;
    g[1, 2] = 7;
    std::cout << "g[1, 2] = " << g[1, 2] << '\n';
}

Output:

1.9.9 2.0.5 2.1.0 2.1.0 
true true true
1.5 <=> 2.0 is less? true
4,6 8,12 true
g[1, 2] = 7

docs.title: Arithmetic operators
docs.text: The canonical pattern, shown for a 2D vector in the example: a member operator+= that modifies *this and returns *this by reference, and a non-member operator+ that takes its left operand by value, uses +=, and returns it.

docs.title: Other operators you'll overload
docs.text:
• operator[] for containers. C++23 allows multiple arguments: m[i, j].
  • operator() makes a function object (functor) — the idea behind lambdas.
  • operator<< with std::ostream for printing.

docs.title: The wrong way: surprising operators
docs.text:
Matrix operator*(const Matrix&, const Matrix&);   // fine: math
Logger& operator<<(Logger&, Level);               // fine: established stream idiom
bool operator&&(const A&, const B&);              // AVOID: loses short-circuit evaluation
Thing& operator,(Thing&, Thing&);                 // AVOID: nobody expects this

Overloaded &&, || and , don't short-circuit / sequence the way the built-ins do. Don't overload them.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Overload operators only with their conventional meaning.
  • In C++20, auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default; gives all six comparisons, member-wise.
  • Comparison categories: strong, weak, partial ordering.
  • Implement + via +=; make symmetric binary operators non-members.
  • Never overload &&, || or ,.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. With only bool operator==(const T&) const defined, does a != b compile in C++20?

Show answer

Yes. C++20 rewrites a != b as !(a == b).

Q2. What comparison category does double <=> double return and why?

Show answer

std::partial_ordering, because NaN is unordered with respect to every value.

Q3. Why take the left operand of operator+ by value?

Show answer

We need a copy to modify anyway; taking it by value lets the compiler move from temporaries and makes the implementation return a += b;.

Q4. Why shouldn't you overload operator&&?

Show answer

The overloaded version is a normal function call: both operands are always evaluated, so short-circuiting is lost.

docs.title: Week 4 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 4.1) Why can't you call a non-const member function through a const Volume&?

Show answer

A const reference only allows operations that promise not to modify the object, i.e. const member functions.

Q2. (from 4.1) What's the type of this inside a const member function of Volume?

Show answer

const Volume*.

Q3. (from 4.2) How many elements does std::vector<int> v{5}; have? And std::vector<int> v(5);?

Show answer

{5}: one element with value 5 (initializer_list). (5): five zero-valued elements.

Q4. (from 4.2) A class declares int a_; int b_; and the constructor writes : b_{1}, a_{b_}. What's a_?

Show answer

Indeterminate (UB to read): a_ is initialized first, from the not-yet-initialized b_. Initialization follows declaration order.

Q5. (from 4.3) Why does RAII make code exception-safe without try/catch at every call site?

Show answer

Destructors of local objects run during stack unwinding, so resources are released whatever path leaves the scope.

Q6. (from 4.3) What goes wrong if a File RAII class is copyable with the default copy constructor?

Show answer

Both copies hold the same FILE* and both destructors call fclose on it — a double close (UB).

Q7. (from 4.4) Why does if (codec) compile with an explicit operator bool, but int n = codec; doesn't?

Show answer

if performs a contextual conversion to bool, which is allowed to use explicit conversion operators. Copy-initialization of int would need an implicit conversion.

Q8. (from 4.4) Does a static member function have a this pointer?

Show answer

No; it isn't called on an object. It can access only static members (or objects passed to it).

Q9. (from 4.5) With only bool operator==(const T&) const defined, does a != b compile in C++20?

Show answer

Yes. C++20 rewrites a != b as !(a == b).

Q10. (from 4.5) What comparison category does double <=> double return and why?

Show answer

std::partial_ordering, because NaN is unordered with respect to every value.

docs.title: Week 5: Value semantics: copy, move, and value categories
docs.text:
This is the week many people describe as "the moment C++ finally made sense". We'll look at what it means to copy an object, then at move semantics — the C++11 feature that lets you transfer resources instead of duplicating them — and the idea underneath it: value categories.

Honest warning: value categories are one of the most confusing topics in C++. We'll go slowly, with lots of printed output so you can see which constructor runs. If it doesn't fully click this week, that's completely normal; it'll click after you use it.

# Lesson Standard Length 5.1 Copy semantics and the Rule of Three C++20 11 min 5.2 Value categories: lvalues, prvalues, xvalues C++20 12 min 5.3 Move semantics, std::move, and the Rules of Five and Zero C++20 12 min 5.4 Copy elision, RVO, and returning by value C++20 9 min 5.5 Aggregates, designated initializers, structured bindings, user-defined literals C++20 11 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 5 programming assignment: A move-aware audio clip
docs.text:
Build class Clip that owns samples (std::vector<float>), a name (std::string) and an id.

  1. Follow the Rule of Zero for storage — but add instrumentation: a static counter of copies and moves using a small member type with custom copy/move that increments counters (so Clip itself still writes no special members).
  2. static Clip make_sine(std::string name, float freq, int n) returning by value.
  3. A Playlist that stores clips in a std::vector<Clip> via a sink add(Clip c).
  4. Show (by printing counters) that building a playlist of 3 clips performs zero copies.
Reference solution examples/week05/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <numbers>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Tally {                       // instrumentation member: counts copies and moves of its owner
    inline static int copies = 0, moves = 0;
    Tally() = default;
    Tally(const Tally&) { ++copies; }
    Tally(Tally&&) noexcept { ++moves; }
    Tally& operator=(const Tally&) { ++copies; return *this; }
    Tally& operator=(Tally&&) noexcept { ++moves; return *this; }
};

class Clip {                         // Rule of Zero: no special members written
public:
    static Clip make_sine(std::string name, float freq, int n) {
        Clip c;
        c.name_ = std::move(name);
        c.samples_.reserve(static_cast<std::size_t>(n));
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
            c.samples_.push_back(std::sin(2.0f * std::numbers::pi_v<float> * freq * static_cast<float>(i) / 48000.0f));
        return c;                     // NRVO / implicit move
    }
    const std::string& name() const { return name_; }
    std::size_t size() const { return samples_.size(); }
private:
    std::string name_;
    std::vector<float> samples_;
    Tally tally_;
};

class Playlist {
public:
    void add(Clip c) { clips_.push_back(std::move(c)); }   // sink
    void print() const { for (const auto& c : clips_) std::cout << c.name() << '(' << c.size() << ") "; std::cout << '\n'; }
private:
    std::vector<Clip> clips_;
};

int main() {
    Playlist p;
    p.add(Clip::make_sine("A4", 440.0f, 480));
    p.add(Clip::make_sine("C5", 523.25f, 480));
    Clip e = Clip::make_sine("E5", 659.25f, 480);
    p.add(std::move(e));
    p.print();
    std::cout << "copies=" << Tally::copies << " moves=" << Tally::moves << '\n';
}

Output:

A4(480) C5(480) E5(480) 
copies=0 moves=7

docs.title: Lesson 5.1: Copy semantics and the Rule of Three
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Write a class that owns a heap buffer with a raw pointer, copy it once, and your program will crash at exit with a double free. Why? The compiler-generated copy just copies the pointer, so two objects think they own the same buffer. Understanding exactly what "copy" means for your class is the foundation for everything this week.

docs.title: The six special member functions
docs.text: For every class, the compiler can generate: default constructor, destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment. The generated copy operations copy each member. For an int or std::string member, that's perfect. For a raw owning pointer, it's a disaster.

docs.title: The wrong way: shallow copy of an owning pointer
docs.text:
class Buffer {
    float* data_; std::size_t n_;
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_{new float[n]{}}, n_{n} {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }
    // no copy operations written: compiler copies the pointer
};
Buffer a{1024};
Buffer b = a;    // b.data_ == a.data_  -> both destructors delete[] it -> double free (UB)

docs.title: The Rule of Three
docs.text:
If a class needs a user-written destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment operator, it almost certainly needs all three.

Because a custom destructor means "I manage a resource", and then copying must decide what happens to that resource: deep copy (duplicate it), forbid copying (= delete), or share it (reference count).

docs.title: A correct deep copy, with copy-and-swap
Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Compiler-generated copies copy each member; for raw owning pointers that means double frees.
  • Rule of Three: a custom destructor, copy ctor or copy assignment usually means you need all three.
  • Copy-and-swap gives safe, exception-safe assignment with little code.
  • Better still: hold resources in members that already copy correctly (Rule of Zero).

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does the implicitly generated copy constructor do?

Show answer

Copy-constructs each base and member in declaration order (memberwise copy).

Q2. Why is copy-and-swap safe for self-assignment?

Show answer

The parameter is a full copy made before anything in *this changes, so swapping with it is fine even if the source was *this.

Q3. Your class has a std::FILE* it closes in the destructor. What are your options for copying?

Show answer

Delete copying (most common), implement a deep copy (open another handle — rarely meaningful), or share ownership with reference counting (e.g. std::shared_ptr with a deleter).

docs.title: Lesson 5.2: Value categories: lvalues, prvalues, xvalues
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: To make moves work, the compiler needs to know one thing about every expression: is this an object that someone still cares about, or one that's about to disappear? If it's about to disappear, it's safe to steal its insides. That's what value categories are — and despite the scary names, the intuition is simple.

docs.title: The intuition: "has a name / identity" vs "about to die"
docs.text:
• An lvalue is an expression that refers to an object with identity that will still exist after the expression: a named variable x, *p, v[0], a function returning T&. You can take its address.
  • A prvalue ("pure rvalue") is a value with no identity yet: 42, a + b, std::string{"hi"}, a function returning T by value. It's a recipe for creating an object.
  • An xvalue ("expiring value") is an object that has identity but which we've declared we're done with: std::move(x), or a function returning T&&.

Grouping them: rvalues = prvalues + xvalues ("can be moved from"); glvalues = lvalues + xvalues ("has identity").

flowchart TD
  E[expression] --> G[glvalue: has identity]
  E --> R[rvalue: can be moved from]
  G --> L[lvalue]
  G --> X[xvalue]
  R --> X
  R --> P[prvalue]

docs.title: Rvalue references: T&&
docs.text:
A T&& parameter binds only to rvalues. So you can overload a function: one version for lvalues (const T&: "I'll copy if needed") and one for rvalues (T&&: "you can steal from this").

examples/week05/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <class T> constexpr const char* category() {
    if constexpr (std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T>) return "lvalue";
    else if constexpr (std::is_rvalue_reference_v<T>) return "xvalue";
    else return "prvalue";
}
#define CATEGORY(...) category<decltype((__VA_ARGS__))>()

void take(const std::string& s) { std::cout << "  take(const&)  [copy if needed]: " << s << '\n'; }
void take(std::string&& s) {
    std::cout << "  take(&&)      [may steal]: " << s << '\n';
    std::cout << "    inside, `s` is an " << CATEGORY(s) << '\n';
}

std::string make() { return "made"; }

int main() {
    std::string name = "named";
    int x = 1;
    std::cout << "x: " << CATEGORY(x) << ", 42: " << CATEGORY(42) << ", x + 1: " << CATEGORY(x + 1)
              << ", std::move(x): " << CATEGORY(std::move(x)) << ", make(): " << CATEGORY(make()) << '\n';

    take(name);                 // lvalue  -> const&
    take(make());               // prvalue -> &&
    take(std::string{"temp"});  // prvalue -> &&
    take(std::move(name));      // xvalue  -> &&
}

Output:

x: lvalue, 42: prvalue, x + 1: prvalue, std::move(x): xvalue, make(): prvalue
  take(const&)  [copy if needed]: named
  take(&&)      [may steal]: made
    inside, `s` is an lvalue
  take(&&)      [may steal]: temp
    inside, `s` is an lvalue
  take(&&)      [may steal]: named
    inside, `s` is an lvalue

Read that output carefully, especially the last line. Inside take(std::string&& s), the parameter s is an lvalue! It has a name, so it's not about to disappear inside the function. That's why, to pass it on as an rvalue, you'd have to say std::move(s) again. This is the #1 confusion about rvalue references: the type is "rvalue reference", the expression s is an lvalue.

docs.title: Seeing categories with decltype
docs.text: decltype((expr)) (double parentheses!) gives T& for lvalues, T&& for xvalues and T for prvalues. The example uses this to print categories — a nice trick for experiments in Compiler Explorer.

docs.title: C++17: guaranteed copy elision and temporary materialization
docs.text:
Since C++17 a prvalue isn't an object until it needs to be: T x = T{}; constructs directly into x — no temporary, no move. The prvalue is only "materialized" into a temporary (becoming an xvalue) when it must be, e.g. when binding to a reference. We'll use this in Lesson 5.4.

Don't memorize the taxonomy

You need two working rules: (1) a named thing is an lvalue, even if its type is T&&; (2) std::move(x) turns x into an rvalue so a move can happen.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • lvalue: has identity and persists; prvalue: a value with no identity yet; xvalue: an object we've marked as expiring.
  • T&& parameters bind only to rvalues; overload on const T& / T&& to copy or steal.
  • A named rvalue reference is an lvalue expression — use std::move again to pass it on.
  • decltype((e)) reveals the value category; C++17 prvalues materialize only when needed.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Classify: v[0] (vector v), v.size(), std::move(v), "hello". Show answer

v[0] lvalue (returns int&); v.size() prvalue; std::move(v) xvalue; a string literal is an lvalue (an array object with static storage).

Q2. Inside void f(Widget&& w), which overload does g(w) call: g(const Widget&) or g(Widget&&)?

Show answer

g(const Widget&). w is a named variable, hence an lvalue. To call the && overload write g(std::move(w)).

Q3. What's the difference between decltype(x) and decltype((x)) for int x?

Show answer

decltype(x) is the declared type int; decltype((x)) treats (x) as an lvalue expression and gives int&.

docs.title: Lesson 5.3: Move semantics, std::move, and the Rules of Five and Zero
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Returning a 4K video frame from a function, or pushing a big buffer into a std::vector, would copy megabytes in C++98. With move semantics, it copies three pointers. That's not a micro-optimization — it changes how you design APIs: you can pass and return big objects by value again, which is simpler and safer. Let's write a move constructor and watch the difference.

docs.title: The idea: steal, then leave the source in a valid state
docs.text:
A move constructor T(T&& other) noexcept takes the resources out of other (pointers, handles) and leaves other valid but unspecified — typically empty. Destroying or reassigning a moved-from object must still work.

examples/week05/lesson03.cpp
#include <cstring>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Counts { int copies = 0, moves = 0; } counts;

class Frame {
public:
    explicit Frame(std::size_t n) : n_{n}, px_{new unsigned char[n]{}} {}
    ~Frame() { delete[] px_; }
    Frame(const Frame& o) : n_{o.n_}, px_{new unsigned char[o.n_]} {
        std::memcpy(px_, o.px_, n_);
        ++counts.copies;
    }
    Frame(Frame&& o) noexcept : n_{std::exchange(o.n_, 0)}, px_{std::exchange(o.px_, nullptr)} {
        ++counts.moves;                          // steal; leave o empty but valid
    }
    Frame& operator=(Frame o) noexcept {         // handles both copy and move assignment
        std::swap(n_, o.n_);
        std::swap(px_, o.px_);
        return *this;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return n_; }
private:
    std::size_t n_;
    unsigned char* px_;
};

struct NoexceptLess {               // move constructor NOT noexcept
    NoexceptLess() = default;
    NoexceptLess(const NoexceptLess&) { ++counts.copies; }
    NoexceptLess(NoexceptLess&&) { ++counts.moves; }
};

int main() {
    Frame a{3840 * 2160 * 4};
    Frame b = a;                 // copy: allocates and memcpy's ~33 MB
    Frame c = std::move(a);      // move: steals the pointer
    std::cout << "copies=" << counts.copies << " moves=" << counts.moves
              << " a.size()=" << a.size() << " c.size()=" << c.size() << '\n';

    counts = {};
    std::vector<Frame> v;
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) v.push_back(Frame{16});   // growth moves (noexcept)
    std::cout << "vector<Frame>: copies=" << counts.copies << " moves=" << counts.moves << '\n';

    counts = {};
    std::vector<NoexceptLess> w;
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) w.emplace_back();          // growth must COPY existing elements
    std::cout << "vector<NoexceptLess>: copies=" << counts.copies << " moves=" << counts.moves << '\n';

    const Frame k{8};
    Frame m = std::move(k);      // const: this silently copies!
    std::cout << "after moving a const: copies=" << counts.copies + 0 << " (one more copy)\n";
    (void)m;
}

Output:

copies=1 moves=1 a.size()=0 c.size()=33177600
vector<Frame>: copies=0 moves=12
vector<NoexceptLess>: copies=7 moves=0
after moving a const: copies=8 (one more copy)

Look at the counts: the moves cost nothing like the copy.

docs.title: std::move doesn't move anything
docs.text:
std::move(x) is just a cast to T&& — it says "I'm done with x, you may steal from it". The actual moving happens in the move constructor/assignment that then gets selected. Two consequences:

  • std::move on a const object silently copies (a const T&& can't bind to T&&, so overload resolution falls back to the copy constructor).
  • After std::move(x), don't use x except to assign to it or destroy it.

docs.title: Why noexcept matters
docs.text: When std::vector grows, it moves elements to the new storage — only if the move constructor is noexcept. Otherwise it copies, so that if a copy throws it can leave the old storage intact (the strong guarantee). Forget noexcept on your move constructor and vector growth silently becomes copies. The example shows both.

docs.title: Rule of Five and Rule of Zero
docs.text:
• Rule of Five: if you write any of destructor / copy ctor / copy assign / move ctor / move assign, think about all five. (Declaring a destructor or copy operation suppresses the implicit moves!)
  • Rule of Zero: better — design classes so they need none. Hold resources in members that manage themselves (std::vector, std::string, std::unique_ptr). Then the compiler-generated operations are correct and as efficient as possible.
struct Track {                     // Rule of Zero: no special members written
    std::string title;
    std::vector<float> samples;
    std::unique_ptr<Decoder> dec;  // makes Track move-only, automatically
};

Common pitfall: return std::move(local);

Don't. It prevents copy elision (next lesson), and return local; already moves automatically. Compilers warn with -Wpessimizing-move.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A move constructor steals resources and leaves the source valid but unspecified (usually empty).
  • std::move is only a cast; moving a const object copies.
  • Mark move operations noexcept, or std::vector will copy on reallocation.
  • Prefer the Rule of Zero; otherwise follow the Rule of Five.
  • Don't write return std::move(local);.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does std::move actually do?

Show answer

static_cast<T&&> — it converts its argument to an xvalue so move overloads can be selected. It performs no moving itself.

Q2. Why might std::vector<T> copy elements during push_back even though T has a move constructor?

Show answer

If the move constructor isn't noexcept (and T is copyable), vector uses copies to keep the strong exception guarantee on reallocation (std::move_if_noexcept).

Q3. Your class declares only a destructor. Does it get an implicit move constructor?

Show answer

No. A user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move operations; moves fall back to (deprecated) implicit copies. Either = default the moves or follow the Rule of Zero.

Q4. Is it OK to call v.size() on a moved-from std::vector?

Show answer

Yes — it's in a valid but unspecified state, so calling functions without preconditions is fine (in practice it's empty). Calling v[0] would not be OK without checking.

docs.title: Lesson 5.4: Copy elision, RVO, and returning by value
docs.text: C++20 · about 9 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Should a function that builds a big vector return it, or take an output parameter void build(std::vector<int>& out)? Old advice said "output parameter, to avoid the copy". Modern C++ says: just return it. Let's see why the compiler makes that free — and the two simple rules for writing parameters that take ownership.

docs.title: Guaranteed elision (C++17)
docs.text: When you return a prvalue — return Widget{args}; — C++17 guarantees the object is constructed directly in the caller's storage. No copy, no move; the type doesn't even need to be copyable or movable.

docs.title: NRVO: named return value optimization
docs.text:
When you return a named local, Widget w; ...; return w;, the compiler is allowed (not required) to construct w directly in the caller's storage. GCC and Clang do this whenever there's a single named object returned on all paths. If it can't, the return still moves automatically (C++11, broadened in C++20), never copies, as long as the type is movable.

examples/week05/lesson04.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Loud {
    std::string tag;
    explicit Loud(std::string t) : tag{std::move(t)} { std::cout << "  construct " << tag << '\n'; }
    Loud(const Loud& o) : tag{o.tag} { std::cout << "  COPY " << tag << '\n'; }
    Loud(Loud&& o) noexcept : tag{std::move(o.tag)} { std::cout << "  move " << tag << '\n'; }
};

Loud make_prvalue() { return Loud{"prvalue"}; }          // guaranteed elision (C++17)
Loud make_named() { Loud w{"named"}; w.tag += "!"; return w; }   // NRVO in practice
Loud make_either(bool b) {
    Loud x{"x"}, y{"y"};
    if (b) return x;     // two candidates: no NRVO, but implicit move (never a copy)
    return y;
}

class Holder {
public:
    explicit Holder(Loud l) : l_{std::move(l)} {}   // sink parameter
private:
    Loud l_;
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "prvalue:\n";  Loud a = make_prvalue();
    std::cout << "named:\n";    Loud b = make_named();
    std::cout << "either:\n";   Loud c = make_either(true);
    std::cout << "sink from lvalue:\n";
    Holder h1{a};                    // copy into parameter, then move
    std::cout << "sink from rvalue:\n";
    Holder h2{std::move(b)};         // move into parameter, then move
    (void)c; (void)h1; (void)h2;
}

Output:

prvalue:
  construct prvalue
named:
  construct named
either:
  construct x
  construct y
  move x
sink from lvalue:
  COPY prvalue
  move prvalue
sink from rvalue:
  move named!
  move named!

Count the "move" lines: zero for the two common patterns. The function returning one of two different locals can't use NRVO, so it moves.

docs.title: Sink parameters: take by value, then move
docs.text:
If a function will store its argument (a constructor storing a name, push_back-like functions), take it by value and std::move it into place:

class Track {
    std::string title_;
public:
    explicit Track(std::string title) : title_{std::move(title)} {}
};
Track a{some_string};          // one copy (into the parameter) + one cheap move
Track b{"literal"};            // constructs the parameter directly + one cheap move
Track c{std::move(s)};         // two cheap moves, no copy

One function handles lvalues and rvalues nearly optimally. (The alternative — overloading on const& and && — saves a move but doubles the code.)

Rules you can apply without thinking

  1. Return by value. Don't std::move the return expression.
  2. Read-only parameter → const T& (or by value for cheap types / string_view / span).
  3. Parameter you'll store → by value + std::move.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Returning a prvalue is guaranteed copy-free since C++17.
  • Returning a named local uses NRVO or, failing that, an implicit move — never write return std::move(x).
  • Return results by value instead of using output parameters.
  • Sink parameters: take by value and std::move into the member.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Can a function return a non-copyable, non-movable type by value in C++17?

Show answer

Yes, if it returns a prvalue (return T{...};), thanks to guaranteed copy elision.

Q2. Why can't the compiler apply NRVO in if (b) return x; return y;?

Show answer

There are two different named objects that might be returned, so neither can be constructed in the caller's storage in advance. The return falls back to an implicit move.

Q3. What's the cost of Track t{name}; with a by-value sink constructor, where name is an lvalue string?

Show answer

One copy (into the parameter) plus one move (into the member).

docs.title: Lesson 5.5: Aggregates, designated initializers, structured bindings, user-defined literals
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Not every type needs constructors and private members. A lot of real code is just data: a config, a point, a parsed header. C++ has a lightweight path for those types — aggregates — and C++17/20 made them really pleasant to use: name the fields when creating them, unpack them by name when reading them. Let's look at the modern toolbox for "plain data".

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
An aggregate is (roughly) an array or a class with no user-declared constructors, no private/protected non-static data members, no virtual functions, and no virtual/private bases. You initialize it with braces listing the members in order:

struct Rgb { std::uint8_t r, g, b; };
Rgb red{255, 0, 0};

docs.title: Designated initializers (C++20)
docs.text:
Naming the members makes the call site self-documenting:

EncoderConfig cfg{.bitrate = 128'000, .vbr = true};   // others get their default member initializers

Rules (stricter than C): designators must appear in declaration order, and you can't mix designated and positional elements. C++20 also allows aggregate init with parentheses, Rgb red(255, 0, 0);, which helps generic code like std::make_unique<Rgb>(255, 0, 0).

docs.title: Structured bindings (C++17)
docs.text:
The reverse: unpack an aggregate, std::pair, std::tuple or array into named variables:

for (const auto& [name, rate] : rates) ...       // map iteration, finally readable
auto [it, inserted] = set.insert(42);

The names are aliases into a hidden object, so auto& binds them by reference to the original. Your own non-aggregate types can opt in by implementing the tuple protocol (std::tuple_size, std::tuple_element, get<I>) — shown in the example.

docs.title: User-defined literals (C++11)
docs.text:
You've used standard ones: "abc"s (string), "abc"sv, 100ms (chrono), 2.0i (complex). You can define your own with operator""_suffix; user suffixes must start with an underscore:

constexpr Hertz operator""_kHz(unsigned long long v) { return Hertz{v * 1000}; }
auto rate = 48_kHz;

They're great for units: 48_kHz can't be mixed up with 48.

examples/week05/lesson05.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>

struct EncoderConfig {
    std::string codec = "aac";
    int bitrate = 96'000;
    int channels = 2;
    bool vbr = false;
};

struct Hertz { unsigned long long value; };
constexpr Hertz operator""_kHz(unsigned long long v) { return Hertz{v * 1000}; }

class Span2 {                               // a non-aggregate that supports structured bindings
public:
    Span2(int b, int e) : b_{b}, e_{e} {}
    template <std::size_t I> int get() const { if constexpr (I == 0) return b_; else return e_; }
private:
    int b_, e_;
};
template <> struct std::tuple_size<Span2> : std::integral_constant<std::size_t, 2> {};
template <std::size_t I> struct std::tuple_element<I, Span2> { using type = int; };

int main() {
    EncoderConfig cfg{.bitrate = 128'000, .vbr = true};
    std::cout << cfg.codec << ' ' << cfg.bitrate << ' ' << cfg.channels << ' ' << cfg.vbr << '\n';

    struct Rgb { std::uint8_t r, g, b; };
    Rgb teal(0, 128, 128);                   // C++20 parenthesized aggregate init
