    auto [r, g, b] = teal;
    std::cout << int{r} << ',' << int{g} << ',' << int{b} << '\n';

    std::map<std::string, int> rates{{"cd", 44'100}, {"dvd", 48'000}};
    for (const auto& [name, rate] : rates) std::cout << name << '=' << rate << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    if (auto [it, inserted] = rates.insert({"cd", 1}); !inserted)
        std::cout << "already had " << it->first << '\n';

    auto [begin, end] = Span2{3, 9};
    std::cout << "span " << begin << ".." << end << '\n';

    using namespace std::chrono_literals;
    auto rate = 48_kHz;
    auto frame = 20ms;
    std::cout << rate.value << " Hz, " << frame.count() << " ms, samples/frame = "
              << rate.value * static_cast<unsigned long long>(frame.count()) / 1000 << '\n';
}

Output:

aac 128000 2 1
0,128,128
cd=44100 dvd=48000 
already had cd
span 3..9
48000 Hz, 20 ms, samples/frame = 960

Common pitfall: adding a constructor removes aggregate-ness

The moment you add any user-declared constructor (even = default since C++20), a struct stops being an aggregate and designated initializers stop compiling. Use default member initializers instead.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Aggregates are plain data types initialized member-wise with braces.
  • C++20 designated initializers name fields at the call site (in declaration order).
  • Structured bindings unpack pairs, tuples, arrays, aggregates — and your types via the tuple protocol.
  • User-defined literals (48_kHz) make units explicit.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Does struct P { int x, y; }; P p{.y = 1, .x = 2}; compile in C++20?

Show answer

No — designators must appear in declaration order (.x before .y).

Q2. In for (auto& [k, v] : m) over a std::map, can you modify k?

Show answer

No: map elements are std::pair<const Key, T>, so k refers to a const key. You can modify v.

Q3. Why must user-defined literal suffixes start with _?

Show answer

Suffixes without an underscore are reserved for the standard library (like s, ms, sv).

docs.title: Week 5 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 5.1) What does the implicitly generated copy constructor do?

Show answer

Copy-constructs each base and member in declaration order (memberwise copy).

Q2. (from 5.1) Why is copy-and-swap safe for self-assignment?

Show answer

The parameter is a full copy made before anything in *this changes, so swapping with it is fine even if the source was *this.

Q3. (from 5.2) Classify: v[0] (vector v), v.size(), std::move(v), "hello". Show answer

v[0] lvalue (returns int&); v.size() prvalue; std::move(v) xvalue; a string literal is an lvalue (an array object with static storage).

Q4. (from 5.2) Inside void f(Widget&& w), which overload does g(w) call: g(const Widget&) or g(Widget&&)?

Show answer

g(const Widget&). w is a named variable, hence an lvalue. To call the && overload write g(std::move(w)).

Q5. (from 5.3) What does std::move actually do?

Show answer

static_cast<T&&> — it converts its argument to an xvalue so move overloads can be selected. It performs no moving itself.

Q6. (from 5.3) Why might std::vector<T> copy elements during push_back even though T has a move constructor?

Show answer

If the move constructor isn't noexcept (and T is copyable), vector uses copies to keep the strong exception guarantee on reallocation (std::move_if_noexcept).

Q7. (from 5.4) Can a function return a non-copyable, non-movable type by value in C++17?

Show answer

Yes, if it returns a prvalue (return T{...};), thanks to guaranteed copy elision.

Q8. (from 5.4) Why can't the compiler apply NRVO in if (b) return x; return y;?

Show answer

There are two different named objects that might be returned, so neither can be constructed in the caller's storage in advance. The return falls back to an implicit move.

Q9. (from 5.5) Does struct P { int x, y; }; P p{.y = 1, .x = 2}; compile in C++20?

Show answer

No — designators must appear in declaration order (.x before .y).

Q10. (from 5.5) In for (auto& [k, v] : m) over a std::map, can you modify k?

Show answer

No: map elements are std::pair<const Key, T>, so k refers to a const key. You can modify v.

docs.title: Week 6: Inheritance and runtime polymorphism
docs.text:
This week covers classic object-oriented C++: base and derived classes, virtual functions, and how the compiler implements them with vtables. We'll also look at the traps — slicing, missing virtual destructors — and at multiple inheritance and RTTI.

A modern perspective runs through the week: inheritance is a tool for runtime polymorphism, not for code reuse. In Weeks 7–8 and 16 you'll see alternatives (templates, std::variant, type erasure) and learn when each fits.

# Lesson Standard Length 6.1 Inheritance basics: base classes, access, construction order C++20 10 min 6.2 Virtual functions, override, final, and how vtables work C++20 12 min 6.3 Abstract classes, interfaces, virtual destructors, and slicing C++20 11 min 6.4 Multiple and virtual inheritance (optional) C++20 9 min 6.5 RTTI: typeid, dynamic_cast, and std::any C++20 9 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 6 programming assignment: A plugin-style effect chain
docs.text:
Design an Effect interface (NVI: public non-virtual process(std::span<float>) that skips disabled effects; private virtual do_process). Implement Gain, Clip and Delay (a simple fixed delay line).

  1. Store effects in std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Effect>>.
  2. Support clone() so a chain can be duplicated.
  3. Process an impulse [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] through the chain and print the result.
  4. No dynamic_cast allowed.
Reference solution examples/week06/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

class Effect {
public:
    virtual ~Effect() = default;
    void process(std::span<float> buf) { if (enabled_) do_process(buf); }
    void set_enabled(bool e) { enabled_ = e; }
    virtual std::unique_ptr<Effect> clone() const = 0;
protected:
    Effect() = default;
    Effect(const Effect&) = default;            // usable by clone() in derived classes only
    Effect& operator=(const Effect&) = delete;
private:
    virtual void do_process(std::span<float> buf) = 0;
    bool enabled_ = true;
};

class Gain final : public Effect {
public:
    explicit Gain(float g) : g_{g} {}
    std::unique_ptr<Effect> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Gain>(*this); }
private:
    void do_process(std::span<float> b) override { for (auto& x : b) x *= g_; }
    float g_;
};

class Clip final : public Effect {
public:
    std::unique_ptr<Effect> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Clip>(*this); }
private:
    void do_process(std::span<float> b) override { for (auto& x : b) x = x > 1 ? 1 : (x < -1 ? -1 : x); }
};

class Delay final : public Effect {
public:
    Delay(std::size_t samples, float mix) : line_(samples), mix_{mix} {}
    std::unique_ptr<Effect> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Delay>(*this); }
private:
    void do_process(std::span<float> b) override {
        for (auto& x : b) {
            const float delayed = line_[pos_];
            line_[pos_] = x;
            pos_ = (pos_ + 1) % line_.size();
            x += mix_ * delayed;
        }
    }
    std::vector<float> line_;
    std::size_t pos_ = 0;
    float mix_;
};

using Chain = std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Effect>>;

Chain clone_chain(const Chain& c) {
    Chain out;
    for (const auto& e : c) out.push_back(e->clone());
    return out;
}

void run(Chain& chain, const char* label) {
    std::vector<float> buf{1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0};
    for (auto& e : chain) e->process(buf);
    std::cout << label << ": ";
    for (float x : buf) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}

int main() {
    Chain chain;
    chain.push_back(std::make_unique<Gain>(3.0f));
    chain.push_back(std::make_unique<Delay>(2, 0.5f));
    chain.push_back(std::make_unique<Clip>());
    Chain copy = clone_chain(chain);
    run(chain, "original");
    copy[2]->set_enabled(false);
    run(copy, "copy, clip off");
}

Output:

original: 1 0 1 0 0 0 
copy, clip off: 3 0 1.5 0 0 0

docs.title: Lesson 6.1: Inheritance basics: base classes, access, construction order
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Suppose every audio effect in your app — gain, echo, low-pass filter — has a name, an enabled flag and a bypass switch. Writing those three things in every class is tedious and error-prone. Inheritance lets a derived class be a kind of base class and get its members. Let's see the mechanics first; next lesson we'll add the real superpower, virtual functions.

docs.title: Is-a relationships
docs.text:
class Effect { ... };                 // base class
class Gain : public Effect { ... };   // Gain *is an* Effect

With public inheritance, a Gain can be used wherever an Effect& or Effect* is expected. That's the only kind of inheritance you'll use regularly. (private inheritance means "implemented in terms of" and is rare; prefer a member.)

Base member is... accessible in derived? accessible to users of derived (public inheritance)? public yes yes protected yes no private no no

docs.title: Construction order
docs.text:
A derived object contains a base subobject. Construction goes base first, then members (in declaration order), then the derived constructor body. Destruction runs in exactly the reverse order. You call a base constructor from the member initializer list. If the derived class adds no state of its own, using Base::Base; (C++11) inherits the base constructors.

examples/week06/lesson01.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Tracer {
    std::string name;
    explicit Tracer(std::string n) : name{std::move(n)} { std::cout << "  + " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Tracer() { std::cout << "  - " << name << '\n'; }
};

class Effect {
public:
    explicit Effect(std::string name) : name_{std::move(name)}, t_{"Effect base"} {}
    const std::string& name() const { return name_; }
    bool enabled() const { return enabled_; }
    void set_enabled(bool e) { enabled_ = e; }
    void process(int n) { std::cout << "  Effect::process(int " << n << ")\n"; }
    void process(double x) { std::cout << "  Effect::process(double " << x << ")\n"; }
protected:
    int processed_ = 0;                 // visible to derived classes only
private:
    std::string name_;
    bool enabled_ = true;
    Tracer t_;
};

class Gain : public Effect {
public:
    Gain(float g) : Effect{"gain"}, t_{"Gain member"}, gain_{g} { std::cout << "  Gain body\n"; }
    using Effect::process;              // un-hide the base overloads
    void process(float x) { ++processed_; std::cout << "  Gain::process(float " << x * gain_ << ")\n"; }
private:
    Tracer t_;
    float gain_;
};

class Mute : public Effect {
public:
    using Effect::Effect;               // inherit constructors
};

int main() {
    std::cout << "construct:\n";
    {
        Gain g{2.0f};
        g.process(1.5f);
        g.process(7);                   // Effect::process(int), thanks to `using`
        Mute m{"mute"};
        std::cout << "  " << g.name() << ' ' << m.name() << '\n';
        std::cout << "destroy:\n";
    }
}

Output:

construct:
  + Effect base
  + Gain member
  Gain body
  Gain::process(float 3)
  Effect::process(int 7)
  + Effect base
  gain mute
destroy:
  - Effect base
  - Gain member
  - Effect base

docs.title: The wrong way: name hiding
docs.text:
struct Base    { void process(int); void process(double); };
struct Derived : Base { void process(int); };   // hides BOTH Base::process overloads
Derived d; d.process(2.5);                     // calls Derived::process(int) with 2 — surprise!

Declaring any process in Derived hides all of the base's process overloads. Bring them back with using Base::process; in Derived.

Pro tip: prefer composition

"Has-a" is usually a member; "is-a" is inheritance. If you inherit only to reuse code, a member object is almost always simpler and more flexible.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Public inheritance models is-a; a derived object contains a base subobject.
  • Construction: bases, then members in declaration order, then the body; destruction is the reverse.
  • A member function in a derived class hides all base overloads with that name; using Base::f; restores them.
  • Prefer composition for code reuse.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. In what order are these constructed: base B, members m1, m2 of derived D, and D's constructor body?

Show answer

B, then m1, then m2 (declaration order), then the body of D's constructor.

Q2. What does using Base::Base; do?

Show answer

Inherits Base's constructors into the derived class (C++11).

Q3. Why might d.process(2.5) call Derived::process(int)?

Show answer

Because Derived declares process, which hides all Base::process overloads; the only candidate takes int and 2.5 converts to it.

docs.title: Lesson 6.2: Virtual functions, override, final, and how vtables work
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Now the payoff. You have a std::vector<Effect*> holding a gain, an echo and a filter, and you want for (auto* e : chain) e->process(buffer); to call the right process for each one. That's dynamic dispatch, and it's what virtual gives you. Let's also peek under the hood, because knowing how it works tells you exactly what it costs.

docs.title: virtual and override
docs.text:
struct Effect {
    virtual ~Effect() = default;
    virtual void process(std::span<float> buf) = 0;   // (= 0: pure virtual; next lesson)
};
struct Gain : Effect {
    void process(std::span<float> buf) override { ... }
};

When a function is virtual, a call through a base reference or pointer runs the most-derived override at run time. Always write override on overrides: if the signature doesn't actually match (a missing const, a different parameter type), the compiler errors instead of silently creating a new, unrelated function.

struct Base { virtual void draw() const; };
struct Oops : Base { void draw(); };            // WRONG: no const -> a new function, not an override
struct Good : Base { void draw() const override; };

final on a function stops further overriding; on a class, stops inheritance. It also helps the optimizer devirtualize calls.

examples/week06/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Effect {
public:
    Effect() { std::cout << "Effect ctor sees name(): " << name() << '\n'; }   // calls Effect::name!
    virtual ~Effect() = default;
    virtual void process(std::span<float> buf) = 0;
    virtual std::string name() const { return "effect"; }
};

class Gain final : public Effect {
public:
    explicit Gain(float g) : g_{g} {}
    void process(std::span<float> buf) override { for (auto& x : buf) x *= g_; }
    std::string name() const override { return "gain"; }
private:
    float g_;
};

class Clip : public Effect {
public:
    void process(std::span<float> buf) override {
        for (auto& x : buf) x = x > 1.0f ? 1.0f : (x < -1.0f ? -1.0f : x);
    }
    std::string name() const override { return "clip"; }
};

struct NoVirtual { float g; };
struct WithVirtual { virtual ~WithVirtual() = default; float g; };

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Effect>> chain;
    chain.push_back(std::make_unique<Gain>(3.0f));
    chain.push_back(std::make_unique<Clip>());

    std::vector<float> buf{0.1f, 0.5f, -0.6f};
    for (const auto& e : chain) {          // dynamic dispatch
        e->process(buf);
        std::cout << e->name() << ": ";
        for (float x : buf) std::cout << x << ' ';
        std::cout << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "sizeof(NoVirtual)=" << sizeof(NoVirtual) << " sizeof(WithVirtual)=" << sizeof(WithVirtual) << '\n';
}

Output:

Effect ctor sees name(): effect
Effect ctor sees name(): effect
gain: 0.3 1.5 -1.8 
clip: 0.3 1 -1 
sizeof(NoVirtual)=4 sizeof(WithVirtual)=16

docs.title: How it works: vtables
docs.text:
The standard doesn't say, but every mainstream compiler does the same thing:

  • Each class with virtual functions has a static table, the vtable, holding pointers to its versions of each virtual function.
  • Each object of such a class holds a hidden pointer, the vptr, to its class's vtable (that's why sizeof grew by 8 in the output).
  • A virtual call is: load the vptr, load the function pointer from a fixed slot, call it.
flowchart LR
  O[Gain object: vptr + gain_] --> V[Gain vtable: ~Gain, process, name]
  V --> F1[Gain::process]
  V --> F2[Effect::name]

So the cost is one or two extra loads and an indirect call, plus — more importantly — the call usually can't be inlined. In a per-sample inner loop that matters; per buffer, it's noise. Design accordingly: make virtual calls coarse-grained (process a whole buffer, not one sample).

docs.title: Virtual calls in constructors and destructors
docs.text: During Effect's constructor, the object is only an Effect yet — the derived part doesn't exist. A virtual call there calls Effect's version, not the derived one. The example shows this.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • virtual + a base pointer/reference = the most-derived override runs at run time.
  • Always mark overrides override; use final to forbid further overriding.
  • Vtable model: one table per class, one hidden vptr per object; virtual calls block inlining.
  • In constructors and destructors, virtual calls resolve to the current class, not the derived one.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does override buy you?

Show answer

A compile error if the function doesn't actually override a base virtual function (e.g. signature mismatch), instead of a silent new function.

Q2. Why did sizeof(WithVirtual) grow?

Show answer

Objects of a polymorphic class carry a hidden vptr (8 bytes on 64-bit), plus padding for alignment.

Q3. What's the main performance cost of a virtual call?

Show answer

Usually not the indirect call itself but the lost inlining and optimization across the call; also possible branch mispredictions. Keep virtual calls coarse-grained.

docs.title: Lesson 6.3: Abstract classes, interfaces, virtual destructors, and slicing
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Two bugs show up in almost every codebase that uses inheritance. First: deleting a derived object through a base pointer, and the derived destructor never runs — a leak. Second: copying a derived object into a base value, and losing everything that made it derived. Both are easy to prevent once you've seen them. Let's see them.

docs.title: Abstract classes and interfaces
docs.text:
A pure virtual function (= 0) has no implementation in the base; a class with one is abstract and can't be instantiated. A class with only pure virtual functions (and a virtual destructor) is C++'s version of an interface:

class AudioSink {
public:
    virtual ~AudioSink() = default;
    virtual void write(std::span<const float>) = 0;
};

docs.title: Bug 1: no virtual destructor
docs.text:
struct Base { ~Base() {} };                        // not virtual
struct Derived : Base { std::vector<int> big; };
Base* p = new Derived;
delete p;     // UB: only ~Base runs; Derived's members are never destroyed

Rule: a base class meant for polymorphic deletion needs a public virtual destructor. (If instead you never delete through the base, make the base destructor protected and non-virtual — that prevents the mistake at compile time.) std::unique_ptr<Base> relies on this too.

docs.title: Bug 2: slicing
docs.text:
void log(Effect e);   // by value!
Gain g{2.0f};
log(g);               // copies only the Effect part: g is "sliced"; virtual calls see an Effect

Pass polymorphic objects by reference or pointer, never by value. To prevent slicing by accident, delete the copy operations of polymorphic bases. If you need to copy a polymorphic object, add a virtual clone():

examples/week06/lesson03.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class AudioSink {                               // interface + NVI
public:
    virtual ~AudioSink() = default;
    AudioSink(const AudioSink&) = delete;       // prevent slicing copies
    AudioSink& operator=(const AudioSink&) = delete;

    void write(std::span<const float> buf) {     // non-virtual: common checks
        if (buf.empty()) return;
        ++writes_;
        do_write(buf);                           // customization point
    }
    int writes() const { return writes_; }
    virtual std::unique_ptr<AudioSink> clone() const = 0;   // polymorphic copy

protected:
    AudioSink() = default;
private:
    virtual void do_write(std::span<const float> buf) = 0;
    int writes_ = 0;
};

class ConsoleSink final : public AudioSink {
public:
    explicit ConsoleSink(std::string tag) : tag_{std::move(tag)} {}
    std::unique_ptr<AudioSink> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<ConsoleSink>(tag_ + "'"); }
private:
    void do_write(std::span<const float> buf) override {
        std::cout << tag_ << " got " << buf.size() << " samples\n";
    }
    std::string tag_;
};

class Probe {
public:
    virtual ~Probe() { std::cout << "~Probe\n"; }
};
class BigProbe : public Probe {
public:
    ~BigProbe() override { std::cout << "~BigProbe (members freed)\n"; }
    std::vector<int> data = std::vector<int>(1000);
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<AudioSink> sink = std::make_unique<ConsoleSink>("speaker");
    const std::vector<float> buf(256);
    sink->write(buf);
    sink->write({});                             // ignored by the NVI wrapper
    auto copy = sink->clone();
    copy->write(buf);
    std::cout << "writes: " << sink->writes() << ' ' << copy->writes() << '\n';

    std::unique_ptr<Probe> p = std::make_unique<BigProbe>();
    p.reset();                                   // virtual dtor: both destructors run
}

Output:

speaker got 256 samples
speaker' got 256 samples
writes: 1 1
~BigProbe (members freed)
~Probe

docs.title: The NVI idiom (non-virtual interface)
docs.text:
A useful design: the public function is non-virtual and does the common work (checks, logging, locking), then calls a private virtual hook. Derived classes customize the hook but can't skip the checks. The example's write() does this.

Pro tip

Enable -Wnon-virtual-dtor and -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor (the latter is in -Wall). clang-tidy's cppcoreguidelines-slicing check catches slicing.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A pure virtual function makes a class abstract; pure-virtual-only classes are interfaces.
  • Polymorphic bases need a public virtual destructor (or a protected non-virtual one).
  • Passing a derived object by value as a base slices it; pass by reference/pointer and delete base copies.
  • Use clone() for polymorphic copies and NVI to keep checks in non-virtual public functions.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What happens with Base* p = new Derived; delete p; if ~Base isn't virtual?

Show answer

Undefined behaviour; in practice only ~Base runs and the Derived part (its members) is never destroyed.

Q2. What is slicing?

Show answer

Copying a derived object into a base-class object, which copies only the base subobject; the derived data and overrides are lost.

Q3. Why make a polymorphic base's copy constructor deleted?

Show answer

To make accidental slicing copies (pass-by-value, assignment to a base object) compile errors.

docs.title: Lesson 6.4: Multiple and virtual inheritance (optional)
docs.text: C++20 · about 9 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Can a class inherit from two base classes? In C++, yes. It's mostly useful for implementing several interfaces at once — a MediaPlayer that is both an AudioSink and a Controllable, say. This lesson is marked optional: you'll rarely write complex multiple inheritance, but you'll meet it in frameworks and you should understand the diamond problem when you see it.

docs.title: Implementing several interfaces
docs.text: This is the safe, common use: each base is an interface (no data), and the class implements all of them.

docs.title: The diamond
docs.text:
If B and C both inherit from A, and D inherits from both B and C, then by default D contains two A subobjects. d.a_member is ambiguous, and converting D* to A* is ambiguous.

flowchart BT
  B --> A
  C --> A
  D --> B
  D --> C

Virtual inheritance (class B : public virtual A) makes B and C share a single A subobject. The price: the most-derived class must construct the virtual base directly, layout is more complex, and access to the virtual base goes through an extra indirection.

examples/week06/lesson04.cpp
#include <iostream>

struct AudioSink { virtual ~AudioSink() = default; virtual void write(int n) = 0; };
struct Controllable { virtual ~Controllable() = default; virtual void pause() = 0; };

class Player : public AudioSink, public Controllable {      // implements two interfaces
public:
    void write(int n) override { std::cout << "write " << n << '\n'; }
    void pause() override { std::cout << "paused\n"; }
};

struct Device { int id = 0; explicit Device(int i) : id{i} {} };
struct Input : virtual Device { Input() : Device{1} {} };
struct Output : virtual Device { Output() : Device{2} {} };
struct Duplex : Input, Output { Duplex() : Device{42} {} };   // most-derived constructs the virtual base

int main() {
    Player p;
    AudioSink* s = &p;
    Controllable* c = &p;
    s->write(128);
    c->pause();
    std::cout << "pointer adjusted? " << std::boolalpha
              << (static_cast<void*>(s) != static_cast<void*>(c)) << '\n';

    Duplex d;
    std::cout << "one shared Device, id=" << d.id << '\n';   // unambiguous thanks to virtual inheritance
}

Output:

write 128
paused
pointer adjusted? true
one shared Device, id=42

docs.title: Pointer adjustment
docs.text:
With multiple bases, converting Player* to Controllable* may change the pointer value: the Controllable subobject lives at an offset inside the Player. That's normal and handled by the compiler — but it's why you must never cast between such pointers with reinterpret_cast or through void* without going back to the exact original type.

Practical advice

Multiple inheritance of interfaces: fine. Multiple inheritance of classes with state: think twice. Virtual inheritance: only when you truly need the shared-base semantics (e.g. std::iostream inherits virtually from std::ios_base via basic_ios).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Multiple inheritance of interfaces is common and safe.
  • A diamond without virtual inheritance duplicates the shared base; virtual inheritance shares it.
  • The most-derived class initializes virtual bases.
  • Converting between base pointers may adjust the address — use static_cast/dynamic_cast, never reinterpret_cast.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. In a non-virtual diamond, how many A subobjects does D have?

Show answer

Two — one via B and one via C.

Q2. With virtual inheritance, who calls the virtual base's constructor?

Show answer

The most-derived class. Initializers for the virtual base in intermediate classes are ignored when they aren't the most-derived.

Q3. Why can static_cast<void*>(s) != static_cast<void*>(c) be true for the same object?

Show answer

The two base subobjects live at different offsets within the derived object.

docs.title: Lesson 6.5: RTTI: typeid, dynamic_cast, and std::any
docs.text: C++20 · about 9 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Sometimes you hold an Effect* and need to know: "is this actually a Reverb?" C++ can answer at run time with RTTI (run-time type information). It's useful, it's occasionally a design smell, and on embedded and some Android builds it's turned off entirely. Let's see the tools and their trade-offs.

docs.title: dynamic_cast
docs.text: dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base_ptr) returns a valid pointer if the object really is a Derived (or derived from it), and nullptr otherwise. With references, failure throws std::bad_cast. It only works on polymorphic types (at least one virtual function).

docs.title: typeid
docs.text: typeid(expr) returns a const std::type_info& describing the dynamic type for polymorphic glvalues. type_info::name() is implementation-defined (GCC/Clang return a mangled name like 6Reverb), so use it for debugging, not for logic. To use types as map keys, wrap them in std::type_index.

docs.title: std::any (C++17)
docs.text:
std::any holds a value of any copyable type and remembers which one; std::any_cast<T> gets it back (throwing std::bad_any_cast on mismatch). It's handy for property bags and plugin metadata, but you lose compile-time type checking — prefer std::variant (Week 9) when the set of types is known.

examples/week06/lesson05.cpp
#include <any>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <typeindex>
#include <typeinfo>
#include <vector>

struct Effect { virtual ~Effect() = default; };
struct Gain : Effect { float g = 1.0f; };
struct Reverb : Effect { float room = 0.5f; };

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Effect>> fx;
    fx.push_back(std::make_unique<Gain>());
    fx.push_back(std::make_unique<Reverb>());

    std::map<std::type_index, std::string> names{{typeid(Gain), "Gain"}, {typeid(Reverb), "Reverb"}};
    for (const auto& e : fx) {
        const Effect& ref = *e;
        std::cout << "dynamic type: " << names[typeid(ref)];
        if (auto* r = dynamic_cast<Reverb*>(e.get())) std::cout << " (room=" << r->room << ')';
        std::cout << '\n';
    }

    try {
        Effect& first = *fx[0];
        auto& r = dynamic_cast<Reverb&>(first);   // it's a Gain: throws
        (void)r;
    } catch (const std::bad_cast&) {
        std::cout << "bad_cast: first effect is not a Reverb\n";
    }

    std::map<std::string, std::any> props{{"rate", 48000}, {"codec", std::string{"opus"}}, {"vbr", true}};
    std::cout << "rate=" << std::any_cast<int>(props["rate"])
              << " codec=" << std::any_cast<std::string>(props["codec"]) << '\n';
    try {
        std::cout << std::any_cast<double>(props["rate"]);
    } catch (const std::bad_any_cast&) {
        std::cout << "bad_any_cast: rate holds an int, not a double\n";
    }
}

Output:

dynamic type: Gain
dynamic type: Reverb (room=0.5)
bad_cast: first effect is not a Reverb
rate=48000 codec=opus
bad_any_cast: rate holds an int, not a double

docs.title: The design smell
docs.text:
if (auto* r = dynamic_cast<Reverb*>(e)) r->set_room(0.8f);
else if (auto* g = dynamic_cast<Gain*>(e)) g->set_gain(2.0f);
// ... a growing chain of casts

A chain of dynamic_casts usually means a virtual function is missing (e->apply_preset(p)), or that the set of types is closed and a std::variant + std::visit would be clearer and faster.

docs.title: No RTTI builds
docs.text: Many embedded and game builds compile with -fno-rtti (and the Android NDK historically defaulted to it; modern NDK CMake toolchains enable RTTI and exceptions by default). Without RTTI, dynamic_cast on polymorphic types and typeid don't compile, and std::any is unavailable with some libraries. Design libraries so the core doesn't require RTTI.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • dynamic_cast checks the dynamic type: null pointer or std::bad_cast on failure.
  • typeid(...).name() is implementation-defined; use std::type_index as a map key.
  • std::any stores any copyable value with runtime type checks; prefer std::variant for closed sets.
  • Chains of dynamic_cast are a design smell; some builds disable RTTI entirely.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does dynamic_cast<D*>(p) return if *p isn't a D?

Show answer

nullptr. (The reference form throws std::bad_cast.)

Q2. Why shouldn't program logic depend on typeid(x).name()?

Show answer

Its contents are implementation-defined (and often mangled); they differ between compilers.

Q3. When is std::variant a better choice than std::any?

Show answer

When the set of possible types is known at compile time: variant is type-checked, needs no heap allocation, and supports exhaustive std::visit.

docs.title: Week 6 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 6.1) In what order are these constructed: base B, members m1, m2 of derived D, and D's constructor body?

Show answer

B, then m1, then m2 (declaration order), then the body of D's constructor.

Q2. (from 6.1) What does using Base::Base; do?

Show answer

Inherits Base's constructors into the derived class (C++11).

Q3. (from 6.2) What does override buy you?

Show answer

A compile error if the function doesn't actually override a base virtual function (e.g. signature mismatch), instead of a silent new function.

Q4. (from 6.2) Why did sizeof(WithVirtual) grow?

Show answer

Objects of a polymorphic class carry a hidden vptr (8 bytes on 64-bit), plus padding for alignment.

Q5. (from 6.3) What happens with Base* p = new Derived; delete p; if ~Base isn't virtual?

Show answer

Undefined behaviour; in practice only ~Base runs and the Derived part (its members) is never destroyed.

Q6. (from 6.3) What is slicing?

Show answer

Copying a derived object into a base-class object, which copies only the base subobject; the derived data and overrides are lost.

Q7. (from 6.4) In a non-virtual diamond, how many A subobjects does D have?

Show answer

Two — one via B and one via C.

Q8. (from 6.4) With virtual inheritance, who calls the virtual base's constructor?

Show answer

The most-derived class. Initializers for the virtual base in intermediate classes are ignored when they aren't the most-derived.

Q9. (from 6.5) What does dynamic_cast<D*>(p) return if *p isn't a D?

Show answer

nullptr. (The reference form throws std::bad_cast.)

Q10. (from 6.5) Why shouldn't program logic depend on typeid(x).name()?

Show answer

Its contents are implementation-defined (and often mangled); they differ between compilers.

docs.title: Week 7: Templates: generic programming
docs.text:
Templates are how C++ writes code once and uses it for many types — without the runtime cost of virtual calls. The whole standard library is built on them. This week goes from function templates to type traits; next week adds concepts and compile-time programming on top.

Honest warning: templates have the worst error messages in the language. We'll show you how to read them, and Week 8's concepts make them dramatically better.

# Lesson Standard Length 7.1 Function templates and argument deduction C++20 11 min 7.2 Class templates, specialization, and CTAD C++20 12 min 7.3 Non-type parameters, variadic templates, and fold expressions C++20 11 min 7.4 Forwarding references and perfect forwarding C++20 10 min 7.5 Type traits, if constexpr, and SFINAE C++20 12 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 7 programming assignment: A generic binary serializer
docs.text:
Write template <typename... Ts> std::vector<std::uint8_t> pack(const Ts&... values) that serializes every argument in order: integers big-endian, bool as one byte, floating-point via std::bit_cast, std::string as a 16-bit length then bytes. Also write std::string hex(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>&).

Unsupported types must be a compile-time error with a readable message.

Starter code examples/week07/assignment_starter.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename... Ts>
std::vector<std::uint8_t> pack(const Ts&... values) {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> out;
    // TODO: fold over values, encoding each
    return out;
}

int main() { return static_cast<int>(pack(1, 2).size()); }
Reference solution examples/week07/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
void put(std::vector<std::uint8_t>& out, const T& v) {
    using U = std::remove_cvref_t<T>;
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<U, bool>) out.push_back(v ? 1 : 0);
    else if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<U>) {
        using UU = std::make_unsigned_t<U>;
        const auto u = static_cast<UU>(v);
        for (int i = sizeof(U) - 1; i >= 0; --i) out.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t>(u >> (8 * i)));
    } else if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<U>) {
        using Bits = std::conditional_t<sizeof(U) == 4, std::uint32_t, std::uint64_t>;
        put(out, std::bit_cast<Bits>(v));
    } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<U, std::string>) {
        put(out, static_cast<std::uint16_t>(v.size()));
        out.insert(out.end(), v.begin(), v.end());
    } else {
        static_assert(sizeof(U) == 0, "pack: unsupported type");
    }
}

template <typename... Ts>
std::vector<std::uint8_t> pack(const Ts&... values) {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> out;
    (put(out, values), ...);
    return out;
}

std::string hex(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& bytes) {
    std::string s;
    char buf[4];
    for (auto b : bytes) { std::snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%02x ", b); s += buf; }
    return s;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << hex(pack(std::int16_t{-2}, true, std::string{"ok"}, 1.5f)) << '\n';
    std::cout << hex(pack()) << "(empty)\n";
}

Output:

ff fe 01 00 02 6f 6b 3f c0 00 00 
(empty)

docs.title: Lesson 7.1: Function templates and argument deduction
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: You've written clamp for int. Now you need it for float, double, and std::chrono::milliseconds. Copy-pasting four versions is how bugs multiply. A function template is a recipe: the compiler stamps out a real function for each type you use — and each one is as fast as if you'd written it by hand.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
template <typename T>
T clamp_to(T v, T lo, T hi) { return v < lo ? lo : (hi < v ? hi : v); }

clamp_to(15, 0, 10);        // T deduced as int
clamp_to(0.7, 0.0, 1.0);    // T deduced as double

The compiler deduces T from the arguments, then instantiates clamp_to<int> — real machine code, no runtime dispatch.

docs.title: The wrong way: conflicting deductions
docs.text:
clamp_to(0.7, 0, 1);   // error: T deduced as double AND int

Deduction doesn't do conversions. Fix it by making the arguments agree (0.0, 1.0), or by specifying T explicitly: clamp_to<double>(0.7, 0, 1).

examples/week07/lesson01.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
T clamp_to(T v, T lo, T hi) { return v < lo ? lo : (hi < v ? hi : v); }

template <typename T>
typename T::value_type sum(const T& c) {          // `typename`: dependent type name
    typename T::value_type total{};
    for (const auto& x : c) total += x;
    return total;
}

void print_all(const auto& c) {                   // abbreviated function template (C++20)
    for (const auto& x : c) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono_literals;
    std::cout << clamp_to(15, 0, 10) << '\n';
    std::cout << clamp_to(0.7, 0.0, 1.0) << '\n';
    std::cout << clamp_to<double>(1.7, 0, 1) << '\n';           // explicit T
    std::cout << clamp_to(250ms, 0ms, 100ms).count() << "ms\n";  // works for any type with <
    std::cout << clamp_to(std::string{"m"}, std::string{"a"}, std::string{"k"}) << '\n';

    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3, 4};
    std::cout << sum(v) << '\n';
    print_all(v);
    print_all(std::vector<std::string>{"templates", "are", "recipes"});
}

Output:

10
0.7
1
100ms
k
10
1 2 3 4 
templates are recipes

docs.title: Abbreviated templates (C++20)
docs.text:
auto in a parameter list makes a function a template:

void print_all(const auto& container);   // same as template <typename C> void print_all(const C&)

docs.title: Templates live in headers
docs.text: A template isn't code until it's instantiated, and the compiler needs the definition to instantiate it. So templates normally go entirely in headers. (Explicit instantiation and modules — Week 15 — are the exceptions.)

docs.title: typename for dependent names
docs.text:
Inside a template, T::value_type could be a type or a static member; the compiler assumes value unless you say typename T::value_type. Since C++20 many contexts no longer need it, but you'll see it everywhere.

Reading template errors

Scroll to the first error, then find the line in your code ("required from here"). The library internals in the middle are rarely the problem.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A function template is a recipe; each set of deduced types instantiates a real function.
  • Deduction requires arguments to agree; no implicit conversions during deduction.
  • auto parameters (C++20) create abbreviated templates.
  • Template definitions usually live in headers; read errors from the first one, looking for your code.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why does clamp_to(0.7, 0, 1) fail?

Show answer

T is deduced as double from the first argument and int from the others; deduction fails because they conflict.

Q2. Do templates have a runtime cost compared to hand-written overloads?

Show answer

No — instantiations are ordinary functions. The costs are compile time and code size.

Q3. Why are templates usually defined in headers?

Show answer

The compiler needs the full definition at the point of instantiation in each translation unit.

docs.title: Lesson 7.2: Class templates, specialization, and CTAD
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: std::vector<int> and std::vector<std::string> are two different classes generated from one template. In this lesson we'll write our own small class template — a fixed-size statistics window for sensor readings — and learn how to customize it for particular types.

docs.title: A class template
docs.text:
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Window { std::array<T, N> data_{}; ... };

Window<float, 4> w;     // a class generated for (float, 4)

Member functions are only instantiated if they're used — so a Window<std::string, 3> compiles fine as long as you don't call mean() on it.

docs.title: Specialization
docs.text:
• Full specialization gives a completely different implementation for one exact set of arguments: template <> struct TypeName<int> { ... };
  • Partial specialization (classes only, not functions) customizes for a pattern: template <typename T> struct TypeName<T*> { ... };

The standard library uses this everywhere (e.g. std::hash<T> specializations, std::vector<bool>, which is a famous cautionary tale: it packs bits and so its operator[] doesn't return a real bool&).

docs.title: CTAD (C++17)
docs.text:
std::pair p{1, 2.5};       // pair<int, double> — no need to spell out the arguments
std::vector v{1, 2, 3};    // vector<int>

The compiler deduces class template arguments from constructor arguments. When that doesn't work the way you want, a deduction guide tells it how.

examples/week07/lesson02.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Window {                                    // fixed-size rolling window
public:
    void push(T v) { data_[next_ % N] = v; ++next_; }
    std::size_t size() const { return next_ < N ? next_ : N; }
    T mean() const {                              // only instantiated if used
        T total{};
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size(); ++i) total += data_[i];
        return total / static_cast<T>(size());
    }
private:
    std::array<T, N> data_{};
    std::size_t next_ = 0;
};

template <typename T> struct TypeName { static std::string get() { return "unknown"; } };
template <> struct TypeName<int> { static std::string get() { return "int"; } };          // full
template <> struct TypeName<float> { static std::string get() { return "float"; } };
template <typename T> struct TypeName<T*> {                                              // partial
    static std::string get() { return "pointer to " + TypeName<T>::get(); }
};

template <typename T>
struct Tagged {
    T value;
    std::string tag;
};
Tagged(const char*, const char*) -> Tagged<std::string>;   // deduction guide

template <typename T> constexpr T pi = T(3.14159265358979323846L);   // variable template
template <typename T> using Grid = std::vector<std::vector<T>>;      // alias template

int main() {
    Window<float, 4> w;
    for (float x : {1.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f, 4.0f, 10.0f}) w.push(x);
    std::cout << "mean of last 4: " << w.mean() << '\n';

    Window<std::string, 2> names;                 // fine: mean() never instantiated
    names.push("a");
    std::cout << "names.size()=" << names.size() << '\n';

    std::cout << TypeName<int>::get() << ", " << TypeName<float**>::get() << ", "
              << TypeName<double>::get() << '\n';

    std::pair p{1, 2.5};                          // CTAD: pair<int, double>
    Tagged t{"hello", "greeting"};                // guide: Tagged<std::string>
    std::cout << p.second << ' ' << t.value.size() << '\n';
    std::cout << pi<float> << ' ' << pi<double> << '\n';
    Grid<int> g(2, std::vector<int>(3, 7));
    std::cout << g.size() << 'x' << g[0].size() << '\n';
}

Output:

mean of last 4: 4.75
names.size()=1
int, pointer to pointer to float, unknown
2.5 5
3.14159 3.14159
2x3

docs.title: Alias and variable templates
docs.text:
template <typename T> using Buffer = std::vector<T, MyAllocator<T>>;
template <typename T> constexpr T pi = T(3.14159265358979323846L);

Pitfall: CTAD with braces and copies

std::vector v{std::vector{1,2}}; is vector<int> (copy), not vector<vector<int>>. CTAD prefers the copy deduction candidate. When in doubt, spell out the type.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Class templates generate a class per argument set; unused members aren't instantiated.
  • Full specialization replaces the template for exact arguments; partial specialization matches patterns (classes only).
  • CTAD deduces class template arguments from constructors; deduction guides steer it.
  • Alias templates and variable templates shorten generic code.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why does Window<std::string, 2> compile even though mean() divides by static_cast<std::string>(size())?

Show answer

Member functions of class templates are only instantiated when used; mean() is never called.

Q2. Can you partially specialize a function template?

Show answer

No. Only class (and variable) templates can be partially specialized; for functions use overloading or if constexpr.

Q3. What type does std::pair p{1, 2.5}; have?

Show answer

std::pair<int, double>, via CTAD.

docs.title: Lesson 7.3: Non-type parameters, variadic templates, and fold expressions
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: How does std::make_unique accept any number of constructor arguments? How does std::format take any number of values? The answer is variadic templates — templates that take packs of types. Combined with fold expressions, they let you write "do this for every argument" in a single line.

docs.title: Non-type template parameters
docs.text: Template parameters can be values, not just types: std::array<int, 8> takes the size 8. Allowed: integers, enums, pointers, auto (C++17), and since C++20 floating-point and structural class types (all public, non-mutable members) — so you can even pass a small string literal wrapper.

docs.title: Parameter packs
docs.text:
template <typename... Args>          // a pack of types
void log(const Args&... args);       // a pack of function parameters
sizeof...(Args)                      // how many

docs.title: Fold expressions (C++17)
docs.text:
Fold over a binary operator:

Fold Expands to (args + ...) a1 + (a2 + (a3)) (... + args) ((a1) + a2) + a3 (init + ... + args) with an initial value — safe for empty packs ((std::cout << args), ...) comma fold: "do this for each" examples/week07/lesson03.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <std::size_t N>
struct Fixed { std::array<char, N> buf{}; };

template <auto Value>                                  // auto NTTP
constexpr auto twice = Value * 2;

template <std::size_t N>
struct Name {                                          // structural type usable as an NTTP (C++20)
    char chars[N]{};
    constexpr Name(const char (&s)[N]) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) chars[i] = s[i]; }
};
template <Name N>
void hello() { std::cout << "hello from " << N.chars << '\n'; }

template <typename... Args>
auto sum(const Args&... args) { return (0 + ... + args); }       // binary left fold, safe if empty

template <typename... Args>
void log(const Args&... args) {
    std::cout << '[' << sizeof...(Args) << " args] ";
    ((std::cout << args << ' '), ...);                              // comma fold
    std::cout << '\n';
}

template <typename T, typename... Args>
bool all_equal(const T& first, const Args&... rest) { return ((first == rest) && ...); }

template <template <typename...> class Container>                 // template template parameter
Container<int> make_ints() { return Container<int>{1, 2, 3}; }

int main() {
    std::cout << sizeof(Fixed<16>) << ' ' << twice<21> << '\n';
    hello<"nttp">();
    std::cout << sum() << ' ' << sum(1, 2, 3) << ' ' << sum(0.5, 1, 2u) << '\n';
    log("rate", 48000, 'k', 1.5);
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << all_equal(3, 3, 3) << ' ' << all_equal(3, 3, 4) << '\n';
    auto v = make_ints<std::vector>();
    std::cout << v.size() << '\n';
}

Output:

16 42
hello from nttp
0 6 3.5
[4 args] rate 48000 k 1.5 
true false
3

docs.title: The old way: recursion
docs.text:
Before C++17 you'd write a base case and a recursive case peeling off one argument at a time. You'll see it in older code; folds and if constexpr replace most of it.

Pro tip

Use std::forward<Args>(args)... to pass a pack along unchanged — that's perfect forwarding, the next lesson.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Templates can take values (NTTPs), including auto and, in C++20, structural class types.
  • typename... Args declares a pack; sizeof... counts it; args... expands it.
  • Fold expressions apply an operator across a pack; the comma fold means 'for each'.
  • Use an initial value in folds when the pack may be empty.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does (0 + ... + args) evaluate to with no arguments?

Show answer

0 — the initial value; without it, an empty + fold is ill-formed.

Q2. How do you count the elements of a parameter pack?

Show answer

sizeof...(Args) (or sizeof...(args)).

Q3. Since C++20, what kinds of class types can be NTTPs?

Show answer

Structural types: literal class types whose bases and non-static members are all public and non-mutable (and themselves structural).

docs.title: Lesson 7.4: Forwarding references and perfect forwarding
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Write a function make_logged<T>(args...) that constructs a T and logs it. If you take the arguments by const&, you force copies of temporaries — moving becomes impossible. If you take them by &&, you can't pass lvalues. You want to pass every argument exactly as it came in. That's perfect forwarding.

docs.title: T&& in a template is special
docs.text:
In a deduced context, T&& is a forwarding reference: it binds to anything.

  • Pass an lvalue std::string s → T = std::string&, and T&& collapses to std::string&.
  • Pass an rvalue → T = std::string, parameter type std::string&&.

Reference collapsing rule: & &, & &&, && & → &; only && && → &&.

Note: std::vector<T>&& or a T&& in a non-template is just an rvalue reference, not a forwarding one.

docs.title: std::forward
docs.text:
Inside the function, a named parameter is always an lvalue. std::forward<T>(arg) casts it back to an rvalue only if it was originally an rvalue. That's how emplace_back and make_unique pass your arguments to the constructor without extra copies.

examples/week07/lesson04.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Track {
    std::string title;
    explicit Track(const std::string& t) : title{t} { std::cout << "  Track(copy title)\n"; }
    explicit Track(std::string&& t) : title{std::move(t)} { std::cout << "  Track(move title)\n"; }
};

template <typename T, typename... Args>
std::unique_ptr<T> make_logged(Args&&... args) {
    std::cout << "make_logged with " << sizeof...(Args) << " arg(s)\n";
    return std::make_unique<T>(std::forward<Args>(args)...);     // perfect forwarding
}

template <typename T>
void bad_wrapper(T&& x) { Track t{x}; }                           // always an lvalue -> copy

template <typename Container>
decltype(auto) first(Container& c) { return c[0]; }              // returns a reference

template <typename T>
void show(T&&) {
    std::cout << (std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T> ? "  T is an lvalue reference\n" : "  T is a non-reference\n");
}

int main() {
    std::string name = "Blue in Green";
    auto a = make_logged<Track>(name);                 // lvalue: copy
    auto b = make_logged<Track>(std::string{"So What"}); // rvalue: move
    std::cout << "bad_wrapper with an rvalue:\n";
    bad_wrapper(std::string{"Freddie Freeloader"});    // copies anyway
    show(name);
    show(std::string{"tmp"});

    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
    first(v) = 100;                                    // decltype(auto) kept int&
    std::cout << "v[0]=" << v[0] << ", name still \"" << name << "\"\n";
}

Output:

make_logged with 1 arg(s)
  Track(copy title)
make_logged with 1 arg(s)
  Track(move title)
bad_wrapper with an rvalue:
  Track(copy title)
  T is an lvalue reference
  T is a non-reference
v[0]=100, name still "Blue in Green"

docs.title: The wrong way
docs.text:
template <typename T> void wrapper(T&& x) { target(x); }             // always passes an lvalue: copies
template <typename T> void wrapper(T&& x) { target(std::move(x)); }  // moves from caller's lvalue: theft!
template <typename T> void wrapper(T&& x) { target(std::forward<T>(x)); }   // right

docs.title: decltype(auto)
docs.text:
If a wrapper returns what it calls, auto would decay references; decltype(auto) preserves the exact return type, references included.

Pitfall

Forwarding-reference overloads are greedy: template <class T> void f(T&&) beats void f(const std::string&) for a non-const std::string lvalue. Avoid overloading on forwarding references, or constrain them with concepts (next week).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • T&& with deduced T is a forwarding reference; it binds to lvalues and rvalues.
  • Reference collapsing: any & wins; only && && stays &&.
  • std::forward<T>(x) preserves the original value category; use it exactly once per argument.
  • decltype(auto) preserves references in return types.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Is void f(std::vector<T>&& v) a forwarding reference?

Show answer

No — only plain T&& with T deduced is a forwarding reference; std::vector<T>&& is an rvalue reference.

Q2. What is T when you call template<class T> void f(T&&) with an lvalue int x?

Show answer

T = int&, so the parameter type collapses to int&.

Q3. Why is std::move(x) wrong inside a forwarding function?

Show answer

It would move from the caller's lvalues too, leaving their objects in a moved-from state unexpectedly.

docs.title: Lesson 7.5: Type traits, if constexpr, and SFINAE
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Sometimes a generic function must do different things for different types: serialize integers as big-endian bytes, floats as IEEE bits, strings as length + characters. <type_traits> lets you ask questions about types at compile time, and if constexpr lets you branch on the answers — with the discarded branch never even compiled.

docs.title: Asking questions about types
docs.text:
std::is_integral_v<T>            // true for int, char, bool...
std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>  // safe to memcpy?
std::is_same_v<T, U>
std::remove_cvref_t<T>           // strip const, volatile and references (C++20)
std::conditional_t<B, X, Y>      // pick a type

_v gives a value, _t gives a type.

docs.title: if constexpr (C++17)
docs.text:
if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) { ... }   // other branch is discarded at compile time

With plain if, both branches must compile for every T. With if constexpr, the discarded branch isn't instantiated — so it may contain code that's invalid for this T.

examples/week07/lesson05.cpp
#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
void encode(std::vector<std::uint8_t>& out, const T& value) {
    using U = std::remove_cvref_t<T>;
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<U, bool>) {
        out.push_back(value ? 1 : 0);
    } else if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<U>) {          // big-endian bytes
        for (int i = sizeof(U) - 1; i >= 0; --i) out.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t>(value >> (8 * i)));
    } else if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<U>) {
        using Bits = std::conditional_t<sizeof(U) == 4, std::uint32_t, std::uint64_t>;
        encode(out, std::bit_cast<Bits>(value));
    } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<U, std::string>) {
        encode(out, static_cast<std::uint16_t>(value.size()));
        out.insert(out.end(), value.begin(), value.end());
    } else {
        static_assert(sizeof(U) == 0, "encode: unsupported type");   // fires only if instantiated
    }
}

// Pre-C++20 detection idiom: does T have .size()?
template <typename, typename = void> struct has_size : std::false_type {};
template <typename T> struct has_size<T, std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<const T&>().size())>> : std::true_type {};

// Pre-C++20 SFINAE overloads
template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<has_size<T>::value, int> = 0>
std::size_t length(const T& t) { return t.size(); }
template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<!has_size<T>::value, int> = 0>
std::size_t length(const T&) { return 1; }

int main() {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> bytes;
    encode(bytes, std::uint16_t{0x1234});
    encode(bytes, true);
    encode(bytes, 1.0f);
    encode(bytes, std::string{"hi"});
    std::cout << std::hex;
    for (auto b : bytes) std::cout << static_cast<int>(b) << ' ';
    std::cout << std::dec << '\n';

    std::cout << "has_size<string>=" << has_size<std::string>::value
              << " has_size<int>=" << has_size<int>::value << '\n';
    std::cout << length(std::string{"abc"}) << ' ' << length(42) << '\n';
    static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<float>);
}

Output:

12 34 1 3f 80 0 0 0 2 68 69 
has_size<string>=1 has_size<int>=0
3 1

docs.title: SFINAE: the old way to constrain templates
docs.text:
"Substitution Failure Is Not An Error": if substituting T into a template's signature fails, that overload is silently removed instead of causing an error. Pre-C++20 code used this with std::enable_if:

template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0>
void encode(T value);

And the detection idiom with std::void_t checks whether an expression is valid ("does T have a .size()?"). It works, but it's cryptic. In C++20, concepts (next week) replace almost all of it. You need to read SFINAE; you rarely need to write it any more.

Pro tip: static_assert your assumptions

static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Header>); next to a memcpy turns a silent future bug into a compile error.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Type traits answer questions (is_integral_v) and transform types (remove_cvref_t) at compile time.
  • if constexpr discards the untaken branch, so it can contain code invalid for that type.
  • SFINAE/enable_if/void_t are the pre-C++20 constraint tools — read them, prefer concepts for new code.
  • static_assert documents and enforces type assumptions.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't a plain if replace if constexpr in encode?

Show answer

Both branches of a plain if must compile for every T; e.g. value >> 8 doesn't compile for std::string.

Q2. Why does static_assert(sizeof(U) == 0, ...) not fire for supported types?

Show answer

It's in a discarded if constexpr branch of a template and depends on U, so it's only evaluated when that branch is instantiated.

Q3. What does SFINAE stand for and what does it do?

Show answer

Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: when substituting template arguments into a signature fails, that candidate is dropped from overload resolution instead of causing a hard error.

docs.title: Week 7 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 7.1) Why does clamp_to(0.7, 0, 1) fail?

Show answer

T is deduced as double from the first argument and int from the others; deduction fails because they conflict.

Q2. (from 7.1) Do templates have a runtime cost compared to hand-written overloads?

Show answer

No — instantiations are ordinary functions. The costs are compile time and code size.

Q3. (from 7.2) Why does Window<std::string, 2> compile even though mean() divides by static_cast<std::string>(size())?

Show answer

Member functions of class templates are only instantiated when used; mean() is never called.

Q4. (from 7.2) Can you partially specialize a function template?

Show answer

No. Only class (and variable) templates can be partially specialized; for functions use overloading or if constexpr.

Q5. (from 7.3) What does (0 + ... + args) evaluate to with no arguments?

Show answer

0 — the initial value; without it, an empty + fold is ill-formed.

Q6. (from 7.3) How do you count the elements of a parameter pack?

Show answer

sizeof...(Args) (or sizeof...(args)).

Q7. (from 7.4) Is void f(std::vector<T>&& v) a forwarding reference?

Show answer

No — only plain T&& with T deduced is a forwarding reference; std::vector<T>&& is an rvalue reference.

Q8. (from 7.4) What is T when you call template<class T> void f(T&&) with an lvalue int x?

Show answer

T = int&, so the parameter type collapses to int&.

Q9. (from 7.5) Why can't a plain if replace if constexpr in encode?

Show answer

Both branches of a plain if must compile for every T; e.g. value >> 8 doesn't compile for std::string.

Q10. (from 7.5) Why does static_assert(sizeof(U) == 0, ...) not fire for supported types?

Show answer

It's in a discarded if constexpr branch of a template and depends on U, so it's only evaluated when that branch is instantiated.

docs.title: Week 8: Concepts, compile-time programming, and lambdas
docs.text:
This week modernizes everything from Week 7. Concepts give templates readable constraints and readable errors. constexpr/consteval move work from run time to compile time. Lambdas and type erasure give you flexible callbacks. We finish with CRTP and C++23's deducing this.

# Lesson Standard Length 8.1 Concepts and requires-clauses C++20 12 min 8.2 constexpr, consteval, constinit, and if consteval C++23 12 min 8.3 Lambdas in depth C++23 11 min 8.4 Callables: std::function, move_only_function, and type erasure C++23 11 min 8.5 CRTP, deducing this, and a taste of metaprogramming C++23 11 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 8 programming assignment: A typed event dispatcher
docs.text:
Build Dispatcher that lets callers subscribe handlers for different event types:

d.on<KeyPressed>([](const KeyPressed& e) { ... });
d.emit(KeyPressed{'a'});

Requirements: constrain events with a concept Event (must be copyable and have a static name), store handlers type-erased in a std::unordered_map<std::type_index, std::vector<std::function<void(const void*)>>>, and print how many handlers ran per emit.

Reference solution examples/week08/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <concepts>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>
#include <typeindex>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

template <typename E>
concept Event = std::copyable<E> && requires { { E::name } -> std::convertible_to<std::string_view>; };

class Dispatcher {
public:
    template <Event E, std::invocable<const E&> F>
    void on(F handler) {
        handlers_[typeid(E)].push_back([h = std::move(handler)](const void* p) { h(*static_cast<const E*>(p)); });
    }
    template <Event E>
    void emit(const E& e) const {
        auto it = handlers_.find(typeid(E));
        const std::size_t n = it == handlers_.end() ? 0 : it->second.size();
        if (n) for (const auto& h : it->second) h(&e);
        std::cout << "  [" << E::name << ": " << n << " handler(s)]\n";
    }
private:
    std::unordered_map<std::type_index, std::vector<std::function<void(const void*)>>> handlers_;
};

struct KeyPressed { static constexpr std::string_view name = "KeyPressed"; char key; };
struct Resized { static constexpr std::string_view name = "Resized"; int w, h; };

int main() {
    Dispatcher d;
    int keys = 0;
    d.on<KeyPressed>([&keys](const KeyPressed& e) { ++keys; std::cout << "key " << e.key << '\n'; });
    d.on<KeyPressed>([](const KeyPressed&) { std::cout << "beep\n"; });
    d.emit(KeyPressed{'a'});
    d.emit(Resized{800, 600});
    d.on<Resized>([](const Resized& r) { std::cout << "resized to " << r.w << 'x' << r.h << '\n'; });
    d.emit(Resized{1024, 768});
    std::cout << "keys=" << keys << '\n';
}

Output:

key a
beep
  [KeyPressed: 2 handler(s)]
  [Resized: 0 handler(s)]
resized to 1024x768
  [Resized: 1 handler(s)]
keys=1

docs.title: Lesson 8.1: Concepts and requires-clauses
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Remember the 200-line template error from Week 7? Concepts fix that. A concept is a named compile-time predicate on types: "T is something you can add and divide". Put it on a template and two things happen: callers get a one-line error that says which requirement failed, and you can overload templates on capabilities cleanly — no SFINAE tricks.

docs.title: Using standard concepts
docs.text:
#include <concepts>
template <std::integral T> T gcd(T a, T b);
void log_count(std::unsigned_integral auto n);         // constrained auto

<concepts> provides std::integral, std::floating_point, std::same_as, std::convertible_to, std::totally_ordered, std::invocable, std::regular, ...; <iterator> and <ranges> add std::input_iterator, std::ranges::range, std::ranges::random_access_range, and more.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
template <typename T>
concept Averageable = requires(T a, T b, std::size_t n) {
    { a + b } -> std::convertible_to<T>;     // expression must compile, result convertible
    { a / n } -> std::convertible_to<T>;
    T{};                                     // default constructible
};

A requires-expression lists expressions that must be valid. It doesn't evaluate them.

docs.title: The payoff: better errors
docs.text:
Call a constrained template with a wrong type and the compiler says "constraints not satisfied" and names the failed requirement — instead of an error buried deep inside the body.

examples/week08/lesson01.cpp
#include <concepts>
#include <cstddef>
#include <forward_list>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
concept Averageable = requires(T a, T b, std::size_t n) {
    { a + b } -> std::convertible_to<T>;
    { a / n } -> std::convertible_to<T>;
    T{};
};

template <Averageable T>
T average(const std::vector<T>& v) {
    T total{};
    for (const auto& x : v) total = total + x;
    return v.empty() ? T{} : total / v.size();
}

template <std::integral T>
T gcd(T a, T b) { while (b != 0) { T t = a % b; a = b; b = t; } return a; }

template <std::input_iterator It>
const char* advance_by(It& it, int n) { while (n-- > 0) ++it; return "step-by-step"; }

template <std::random_access_iterator It>                       // more constrained: wins when it matches
const char* advance_by(It& it, int n) { it += n; return "jump"; }

void print_count(std::unsigned_integral auto n) { std::cout << "count=" << n << '\n'; }

template <typename T>
    requires std::totally_ordered<T> && std::copyable<T>
T largest(T a, T b) { return a < b ? b : a; }

int main() {
    std::cout << average(std::vector<double>{1.0, 2.0, 4.5}) << '\n';
    std::cout << gcd(48, 18) << '\n';

    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    std::list<int> l{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    auto vi = v.begin();
    auto li = l.begin();
    std::cout << advance_by(vi, 3) << " -> " << *vi << '\n';
    std::cout << advance_by(li, 3) << " -> " << *li << '\n';

    print_count(3u);
    std::cout << largest(std::string{"pear"}, std::string{"apple"}) << '\n';
    static_assert(!Averageable<std::string>);       // no string / size_t
}

Output:

2.5
6
jump -> 4
step-by-step -> 4
count=3
pear

docs.title: Overloading by constraints
docs.text:
If two overloads both match, the more constrained one wins (if one's constraints subsume the other's). That's how the example picks a faster advance_by for random-access iterators. Subsumption only works through named concepts — not through arbitrary boolean expressions — another reason to name your concepts.

Pro tip

Constrain on what you use, not on what you think the type "is". requires { a + b } is better than "must be a number" if all you do is add.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A concept is a named compile-time predicate; constrain templates with it.
  • requires expressions list operations that must compile, optionally with result constraints.
  • Constrained templates produce short, specific errors.
  • When overloads both match, the more constrained one (by subsumption of named concepts) wins.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does { a + b } -> std::convertible_to<T>; require?

Show answer

That a + b is a valid expression and its result type is convertible to T.

Q2. Why did advance_by on a std::vector iterator choose the "jump" version?

Show answer

Both overloads match, but std::random_access_iterator subsumes std::input_iterator, so the more constrained overload wins.

Q3. Does a requires-expression evaluate its expressions at run time?

Show answer

No — they're unevaluated operands; only their validity is checked at compile time.

docs.title: Lesson 8.2: constexpr, consteval, constinit, and if consteval
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A DSP filter needs a 256-entry sine table. You can compute it at startup — or have the compiler compute it so it's baked into the binary, costs zero time at run time, and fits in read-only flash on a microcontroller. That's constexpr. Its siblings consteval and constinit give you stronger guarantees.

docs.title: constexpr: may run at compile time
docs.text: A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time if its arguments are constants and its result is needed as a constant; otherwise it runs normally. Since C++20, constexpr functions can use loops, std::vector/std::string (as long as the memory is freed before evaluation ends), virtual calls, and try blocks. UB during constant evaluation is a compile error — a free UB detector for your tests.

docs.title: consteval: must run at compile time
docs.text: An immediate function. Every call must produce a constant — great for validating format strings, units, or IDs at compile time.

docs.title: constinit: initialized at compile time, mutable afterwards
docs.text:
constinit asserts that a global/static variable has static initialization (no dynamic initializer at startup). This kills the static initialization order fiasco — where one global's constructor uses another global from a different .cpp file that hasn't been initialized yet.

examples/week08/lesson02.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

constexpr double sin_approx(double x) {           // Taylor series: constexpr-friendly
    double term = x, sum = x;
    for (int n = 1; n < 10; ++n) { term *= -x * x / ((2 * n) * (2 * n + 1)); sum += term; }
    return sum;
}

template <std::size_t N>
constexpr std::array<std::int16_t, N> make_sine_table() {
    std::array<std::int16_t, N> t{};
    constexpr double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        double x = 2 * pi * static_cast<double>(i) / N;
        if (x > pi) x -= 2 * pi;                  // keep the series accurate
        t[i] = static_cast<std::int16_t>(sin_approx(x) * 32767);
    }
    return t;
}
constexpr auto sine = make_sine_table<256>();    // computed by the compiler
static_assert(sine[64] > 32700);                 // a compile-time test

constexpr int sum_squares(int n) {               // C++20: std::vector in constant evaluation
    std::vector<int> v(static_cast<std::size_t>(n));
    std::iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 1);
    int s = 0;
    for (int x : v) s += x * x;
    return s;
}
static_assert(sum_squares(3) == 14);

consteval std::uint32_t fourcc(std::string_view s) {   // must be compile time
    if (s.size() != 4) throw "fourcc needs exactly 4 chars";   // compile error if hit
    return std::uint32_t(s[0]) | std::uint32_t(s[1]) << 8 | std::uint32_t(s[2]) << 16 | std::uint32_t(s[3]) << 24;
}

constexpr double fast_sqrt(double x) {
    if consteval { double r = x; for (int i = 0; i < 30; ++i) r = 0.5 * (r + x / r); return r; }
    else { return std::sqrt(x); }                // run time: use the library
}

constinit int frame_counter = 0;                 // statically initialized; still mutable

int main() {
    std::cout << "sine[0]=" << sine[0] << " sine[64]=" << sine[64] << " sine[192]=" << sine[192] << '\n';
    std::cout << "sum_squares(10)=" << sum_squares(10) << '\n';
    constexpr auto riff = fourcc("RIFF");
    std::cout << std::hex << "RIFF=0x" << riff << std::dec << '\n';
    constexpr double s2 = fast_sqrt(2.0);
    volatile double two = 2.0;
    std::cout << s2 << ' ' << fast_sqrt(two) << '\n';
    ++frame_counter;
    std::cout << "frame_counter=" << frame_counter << '\n';
}

Output:

sine[0]=0 sine[64]=32767 sine[192]=-32767
sum_squares(10)=385
RIFF=0x46464952
1.41421 1.41421
frame_counter=1

docs.title: if consteval (C++23)
docs.text:
Inside a constexpr function, choose a compile-time-friendly path vs. a fast run-time path (e.g. an intrinsic or a lookup table that isn't constexpr). It replaces if (std::is_constant_evaluated()), which had a famous trap: inside if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated()) it's always true.

Pro tip: test with static_assert

If your parsing or math is constexpr, add static_assert(parse("42") == 42); — tests that run every time you compile, and that fail on UB.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • constexpr functions may run at compile time; constant evaluation rejects UB.
  • consteval functions must run at compile time — great for validating literals.
  • constinit guarantees static initialization, avoiding the initialization order fiasco.
  • if consteval (C++23) picks a compile-time path vs. a run-time path.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's the difference between constexpr and consteval functions?

Show answer

constexpr functions can be evaluated at compile time; consteval functions must be (every call is a constant expression).

Q2. Does constinit make a variable const?

Show answer

No — it only guarantees compile-time (static) initialization; the variable remains mutable.

Q3. What happens if a constexpr computation used in a static_assert overflows a signed int?

Show answer

Compile error: undefined behaviour isn't allowed in constant evaluation.

docs.title: Lesson 8.3: Lambdas in depth
docs.text: C++23 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Sorting tracks by duration, filtering sensor readings above a threshold, registering a callback for "new frame ready" — all need a small function right where you use it. Lambdas are that. And they're not slow: each lambda is a tiny class the compiler can inline completely.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
[captures](params) mutable -> ReturnType { body }

A lambda creates an object of a unique, unnamed class with an operator(). Captures become its members.

Capture Meaning [x] copy x [&x] reference to x [=] / [&] everything used, by copy / by reference [p = std::move(ptr)] init capture (C++14): move-only values, renaming [this] / [*this] the object by pointer / by copy (C++17)

docs.title: The wrong way: dangling reference captures
docs.text:
std::function<int()> make_counter() {
    int count = 0;
    return [&count] { return ++count; };   // count dies when make_counter returns: UB
}

Capturing by reference is fine for lambdas used immediately (e.g. passed to std::sort). For lambdas that are stored (callbacks, threads), capture by value or init-capture.

examples/week08/lesson03.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Track { std::string title; int seconds; };

class Player {
public:
    auto make_logger() const { return [*this] { std::cout << "player volume " << volume_ << '\n'; }; }  // copy of *this
    int volume_ = 7;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Track> tracks{{"So What", 562}, {"Blue in Green", 337}, {"All Blues", 693}};

    std::ranges::sort(tracks, [](const Track& a, const Track& b) { return a.seconds < b.seconds; });
    for (const auto& t : tracks) std::cout << t.title << " (" << t.seconds << "s)\n";

    int threshold = 400;
    auto longer = std::ranges::count_if(tracks, [threshold](const Track& t) { return t.seconds > threshold; });
    std::cout << longer << " tracks longer than " << threshold << "s\n";

    auto counter = [n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; };   // init capture + mutable
    auto copy = counter;
    std::cout << counter() << counter() << ' ' << copy() << '\n';

    auto owned = std::make_unique<std::string>("owned buffer");
    auto task = [buf = std::move(owned)] { return buf->size(); };   // move-only capture
    std::cout << "task sees " << task() << " chars\n";

    auto add = [](const auto& a, const auto& b) { return a + b; };   // generic
    std::cout << add(1, 2) << ' ' << add(std::string{"a"}, std::string{"b"}) << '\n';

    auto first_or = []<typename T>(const std::vector<T>& v, T fallback) { return v.empty() ? fallback : v.front(); };
    std::cout << first_or(std::vector<int>{}, -1) << '\n';

    constexpr auto square = [](int x) { return x * x; };
    static_assert(square(5) == 25);

    auto cube = [](int x) static { return x * x * x; };   // C++23: no `this` needed
    std::cout << cube(3) << '\n';

    Player p;
    auto log = p.make_logger();
    p.volume_ = 11;
    log();                                                // still 7: captured a copy

    const std::string mode = [&] { return threshold > 300 ? std::string{"long"} : std::string{"short"}; }();
    std::cout << "mode=" << mode << '\n';
}

Output:

Blue in Green (337s)
So What (562s)
All Blues (693s)
2 tracks longer than 400s
12 1
task sees 12 chars
3 ab
-1
27
player volume 7
mode=long

docs.title: Generic and template lambdas
docs.text: [](const auto& a, const auto& b) is a generic lambda (a template operator()). C++20 template lambdas []<typename T>(const std::vector<T>& v) let you name the type.

docs.title: IILE: initialize a const with complex logic
docs.text:
const auto config = [&] { Config c; /* many steps */ return c; }();

Pro tip

mutable lets a by-copy lambda modify its own copies. State lives in the lambda object, so copies of the lambda have independent state.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
