Key takeaways

  • A lambda is an object of an unnamed class; captures are its members.
  • Capture by reference only for lambdas used before the captured variables die.
  • Init captures move in move-only state; mutable allows modifying copies.
  • Generic, template, constexpr and (C++23) static lambdas cover most callback needs.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is [&count] dangerous in a returned lambda?

Show answer

The lambda outlives count, a local variable; calling it later reads a dangling reference (UB).

Q2. Why did copy() print 1 while counter printed 1 then 2?

Show answer

copy was copied from counter before it was called, so it has its own independent n.

Q3. How do you capture a std::unique_ptr into a lambda?

Show answer

With an init capture: [p = std::move(ptr)] { ... }.

docs.title: Lesson 8.4: Callables: std::function, move_only_function, and type erasure
docs.text: C++23 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Lambdas each have a unique type. So how do you store different callbacks in one std::vector? Or keep a callback as a class member without making the whole class a template? You need a type that can hold "any callable with signature void(int)". That's std::function — and understanding how it works teaches you type erasure, one of the most powerful designs in C++.

docs.title: The standard wrappers
docs.text:
Wrapper Owns? Copyable? Notes std::function<R(Args...)> yes yes (requires copyable callable) may heap-allocate; small-buffer optimization common std::move_only_function<R(Args...)> (C++23) yes move-only can hold lambdas capturing unique_ptr; const-correct std::function_ref<R(Args...)> (C++26) no yes cheap non-owning view for parameters plain template parameter F&& — — zero overhead, but makes your function a template

Rule of thumb: function parameters that call immediately → template or (C++26) function_ref; stored callbacks → std::function or std::move_only_function.

docs.title: std::invoke
docs.text:
Calls anything callable uniformly: functions, lambdas, and member function pointers (std::invoke(&Track::title, t)). Generic code uses it so that users can pass member pointers too.

examples/week08/lesson04.cpp
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Track { std::string title; int seconds; int duration_min() const { return seconds / 60; } };

class EventBus {                                     // stored callbacks
public:
    void subscribe(std::function<void(const std::string&)> cb) { subs_.push_back(std::move(cb)); }
    void publish(const std::string& e) const { for (const auto& s : subs_) s(e); }
private:
    std::vector<std::function<void(const std::string&)>> subs_;
};

// Hand-written type erasure: anything with a draw() member
class AnyDrawable {
public:
    template <typename T>
    AnyDrawable(T obj) : self_{std::make_unique<Model<T>>(std::move(obj))} {}
    void draw() const { self_->draw(); }
private:
    struct Concept { virtual ~Concept() = default; virtual void draw() const = 0; };
    template <typename T>
    struct Model final : Concept {
        explicit Model(T o) : obj{std::move(o)} {}
        void draw() const override { obj.draw(); }
        T obj;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Concept> self_;
};
struct Circle { void draw() const { std::cout << "  circle\n"; } };
struct Label { std::string text; void draw() const { std::cout << "  label: " << text << '\n'; } };

int main() {
    EventBus bus;
    int received = 0;
    bus.subscribe([&received](const std::string& e) { ++received; std::cout << "ui got " << e << '\n'; });
    bus.subscribe([](const std::string& e) { std::cout << "logger got " << e << '\n'; });
    bus.publish("track-changed");

    std::move_only_function<int()> job = [p = std::make_unique<int>(41)] { return *p + 1; };
    std::cout << "move_only_function: " << job() << '\n';

    Track t{"So What", 562};
    std::cout << std::invoke(&Track::title, t) << ' ' << std::invoke(&Track::duration_min, t) << "min\n";

    auto add = [](int a, int b) { return a + b; };
    auto add10 = std::bind_front(add, 10);
    std::cout << add10(5) << ' ' << received << '\n';

    std::vector<AnyDrawable> scene{Circle{}, Label{"hello"}};
    for (const auto& d : scene) d.draw();
}

Output:

ui got track-changed
logger got track-changed
move_only_function: 42
So What 9min
15 1
  circle
  label: hello

docs.title: How type erasure works
docs.text:
Inside, std::function holds a pointer to an abstract "concept" interface, and a templated "model" that implements it for the concrete callable type. The template is only visible at construction; afterwards the type is "erased" behind a virtual call. The example builds a tiny AnyDrawable the same way — runtime polymorphism without requiring your types to inherit from anything.

Costs

Calling through std::function is an indirect call that's hard to inline, and storing a large lambda may allocate. Fine for event callbacks; avoid in per-sample DSP loops.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::function stores any copyable callable with a given signature; std::move_only_function (C++23) allows move-only ones.
  • std::function_ref (C++26) is a non-owning view for parameters.
  • std::invoke calls functions, lambdas and member pointers uniformly.
  • Type erasure = abstract concept + templated model, hidden behind a value-semantic wrapper.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't std::function hold a lambda that captures a std::unique_ptr?

Show answer

std::function requires the callable to be copyable; such a lambda is move-only. Use std::move_only_function.

Q2. When should a function take a template F&& instead of std::function?

Show answer

When it calls the callable immediately and doesn't store it — the template has no type-erasure overhead and inlines.

Q3. In type erasure, where does the concrete type survive?

Show answer

Only inside the templated Model<T>, created in the wrapper's constructor template; the wrapper itself sees only the abstract Concept.

docs.title: Lesson 8.5: CRTP, deducing this, and a taste of metaprogramming
docs.text: C++23 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Virtual functions cost an indirect call and block inlining. If you know all types at compile time, you can get polymorphism with zero runtime cost: the base class template knows the derived type and calls it directly. That's CRTP — and C++23's "deducing this" makes much of it simpler. This lesson is intermediate-to-advanced; it's fine to skim the metaprogramming part on a first pass.

docs.title: CRTP
docs.text:
template <typename Derived>
struct Shape {
    double area() const { return static_cast<const Derived&>(*this).area_impl(); }
};
struct Square : Shape<Square> { double area_impl() const; };

The base is parameterized by the derived class, so the call is resolved at compile time. Uses: mixins (add operator!= from operator==, add counting, add clone()), and static interfaces in performance code. Downsides: no common base type for a heterogeneous container, and more template code.

docs.title: Deducing this (C++23)
docs.text:
An explicit object parameter makes the object a normal, deducible parameter:

struct Counter {
    template <typename Self>
    auto& get(this Self& self) { return self.value; }   // one function for const and non-const
};

This removes duplicated const/non-const overloads, enables recursive lambdas, and replaces many CRTP mixins — this auto& self deduces the derived type even when the function is declared in a base.

examples/week08/lesson05.cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <utility>

template <typename Derived>
struct Shape {                                         // CRTP static interface
    double area() const { return static_cast<const Derived&>(*this).area_impl(); }
};
struct Square : Shape<Square> { double s; explicit Square(double x) : s{x} {} double area_impl() const { return s * s; } };
struct Circle : Shape<Circle> { double r; explicit Circle(double x) : r{x} {} double area_impl() const { return 3.14159 * r * r; } };

template <typename T>
double total_area(const Shape<T>& a, const Shape<T>& b) { return a.area() + b.area(); }

template <typename Derived>
struct InstanceCounter {                               // CRTP mixin: per-class counter
    inline static int count = 0;
    InstanceCounter() { ++count; }
};
struct Widget : InstanceCounter<Widget> {};
struct Gadget : InstanceCounter<Gadget> {};

struct Buffer {
    std::string data = "abc";
    template <typename Self>
    auto& get(this Self& self) { return self.data; }    // deducing this: const and non-const in one
};

struct Base {
    void describe(this const auto& self) { std::cout << "I am " << self.name() << '\n'; }
};
struct Mic : Base { std::string name() const { return "a microphone"; } };

template <typename Tuple, std::size_t... I>
void print_tuple_impl(const Tuple& t, std::index_sequence<I...>) {
    ((std::cout << (I == 0 ? "" : ", ") << std::get<I>(t)), ...);
}
template <typename... Ts>
void print_tuple(const std::tuple<Ts...>& t) {
    std::cout << '(';
    print_tuple_impl(t, std::index_sequence_for<Ts...>{});
    std::cout << ")\n";
}

int main() {
    std::cout << total_area(Square{2}, Square{3}) << ' ' << Circle{1}.area() << '\n';
    Widget w1, w2; Gadget g1;
    std::cout << "widgets=" << Widget::count << " gadgets=" << Gadget::count << '\n';

    Buffer b;
    b.get() += "d";
    const Buffer& cb = b;
    std::cout << cb.get() << '\n';                     // const version, same function

    Mic{}.describe();

    auto fib = [](this auto self, int n) -> int { return n < 2 ? n : self(n - 1) + self(n - 2); };  // recursive lambda
    std::cout << "fib(10)=" << fib(10) << '\n';
    print_tuple(std::tuple{1, 2.5, std::string{"three"}});
    (void)w1; (void)w2; (void)g1;
}

Output:

13 3.14159
widgets=2 gadgets=1
abcd
I am a microphone
fib(10)=55
(1, 2.5, three)

docs.title: Metaprogramming in one breath
docs.text: Templates are Turing complete; you can compute with types. Modern code mostly uses constexpr for values and concepts for constraints, but std::index_sequence (compile-time list of indices) is still everyday useful, e.g. for iterating over a tuple — see the example's print_tuple. Expression templates (used by Eigen and similar libraries) build an expression tree as types so that a + b + c on vectors runs as one loop with no temporaries — a topic for further reading.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • CRTP gives compile-time polymorphism and mixins with no virtual calls.
  • Deducing this (C++23) deduces the object's type: one function for const/non-const, recursive lambdas, simpler mixins.
  • Use std::index_sequence to expand over tuple elements at compile time.
  • Pick dynamic polymorphism for open, runtime sets of types; static for known types in hot paths.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's the main limitation of CRTP vs virtual functions?

Show answer

No common base type: Shape<Square> and Shape<Circle> are unrelated, so you can't store them in one container and choose at run time.

Q2. What does template <typename Self> auto& get(this Self& self) replace?

Show answer

A pair of overloads T& get() and const T& get() const (and possibly && versions).

Q3. Why does InstanceCounter<Widget>::count differ from InstanceCounter<Gadget>::count?

Show answer

They're different class template instantiations, each with its own static member.

docs.title: Week 8 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 8.1) What does { a + b } -> std::convertible_to<T>; require?

Show answer

That a + b is a valid expression and its result type is convertible to T.

Q2. (from 8.1) Why did advance_by on a std::vector iterator choose the "jump" version?

Show answer

Both overloads match, but std::random_access_iterator subsumes std::input_iterator, so the more constrained overload wins.

Q3. (from 8.2) What's the difference between constexpr and consteval functions?

Show answer

constexpr functions can be evaluated at compile time; consteval functions must be (every call is a constant expression).

Q4. (from 8.2) Does constinit make a variable const?

Show answer

No — it only guarantees compile-time (static) initialization; the variable remains mutable.

Q5. (from 8.3) Why is [&count] dangerous in a returned lambda?

Show answer

The lambda outlives count, a local variable; calling it later reads a dangling reference (UB).

Q6. (from 8.3) Why did copy() print 1 while counter printed 1 then 2?

Show answer

copy was copied from counter before it was called, so it has its own independent n.

Q7. (from 8.4) Why can't std::function hold a lambda that captures a std::unique_ptr?

Show answer

std::function requires the callable to be copyable; such a lambda is move-only. Use std::move_only_function.

Q8. (from 8.4) When should a function take a template F&& instead of std::function?

Show answer

When it calls the callable immediately and doesn't store it — the template has no type-erasure overhead and inlines.

Q9. (from 8.5) What's the main limitation of CRTP vs virtual functions?

Show answer

No common base type: Shape<Square> and Shape<Circle> are unrelated, so you can't store them in one container and choose at run time.

Q10. (from 8.5) What does template <typename Self> auto& get(this Self& self) replace?

Show answer

A pair of overloads T& get() and const T& get() const (and possibly && versions).

docs.title: Week 9: Error handling and undefined behaviour
docs.text:
Every real program fails: files are missing, packets are corrupt, memory runs out. This week compares C++'s error-handling tools — exceptions, std::optional, std::expected, error codes, assertions — and gives you a rule for choosing. We end with a catalogue of undefined behaviour, the class of bug that makes C++ uniquely dangerous, and the tools that catch it.

# Lesson Standard Length 9.1 Exceptions: throw, try, catch, and stack unwinding C++20 11 min 9.2 Exception safety guarantees and noexcept C++20 11 min 9.3 std::optional and std::variant C++23 11 min 9.4 std::expected, error codes, and choosing a strategy C++23 12 min 9.5 Assertions, contracts preview, and the undefined behaviour catalogue C++23 14 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 9 programming assignment: A robust config parser
docs.text:
Parse lines of the form key=value into a Config { int sample_rate; int channels; std::string device; }.

  • Return std::expected<Config, ConfigError> where ConfigError holds a line number and a message.
  • Unknown keys, missing =, non-numeric numbers, out-of-range values and missing required keys are errors.
  • Use std::from_chars (no exceptions in the parser).
  • Print the result for one valid and three invalid inputs.
Reference solution examples/week09/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <charconv>
#include <expected>
#include <iostream>
#include <optional>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

struct Config { int sample_rate = 0; int channels = 0; std::string device; };
struct ConfigError { int line; std::string message; };

std::expected<int, std::string> to_int(std::string_view s, int lo, int hi) {
    int v{};
    auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v);
    if (ec != std::errc{} || p != s.data() + s.size()) return std::unexpected{"not a number: '" + std::string{s} + "'"};
    if (v < lo || v > hi) return std::unexpected{"out of range: " + std::string{s}};
    return v;
}

std::expected<Config, ConfigError> parse(const std::string& text) {
    Config c;
    std::istringstream in{text};
    std::string line;
    int n = 0;
    while (std::getline(in, line)) {
        ++n;
        if (line.empty() || line[0] == '#') continue;
        auto eq = line.find('=');
        if (eq == std::string::npos) return std::unexpected{ConfigError{n, "missing '='"}};
        std::string_view key{line.data(), eq}, value{line.data() + eq + 1, line.size() - eq - 1};
        if (key == "sample_rate") {
            auto v = to_int(value, 8000, 192000);
            if (!v) return std::unexpected{ConfigError{n, v.error()}};
            c.sample_rate = *v;
        } else if (key == "channels") {
            auto v = to_int(value, 1, 8);
            if (!v) return std::unexpected{ConfigError{n, v.error()}};
            c.channels = *v;
        } else if (key == "device") {
            c.device = value;
        } else {
            return std::unexpected{ConfigError{n, "unknown key '" + std::string{key} + "'"}};
        }
    }
    if (c.sample_rate == 0 || c.channels == 0) return std::unexpected{ConfigError{n, "sample_rate and channels are required"}};
    return c;
}

int main() {
    for (const char* text : {"# audio\nsample_rate=48000\nchannels=2\ndevice=hw:0\n",
                             "sample_rate=48k\nchannels=2\n",
                             "sample_rate=48000\nchanels=2\n",
                             "channels=2\n"}) {
        auto r = parse(text);
        if (r) std::cout << "ok: " << r->sample_rate << " Hz, " << r->channels << " ch, device '" << r->device << "'\n";
        else std::cout << "line " << r.error().line << ": " << r.error().message << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

ok: 48000 Hz, 2 ch, device 'hw:0'
line 1: not a number: '48k'
line 2: unknown key 'chanels'
line 1: sample_rate and channels are required

docs.title: Lesson 9.1: Exceptions: throw, try, catch, and stack unwinding
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: You're parsing a playlist file. Fifteen functions deep, you discover the file is corrupt. With error codes, every one of those fifteen functions must check and pass the error up. Exceptions jump straight to the code that can handle it — and RAII ensures everything in between is cleaned up on the way. That's the idea; the details (what to throw, what to catch, what it costs) are this lesson.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
if (!file) throw std::runtime_error{"cannot open " + path};
...
try { load(path); }
catch (const std::runtime_error& e) { std::cerr << e.what(); }
  • Throw by value, catch by const&. Catching by value slices and copies.
  • Handlers are tried in order; put derived types before base types.
  • catch (...) catches anything; throw; rethrows the current exception unchanged.

docs.title: Stack unwinding
docs.text:
When an exception propagates, every fully constructed local object on the way is destroyed — that's why RAII (Week 4) makes exception-safe code natural. The example prints destructors as the stack unwinds. If no handler is found, std::terminate is called (and whether the stack is unwound first is implementation-defined).

examples/week09/lesson01.cpp
#include <exception>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>

struct Guard {
    std::string name;
    explicit Guard(std::string n) : name{std::move(n)} {}
    ~Guard() { std::cout << "  ~Guard(" << name << ")\n"; }
};

class ParseError : public std::runtime_error {
public:
    ParseError(const std::string& what, int line) : std::runtime_error{what}, line_{line} {}
    int line() const { return line_; }
private:
    int line_;
};

int parse_duration(const std::string& field, int line) {
    Guard g{"parse_duration"};
    std::size_t used = 0;
    int v = std::stoi(field, &used);                  // may throw std::invalid_argument
    if (used != field.size()) throw ParseError{"trailing junk in '" + field + "'", line};
    return v;
}

void load_playlist() {
    Guard g{"load_playlist"};
    try {
        parse_duration("12x", 7);
    } catch (...) {
        std::throw_with_nested(std::runtime_error{"while loading playlist.m3u"});
    }
}

void print_nested(const std::exception& e, int depth = 0) {
    std::cout << std::string(depth * 2, ' ') << "- " << e.what() << '\n';
    try { std::rethrow_if_nested(e); }
    catch (const std::exception& inner) { print_nested(inner, depth + 1); }
}

int main() {
    try {
        load_playlist();
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught:\n";
        print_nested(e);
    }

    try {
        parse_duration("abc", 3);
    } catch (const ParseError& e) {                   // most specific first
        std::cout << "ParseError at line " << e.line() << '\n';
    } catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) {
        std::cout << "invalid_argument from stoi\n";
    }

    std::exception_ptr saved;
    try { throw std::out_of_range{"index 9"}; } catch (...) { saved = std::current_exception(); }
    try { std::rethrow_exception(saved); }
    catch (const std::logic_error& e) { std::cout << "transported: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
}

Output:

  ~Guard(parse_duration)
  ~Guard(load_playlist)
caught:
- while loading playlist.m3u
  - trailing junk in '12x'
  ~Guard(parse_duration)
invalid_argument from stoi
transported: index 9

docs.title: The standard hierarchy
docs.text: std::exception ← std::logic_error (bugs: invalid_argument, out_of_range, length_error) and std::runtime_error (environment: range_error, overflow_error, system_error), plus bad_alloc, bad_cast, bad_variant_access, bad_optional_access... Derive your own from std::runtime_error and add context.

docs.title: Nesting and transporting
docs.text: std::throw_with_nested wraps the current exception inside a new one with more context ("while loading playlist X: cannot open file Y"). std::exception_ptr lets you carry an exception to another thread — std::future uses it.

docs.title: Costs and no-exception builds
docs.text: Mainstream implementations use "zero-cost" tables: no cost on the happy path, but a throw is slow (microseconds) and binaries grow. So: exceptions for exceptional failures, not for control flow. Some domains (games, embedded, parts of Android/Google code) compile with -fno-exceptions; then throw doesn't compile and allocation failure terminates. Lesson 4 shows the alternatives.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Throw by value, catch by const&, most-derived handlers first.
  • Stack unwinding destroys locals, so RAII makes cleanup automatic.
  • Use throw_with_nested for context and exception_ptr to transport exceptions.
  • Exceptions are free when not thrown but slow when thrown; reserve them for genuinely exceptional failures.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why catch by const& rather than by value?

Show answer

Catching by value copies and slices derived exceptions to the caught type; a reference preserves the dynamic type and avoids the copy.

Q2. What happens if an exception is never caught?

Show answer

std::terminate is called.

Q3. What's the difference between throw; and throw e; in a handler?

Show answer

throw; rethrows the original exception object unchanged; throw e; throws a copy of e's static type, possibly slicing.

docs.title: Lesson 9.2: Exception safety guarantees and noexcept
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Imagine a Playlist::add that throws halfway through: the track count was incremented but the track wasn't stored. Now the object is lying. Exception safety is about what state your objects are in after an exception. There are three standard levels of promise, and choosing deliberately is what makes C++ code robust.

docs.title: The three guarantees
docs.text:
Guarantee Promise Example No-throw never throws destructors, swap, move operations (ideally) Strong commit or rollback: on failure, state is unchanged std::vector::push_back (with noexcept moves or copyable types) Basic no leaks, invariants hold, but state may have changed most operations

No guarantee at all = a bug.

docs.title: The wrong way
noexcept
docs.text:
noexcept promises a function won't throw. If it throws anyway, std::terminate is called — no unwinding guaranteed. Why bother?

  1. Containers check it: std::vector moves during reallocation only if the move constructor is noexcept (or the type isn't copyable). You saw the copy counts in Week 5.
  2. It documents intent and enables optimizations.

Destructors are noexcept by default; never let an exception escape one (throwing during unwinding calls std::terminate).

Conditional form: void swap(T& other) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_swappable_v<U>). The noexcept(expr) operator asks whether an expression can throw.

Pro tip

Mark move constructors, move assignment, swap, and destructors noexcept. Don't sprinkle noexcept on everything else — if a function might ever need to throw, removing noexcept later is a breaking change.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Know the three guarantees: no-throw, strong (commit/rollback), basic (valid but changed).
  • Recipe: do all throwing work first, then commit with no-throw operations.
  • noexcept moves let containers move instead of copy; violating noexcept calls std::terminate.
  • Never let exceptions escape destructors.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What guarantee does add_bad provide?

Show answer

Not even the basic guarantee in a meaningful sense: the class invariant (count == size) is broken after the exception.

Q2. Why does std::vector care whether your move constructor is noexcept?

Show answer

To keep push_back's strong guarantee during reallocation: if a move could throw midway, the old buffer would be partially moved-from, so it copies instead.

Q3. What does noexcept(p.consistent()) evaluate to here and why?

Show answer

false, because consistent() isn't declared noexcept — the operator checks declarations, not actual behaviour.

docs.title: Lesson 9.3: std::optional and std::variant
docs.text: C++23 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: "Find the track with this ID" — the track might not exist. That's not an error worth an exception; it's a normal outcome. Returning -1 or nullptr as a magic value is how bugs are born. std::optional says "maybe a value" in the type. And when the answer can be one of several types — a JSON value that's a number, a string or a list — std::variant gives you a type-safe union.

docs.title: std::optional<T>
docs.text:
std::optional<Track> find(int id);
if (auto t = find(42)) use(*t);         // contextually converts to bool
find(42).value_or(default_track);

*opt on an empty optional is UB; opt.value() throws std::bad_optional_access. C++23 adds monadic operations so you can chain steps without nested ifs:

parse_int(s).transform([](int x) { return x * 2; })   // map the value if present
            .and_then(validate)                      // next step that also returns optional
            .value_or(0);

docs.title: std::variant<Ts...>
docs.text:
A variant holds exactly one of its alternatives, knows which, and won't let you read the wrong one. Read it with std::visit and a visitor that handles every alternative — the compiler checks exhaustiveness. The overload pattern builds a visitor from lambdas:

template <class... Fs> struct overloaded : Fs... { using Fs::operator()...; };
examples/week09/lesson03.cpp
#include <charconv>
#include <iostream>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <variant>
#include <vector>

std::optional<int> parse_int(std::string_view s) {
    int v{};
    auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v);
    if (ec != std::errc{} || p != s.data() + s.size()) return std::nullopt;
    return v;
}
std::optional<int> valid_bpm(int bpm) { return bpm >= 20 && bpm <= 300 ? std::optional{bpm} : std::nullopt; }

template <class... Fs> struct overloaded : Fs... { using Fs::operator()...; };

using Json = std::variant<std::monostate, double, std::string, std::vector<double>>;

std::string describe(const Json& j) {
    return std::visit(overloaded{
        [](std::monostate) { return std::string{"null"}; },
        [](double d) { return "number " + std::to_string(d); },
        [](const std::string& s) { return "string \"" + s + '"'; },
        [](const std::vector<double>& v) { return "array of " + std::to_string(v.size()); },
    }, j);
}

int main() {
    for (std::string_view s : {"120", "12x", "999"}) {
        auto bpm = parse_int(s).and_then(valid_bpm).transform([](int b) { return b * 2; });
        std::cout << s << " -> " << (bpm ? std::to_string(*bpm) + " half-beats/min" : std::string{"invalid"}) << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "value_or: " << parse_int("oops").value_or(-1) << '\n';
    try { (void)parse_int("x").value(); } catch (const std::bad_optional_access&) { std::cout << "bad_optional_access\n"; }

    std::vector<Json> values{Json{}, 3.5, std::string{"hi"}, std::vector<double>{1, 2, 3}};
    for (const auto& j : values) std::cout << describe(j) << '\n';

    Json j = 2.0;
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << std::holds_alternative<double>(j) << ' ' << j.index() << '\n';
    if (auto* s = std::get_if<std::string>(&j)) std::cout << *s; else std::cout << "not a string\n";
    try { (void)std::get<std::string>(j); } catch (const std::bad_variant_access&) { std::cout << "bad_variant_access\n"; }
}

Output:

120 -> 240 half-beats/min
12x -> invalid
999 -> invalid
value_or: -1
bad_optional_access
null
number 3.500000
string "hi"
array of 3
true 1
not a string
bad_variant_access

docs.title: variant vs. inheritance
docs.text:
Both model "one of several kinds". Variant: closed set of types, value semantics, no heap allocation, adding an operation is easy (write a new visitor). Inheritance: open set of types, adding a type is easy. This trade-off is called the expression problem.

Pitfall

std::variant<bool, std::string> v = "text"; — before C++20's fix (P0608) this chose bool! Modern compilers choose std::string, but be explicit with string literals in variants.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::optional encodes 'maybe a value' in the type; avoid magic sentinel values.
  • C++23 and_then/transform/or_else chain optional steps.
  • std::variant is a type-safe union; std::visit with the overload pattern handles every alternative.
  • Variant suits closed sets of types; inheritance suits open sets.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What happens on *opt when opt is empty?

Show answer

Undefined behaviour. Use value() (throws) or check first.

Q2. What's the difference between and_then and transform on optional?

Show answer

transform maps the value with a function returning a plain value; and_then takes a function that itself returns an optional, flattening the result.

Q3. Why use std::monostate as the first alternative?

Show answer

To give the variant a cheap default/'empty' state, e.g. when the other alternatives aren't default constructible or to represent null.

docs.title: Lesson 9.4: std::expected, error codes, and choosing a strategy
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: std::optional tells you that something failed but not why. Exceptions tell you why, but they're invisible in function signatures and unavailable in some builds. std::expected<T, E> (C++23) is the middle path: a value or an error, explicit in the type, cheap, and works with -fno-exceptions. Let's see it — and then settle the big question: which tool when?

docs.title: std::expected
docs.text:
std::expected<Header, ParseError> parse_header(std::span<const std::byte>);

auto h = parse_header(bytes);
if (!h) report(h.error());
else use(*h);

Construct an error with return std::unexpected{ParseError::truncated};. Like optional, C++23 gives it and_then, transform, or_else and transform_error, so a pipeline of fallible steps reads top to bottom.

docs.title: std::error_code
docs.text:
The older standard mechanism, used by <filesystem>, <system_error> and networking-style APIs. An error_code is an integer plus a category (generic, system, or your own), so codes from different subsystems don't collide. Many std functions have two overloads: one that throws std::system_error, one that takes std::error_code&.

examples/week09/lesson04.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <expected>
#include <filesystem>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>
#include <vector>

enum class ParseError { too_short, bad_magic, bad_channels };

std::string to_string(ParseError e) {
    switch (e) {
        case ParseError::too_short: return "too short";
        case ParseError::bad_magic: return "bad magic";
        case ParseError::bad_channels: return "bad channel count";
    }
    return "?";
}

struct Header { int channels; int rate; };

[[nodiscard]] std::expected<std::vector<std::uint8_t>, ParseError> check_size(std::vector<std::uint8_t> b) {
    if (b.size() < 6) return std::unexpected{ParseError::too_short};
    return b;
}
[[nodiscard]] std::expected<std::vector<std::uint8_t>, ParseError> check_magic(std::vector<std::uint8_t> b) {
    if (b[0] != 'S' || b[1] != 'N') return std::unexpected{ParseError::bad_magic};
    return b;
}
[[nodiscard]] std::expected<Header, ParseError> decode(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& b) {
    if (b[2] == 0 || b[2] > 8) return std::unexpected{ParseError::bad_channels};
    return Header{b[2], (b[3] << 16) | (b[4] << 8) | b[5]};
}

void report(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& bytes) {
    auto result = check_size(bytes).and_then(check_magic).and_then(decode)
                      .transform([](Header h) { return std::to_string(h.channels) + "ch @ " + std::to_string(h.rate) + " Hz"; })
                      .transform_error(to_string);
    std::cout << (result ? "ok: " + *result : "error: " + result.error()) << '\n';
}

int main() {
    report({'S', 'N', 2, 0x00, 0xBB, 0x80});
    report({'S', 'N', 2});
    report({'X', 'X', 2, 0, 0, 0});
    report({'S', 'N', 0, 0, 0, 0});

    std::error_code ec;
    auto size = std::filesystem::file_size("/definitely/not/here.wav", ec);   // non-throwing overload
    std::cout << "file_size failed? " << std::boolalpha << static_cast<bool>(ec)
              << " (no_such_file: " << (ec == std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) << ")\n";
    (void)size;
    try {
        (void)std::filesystem::file_size("/definitely/not/here.wav");           // throwing overload
    } catch (const std::filesystem::filesystem_error& e) {
        std::cout << "filesystem_error code matches: " << (e.code() == std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

ok: 2ch @ 48000 Hz
error: too short
error: bad magic
error: bad channel count
file_size failed? true (no_such_file: true)
filesystem_error code matches: true

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
There's no single right answer, but here's a defensible default:

Situation Use A bug (precondition violated, impossible state) assert / contract / terminate — don't "handle" bugs Rare failure, far from where it can be handled, exceptions enabled exception Failure is a normal, expected outcome, handled by the caller std::expected<T, E> "Not found" with no further information needed std::optional<T> Interop with OS / filesystem APIs std::error_code Constructors exceptions (or a factory returning expected)

Mark result-returning functions [[nodiscard]] so ignoring an error is a warning. (std::expected itself is not marked nodiscard by every library, so put it on your functions.)

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::expected<T, E> makes failure explicit in the type and works without exceptions.
  • Chain fallible steps with and_then, map values with transform, map errors with transform_error.
  • std::error_code pairs a value with a category; many std APIs offer throwing and error_code& overloads.
  • Bugs → assert/terminate; expected outcomes → expected/optional; rare far-away failures → exceptions.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. How do you return an error from a function returning std::expected<int, std::string>?

Show answer

return std::unexpected{std::string{"message"}}; (or std::unexpected("message") where convertible).

Q2. Why compare ec == std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory instead of ec.value() == 2?

Show answer

The comparison goes through error categories/conditions and is portable; raw values differ between platforms and categories.

Q3. Should a violated precondition (a caller bug) be reported with std::expected?

Show answer

Usually no — bugs should be caught by assertions/contracts and fixed, not returned as recoverable errors.

docs.title: Lesson 9.5: Assertions, contracts preview, and the undefined behaviour catalogue
docs.text: C++23 · about 14 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Undefined behaviour (UB) is the scariest phrase in C++. It doesn't mean "crashes"; it means the standard places no requirements — the optimizer may assume it never happens, and your program can do anything, including appear to work until the day it doesn't. This lesson is your field guide: what UB looks like, how to catch it, and how assertions (and soon contracts) help you state your assumptions.

docs.title: Three kinds of "it depends"
docs.text: Term Meaning Example Implementation-defined each implementation picks and documents sizeof(long), right shift of negative ints (pre-C++20) Unspecified one of several valid outcomes, not documented order of evaluation of function arguments Undefined no requirements at all signed overflow, out-of-bounds access

docs.title: The UB catalogue
docs.text: UB Example Catch it with Out-of-bounds access v[v.size()] ASan, -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS, .at() Use after free / dangling reference to a destroyed local, iterator after push_back ASan Double free / mismatched new[]/delete ASan Signed integer overflow INT_MAX + 1 UBSan, constexpr tests Shift too far / negative shift 1 << 32 UBSan Reading uninitialized variables int x; use(x); MSan, -Wuninitialized, C++26 makes it "erroneous" Null pointer dereference UBSan, ASan Strict aliasing violation *(float*)&some_int -fstrict-aliasing warnings; use std::bit_cast Data race two threads, one writes, no sync TSan Misaligned access casting a char* buffer to int* UBSan Modifying a const object const_cast then write — Infinite loop without side effects while(true){} with no I/O/atomics — Returning without a value from non-void -Wreturn-type Violating std::unreachable() debug builds

docs.title: Why the optimizer makes it worse
Assertions
docs.text: assert(cond) checks a condition in debug builds and is removed when NDEBUG is defined. Use it for internal invariants — things that are true unless there's a bug. static_assert does the same at compile time.

docs.title: Contracts (C++26 preview)
docs.text:
C++26 adds contract assertions as language syntax:

int isqrt(int x)
    pre(x >= 0)
    post(r: r * r <= x);
// inside a body: contract_assert(cond);

The build chooses an evaluation semantic (ignore, observe, enforce, quick-enforce) and you can install a violation handler. Compiler support is arriving in 2025–2026 (GCC trunk has an implementation); treat this as a preview and keep using assert today.

Pro tip: the debug-build safety net

Add -fsanitize=address,undefined -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS (libstdc++) or -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_DEBUG (libc++) to your test builds. Week 15 makes this a habit.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • UB means no requirements; optimizers assume it never happens and may delete your checks.
  • Check before an operation that could overflow; use std::bit_cast instead of type punning.
  • Use assert for internal invariants, static_assert for compile-time ones; contracts (C++26) are coming.
  • Run tests under ASan/UBSan/TSan and library hardening modes to catch UB early.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can x + 1 < x be optimized to false?

Show answer

Signed overflow is UB, so the compiler may assume it doesn't happen; then x + 1 is always greater than x.

Q2. Is the order of evaluation of function arguments undefined, unspecified or implementation-defined?

Show answer

Unspecified — the compiler can pick any order and need not document it; it's not UB by itself.

Q3. What happens to assert in a release build with -DNDEBUG?

Show answer

It expands to nothing; the condition isn't evaluated (so never put side effects in an assert).

docs.title: Week 9 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 9.1) Why catch by const& rather than by value?

Show answer

Catching by value copies and slices derived exceptions to the caught type; a reference preserves the dynamic type and avoids the copy.

Q2. (from 9.1) What happens if an exception is never caught?

Show answer

std::terminate is called.

Q3. (from 9.2) What guarantee does add_bad provide?

Show answer

Not even the basic guarantee in a meaningful sense: the class invariant (count == size) is broken after the exception.

Q4. (from 9.2) Why does std::vector care whether your move constructor is noexcept?

Show answer

To keep push_back's strong guarantee during reallocation: if a move could throw midway, the old buffer would be partially moved-from, so it copies instead.

Q5. (from 9.3) What happens on *opt when opt is empty?

Show answer

Undefined behaviour. Use value() (throws) or check first.

Q6. (from 9.3) What's the difference between and_then and transform on optional?

Show answer

transform maps the value with a function returning a plain value; and_then takes a function that itself returns an optional, flattening the result.

Q7. (from 9.4) How do you return an error from a function returning std::expected<int, std::string>?

Show answer

return std::unexpected{std::string{"message"}}; (or std::unexpected("message") where convertible).

Q8. (from 9.4) Why compare ec == std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory instead of ec.value() == 2?

Show answer

The comparison goes through error categories/conditions and is portable; raw values differ between platforms and categories.

Q9. (from 9.5) Why can x + 1 < x be optimized to false?

Show answer

Signed overflow is UB, so the compiler may assume it doesn't happen; then x + 1 is always greater than x.

Q10. (from 9.5) Is the order of evaluation of function arguments undefined, unspecified or implementation-defined?

Show answer

Unspecified — the compiler can pick any order and need not document it; it's not UB by itself.

docs.title: Week 10: The standard library I: containers and iterators
docs.text:
Choosing the right container is one of the highest-leverage decisions in C++ — often worth more than any micro-optimization. This week tours every standard container, explains its complexity and memory layout, and gives you a decision procedure. The short version, which we'll justify with measurements: default to std::vector.

# Lesson Standard Length 10.1 std::vector in depth C++20 12 min 10.2 array, deque, list, and forward_list C++20 10 min 10.3 Associative and unordered containers C++20 12 min 10.4 Container adaptors, flat_map and flat_set C++23 10 min 10.5 Views over data: span, mdspan, string_view, and inplace_vector (preview) C++23 11 min 10.6 Iterators and iterator categories C++20 11 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 10 programming assignment: An LRU cache
docs.text:
Implement LruCache<Key, Value> with capacity N:

  • std::optional<Value> get(const Key&) — returns the value and marks it most-recently used.
  • void put(Key, Value) — inserts/updates; evicts the least-recently used entry when full.
  • Both operations must be O(1) average: use std::list for recency order and std::unordered_map from key to list iterator (this is the classic case where list's stable iterators and splice shine).
Reference solution examples/week10/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <list>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

template <typename Key, typename Value>
class LruCache {
public:
    explicit LruCache(std::size_t cap) : cap_{cap} {}
    std::optional<Value> get(const Key& k) {
        auto it = index_.find(k);
        if (it == index_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, it->second);     // O(1) move to front
        return it->second->second;
    }
    void put(Key k, Value v) {
        if (auto it = index_.find(k); it != index_.end()) {
            it->second->second = std::move(v);
            order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, it->second);
            return;
        }
        if (order_.size() == cap_) {
            std::cout << "  evict " << order_.back().first << '\n';
            index_.erase(order_.back().first);
            order_.pop_back();
        }
        order_.emplace_front(k, std::move(v));
        index_[std::move(k)] = order_.begin();
    }
private:
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::list<std::pair<Key, Value>> order_;
    std::unordered_map<Key, typename std::list<std::pair<Key, Value>>::iterator> index_;
};

int main() {
    LruCache<std::string, int> c{2};
    c.put("kick", 1);
    c.put("snare", 2);
    std::cout << "get kick: " << c.get("kick").value_or(-1) << '\n';
    c.put("hat", 3);                     // evicts snare (least recently used)
    std::cout << "get snare: " << c.get("snare").value_or(-1) << '\n';
    std::cout << "get hat: " << c.get("hat").value_or(-1) << '\n';
}

Output:

get kick: 1
  evict snare
get snare: -1
get hat: 3

docs.title: Lesson 10.1: std::vector in depth
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: std::vector is a contiguous, growable array — and contiguous memory is what modern CPUs love: caches prefetch it, SIMD chews through it. Even for operations where a linked list "should" win on paper, vector often wins in practice. Let's understand it deeply: growth, invalidation, and the idioms that keep it fast.

docs.title: Size, capacity and growth
docs.text:
A vector owns a heap buffer with capacity() slots, of which size() are in use. When you push_back into a full vector, it allocates a bigger buffer (typically 1.5× or 2×), moves the elements over, and frees the old one. Growth is geometric, so push_back is amortized O(1). If you know the final size, reserve(n) avoids all the reallocations.

examples/week10/lesson01.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Sample { int t; float v; Sample(int tt, float vv) : t{tt}, v{vv} {} };

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;
    std::size_t last_cap = v.capacity();
    int reallocs = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
        v.push_back(i);
        if (v.capacity() != last_cap) { ++reallocs; last_cap = v.capacity(); }
    }
    std::cout << "size=" << v.size() << " reallocations=" << reallocs << " (geometric growth; count is implementation-specific)\n";

    std::vector<int> r;
    r.reserve(1000);
    const int* before = r.data();
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) r.push_back(i);
    std::cout << "with reserve: buffer moved? " << std::boolalpha << (before != r.data()) << '\n';

    std::vector<Sample> samples;
    samples.emplace_back(0, 0.5f);                   // constructed in place
    samples.push_back(Sample{1, 0.25f});
    std::cout << "samples=" << samples.size() << '\n';

    std::vector<int> data{5, 0, 3, 0, 0, 7, 1};
    std::vector<int> copy = data;
    auto removed = std::erase_if(data, [](int x) { return x == 0; });             // C++20
    copy.erase(std::remove(copy.begin(), copy.end(), 0), copy.end());              // classic idiom
    std::cout << "removed " << removed << ": ";
    for (int x : data) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << "| idiom gives same? " << (data == copy) << '\n';

    std::vector<int> work{1, 0, 2};                  // safe modification while iterating: indices
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < work.size(); ++i)
        if (work[i] == 0) work.push_back(9);
    std::cout << "work.size()=" << work.size() << '\n';

    std::vector<bool> flags(10);
    flags[3] = true;
    auto proxy = flags[3];                            // a proxy, not bool&
    std::cout << "vector<bool> proxy reads " << static_cast<bool>(proxy) << '\n';
}

Output (yours may differ: timing/threads):

size=1000 reallocations=11 (geometric growth; count is implementation-specific)
with reserve: buffer moved? false
samples=2
removed 3: 5 3 7 1 | idiom gives same? true
work.size()=4
vector<bool> proxy reads true

docs.title: Iterator invalidation: the classic bug
docs.text:
for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)
    if (*it == 0) v.push_back(1);     // WRONG: push_back may reallocate -> `it` dangles (UB)

Rules for vector: a reallocation invalidates all iterators, pointers and references; insert/erase without reallocation invalidate those at or after the point. Holding &v[0] across a push_back is the same bug. Prefer indices when you must modify while iterating, or collect changes and apply them after.

docs.title: Erasing elements
docs.text: C++20's std::erase_if(v, pred) does it in one line. Before C++20 you'd use the erase-remove idiom: v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end()); — remove_if only shuffles the kept elements forward; erase chops off the tail.

docs.title: emplace_back vs push_back
docs.text:
emplace_back(args...) constructs the element in place from constructor arguments; push_back(obj) copies or moves an existing object. For an already-built object they're the same. Note emplace_back can call explicit constructors, which can hide mistakes — prefer push_back unless you're constructing in place.

std::vector<bool> is not a container of bools

It packs bits, so v[i] returns a proxy object, not bool&; auto& b = v[0]; doesn't compile and &v[0] isn't a bool*. Use std::vector<char>, std::bitset or std::vector<std::uint8_t> when you need real elements.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • vector is contiguous and cache-friendly; growth is geometric so push_back is amortized O(1).
  • reserve when you know the size; reallocation invalidates all iterators, pointers and references.
  • Use std::erase_if (C++20) or erase-remove to delete elements.
  • std::vector<bool> is a bit-packed special case with proxy references.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is push_back amortized O(1) even though reallocation is O(n)?

Show answer

Capacity grows geometrically, so the total copying cost over n insertions is O(n) — O(1) per insertion on average.

Q2. After v.push_back(x) causes a reallocation, which iterators are valid?

Show answer

None of the old ones: all iterators, pointers and references into the vector are invalidated.

Q3. What does std::remove actually do?

Show answer

It moves the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end; it doesn't change the size — you must erase the tail.

docs.title: Lesson 10.2: array, deque, list, and forward_list
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
std::vector is the default, but not the only answer. A fixed-size table of filter coefficients doesn't need the heap at all (std::array). A queue that grows at both ends wants std::deque. And sometimes you genuinely need stable element addresses or O(1) splicing (std::list). Let's see when each one earns its place — and measure why lists usually don't.

Container Layout Fast operations Iterators stable? array<T,N> inline, fixed everything; no heap yes (never reallocates) vector<T> contiguous heap block back insert/erase, random access until reallocation deque<T> blocks of elements front and back insert, random access references stable for end inserts; iterators not list<T> doubly linked nodes insert/erase anywhere given an iterator, splice yes forward_list<T> singly linked nodes same, less memory, forward only yes

docs.title: Big-O isn't everything
docs.text:
Inserting in the middle of a list is O(1) — once you have the iterator. Finding the position is O(n) pointer chasing, with a likely cache miss per node. A vector insert is O(n) but it's a memmove of contiguous memory, which modern CPUs do extremely fast. The example times both (timings are printed for you to look at on your machine; they vary).

examples/week10/lesson02.cpp
#include <array>
#include <chrono>
#include <deque>
#include <forward_list>
#include <iostream>
#include <list>
#include <vector>

template <typename C>
long long insert_middle_ms(int n) {
    C c;
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        auto it = c.begin();
        std::advance(it, static_cast<long>(c.size() / 2));   // find the middle: O(n) either way
        c.insert(it, i);
    }
    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    return std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(t1 - t0).count();
}

int main() {
    constexpr auto coeffs = std::to_array({0.25f, 0.5f, 0.25f});   // no heap, size deduced
    static_assert(coeffs.size() == 3);

    std::deque<int> dq{2, 3};
    dq.push_front(1);
    dq.push_back(4);
    std::cout << "deque: " << dq.front() << ".." << dq.back() << " [2]=" << dq[2] << '\n';

    std::list<int> a{1, 2, 3}, b{10, 20};
    auto keep = a.begin();                                  // iterator to 1
    a.splice(std::next(a.begin()), b);                      // O(1): moves nodes, no copies
    std::cout << "list after splice: ";
    for (int x : a) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << "| b.size()=" << b.size() << " | iterator still valid: " << *keep << '\n';

    std::forward_list<int> fl{3, 2, 1};
    fl.push_front(4);
    fl.sort();
    std::cout << "forward_list sorted front: " << fl.front() << '\n';

    const int n = 20000;
    std::cout << "insert " << n << " in the middle (your timings will differ):\n";
    std::cout << "  vector: " << insert_middle_ms<std::vector<int>>(n) << " ms\n";
    std::cout << "  list:   " << insert_middle_ms<std::list<int>>(n) << " ms\n";
}

Output (yours may differ: timing/threads):

deque: 1..4 [2]=3
list after splice: 1 10 20 2 3 | b.size()=0 | iterator still valid: 1
forward_list sorted front: 1
insert 20000 in the middle (your timings will differ):
  vector: 2 ms
  list:   158 ms

docs.title: When list really wins
docs.text:
• You need iterators/pointers to elements to stay valid while others are inserted/erased (e.g. an LRU cache: list + unordered_map of iterators).
  • You move ranges between lists with splice in O(1) without copying elements.
  • Elements are huge and non-movable.

std::to_array (C++20) creates a std::array with the size deduced: auto a = std::to_array({1, 2, 3});.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::array for fixed sizes (no heap); deque for both-end queues; vector for almost everything else.
  • Linked lists have O(1) insertion given an iterator but terrible cache behaviour; finding the position dominates.
  • Choose list for stable iterators and O(1) splice, not for 'fast insertion'.
  • Measure on your hardware — complexity classes hide constant factors.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is vector typically faster than list at 'insert in the middle' for ints?

Show answer

Finding the middle is O(n) for both, but vector's traversal and shift are contiguous memory operations that are cache- and prefetch-friendly, while the list chases pointers with cache misses.

Q2. What does splice do and why is it O(1)?

Show answer

It relinks nodes from one list into another without copying or allocating; only pointers change.

Q3. Does std::array allocate on the heap?

Show answer

No — its elements are stored inline in the object (on the stack for a local).

docs.title: Lesson 10.3: Associative and unordered containers
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: "Look up a sample by its name." "Count how many times each word appears." "Keep events sorted by time." These are the jobs of associative containers. You have two families: tree-based (map, set), sorted with O(log n) operations, and hash-based (unordered_map, unordered_set), unsorted with O(1) average. Knowing their APIs well — try_emplace, contains, heterogeneous lookup — avoids a lot of slow, buggy code.

docs.title: The operator[] trap
docs.text:
std::map<std::string, int> counts;
if (counts["drums"] > 0) ...     // WRONG for a lookup: inserts "drums" -> 0 if missing!

operator[] inserts a default value when the key is missing (and so doesn't work on a const map). For lookups use find, contains (C++20) or at (throws if missing).

docs.title: Insertion done right
docs.text:
• try_emplace(key, args...) — constructs the value only if the key is absent.
  • insert_or_assign(key, value) — explicit upsert, tells you which happened.

docs.title: Heterogeneous lookup
docs.text:
With std::map<std::string, int>, m.find("drums") creates a temporary std::string. Use a transparent comparator, std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>>, and lookups with std::string_view or const char* allocate nothing. For unordered containers (C++20) you need a transparent hash and std::equal_to<>.

examples/week10/lesson03.cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <set>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <unordered_map>

struct NoteKey {
    int octave; char name;
    bool operator==(const NoteKey&) const = default;
    auto operator<=>(const NoteKey&) const = default;
};
template <> struct std::hash<NoteKey> {
    std::size_t operator()(const NoteKey& k) const noexcept {
        std::size_t h = std::hash<int>{}(k.octave);
        h ^= std::hash<char>{}(k.name) + 0x9e3779b9 + (h << 6) + (h >> 2);   // hash_combine
        return h;
    }
};

struct StringHash {                                       // transparent hash (C++20 lookup)
    using is_transparent = void;
    std::size_t operator()(std::string_view s) const { return std::hash<std::string_view>{}(s); }
};

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>> counts;       // transparent comparator
    for (std::string_view w : {"kick", "snare", "kick", "hat", "kick"}) ++counts[std::string{w}];
    for (const auto& [word, n] : counts) std::cout << word << '=' << n << ' ';   // sorted
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::cout << std::boolalpha << "contains(\"tom\") " << counts.contains("tom")
              << ", size still " << counts.size() << '\n';
    (void)counts["tom"];                                   // the trap: inserts!
    std::cout << "after operator[]: size " << counts.size() << '\n';

    auto [it, inserted] = counts.try_emplace("kick", 100);
    std::cout << "try_emplace kick inserted? " << inserted << " value " << it->second << '\n';
    auto [it2, ins2] = counts.insert_or_assign("hat", 9);
    std::cout << "insert_or_assign hat inserted? " << ins2 << " value " << it2->second << '\n';

    auto lo = counts.lower_bound("j"), hi = counts.upper_bound("s");     // range query
    std::cout << "keys in [j, s]: ";
    for (auto i = lo; i != hi; ++i) std::cout << i->first << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::unordered_map<std::string, int, StringHash, std::equal_to<>> bpm{{"techno", 130}, {"house", 124}};
    std::string_view genre = "house";
    if (auto f = bpm.find(genre); f != bpm.end()) std::cout << genre << " -> " << f->second << '\n';   // no temp string

    std::unordered_map<NoteKey, double> freq{{{4, 'A'}, 440.0}, {{5, 'A'}, 880.0}};
    std::cout << "A4=" << freq.at({4, 'A'}) << '\n';

    std::set<int> s1{1, 3, 5}, s2{2, 3, 4};
    s1.merge(s2);                                          // moves nodes; duplicates stay in s2
    std::cout << "merged size " << s1.size() << ", left in s2: " << *s2.begin() << '\n';
    auto node = s1.extract(5);
    node.value() = 50;                                     // change a key without reallocating
    s1.insert(std::move(node));
    std::cout << "largest now " << *s1.rbegin() << '\n';
}

Output:

hat=1 kick=3 snare=1 
contains("tom") false, size still 3
after operator[]: size 4
try_emplace kick inserted? false value 3
insert_or_assign hat inserted? false value 9
keys in [j, s]: kick 
house -> 124
A4=440
merged size 5, left in s2: 3
largest now 50

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text: map needs operator< (or a comparator) — <=> from Week 4 provides it. unordered_map needs a hash: specialize std::hash<Key> or pass a hasher type. Combine field hashes carefully (the example uses a simple boost::hash_combine-style mix).

docs.title: Which one?
docs.text:
Need Use Sorted iteration, range queries (lower_bound) map/set Fastest average lookup, no order needed unordered_map/unordered_set Small, mostly-read data sorted vector or flat_map (next lesson)

Node handles (extract/merge, C++17) move elements between maps — even change a key — without reallocating.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • operator[] inserts on a miss; use find, contains or at for lookups.
  • Use try_emplace and insert_or_assign for clear insertion semantics.
  • Transparent comparators/hashes enable lookups by string_view without temporaries.
  • Tree containers are ordered (range queries); hash containers are faster on average but unordered.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why doesn't counts["x"] compile on a const std::map?

Show answer

operator[] may insert, so it's non-const; use at or find.

Q2. What do you need for heterogeneous lookup in std::unordered_map (C++20)?

Show answer

A transparent hash (with is_transparent) and a transparent equality such as std::equal_to<>.

Q3. What's the advantage of extract + insert over erase + insert?

Show answer

The node is reused — no deallocation/allocation and no copy of the value — and you can even modify the key.

docs.title: Lesson 10.4: Container adaptors, flat_map and flat_set
docs.text: C++23 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A task scheduler needs "give me the highest-priority job". An undo system needs "last in, first out". These aren't new data structures — they're interfaces on top of existing containers, called adaptors. And C++23 adds flat_map, a map that stores its data in sorted vectors, because for many workloads that beats a tree by a wide margin.

docs.title: Adaptors
flat_map and flat_set (C++23)
docs.text:
They keep keys (and values) in sorted contiguous containers and binary-search them. Compared with std::map:

  • Lookups and iteration: faster (cache-friendly, no pointer chasing).
  • Insertions/erasures in the middle: O(n) (elements shift).
  • Iterators invalidated by insertions (unlike map).

Great for data that's built once and read many times — configs, lookup tables, small maps. Compiler status: libc++ ships them; GCC's libstdc++ added <flat_map> in GCC 15. The second example is therefore marked "may be unsupported" in our checker. Before C++23, a sorted std::vector + std::lower_bound gives you the same thing by hand.

examples/week10/lesson04_flat.cpp
#include <flat_map>
#include <flat_set>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::flat_map<std::string, int> rates{{"cd", 44100}, {"dvd", 48000}, {"hires", 96000}};
    rates["phone"] = 8000;
    for (const auto& [k, v] : rates) std::cout << k << '=' << v << ' ';   // sorted, contiguous
    std::cout << '\n';
    std::cout << "keys stored contiguously: " << rates.keys().size() << '\n';

    std::flat_set<int> ids{5, 1, 3, 1};
    std::cout << "unique sorted ids: ";
    for (int i : ids) std::cout << i << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

cd=44100 dvd=48000 hires=96000 phone=8000 
keys stored contiguously: 4
unique sorted ids: 1 3 5

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • stack, queue and priority_queue are adaptors over other containers.
  • pop() returns void; read top()/front() first.
  • priority_queue is a max-heap by default; use std::greater<> for a min-heap.
  • flat_map/flat_set (C++23) store sorted contiguous data: fast lookup, slower mid insertion.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why does std::stack::pop() return void?

Show answer

Returning the removed element by value could throw (during the copy) after the element was already removed, losing it; splitting top() and pop() keeps the strong guarantee.

Q2. How do you make a min-heap with std::priority_queue?

Show answer

std::priority_queue<T, std::vector<T>, std::greater<>>.

Q3. When is flat_map a worse choice than map?

Show answer

When you do frequent insertions/erasures in a large container (O(n) shifts), or need iterators/references stable across insertions.

docs.title: Lesson 10.5: Views over data: span, mdspan, string_view, and inplace_vector (preview)
docs.text: C++23 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A function that processes audio shouldn't care whether the samples live in a std::vector, a std::array, a C array from a driver, or memory-mapped file data. It needs "a pointer and a length". Views give exactly that, safely typed. std::span does 1-D; C++23's std::mdspan does images, matrices and multichannel audio; and C++26's std::inplace_vector gives a vector with fixed capacity and no heap — ideal for embedded.

docs.title: std::span<T> recap
docs.text: From Week 3: a non-owning (pointer, size) view over contiguous data. std::span<const float> for read-only parameters; fixed extent std::span<float, 4> encodes the size in the type. subspan, first, last slice without copying.

docs.title: std::mdspan (C++23)
docs.text:
A view over contiguous memory interpreted as N dimensions:

std::mdspan img(pixels.data(), height, width);   // 2-D view
img[y, x] = 255;                                  // C++23 multidimensional subscript

The layout policy decides how indices map to memory: layout_right (row-major, C style, default), layout_left (column-major, Fortran/BLAS style), layout_stride. Extents can be static or dynamic. Support: libc++ (Clang 17+) and libstdc++ (GCC 15+); older toolchains lack it, so the example is marked "may be unsupported" in our checker.

examples/week10/lesson05.cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <mdspan>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

float peak(std::span<const float> s) {
    float p = 0;
    for (float x : s) p = (x < 0 ? -x : x) > p ? (x < 0 ? -x : x) : p;
    return p;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<float> interleaved{0.1f, -0.9f, 0.4f, 0.2f, -0.3f, 0.8f};   // L R L R L R
    std::cout << "peak(all)=" << peak(interleaved) << " peak(first 2)=" << peak(std::span{interleaved}.first(2)) << '\n';

    // View the same memory as frames x channels
    std::mdspan audio(interleaved.data(), 3, 2);
    for (std::size_t ch = 0; ch < audio.extent(1); ++ch) {
        float p = 0;
        for (std::size_t f = 0; f < audio.extent(0); ++f) {
            float a = audio[f, ch] < 0 ? -audio[f, ch] : audio[f, ch];
            if (a > p) p = a;
        }
        std::cout << "channel " << ch << " peak " << p << '\n';
    }

    std::vector<int> pixels(4 * 3, 0);
    std::mdspan img(pixels.data(), 3, 4);           // 3 rows x 4 cols, row-major
    img[1, 2] = 255;
    std::cout << "pixel (1,2) is element " << (&img[1, 2] - pixels.data()) << " in memory\n";

    std::mdspan<int, std::extents<std::size_t, 3, 4>, std::layout_left> col_major(pixels.data());
    std::cout << "column-major (1,2) is element " << (&col_major[1, 2] - pixels.data()) << '\n';
}

Output:

peak(all)=0.9 peak(first 2)=0.9
channel 0 peak 0.4
channel 1 peak 0.9
pixel (1,2) is element 6 in memory
column-major (1,2) is element 7

docs.title: Lifetime: views never own
docs.text:
std::span<int> bad() { std::vector<int> v{1,2,3}; return v; }   // dangling view!

A view is only valid while the data it refers to is alive and not reallocated. Never return a view to a local; be careful storing views in members.

docs.title: std::inplace_vector<T, N> (C++26 preview)
docs.text:
A vector with capacity fixed at compile time, elements stored inline — no allocation, ever. push_back past capacity throws, and try_push_back returns null instead. It's perfect for embedded systems and for "small lists" in hot code. No major standard library shipped it at the time of writing, so we don't compile an example here; the Week 16 embedded lesson and the ring-buffer capstone build similar fixed-capacity containers by hand.

// C++26 (not compiled in this course yet)
std::inplace_vector<int, 8> v;
v.push_back(1);
if (!v.try_push_back(2)) { /* full */ }

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::span is the standard 1-D view; prefer it for buffer parameters.
  • std::mdspan (C++23) views memory as N dimensions with pluggable layouts.
  • Views never own; returning a view to local data dangles.
  • std::inplace_vector (C++26) is a fixed-capacity, no-heap vector — shown as a preview.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. In a row-major 3×4 mdspan, which memory element is [1, 2]?

Show answer

Element 1*4 + 2 = 6.

Q2. What's wrong with std::span<int> f() { std::vector<int> v{1}; return v; }?

Show answer

The span refers to v's buffer, which is destroyed when f returns — a dangling view.

Q3. What happens when you push_back into a full std::inplace_vector?

Show answer

It throws std::bad_alloc; try_push_back returns a null pointer instead.

docs.title: Lesson 10.6: Iterators and iterator categories
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Iterators are the glue of the standard library: algorithms don't know about containers, only about iterators. If you make your data structure provide iterators, every algorithm — sort, find, accumulate, range-for, ranges — works on it for free. This lesson shows the categories and builds an iterator for a ring buffer, the core of our embedded capstone.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Each category adds capabilities; algorithms require the weakest category they need:

Category Adds Example input read once, ++ istream_iterator forward multi-pass forward_list bidirectional -- list, map random access + n, [], < deque contiguous (C++20) elements adjacent in memory vector, array, span

std::sort needs random access, which is why std::list has its own sort() member.

docs.title: Adaptors
docs.text:
• std::back_inserter(v) — an output iterator that calls push_back.
  • std::make_reverse_iterator, rbegin/rend.
  • std::make_move_iterator — moves instead of copies when used with algorithms.
  • std::istream_iterator<T> — reads values from a stream.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
A C++20 iterator needs: value_type, difference_type, operator*, operator++ (pre and post), and operator==. Satisfying std::forward_iterator then gets you every forward algorithm. Use static_assert with the concept to check.

examples/week10/lesson06.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <numeric>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Ring {
public:
    void push(T v) { data_[(head_ + size_) % N] = v; if (size_ < N) ++size_; else head_ = (head_ + 1) % N; }

    class iterator {
    public:
        using value_type = T;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        iterator() = default;
        iterator(const Ring* r, std::size_t i) : r_{r}, i_{i} {}
        const T& operator*() const { return r_->data_[(r_->head_ + i_) % N]; }
        iterator& operator++() { ++i_; return *this; }
        iterator operator++(int) { auto t = *this; ++i_; return t; }
        bool operator==(const iterator& o) const { return i_ == o.i_; }
    private:
        const Ring* r_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t i_ = 0;
    };
    iterator begin() const { return {this, 0}; }
    iterator end() const { return {this, size_}; }
private:
    std::array<T, N> data_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0, size_ = 0;
};
static_assert(std::forward_iterator<Ring<int, 4>::iterator>);

int main() {
    Ring<int, 4> r;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 6; ++i) r.push(i);              // keeps the last 4
    for (int x : r) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << "| sum=" << std::accumulate(r.begin(), r.end(), 0)
              << " max=" << *std::max_element(r.begin(), r.end()) << '\n';

    std::vector<int> copy;
    std::copy(r.begin(), r.end(), std::back_inserter(copy));
    std::cout << "copied " << copy.size() << ", reversed: ";
    for (auto it = copy.rbegin(); it != copy.rend(); ++it) std::cout << *it << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::istringstream in{"3 1 4 1 5"};
    std::vector<int> parsed{std::istream_iterator<int>{in}, std::istream_iterator<int>{}};
    std::cout << "parsed " << parsed.size() << " ints, distance(begin,end)=" << std::distance(parsed.begin(), parsed.end()) << '\n';

    std::vector<std::string> src{"a", "b"}, dst;
    std::copy(std::make_move_iterator(src.begin()), std::make_move_iterator(src.end()), std::back_inserter(dst));
    std::cout << "moved: " << dst[0] << dst[1] << ", ssize=" << std::ssize(dst) << '\n';
    auto it = std::next(parsed.begin(), 2);
    std::cout << "third element: " << *it << ", prev: " << *std::prev(it) << '\n';
}

Output:

3 4 5 6 | sum=18 max=6
copied 4, reversed: 6 5 4 3 
parsed 5 ints, distance(begin,end)=5
moved: ab, ssize=2
third element: 4, prev: 1

docs.title: Sentinels
docs.text: In C++20 ranges, the end of a range can be a different type than the iterator — a sentinel. E.g. "until the null terminator" doesn't need a precomputed end pointer. We'll use this in Week 11.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Algorithms work on iterators; the category determines which algorithms apply.
  • Iterator adaptors (back_inserter, reverse, move, stream) connect containers, streams and algorithms.
  • A custom iterator with a few members unlocks the whole algorithm library; check with C++20 concepts.
  • Sentinels let a range's end be a different type than its iterator.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't you call std::sort on a std::list?

Show answer

std::sort requires random-access iterators; list iterators are only bidirectional. Use list::sort().

Q2. What does std::back_inserter(v) do when assigned to?

Show answer

Calls v.push_back(value).

Q3. What minimum members does a C++20 forward iterator need?

Show answer

value_type, difference_type, operator*, pre- and post-increment, equality comparison, and default constructibility.

docs.title: Week 10 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 10.1) Why is push_back amortized O(1) even though reallocation is O(n)?

Show answer

Capacity grows geometrically, so the total copying cost over n insertions is O(n) — O(1) per insertion on average.

Q2. (from 10.1) After v.push_back(x) causes a reallocation, which iterators are valid?

Show answer

None of the old ones: all iterators, pointers and references into the vector are invalidated.

Q3. (from 10.2) Why is vector typically faster than list at 'insert in the middle' for ints?

Show answer

Finding the middle is O(n) for both, but vector's traversal and shift are contiguous memory operations that are cache- and prefetch-friendly, while the list chases pointers with cache misses.

Q4. (from 10.2) What does splice do and why is it O(1)?

Show answer

It relinks nodes from one list into another without copying or allocating; only pointers change.

Q5. (from 10.3) Why doesn't counts["x"] compile on a const std::map?

Show answer

operator[] may insert, so it's non-const; use at or find.

Q6. (from 10.3) What do you need for heterogeneous lookup in std::unordered_map (C++20)?

Show answer

A transparent hash (with is_transparent) and a transparent equality such as std::equal_to<>.

Q7. (from 10.4) Why does std::stack::pop() return void?

Show answer

Returning the removed element by value could throw (during the copy) after the element was already removed, losing it; splitting top() and pop() keeps the strong guarantee.

Q8. (from 10.4) How do you make a min-heap with std::priority_queue?

Show answer

std::priority_queue<T, std::vector<T>, std::greater<>>.

Q9. (from 10.5) In a row-major 3×4 mdspan, which memory element is [1, 2]?

Show answer

Element 1*4 + 2 = 6.

Q10. (from 10.5) What's wrong with std::span<int> f() { std::vector<int> v{1}; return v; }?

Show answer

The span refers to v's buffer, which is destroyed when f returns — a dangling view.

Q11. (from 10.6) Why can't you call std::sort on a std::list?

Show answer

std::sort requires random-access iterators; list iterators are only bidirectional. Use list::sort().

Q12. (from 10.6) What does std::back_inserter(v) do when assigned to?

Show answer

Calls v.push_back(value).

docs.title: Week 11: The standard library II: algorithms and ranges
docs.text:
"No raw loops" is a famous piece of C++ advice (from Sean Parent). It doesn't mean loops are evil; it means that most loops are a well-known algorithm in disguise, and naming the algorithm makes code shorter, clearer and often faster. This week covers the <algorithm> and <numeric> toolbox, then C++20 ranges, which make algorithms composable.

# Lesson Standard Length 11.1 Algorithms I: searching, counting, sorting C++20 12 min 11.2 Algorithms II: transforming, removing, and numeric C++23 11 min 11.3 Ranges and views C++23 13 min 11.4 Utilities: pair, tuple, apply, function objects, and friends C++23 10 min 11.5 Generators and lazy sequences with std::generator (C++23) C++23 9 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 11 programming assignment: A log analysis pipeline
docs.text:
Given lines like "12:00:01 WARN disk 91%", write range pipelines (no raw for loops except for printing) to:

  1. Count lines per level (INFO, WARN, ERROR) using std::ranges::count_if.
  2. Collect the messages of the first 2 ERROR lines into a std::vector<std::string> with std::ranges::to.
  3. Print the line numbers (1-based) of all WARN lines using views::enumerate.
Reference solution examples/week11/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

std::string_view level(std::string_view line) {
    auto s = line.substr(line.find(' ') + 1);
    return s.substr(0, s.find(' '));
}
std::string_view message(std::string_view line) {
    auto s = line.substr(line.find(' ') + 1);
    return s.substr(s.find(' ') + 1);
}

int main() {
    std::vector<std::string_view> log{"12:00:01 INFO start", "12:00:02 WARN disk 91%", "12:00:03 ERROR write failed",
                                      "12:00:04 INFO retry", "12:00:05 ERROR write failed again", "12:00:06 WARN fan",
                                      "12:00:07 ERROR giving up"};
    for (std::string_view lv : {"INFO", "WARN", "ERROR"})
        std::cout << lv << ": " << std::ranges::count_if(log, [lv](auto l) { return level(l) == lv; }) << '\n';

    auto errors = log | std::views::filter([](auto l) { return level(l) == "ERROR"; })
                      | std::views::transform([](auto l) { return std::string{message(l)}; })
                      | std::views::take(2)
                      | std::ranges::to<std::vector>();
    for (const auto& e : errors) std::cout << "error: " << e << '\n';

    std::cout << "WARN on lines:";
    for (auto [i, l] : std::views::enumerate(log))
        if (level(l) == "WARN") std::cout << ' ' << i + 1;
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

INFO: 2
WARN: 2
ERROR: 3
error: write failed
error: write failed again
WARN on lines: 2 6

docs.title: Lesson 11.1: Algorithms I: searching, counting, sorting
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: You have 10,000 recorded takes and want: the first one that's clipped, how many are longer than a minute, the top 5 by loudness, and the median duration. Each of those is a one-liner with the right algorithm — and each of the "obvious" hand-written loops has a subtle bug or a worse complexity. Let's learn the toolbox.

docs.title: Finding and counting
docs.text:
