find_if, count_if, any_of/all_of/none_of replace most "search loops". In C++20, prefer the std::ranges:: versions: they take the container directly and support projections — a function applied to each element before comparing:

std::ranges::sort(takes, {}, &Take::loudness);   // sort by a member: no lambda needed

docs.title: Choosing a sort
docs.text: Need Algorithm Complexity fully sorted sort O(n log n) equal elements keep their order stable_sort O(n log n), may allocate only the top k, sorted partial_sort O(n log k) only the k-th element (e.g. median) nth_element O(n) average

docs.title: The comparator rule
docs.text:
Comparators must be a strict weak ordering: comp(a, a) is false, and it's transitive. <= breaks the rule — and with std::sort that's UB that can read out of bounds, not just "sort wrongly".

examples/week11/lesson01.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Take { std::string name; int seconds; double loudness; bool clipped; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Take> takes{{"t1", 45, -14.0, false}, {"t2", 75, -9.5, true}, {"t3", 62, -11.0, false},
                            {"t4", 30, -20.0, false}, {"t5", 90, -8.0, true}, {"t6", 62, -12.5, false}};

    auto first_clip = std::ranges::find_if(takes, &Take::clipped);              // projection as predicate
    std::cout << "first clipped: " << first_clip->name << '\n';
    auto long_ones = std::ranges::count_if(takes, [](int s) { return s > 60; }, &Take::seconds);
    std::cout << "longer than 60s: " << long_ones << '\n';
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << "all under 2 min? "
              << std::ranges::all_of(takes, [](int s) { return s < 120; }, &Take::seconds) << '\n';

    auto by_loud = takes;
    std::ranges::partial_sort(by_loud, by_loud.begin() + 2, std::ranges::greater{}, &Take::loudness);
    std::cout << "top 2 loudest: " << by_loud[0].name << ' ' << by_loud[1].name << '\n';

    std::vector<int> durations;
    for (const auto& t : takes) durations.push_back(t.seconds);
    auto mid = durations.begin() + static_cast<long>(durations.size() / 2);
    std::ranges::nth_element(durations, mid);
    std::cout << "median-ish duration: " << *mid << '\n';

    auto stable = takes;
    std::ranges::stable_sort(stable, {}, &Take::seconds);                    // t3 stays before t6
    for (const auto& t : stable) std::cout << t.name << '(' << t.seconds << ") ";
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::ranges::sort(durations);
    auto [lo, hi] = std::ranges::equal_range(durations, 62);
    std::cout << "takes of exactly 62s: " << (hi - lo) << ", lower_bound(60) -> " << *std::ranges::lower_bound(durations, 60) << '\n';
    auto [mn, mx] = std::ranges::minmax(durations);
    std::cout << "min " << mn << " max " << mx << " clamp(200) " << std::clamp(200, mn, mx) << '\n';
}

Output:

first clipped: t2
longer than 60s: 4
all under 2 min? true
top 2 loudest: t5 t2
median-ish duration: 62
t4(30) t1(45) t3(62) t6(62) t2(75) t5(90) 
takes of exactly 62s: 2, lower_bound(60) -> 62
min 30 max 90 clamp(200) 90

docs.title: Binary search on sorted data
docs.text: lower_bound returns the first element not less than the value; upper_bound the first greater; equal_range both. They're O(log n) — if the range is sorted by the same comparison.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Name your loops: find_if, count_if, any_of… say what they do.
  • Projections (&Take::seconds) let range algorithms work on a member without lambdas.
  • Pick the cheapest sort: partial_sort for top-k, nth_element for medians, stable_sort to keep order.
  • Comparators must be strict weak orderings; <= is UB with std::sort.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's the complexity of nth_element?

Show answer

O(n) on average.

Q2. Why is [](int a, int b){ return a <= b; } a broken comparator?

Show answer

It's not irreflexive (comp(a, a) is true), so it's not a strict weak ordering; std::sort may misbehave or read out of bounds.

Q3. What does std::ranges::sort(v, {}, &T::x) do?

Show answer

Sorts v by member x using the default comparator std::ranges::less on the projected values.

docs.title: Lesson 11.2: Algorithms II: transforming, removing, and numeric
docs.text: C++23 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Normalize a buffer, keep only the takes above a threshold, compute RMS loudness, build a running total — these are transforms, filters and reductions. The standard library has them all, including parallel-ready versions (reduce, transform_reduce) that we'll run on multiple cores in Week 14.

docs.title: Transform, filter, replace
docs.text:
std::ranges::transform(in, out.begin(), [](float x) { return x * gain; });
std::ranges::copy_if(takes, std::back_inserter(good), is_good);

Output algorithms write through an iterator; they never grow the destination. Writing into an empty vector's begin() is UB — use std::back_inserter or size the destination first.

docs.title: Removing duplicates
docs.text: unique removes consecutive duplicates (so sort first) and, like remove, returns the new end — then erase.

docs.title: Numeric reductions
docs.text:
• accumulate(first, last, init) — left fold, strictly in order. The init type decides the result type: accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) on doubles sums into an int!
  • reduce — like accumulate but may reorder (associative + commutative ops), enabling parallelism.
  • transform_reduce — map then reduce: dot products, RMS.
  • partial_sum / inclusive_scan / exclusive_scan — running totals.
  • C++23 std::ranges::fold_left — the ranges-style accumulate.
examples/week11/lesson02.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <numeric>
#include <random>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> buf{0.5, -0.25, 0.75, -0.5};
    std::vector<double> loud(buf.size());
    std::ranges::transform(buf, loud.begin(), [](double x) { return x * 2.0; });

    std::vector<double> clipped;
    std::ranges::copy_if(loud, std::back_inserter(clipped), [](double x) { return std::abs(x) > 1.0; });
    std::cout << "samples over full scale after gain: " << clipped.size() << '\n';

    auto wrong = std::accumulate(buf.begin(), buf.end(), 0);       // int init: sums truncated values!
    auto right = std::accumulate(buf.begin(), buf.end(), 0.0);
    std::cout << "accumulate with 0: " << wrong << ", with 0.0: " << right << '\n';

    double rms = std::sqrt(std::transform_reduce(buf.begin(), buf.end(), buf.begin(), 0.0) / static_cast<double>(buf.size()));
    std::cout << "rms = " << rms << '\n';
    std::cout << "fold_left = " << std::ranges::fold_left(buf, 0.0, std::plus<>{}) << '\n';

    std::vector<int> frames{3, 1, 4, 1, 5};
    std::vector<int> offsets(frames.size());
    std::exclusive_scan(frames.begin(), frames.end(), offsets.begin(), 0);     // where each chunk starts
    for (int o : offsets) std::cout << o << ' ';
    std::cout << "(offsets)\n";

    std::vector<int> ids(6);
    std::iota(ids.begin(), ids.end(), 100);
    std::ranges::rotate(ids, ids.begin() + 2);
    std::ranges::reverse(ids);
    std::cout << "ids: ";
    for (int i : ids) std::cout << i << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::vector<std::string> tags{"rock", "jazz", "rock", "funk", "jazz"};
    std::ranges::sort(tags);
    auto [first, last] = std::ranges::unique(tags);
    tags.erase(first, last);
    std::cout << "unique tags: " << tags.size() << '\n';

    std::vector<std::string> a{"funk", "jazz", "rock"}, b{"jazz", "pop"}, both;
    std::ranges::set_intersection(a, b, std::back_inserter(both));
    std::cout << "in both: " << both[0] << '\n';

    std::mt19937 rng{42};
    std::ranges::shuffle(ids, rng);                                 // deterministic for a given seed+library
    std::cout << "gcd(48000,44100)=" << std::gcd(48000, 44100) << " lcm=" << std::lcm(48000, 44100)
              << " midpoint(2e9,2.1e9)=" << std::midpoint(2'000'000'000, 2'100'000'000) << '\n';
}

Output:

samples over full scale after gain: 1
accumulate with 0: 0, with 0.0: 0.5
rms = 0.53033
fold_left = 0.5
0 3 4 8 9 (offsets)
ids: 101 100 105 104 103 102 
unique tags: 3
in both: jazz
gcd(48000,44100)=300 lcm=7056000 midpoint(2e9,2.1e9)=2050000000

docs.title: Set and heap algorithms
docs.text:
On sorted ranges, set_intersection, set_union, set_difference and includes run in linear time. Heap algorithms let you keep a heap inside your own vector — what priority_queue uses internally.

Pro tip: std::midpoint

(a + b) / 2 can overflow; std::midpoint(a, b) (C++20) can't. It also handles pointers and floats correctly.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Output algorithms write through iterators; use back_inserter or pre-size the destination.
  • unique and remove return a new end; erase the tail.
  • accumulate's init value sets the result type — 0 vs 0.0 matters.
  • reduce/transform_reduce allow reordering (and parallelism); scans give running totals.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's wrong with std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) for std::vector<double>?

Show answer

The accumulator is int, so each partial sum is converted to int — the result is truncated.

Q2. Why must you sort before std::unique to remove all duplicates?

Show answer

unique only collapses consecutive equal elements.

Q3. How does reduce differ from accumulate?

Show answer

reduce may apply the operation in any order/grouping (requiring associativity and commutativity for deterministic results), which enables parallel execution; accumulate is strictly left-to-right.

docs.title: Lesson 11.3: Ranges and views
docs.text: C++23 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: "Take the clipped takes, get their names, uppercase them, first three." With classic algorithms that's three temporary vectors and a loop. With C++20 ranges it's one readable pipeline that runs lazily — no temporaries, nothing computed until you iterate. This is the biggest change to everyday C++ style since lambdas.

docs.title: Views and pipes
docs.text:
A view is a lightweight, lazy range adaptor. Compose them with |:

auto names = takes | std::views::filter(&Take::clipped)
                   | std::views::transform(&Take::name)
                   | std::views::take(3);
for (const auto& n : names) ...      // work happens here, element by element

C++23 adds std::ranges::to<std::vector>() to materialize a pipeline, plus many views: zip, enumerate, chunk, slide, stride, adjacent, cartesian_product, join_with.

examples/week11/lesson03.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <cctype>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <ranges>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

struct Take { std::string name; int seconds; bool clipped; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Take> takes{{"intro", 30, false}, {"verse", 62, true}, {"chorus", 45, true},
                            {"bridge", 20, false}, {"outro", 75, true}, {"coda", 15, true}};

    auto upper = [](std::string s) { for (auto& c : s) c = static_cast<char>(std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))); return s; };
    auto names = takes | std::views::filter(&Take::clipped)
                       | std::views::transform(&Take::name)
                       | std::views::transform(upper)
                       | std::views::take(3);
    for (const auto& n : names) std::cout << n << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    auto squares = std::views::iota(1) | std::views::transform([](int i) { return i * i; })
                                       | std::views::take_while([](int x) { return x < 50; });
    auto v = squares | std::ranges::to<std::vector>();                  // C++23
    std::cout << "squares < 50: " << v.size() << " values, last " << v.back() << '\n';

    for (auto [i, t] : std::views::enumerate(takes) | std::views::take(2))   // C++23
        std::cout << i << ':' << t.name << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::vector<int> left{1, 2, 3}, right{10, 20, 30};
    for (auto [l, r] : std::views::zip(left, right)) std::cout << l + r << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::vector<int> samples{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7};
    for (auto chunk : samples | std::views::chunk(3)) std::cout << '[' << std::ranges::fold_left(chunk, 0, std::plus<>{}) << ']';
    std::cout << " <- sums of chunks of 3\n";
    for (auto w : samples | std::views::slide(3)) std::cout << w[1] << ' ';
    std::cout << "<- centers of sliding windows\n";

    std::string_view csv = "kick,snare,hat";
    for (auto part : csv | std::views::split(',')) std::cout << std::string_view{part} << '|';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::map<std::string, int> bpm{{"house", 124}, {"techno", 130}};
    for (const auto& k : bpm | std::views::keys) std::cout << k << ' ';
    for (int b : bpm | std::views::values | std::views::reverse) std::cout << b << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    auto r = std::ranges::find(std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3}, 2);           // temporary: returns `dangling`
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(r), std::ranges::dangling>);
}

Output:

VERSE CHORUS OUTRO 
squares < 50: 7 values, last 49
0:intro 1:verse 
11 22 33 
[6][15][7] <- sums of chunks of 3
2 3 4 5 6 <- centers of sliding windows
kick|snare|hat|
house techno 130 124

docs.title: Laziness has consequences
docs.text:
1. Views don't own (except owning_view). A view over a temporary vector dangles; the library catches some cases by returning std::ranges::dangling from algorithms called on temporaries.
  2. Some views cache. filter_view::begin() caches its result, so iterating a filter view while modifying the underlying elements that affect the predicate is a bug, and a const filter view isn't iterable.
  3. Re-iterating recomputes. A transform over an expensive function runs it again each pass; materialize with ranges::to if you iterate many times.

docs.title: Generators of values
docs.text:
std::views::iota(1, 11) counts; std::views::iota(1) is infinite — combine with take. std::views::istream<int>(in) reads from a stream lazily.

Pro tip: debugging

If a pipeline won't compile, build it up one adaptor at a time. Ranges errors are long, but the first "constraints not satisfied" line usually names the culprit view.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Views are lazy, composable with |, and don't own their data.
  • C++23 adds ranges::to, zip, enumerate, chunk, slide and more.
  • Mind laziness: dangling views, caching in filter, recomputation on re-iteration.
  • Range algorithms on temporaries return std::ranges::dangling to prevent use-after-free.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. When does the work in takes | views::filter(f) | views::transform(g) happen?

Show answer

Lazily, element by element, as you iterate the resulting view — nothing is computed when the pipeline is built.

Q2. How do you turn a view into a std::vector in C++23?

Show answer

view | std::ranges::to<std::vector>().

Q3. Why does std::ranges::find(std::vector<int>{1,2,3}, 2) return std::ranges::dangling?

Show answer

The argument is a temporary non-borrowed range; an iterator into it would dangle after the full expression, so the library returns a placeholder type that can't be dereferenced.

docs.title: Lesson 11.4: Utilities: pair, tuple, apply, function objects, and friends
docs.text: C++23 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: The <utility>, <tuple> and <functional> headers are full of small tools that remove boilerplate: returning several values, calling a function with arguments stored in a tuple, flipping a predicate, resetting a member while returning its old value. Individually tiny; together they make code noticeably cleaner.

docs.title: Pairs and tuples
docs.text:
std::tuple<int, std::string, double> groups values without naming a struct. Access with std::get<0>(t) or std::get<std::string>(t) (if the type is unique) — or, better, structured bindings. Honest advice: if the tuple escapes a small scope, a named struct with named fields is clearer.

std::tie(a, b) = f(); assigns into existing variables; std::tie(x.a, x.b) < std::tie(y.a, y.b) was the pre-<=> way to write lexicographic comparisons.

docs.title: std::apply
docs.text:
Calls a function with a tuple's elements as arguments — the bridge between stored arguments and calls (used by thread pools and deferred tasks).

examples/week11/lesson04.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::tuple<int, std::string, double> parse_line() { return {7, "So What", 562.5}; }

struct Mixer {
    Mixer(int ch, std::string n) : channels{ch}, name{std::move(n)} {}
    int channels; std::string name;
};

enum class Codec : unsigned char { pcm = 1, opus = 2 };

void bump(int& x) { ++x; }

int main() {
    auto [id, title, secs] = parse_line();
    std::cout << id << ' ' << title << ' ' << secs << '\n';

    auto t = parse_line();
    std::cout << std::get<std::string>(t) << " / " << std::get<0>(t) << '\n';
    auto bigger = std::tuple_cat(t, std::make_tuple('x'));
    std::cout << "tuple_cat size: " << std::tuple_size_v<decltype(bigger)> << '\n';

    int a = 0; std::string b;
    std::tie(a, b, std::ignore) = parse_line();
    std::cout << "tie: " << a << ' ' << b << '\n';

    auto args = std::make_tuple(3, 4);
    std::cout << "apply: " << std::apply(std::plus<>{}, args) << '\n';
    auto m = std::make_from_tuple<Mixer>(std::make_tuple(2, std::string{"main"}));
    std::cout << "make_from_tuple: " << m.name << ' ' << m.channels << '\n';

    std::vector<int> v{5, 2, 8, 1};
    std::ranges::sort(v, std::greater<>{});
    auto is_even = [](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; };
    std::cout << "first odd: " << *std::ranges::find_if(v, std::not_fn(is_even)) << '\n';

    int counter = 10;
    int old = std::exchange(counter, 0);
    std::cout << "exchange: old " << old << " new " << counter << '\n';
    std::cout << "to_underlying(opus) = " << static_cast<int>(std::to_underlying(Codec::opus)) << '\n';

    int n = 1;
    auto f = std::bind_front(bump, std::ref(n));   // without std::ref, bump would modify a copy
    f(); f();
    std::cout << "n after ref binding: " << n << '\n';
}

Output:

7 So What 562.5
So What / 7
tuple_cat size: 4
tie: 7 So What
apply: 7
make_from_tuple: main 2
first odd: 5
exchange: old 10 new 0
to_underlying(opus) = 2
n after ref binding: 3

docs.title: Function objects
docs.text: std::plus<>, std::less<>, std::greater<> (the <> forms are transparent and generic). C++20 adds std::ranges::less (concept-constrained) and std::identity (the default projection). std::not_fn(pred) negates a predicate.

docs.title: Small helpers
docs.text:
• std::exchange(x, new) — set and return the old value: perfect for move constructors.
  • std::as_const(x) — get a const reference (call const overloads).
  • std::to_underlying(e) (C++23) — enum to its underlying integer.
  • std::ref(x) — pass by reference through APIs that copy (like std::thread or std::bind).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Use tuples locally and structured bindings to unpack; prefer named structs for public APIs.
  • std::apply calls a function with a tuple's elements; make_from_tuple constructs an object.
  • Transparent function objects (std::less<>) and std::not_fn replace small lambdas.
  • std::exchange, std::as_const, std::to_underlying and std::ref remove common boilerplate.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does std::exchange(x, 0) return?

Show answer

The old value of x; x is set to 0.

Q2. Why is std::ref(n) needed in std::bind_front(bump, std::ref(n))?

Show answer

bind_front stores copies of its arguments; std::ref stores a reference wrapper so bump modifies the original n.

Q3. When does std::get<std::string>(t) fail to compile?

Show answer

When the tuple has zero or more than one element of type std::string.

docs.title: Lesson 11.5: Generators and lazy sequences with std::generator (C++23)
docs.text: C++23 · about 9 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Some sequences are easiest to describe as a loop that produces values one at a time: walk a directory tree, read packets until EOF, generate an infinite stream of test tones. std::generator lets you write that loop with co_yield and hand it out as a range that callers can pipe through views. It's a preview of coroutines, which Week 14 explains properly.

docs.title: Writing a generator
docs.text:
std::generator<int> fibonacci() {
    int a = 0, b = 1;
    while (true) { co_yield a; a = std::exchange(b, a + b); }
}
for (int x : fibonacci() | std::views::take(10)) ...

The function body runs only as far as needed: each co_yield suspends it until the caller asks for the next value. Infinite sequences are fine as long as the consumer stops.

examples/week11/lesson05.cpp
#include <generator>
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::generator<long long> fibonacci() {
    long long a = 0, b = 1;
    while (true) {
        co_yield a;
        a = std::exchange(b, a + b);
    }
}

std::generator<std::string> packets(std::vector<std::string> wire) {   // by value: no dangling
    for (auto& p : wire) {
        if (p == "EOF") co_return;
        co_yield "pkt:" + p;
    }
}

struct Node { std::string name; std::vector<Node> children; };

std::generator<const std::string&> walk(const Node& n) {
    co_yield n.name;
    for (const auto& c : n.children) co_yield std::ranges::elements_of(walk(c));
}

int main() {
    for (auto x : fibonacci() | std::views::drop(5) | std::views::take(5)) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
    for (const auto& p : packets({"a", "b", "EOF", "c"})) std::cout << p << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
    Node root{"root", {{"drums", {{"kick", {}}, {"snare", {}}}}, {"bass", {}}}};
    for (const auto& name : walk(root)) std::cout << name << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

5 8 13 21 34 
pkt:a pkt:b 
root drums kick snare bass

docs.title: Recursive generators
docs.text: co_yield std::ranges::elements_of(child_generator()); yields everything from a nested generator — handy for tree traversals.

docs.title: Support status (honest)
docs.text:
std::generator is C++23 and is implemented in GCC 14's libstdc++, and in MSVC. libc++ (used by Clang on macOS and by our local test compiler) did not ship it at the time of writing, so this example is marked "may be unsupported": our CI compiles and runs it with GCC. If your toolchain lacks it, Week 14 shows how to write a minimal generator yourself.

Lifetime pitfall

A generator that takes parameters by reference keeps referring to them while suspended. Passing a temporary (gen(std::string{"x"})) leaves a dangling reference after the first suspension. Take coroutine parameters by value.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::generator<T> turns a co_yield loop into a lazy input range.
  • Generators compose with views; infinite generators are fine if the consumer stops.
  • std::ranges::elements_of yields from nested generators (recursion).
  • Take generator parameters by value; library support is still uneven (GCC 14+, MSVC).

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What happens at co_yield a;?

Show answer

The generator produces a to the consumer and suspends; it resumes from that point when the consumer asks for the next value.

Q2. Why is std::generator<int> g(const std::string& s) risky?

Show answer

The coroutine may outlive the referenced argument (e.g. a temporary), leaving a dangling reference when resumed.

Q3. Is a generator a forward range?

Show answer

No — it's an input range: single-pass; you can iterate it only once.

docs.title: Week 11 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 11.1) What's the complexity of nth_element?

Show answer

O(n) on average.

Q2. (from 11.1) Why is [](int a, int b){ return a <= b; } a broken comparator?

Show answer

It's not irreflexive (comp(a, a) is true), so it's not a strict weak ordering; std::sort may misbehave or read out of bounds.

Q3. (from 11.2) What's wrong with std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) for std::vector<double>?

Show answer

The accumulator is int, so each partial sum is converted to int — the result is truncated.

Q4. (from 11.2) Why must you sort before std::unique to remove all duplicates?

Show answer

unique only collapses consecutive equal elements.

Q5. (from 11.3) When does the work in takes | views::filter(f) | views::transform(g) happen?

Show answer

Lazily, element by element, as you iterate the resulting view — nothing is computed when the pipeline is built.

Q6. (from 11.3) How do you turn a view into a std::vector in C++23?

Show answer

view | std::ranges::to<std::vector>().

Q7. (from 11.4) What does std::exchange(x, 0) return?

Show answer

The old value of x; x is set to 0.

Q8. (from 11.4) Why is std::ref(n) needed in std::bind_front(bump, std::ref(n))?

Show answer

bind_front stores copies of its arguments; std::ref stores a reference wrapper so bump modifies the original n.

Q9. (from 11.5) What happens at co_yield a;?

Show answer

The generator produces a to the consumer and suspends; it resumes from that point when the consumer asks for the next value.

Q10. (from 11.5) Why is std::generator<int> g(const std::string& s) risky?

Show answer

The coroutine may outlive the referenced argument (e.g. a temporary), leaving a dangling reference when resumed.

docs.title: Week 12: The standard library III: memory, text, files, and time
docs.text:
This week covers the parts of the standard library you'll touch in every real program: smart pointers and allocators for memory, std::format/std::print for text, <filesystem> for files, <chrono> for time, plus a tour of the remaining utility headers. Lots of APIs, so we focus on idioms and pitfalls.

# Lesson Standard Length 12.1 unique_ptr and custom deleters C++20 11 min 12.2 shared_ptr, weak_ptr, and ownership graphs C++20 11 min 12.3 Allocators and polymorphic memory resources (pmr) C++20 11 min 12.4 Text: std::format, std::print, iostreams, charconv, and Unicode C++23 13 min 12.5 std::filesystem C++20 10 min 12.6 std::chrono: durations, clocks, calendars, and time zones C++20 12 min 12.7 A tour of the rest: random, regex, math, bits, limits, and more C++23 12 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 12 programming assignment: A media library scanner
docs.text:
Write a tool that scans a directory tree for audio files (.wav, .flac, .mp3), and prints a report: count per extension, total size, and the 3 largest files — formatted as an aligned table with std::println.

Create a test directory under fs::temp_directory_path() with a few files of known sizes, run the scan, then remove it. Use error_code overloads for cleanup, and sort results for deterministic output.

Reference solution examples/week12/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdint>
#include <filesystem>
#include <fstream>
#include <map>
#include <print>
#include <ranges>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>
#include <vector>

namespace fs = std::filesystem;

struct FileInfo { std::string rel; std::uintmax_t size; };

int main() {
    const fs::path root = fs::temp_directory_path() / "cpp_course_scan";
    std::error_code ec;
    fs::remove_all(root, ec);
    fs::create_directories(root / "album1");
    fs::create_directories(root / "album2");
    struct Make { const char* name; std::size_t size; };
    for (auto [name, size] : {Make{"album1/a.wav", 4000}, Make{"album1/b.flac", 2500}, Make{"album2/c.mp3", 900},
                              Make{"album2/d.wav", 6000}, Make{"album2/notes.txt", 100}}) {
        std::ofstream{root / name, std::ios::binary} << std::string(size, 'x');
    }

    std::map<std::string, int> per_ext;
    std::vector<FileInfo> files;
    std::uintmax_t total = 0;
    for (const auto& e : fs::recursive_directory_iterator(root, ec)) {
        if (!e.is_regular_file()) continue;
        auto ext = e.path().extension().string();
        if (ext != ".wav" && ext != ".flac" && ext != ".mp3") continue;
        ++per_ext[ext];
        files.push_back({fs::relative(e.path(), root).generic_string(), e.file_size()});
        total += e.file_size();
    }
    std::ranges::sort(files, [](const FileInfo& a, const FileInfo& b) { return a.size != b.size ? a.size > b.size : a.rel < b.rel; });

    std::println("{:<8}{:>6}", "ext", "count");
    for (const auto& [ext, n] : per_ext) std::println("{:<8}{:>6}", ext, n);
    std::println("total: {} files, {} bytes", files.size(), total);
    std::println("largest:");
    for (const auto& f : files | std::views::take(3)) std::println("  {:<16}{:>8}", f.rel, f.size);

    fs::remove_all(root, ec);
    std::println("cleanup ok: {}", !ec);
}

Output:

ext      count
.flac        1
.mp3         1
.wav         2
total: 4 files, 13400 bytes
largest:
  album2/d.wav        6000
  album1/a.wav        4000
  album1/b.flac       2500
cleanup ok: true

docs.title: Lesson 12.1: unique_ptr and custom deleters
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Back in Week 3 we saw how raw new/delete leaks and double-frees. std::unique_ptr fixes that with zero overhead: it's exactly one pointer, and its destructor calls delete. With a custom deleter it manages any resource — FILE*, a codec handle from a C library, an OpenGL texture. It should be your default for owning heap objects.

docs.title: Unique ownership
docs.text:
auto codec = std::make_unique<Codec>(48000);   // owns the Codec
auto other = std::move(codec);                 // ownership transferred; codec is now null

unique_ptr is move-only, so "who owns this" is visible in the code: you can't accidentally share it.

docs.title: Custom deleters for C resources
docs.text:
struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept { std::fclose(f); } };
using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;

A stateless function-object deleter keeps sizeof(File) == sizeof(FILE*). A function-pointer deleter adds a pointer's worth of size. C++23's std::out_ptr adapts a unique_ptr to C APIs that return a resource through a T** out-parameter.

examples/week12/lesson01.cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Codec {
    explicit Codec(int rate) : rate{rate} { std::cout << "  Codec(" << rate << ") opened\n"; }
    ~Codec() { std::cout << "  Codec(" << rate << ") closed\n"; }
    int rate;
};

struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept { if (f) { std::fclose(f); std::cout << "  file closed\n"; } } };
using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;

// A C-style API that returns a resource through an out-parameter
int c_open_codec(int rate, Codec** out) { *out = new Codec{rate}; return 0; }

void use(const Codec& c) { std::cout << "  using codec at " << c.rate << '\n'; }      // borrows
void sink(std::unique_ptr<Codec> c) { std::cout << "  sink took " << c->rate << '\n'; } // takes ownership

int main() {
    {
        auto a = std::make_unique<Codec>(44100);
        use(*a);
        auto b = std::move(a);                                   // transfer
        std::cout << "  a is " << (a ? "set" : "null") << '\n';
        sink(std::move(b));                                      // destroyed at the end of sink
        std::cout << "after sink\n";
    }
    {
        File f{std::tmpfile()};
        std::fputs("hello", f.get());
        std::cout << "  sizeof(File)==sizeof(FILE*)? " << std::boolalpha << (sizeof(File) == sizeof(std::FILE*)) << '\n';
    }
    {
        std::unique_ptr<Codec> c;
        c_open_codec(96000, std::out_ptr(c));                    // C++23
        std::cout << "  out_ptr filled codec at " << c->rate << '\n';
    }
    auto buf = std::make_unique_for_overwrite<char[]>(4096);    // no zeroing: we'll overwrite it
    buf[0] = 'x';
    std::cout << "buffer starts with " << buf[0] << '\n';
}

Output:

  Codec(44100) opened
  using codec at 44100
  a is null
  sink took 44100
  Codec(44100) closed
after sink
  sizeof(File)==sizeof(FILE*)? true
  file closed
  Codec(96000) opened
  out_ptr filled codec at 96000
  Codec(96000) closed
buffer starts with x

docs.title: Passing smart pointers (C++ Core Guidelines R.30–R.37)
docs.text: You want to... Parameter type just use the object T& or T* (nullable) — not a smart pointer take ownership std::unique_ptr<T> by value maybe reseat the caller's pointer std::unique_ptr<T>& share ownership std::shared_ptr<T> by value

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Two unique_ptrs from the same raw pointer → double free.
  • unique_ptr<T> for an array allocated with new[] → use unique_ptr<T[]> (or better, std::vector).
  • release() gives up ownership without deleting — the caller must now free it.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • unique_ptr is zero-overhead exclusive ownership; transfer it with std::move.
  • Custom deleters manage any resource; stateless deleters add no size.
  • Pass T&/T* to functions that only use an object; pass unique_ptr by value to transfer ownership.
  • std::out_ptr (C++23) bridges smart pointers and C out-parameter APIs.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>) on a typical 64-bit platform?

Show answer

8 bytes — the same as a raw pointer (with the default deleter).

Q2. How should a function that only reads a Codec take it?

Show answer

By const Codec& (or const Codec* if null is allowed), not by smart pointer.

Q3. What does release() do?

Show answer

Returns the raw pointer and sets the unique_ptr to null without deleting; the caller becomes responsible for freeing it.

docs.title: Lesson 12.2: shared_ptr, weak_ptr, and ownership graphs
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Sometimes ownership really is shared: an audio buffer used by the player and the waveform view, and it should live as long as either needs it. std::shared_ptr counts owners and frees the object when the last one goes. It's convenient — and easy to overuse. Let's learn the cost, the cycle trap, and weak_ptr.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A shared_ptr is two pointers: one to the object, one to a control block holding the strong count, weak count and deleter. Copying increments the strong count atomically (thread-safe counting, not thread-safe object access). make_shared allocates object and control block together: one allocation, better locality.

docs.title: The cycle trap
docs.text:
struct Node { std::shared_ptr<Node> next; std::shared_ptr<Node> prev; };   // a <-> b

If a.next = b and b.prev = a, neither count reaches zero — leak. Make the back-edge a std::weak_ptr: it observes without owning. Call lock() to get a temporary shared_ptr (null if the object is gone).

examples/week12/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Buffer {
    std::string name;
    explicit Buffer(std::string n) : name{std::move(n)} {}
    ~Buffer() { std::cout << "  ~Buffer(" << name << ")\n"; }
};

struct Track;
struct Album {
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Track>> tracks;     // owns tracks
    ~Album() { std::cout << "  ~Album\n"; }
};
struct Track {
    std::weak_ptr<Album> album;                     // back-edge: observes, doesn't own
    ~Track() { std::cout << "  ~Track\n"; }
};

class Session : public std::enable_shared_from_this<Session> {
public:
    std::shared_ptr<Session> self() { return shared_from_this(); }
};

int main() {
    {
        auto buf = std::make_shared<Buffer>("pcm");
        auto view = buf;                            // second owner
        std::cout << "use_count=" << buf.use_count() << '\n';
        buf.reset();
        std::cout << "after reset, view still alive: " << view->name << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "--- album with weak back-edges\n";
    {
        auto album = std::make_shared<Album>();
        auto t = std::make_shared<Track>();
        t->album = album;
        album->tracks.push_back(t);
        if (auto a = t->album.lock()) std::cout << "  track's album has " << a->tracks.size() << " track(s)\n";
    }                                               // everything freed: no cycle
    std::cout << "--- weak_ptr expiry\n";
    std::weak_ptr<Buffer> watcher;
    {
        auto b = std::make_shared<Buffer>("temp");
        watcher = b;
        std::cout << "  expired? " << std::boolalpha << watcher.expired() << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "  expired? " << watcher.expired() << '\n';

    auto s = std::make_shared<Session>();
    auto s2 = s->self();
    std::cout << "session owners: " << s.use_count() << '\n';

    struct Pair { int a = 1; int b = 2; };
    auto p = std::make_shared<Pair>();
    std::shared_ptr<int> just_b(p, &p->b);          // aliasing: shares p's ownership
    p.reset();
    std::cout << "aliased member still valid: " << *just_b << '\n';
}

Output:

use_count=2
after reset, view still alive: pcm
  ~Buffer(pcm)
--- album with weak back-edges
  track's album has 1 track(s)
  ~Album
  ~Track
--- weak_ptr expiry
  expired? false
  ~Buffer(temp)
  expired? true
session owners: 2
aliased member still valid: 2

docs.title: enable_shared_from_this
docs.text: Inside a member function you sometimes need a shared_ptr to this (e.g. to register a callback that keeps the object alive). Creating std::shared_ptr<T>(this) makes a second control block → double delete. Inherit std::enable_shared_from_this<T> and call shared_from_this() instead.

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Prefer unique_ptr; reach for shared_ptr only for genuinely shared lifetime. A unique_ptr converts to a shared_ptr later if needed.
  • Don't pass shared_ptr by value "just in case" — each copy is an atomic increment and decrement.
  • The aliasing constructor shares ownership of an object while pointing to one of its members.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • shared_ptr = object pointer + control block with atomic counts; make_shared allocates once.
  • Cycles of shared_ptr leak; use weak_ptr for back-edges and lock() to access.
  • Use enable_shared_from_this instead of shared_ptr<T>(this).
  • Prefer unique_ptr; don't pass shared_ptr by value unless you're sharing ownership.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Is shared_ptr thread-safe?

Show answer

The reference counting is (atomic); accessing the pointed-to object or assigning to the same shared_ptr instance from several threads is not (use std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> for the latter).

Q2. How does weak_ptr break a cycle?

Show answer

It doesn't contribute to the strong count, so the objects can be destroyed when external owners go away.

Q3. What goes wrong with return std::shared_ptr<Session>(this);?

Show answer

It creates a second, independent control block; both will delete the object — double free.

docs.title: Lesson 12.3: Allocators and polymorphic memory resources (pmr)
docs.text: C++20 · about 11 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: In a real-time audio callback you're not allowed to call malloc — it may take a lock and blow your 2 ms deadline. In a game, you want all per-frame allocations to come from one arena that's reset each frame. Allocators let you keep using std::vector and std::string while controlling where their memory comes from. C++17's pmr makes this practical.

docs.title: Classic allocators — and why they were painful
docs.text: Containers take an allocator template parameter: std::vector<int, MyAlloc<int>>. But the allocator is part of the type, so a vector<int, A> can't be passed where vector<int> is expected. That limited their use.

docs.title: std::pmr (C++17)
docs.text:
std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator holds a pointer to a std::pmr::memory_resource and forwards to it via virtual calls. std::pmr::vector<int> is one type regardless of the resource. The standard resources:

Resource Behaviour monotonic_buffer_resource bump-pointer arena; deallocate is a no-op; free all at once. Very fast. unsynchronized_pool_resource pools of fixed-size blocks; single-threaded synchronized_pool_resource same, thread-safe new_delete_resource() the global heap null_memory_resource() throws on any allocation — great as an upstream to prove you never hit the heap examples/week12/lesson03.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

static std::size_t g_allocs = 0;
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {                     // replaced global operator new: count calls
    ++g_allocs;
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

int main() {
    std::size_t before = g_allocs;
    {
        std::vector<std::string> v;
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) v.push_back("a fairly long string number " + std::to_string(i));
    }
    std::cout << "std::vector<std::string>: " << (g_allocs - before > 0 ? "heap allocations happened" : "no heap") << '\n';

    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, 4096> stack_buf;
    before = g_allocs;
    {
        std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena{stack_buf.data(), stack_buf.size(), std::pmr::null_memory_resource()};
        std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> v{&arena};
        v.reserve(4);
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
            std::pmr::string s{"a fairly long string number ", &arena};
            s += static_cast<char>('0' + i);
            v.push_back(std::move(s));
        }
        std::cout << "pmr in arena: " << v.size() << " strings, last = \"" << v.back() << "\"\n";
        std::cout << "element uses the same arena? " << std::boolalpha
                  << (v.back().get_allocator().resource() == &arena) << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "global allocations during pmr block: " << (g_allocs - before) << '\n';

    try {
        std::array<std::byte, 16> tiny;
        std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource small{tiny.data(), tiny.size(), std::pmr::null_memory_resource()};
        std::pmr::vector<int> v{&small};
        v.resize(100);                                   // needs more than 16 bytes
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
        std::cout << "null_memory_resource caught an overflow of the arena\n";
    }
}

Output:

std::vector<std::string>: heap allocations happened
pmr in arena: 4 strings, last = "a fairly long string number 3"
element uses the same arena? true
global allocations during pmr block: 0
null_memory_resource caught an overflow of the arena

The example builds a vector of strings inside a stack buffer and proves no heap allocation happens by using null_memory_resource() as the fallback. Note that pmr containers propagate the allocator to their elements (pmr::string inside pmr::vector uses the same arena).

docs.title: Replacing global operator new
docs.text:
You can replace operator new/operator delete globally to count or trace allocations — useful in tests ("this function must not allocate"). The example counts global allocations.

Pitfall

A monotonic arena never reuses memory until it's destroyed or release()d. Great for per-frame or per-request work; bad for long-lived containers that grow and shrink.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Allocators control where container memory comes from; classic ones are part of the type.
  • std::pmr containers share one type and take a memory_resource* at run time.
  • monotonic_buffer_resource is a fast arena; null_memory_resource proves no heap fallback.
  • Replacing global operator new lets tests count or forbid allocations.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't you pass std::vector<int, MyAlloc<int>> to a function taking const std::vector<int>&?

Show answer

The allocator is a template parameter, so they're different types.

Q2. What does deallocate do on a monotonic_buffer_resource?

Show answer

Nothing — memory is only reclaimed when the resource is released or destroyed.

Q3. Why use null_memory_resource() as an upstream?

Show answer

Any allocation that doesn't fit the buffer throws bad_alloc instead of silently using the heap, proving the code stays within the arena.

docs.title: Lesson 12.4: Text: std::format, std::print, iostreams, charconv, and Unicode
docs.text: C++23 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Printing a table of meter readings with aligned columns used to mean either printf (fast, type-unsafe) or iostreams (type-safe, verbose, slow, stateful). C++20's std::format and C++23's std::print give you Python-style formatting that's type-safe, checked at compile time, and fast. We'll also cover the fastest number parsing in the library (from_chars) and the state of Unicode.

docs.title: std::format and std::print
docs.text:
std::println("{:<10} {:>8.2f} dB", name, level);    // left-align 10, right-align 8 with 2 decimals

Format spec mini-language: {index:fill align sign # 0 width .precision type}. Examples: {:08.3f}, {:#x}, {:^20}, {:+}. The format string is checked at compile time: a mismatch like {:d} with a string is a compile error. For runtime format strings use std::vformat / std::runtime_format (C++26).

C++23 formats ranges too: std::println("{}", vec) prints [1, 2, 3].

docs.title: Custom types
docs.text:
Specialize std::formatter<T>: implement parse (or inherit from an existing formatter) and format.

examples/week12/lesson04.cpp
#include <charconv>
#include <format>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <print>
#include <ranges>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <system_error>
#include <vector>

struct Level { double db; };

template <>
struct std::formatter<Level> : std::formatter<double> {        // reuse double's spec parsing
    auto format(const Level& l, std::format_context& ctx) const {
        auto out = std::formatter<double>::format(l.db, ctx);
        return std::format_to(out, " dB");
    }
};

int main() {
    std::println("{:<8}|{:>8}|{:^8}|", "left", "right", "mid");
    std::println("{:08.3f} {:+d} {:#x} {:#b} {:e}", 3.14159, 42, 255, 5, 12345.678);
    std::println("{1} before {0}", "world", "hello");
    std::println("{:>10.1f}", Level{-3.25});
    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
#if defined(__cpp_lib_format_ranges)
    std::println("ranges: {}", v);                  // C++23 range formatting (GCC 15+, Clang 16+)
#else
    std::println("ranges: [{}, {}, {}]", v[0], v[1], v[2]);   // fallback for GCC 14
#endif
    std::string s = std::format("{}-{:03}", "take", 7);
    std::cout << s << '\n';

    std::cout << std::hex << 255 << ' ' << 16 << std::dec << ' ' << 16 << '\n';   // hex was sticky
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << 2.0 / 3 << '\n';
    std::cout.unsetf(std::ios::floatfield);

    std::istringstream in{"48000 2 stereo"};
    int rate = 0, ch = 0; std::string mode;
    in >> rate >> ch >> mode;
    std::cout << rate << '/' << ch << '/' << mode << '\n';

    std::string_view text = "1234abc";
    int value = 0;
    auto [ptr, ec] = std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value);
    std::cout << "parsed " << value << ", stopped at '" << ptr << "', ok=" << (ec == std::errc{}) << '\n';
    char buf[32];
    auto res = std::to_chars(buf, buf + sizeof buf, 0.1 + 0.2);       // shortest round-trip repr
    std::cout << "to_chars(0.1+0.2) = " << std::string_view(buf, static_cast<std::size_t>(res.ptr - buf)) << '\n';

    std::u8string_view word = u8"caf\u00e9";
    std::cout << "u8\"cafe-acute\" has " << word.size() << " bytes for 4 characters\n";
}

Output:

left    |   right|  mid   |
0003.142 +42 0xff 0b101 1.234568e+04
hello before world
      -3.2 dB
ranges: [1, 2, 3]
take-007
ff 10 16
0.67
48000/2/stereo
parsed 1234, stopped at 'abc', ok=1
to_chars(0.1+0.2) = 0.30000000000000004
u8"cafe-acute" has 5 bytes for 4 characters

docs.title: iostreams: still everywhere
docs.text: You'll still use std::cout, std::ifstream and std::stringstream. Know their pitfalls: manipulators like std::hex and std::setprecision are sticky (they stay set), std::endl flushes (slow in loops — use '\n'), and std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false) speeds up console I/O when you don't mix with C stdio.

docs.title: from_chars / to_chars
docs.text: Locale-independent, non-allocating, non-throwing, and the fastest conversions available. Always check the returned ec and the end pointer.

docs.title: Unicode: the honest version
docs.text: std::string holds bytes; it doesn't know about characters. u8"..." literals are char8_t (C++20), which doesn't convert implicitly to char. size() counts bytes, not characters. For real text processing (normalization, case folding, grapheme clusters) use a library such as ICU. std::print writes UTF-8 correctly to Unicode-capable terminals, which iostreams on Windows historically did not.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • std::format/std::println give type-safe, compile-time-checked, Python-style formatting.
  • Specialize std::formatter<T> (often by inheriting an existing one) for your types.
  • iostream manipulators are sticky; prefer '\n' over std::endl in loops.
  • from_chars/to_chars are the fastest, locale-free conversions; std::string is bytes, not characters.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What happens if you write std::format("{:d}", std::string{"x"})?

Show answer

A compile-time error: the format string is checked against the argument types.

Q2. Why can std::endl make output slow?

Show answer

It flushes the stream every time; in a loop that defeats buffering.

Q3. How many bytes does u8"é" (one character, U+00E9) use, excluding the terminator?

Show answer

Two bytes in UTF-8.

docs.title: Lesson 12.5: std::filesystem
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Batch-converting a folder of WAV files, cleaning up old logs, finding every .json preset under a directory — before C++17 these needed POSIX or Win32 calls. std::filesystem makes them portable. It also has a few sharp edges around errors and races that we'll point out.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: std::filesystem::path handles separators and pieces: p / "sub" / "file.wav", p.filename(), p.stem(), p.extension(), p.parent_path(), p.replace_extension(".flac"). It's just a string manipulation type — a path doesn't have to exist.

docs.title: Walking directories
docs.text:
directory_iterator lists one directory; recursive_directory_iterator walks the tree. Iteration order is unspecified — sort if you need determinism.

examples/week12/lesson05.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <filesystem>
#include <fstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <string>
#include <system_error>
#include <vector>

namespace fs = std::filesystem;

int main() {
    const fs::path root = fs::temp_directory_path() / "cpp_course_fs_demo";
    fs::remove_all(root);                                          // start clean
    fs::create_directories(root / "presets" / "drums");

    for (const char* name : {"presets/kick.json", "presets/drums/snare.json", "presets/readme.txt"}) {
        std::ofstream out{root / name, std::ios::binary};
        out << "{\"name\": \"" << fs::path{name}.stem().string() << "\"}";
    }

    fs::path p = root / "presets" / "kick.json";
    std::cout << "filename=" << p.filename() << " stem=" << p.stem() << " ext=" << p.extension() << '\n';
    std::cout << "as flac: " << fs::path{p}.replace_extension(".flac").filename() << '\n';

    std::vector<std::string> found;
    for (const auto& entry : fs::recursive_directory_iterator(root))
        if (entry.is_regular_file() && entry.path().extension() == ".json")
            found.push_back(fs::relative(entry.path(), root).generic_string());
    std::ranges::sort(found);                                       // iteration order is unspecified
    for (const auto& f : found) std::cout << "json: " << f << '\n';

    std::ifstream in{p, std::ios::binary};
    std::string content{std::istreambuf_iterator<char>{in}, {}};
    std::cout << "content: " << content << " (" << fs::file_size(p) << " bytes)\n";

    std::error_code ec;
    fs::remove(root / "does-not-exist.txt", ec);                    // no TOCTOU, no exception
    std::cout << "remove missing file -> error? " << std::boolalpha << static_cast<bool>(ec) << '\n';
    fs::rename(root / "presets" / "readme.txt", root / "README.txt");
    std::cout << "renamed exists: " << fs::exists(root / "README.txt") << '\n';
    std::cout << "removed " << fs::remove_all(root) << " entries\n";
}

Output:

filename="kick.json" stem="kick" ext=".json"
as flac: "kick.flac"
json: presets/drums/snare.json
json: presets/kick.json
content: {"name": "kick"} (16 bytes)
remove missing file -> error? false
renamed exists: true
removed 6 entries

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Almost every function has two overloads: one throws std::filesystem::filesystem_error, one takes std::error_code& (Week 9). Use the error_code form when failure is expected (e.g. "delete if exists").

docs.title: The TOCTOU trap
docs.text:
if (fs::exists(p)) fs::remove(p);   // another process may delete p in between ("time of check to time of use")

Just do the operation and handle the error: fs::remove(p, ec);. Filesystems are shared, concurrent state.

docs.title: Reading and writing files
docs.text: std::ofstream out{path, std::ios::binary} / std::ifstream. Streams don't throw by default — check if (!in) or enable exceptions with in.exceptions(...). For a whole file: std::string data{std::istreambuf_iterator<char>{in}, {}};.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • fs::path composes and dissects paths portably; it doesn't need to exist.
  • Directory iteration order is unspecified; sort when you need determinism.
  • Use error_code overloads when failure is normal; avoid check-then-act (TOCTOU) races.
  • Streams don't throw by default — check their state.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's wrong with if (fs::exists(p)) fs::remove(p);?

Show answer

A race: the file can change between the check and the removal; just call fs::remove(p, ec) and inspect ec.

Q2. Does recursive_directory_iterator visit files in alphabetical order?

Show answer

Not necessarily — the order is unspecified.

Q3. What does fs::remove (error_code overload) report for a missing file?

Show answer

It returns false and leaves ec clear — a missing file isn't an error for remove.

docs.title: Lesson 12.6: std::chrono: durations, clocks, calendars, and time zones
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: "Wait 50 ms." "How long did encoding take?" "What's the date three months from now?" "What time is this UTC timestamp in India?" Getting time wrong produces subtle bugs: mixing up seconds and milliseconds, using a wall clock that jumps for measuring intervals, or doing time-zone math by hand. <chrono> makes units part of the type, so many of those bugs become compile errors.

docs.title: Durations carry units
docs.text:
using namespace std::chrono_literals;
auto timeout = 250ms;
std::chrono::seconds s = 3min;          // OK: lossless conversion is implicit
std::chrono::seconds t = 1500ms;        // compile error: lossy! use duration_cast/floor/round

docs.title: Pick the right clock
docs.text: Clock Use for steady_clock measuring intervals and timeouts (never goes backwards) system_clock wall-clock time, timestamps, dates high_resolution_clock usually an alias of one of the above — don't rely on it

docs.title: Calendars and time zones (C++20)
docs.text:
2026y/std::chrono::March/31 is a year_month_day. Adding months to the 31st gives an invalid date that you must handle explicitly (clamp to last day, or overflow into the next month) — chrono makes you choose. zoned_time converts between UTC and IANA time zones using the time-zone database.

examples/week12/lesson06.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <format>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    using namespace std::chrono_literals;

    auto timeout = 250ms;
    seconds s = 3min;                                       // lossless: implicit
    auto t = duration_cast<seconds>(1500ms);                 // lossy: explicit (truncates)
    std::cout << timeout.count() << "ms, " << s.count() << "s, " << t.count() << "s, round="
              << round<seconds>(1500ms).count() << "s\n";
    std::cout << std::format("{} + {} = {}\n", 1h, 30min, 1h + 30min);

    auto start = steady_clock::now();
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(20ms);
    auto elapsed = duration_cast<milliseconds>(steady_clock::now() - start);
    std::cout << "slept at least 20ms? " << std::boolalpha << (elapsed >= 20ms) << '\n';

    year_month_day release = 2026y / January / 31;
    auto next_month = release + months{1};                   // 2026-02-31: not a valid date
    std::cout << "valid? " << next_month.ok() << '\n';
    auto clamped = next_month.year() / next_month.month() / last;
    std::cout << "clamped to " << year_month_day{clamped} << '\n';
    auto overflowed = year_month_day{sys_days{next_month}};  // normalizes into March
    std::cout << "overflowed to " << overflowed << '\n';
    std::cout << "weekday of 2026-11-03: " << weekday{sys_days{2026y / November / 3}} << '\n';
    auto days_left = sys_days{2026y / December / 25} - sys_days{2026y / November / 3};
    std::cout << "days until 2026-12-25: " << days_left.count() << '\n';

    sys_seconds stamp = sys_days{2026y / November / 3} + 9h + 30min;
    std::cout << std::format("UTC stamp: {:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}\n", stamp);
}

Output:

250ms, 180s, 1s, round=2s
1h + 30min = 90min
slept at least 20ms? true
valid? false
clamped to 2026-02-28
overflowed to 2026-03-03
weekday of 2026-11-03: Tue
days until 2026-12-25: 52
UTC stamp: 2026-11-03 09:30

Time-zone support needs the tz database at run time and library support (GCC 14 and MSVC have it; libc++ support is recent/partial), so that part is a separate example marked "may be unsupported":

examples/week12/lesson06_tz.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <format>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    sys_seconds stamp = sys_days{2026y / November / 3} + 9h + 30min;   // 09:30 UTC
    zoned_time india{"Asia/Kolkata", stamp};
    zoned_time ny{"America/New_York", stamp};
    std::cout << std::format("India:    {:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z}\n", india);
    std::cout << std::format("New York: {:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z}\n", ny);
}

Output:

India:    2026-11-03 15:00 IST
New York: 2026-11-03 04:30 EST

Pro tip

Store and transmit timestamps in UTC (system_clock / sys_seconds); convert to local time zones only for display.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Durations encode units; lossy conversions require duration_cast, floor, ceil or round.
  • Use steady_clock for intervals, system_clock for timestamps.
  • C++20 calendar types make invalid dates explicit; you choose how to normalize.
  • Store UTC; convert with zoned_time only for display (needs tzdb support).

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why does std::chrono::seconds s = 1500ms; not compile?

Show answer

The conversion would lose information (truncate), so it must be explicit.

Q2. Which clock should measure how long a function takes?

Show answer

std::chrono::steady_clock — it's monotonic and unaffected by wall-clock adjustments.

Q3. What is 2026y/January/31 + months{1}?

Show answer

2026-02-31, an invalid year_month_day (ok() is false) that you must clamp or normalize.

docs.title: Lesson 12.7: A tour of the rest: random, regex, math, bits, limits, and more
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: The standard library has many smaller headers that each solve one problem well — and a couple that are famously slow or awkward. This lesson is a guided tour: what each is for, the idiomatic call, and the one pitfall to remember.

docs.title: <random>: never rand()
docs.text:
std::mt19937 rng{std::random_device{}()};          // engine, seeded
std::uniform_int_distribution<int> die{1, 6};      // distribution
int roll = die(rng);

rand() % 6 is biased and low quality. Engines are deterministic given a seed (great for reproducible tests); distributions shape the output. Note: distributions are not guaranteed to produce identical sequences across standard library implementations — only engines are.

docs.title: <regex>: correct but slow
docs.text: std::regex works, but common implementations are slow and can blow the stack on long inputs. Fine for config parsing; for hot paths use a dedicated library (RE2, PCRE2, CTRE) or hand-written parsing.

docs.title: Math, constants and limits
docs.text: <numbers> (C++20) gives std::numbers::pi, e, sqrt2... <cmath> has std::hypot, std::lerp (C++20), special functions (std::beta, std::cyl_bessel_j). std::numeric_limits<T> tells you max(), lowest(), epsilon(), infinity(). Remember: numeric_limits<float>::min() is the smallest positive normal value, not the most negative!

docs.title: Debugging helpers
docs.text:
std::source_location::current() (C++20) gives file, line and function — a macro-free logging helper. std::stacktrace (C++23) captures a call stack (library support varies; GCC needs -lstdc++exp), so it's mentioned but not compiled here.

examples/week12/lesson07.cpp
#include <bitset>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>
#include <numbers>
#include <random>
#include <regex>
#include <source_location>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

void log(std::string_view msg, std::source_location loc = std::source_location::current()) {
    std::cout << "[" << loc.function_name() << ":" << loc.line() << "] " << msg << '\n';
}

int main() {
    std::mt19937 rng{12345};                                   // fixed seed: reproducible engine
    std::mt19937 rng2{12345};
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same seed, same first value: " << (rng() == rng2()) << '\n';
    std::uniform_int_distribution<int> die{1, 6};
    int counts[7]{};
    for (int i = 0; i < 6000; ++i) ++counts[die(rng)];
    bool roughly_uniform = true;
    for (int f = 1; f <= 6; ++f) roughly_uniform = roughly_uniform && counts[f] > 850 && counts[f] < 1150;
    std::cout << "6000 rolls roughly uniform: " << roughly_uniform << '\n';

    std::regex tag{R"((\w+)=(\d+))"};
    std::string cfg = "rate=48000 bits=24 ch=2";
    for (std::sregex_iterator it{cfg.begin(), cfg.end(), tag}, end; it != end; ++it)
        std::cout << (*it)[1] << " -> " << (*it)[2] << "; ";
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::cout << "pi=" << std::numbers::pi << " hypot(3,4)=" << std::hypot(3.0, 4.0)
              << " lerp(0,10,0.25)=" << std::lerp(0.0, 10.0, 0.25) << '\n';
    std::cout << "int max=" << std::numeric_limits<int>::max()
              << " float min (smallest positive normal)=" << std::numeric_limits<float>::min()
              << " float lowest=" << std::numeric_limits<float>::lowest() << '\n';
    std::cout << "0.1+0.2==0.3? " << (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
              << ", within epsilon? " << (std::abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon()) << '\n';

    std::bitset<8> status{"10010110"};
    status.set(0);
    std::cout << "status=" << status << " count=" << status.count() << " bit7=" << status.test(7) << '\n';

    log("hello from source_location");
}

Output:

same seed, same first value: true
6000 rolls roughly uniform: true
rate -> 48000; bits -> 24; ch -> 2; 
pi=3.14159 hypot(3,4)=5 lerp(0,10,0.25)=2.5
int max=2147483647 float min (smallest positive normal)=1.17549e-38 float lowest=-3.40282e+38
0.1+0.2==0.3? false, within epsilon? true
status=10010111 count=5 bit7=true
[int main():45] hello from source_location

docs.title: std::bitset and <locale>
docs.text: std::bitset<N> is a fixed-size bit array with count(), test(), and string conversion — handy for flags and register maps. <locale> controls number formatting, character classification and collation; it's global, stateful and slow, which is why std::format and from_chars are locale-independent by default.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Use <random> engines + distributions; never rand() % n.
  • std::regex is correct but slow; avoid it in hot paths.
  • <numbers>, <cmath> and numeric_limits cover constants, math and type limits (min() is positive for floats!).
  • source_location replaces __FILE__/__LINE__ macros; bitset handles flags.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is rand() % 6 a poor die?

Show answer

rand() is low-quality and % introduces bias when RAND_MAX+1 isn't a multiple of 6; use std::uniform_int_distribution with a good engine.

Q2. What is std::numeric_limits<float>::min()?

Show answer

The smallest positive normalized float (~1.18e-38), not the most negative value — that's lowest().

Q3. Are std::uniform_int_distribution results identical across GCC and Clang for the same seed?

Show answer

Not guaranteed — engines are specified exactly, but distribution algorithms are implementation-specific.

docs.title: Week 12 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 12.1) What's sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>) on a typical 64-bit platform?

Show answer

8 bytes — the same as a raw pointer (with the default deleter).

Q2. (from 12.1) How should a function that only reads a Codec take it?

Show answer

By const Codec& (or const Codec* if null is allowed), not by smart pointer.

Q3. (from 12.2) Is shared_ptr thread-safe?

Show answer

The reference counting is (atomic); accessing the pointed-to object or assigning to the same shared_ptr instance from several threads is not (use std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> for the latter).

Q4. (from 12.2) How does weak_ptr break a cycle?

Show answer

It doesn't contribute to the strong count, so the objects can be destroyed when external owners go away.

Q5. (from 12.3) Why can't you pass std::vector<int, MyAlloc<int>> to a function taking const std::vector<int>&?

Show answer

The allocator is a template parameter, so they're different types.

Q6. (from 12.3) What does deallocate do on a monotonic_buffer_resource?

Show answer

Nothing — memory is only reclaimed when the resource is released or destroyed.

Q7. (from 12.4) What happens if you write std::format("{:d}", std::string{"x"})?

Show answer

A compile-time error: the format string is checked against the argument types.

Q8. (from 12.4) Why can std::endl make output slow?

Show answer

It flushes the stream every time; in a loop that defeats buffering.

Q9. (from 12.5) What's wrong with if (fs::exists(p)) fs::remove(p);?

Show answer

A race: the file can change between the check and the removal; just call fs::remove(p, ec) and inspect ec.

Q10. (from 12.5) Does recursive_directory_iterator visit files in alphabetical order?

Show answer

Not necessarily — the order is unspecified.

Q11. (from 12.6) Why does std::chrono::seconds s = 1500ms; not compile?

Show answer

The conversion would lose information (truncate), so it must be explicit.

Q12. (from 12.6) Which clock should measure how long a function takes?

Show answer

std::chrono::steady_clock — it's monotonic and unaffected by wall-clock adjustments.

Q13. (from 12.7) Why is rand() % 6 a poor die?

Show answer

rand() is low-quality and % introduces bias when RAND_MAX+1 isn't a multiple of 6; use std::uniform_int_distribution with a good engine.

Q14. (from 12.7) What is std::numeric_limits<float>::min()?

Show answer

The smallest positive normalized float (~1.18e-38), not the most negative value — that's lowest().

docs.title: Week 13: Concurrency I: threads, locks, and synchronization
docs.text:
Your phone has 8 cores; a single-threaded program uses one. This week we learn to use the rest safely: starting threads, protecting shared data, waiting for events, and getting results back. Honest warning: concurrency bugs are the hardest bugs in software — they hide in testing and appear in production. Every example here runs under ThreadSanitizer in CI, and you should run yours under it too.

# Lesson Standard Length 13.1 Threads, jthread, and cooperative cancellation C++20 12 min 13.2 Data races, mutexes, and deadlock C++20 13 min 13.3 Condition variables and a thread-safe queue C++20 12 min 13.4 Futures, promises, async, and packaged_task C++20 10 min 13.5 Latches, barriers, semaphores, and thread_local C++20 10 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 13 programming assignment: Parallel file checksum
docs.text:
Compute a checksum (sum of bytes mod 2^32) of 64 simulated "files" (vectors of bytes generated deterministically) using a fixed number of worker threads pulling indices from a shared work queue. Use a std::latch to start all workers simultaneously, a mutex-protected result map, and print results in index order plus the grand total. Must be TSan-clean and give the same output as a sequential computation.

Reference solution examples/week13/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <atomic>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <latch>
#include <map>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::uint8_t> make_file(int id) {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> data(1000 + static_cast<std::size_t>(id) * 37);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < data.size(); ++i) data[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>((i * 31 + static_cast<std::size_t>(id)) & 0xFF);
    return data;
}
std::uint32_t checksum(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& d) {
    std::uint32_t s = 0;
    for (auto b : d) s += b;
    return s;
}

int main() {
    constexpr int files = 64, workers = 4;
    std::atomic<int> next{0};
    std::latch start{workers + 1};
    std::mutex m;
    std::map<int, std::uint32_t> results;
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> pool;
        for (int w = 0; w < workers; ++w)
            pool.emplace_back([&] {
                start.arrive_and_wait();
                for (int id; (id = next.fetch_add(1)) < files;) {
                    auto sum = checksum(make_file(id));
                    std::lock_guard lock{m};
                    results[id] = sum;
                }
            });
        start.arrive_and_wait();                      // release everyone at once
    }
    std::uint32_t total = 0, sequential = 0;
    for (auto [id, sum] : results) {
        if (id < 3 || id == files - 1) std::cout << "file " << id << ": " << sum << '\n';
        total += sum;
    }
    for (int id = 0; id < files; ++id) sequential += checksum(make_file(id));
    std::cout << results.size() << " files, total " << total
              << (total == sequential ? " (matches sequential)" : " (MISMATCH)") << '\n';
}

Output:

file 0: 127572
file 1: 131967
file 2: 136891
file 63: 424602
64 files, total 17663328 (matches sequential)

docs.title: Lesson 13.1: Threads, jthread, and cooperative cancellation
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Suppose you're decoding 200 audio files. One at a time takes 40 seconds; spread across 8 cores, about 5. A thread is an independent flow of execution sharing your process's memory. That sharing is the power — and the danger. Let's start with the mechanics: starting, joining, and stopping threads cleanly.

docs.title: std::thread and its trap
docs.text:
std::thread t{work};
// if we forget t.join() and t goes out of scope -> std::terminate()!

A joinable std::thread destroyed without join() or detach() calls std::terminate. And detach() is almost always wrong: the thread may outlive the data it uses.

docs.title: std::jthread (C++20): use this by default
docs.text:
jthread joins automatically in its destructor, and carries a std::stop_token so you can ask it to stop. Cancellation is cooperative: the thread checks stop_requested() and exits on its own. There's no safe way to kill a thread from outside.

examples/week13/lesson01.cpp
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <stop_token>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

void decode(int file_id, int& result) { result = file_id * file_id; }   // pretend work

int main() {
    std::vector<int> results(4);
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> workers;
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) workers.emplace_back(decode, i + 1, std::ref(results[i]));
    }                                                  // all jthreads join here
    for (int r : results) std::cout << r << ' ';
    std::cout << "<- decoded\n";

    std::atomic<int> ticks{0};
    {
        std::jthread meter{[&ticks](std::stop_token st) {
            std::stop_callback on_stop{st, [] { std::cout << "stop requested\n"; }};
            while (!st.stop_requested()) {
                ++ticks;
                std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds{1});
            }
        }};
        while (ticks < 5) std::this_thread::yield();
        meter.request_stop();                          // cooperative: the thread notices and exits
    }                                                  // and is joined
    std::cout << "meter ran at least 5 ticks: " << std::boolalpha << (ticks >= 5) << '\n';

    std::thread classic{[] {}};
    classic.join();                                    // forget this and std::terminate() is called
    std::cout << "hardware threads known: " << (std::thread::hardware_concurrency() > 0) << '\n';
}

Output:

1 4 9 16 <- decoded
stop requested
meter ran at least 5 ticks: true
hardware threads known: true

docs.title: Arguments are copied
docs.text: std::thread{f, x} copies x into the thread's storage. To pass a reference use std::ref(x) — and make sure x outlives the thread. Passing a pointer or reference to a local that goes out of scope is the classic dangling bug.

docs.title: How many threads?
docs.text: std::thread::hardware_concurrency() hints at the number of hardware threads (may return 0 if unknown). More threads than cores for CPU-bound work just adds context switches.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A joinable std::thread that's destroyed calls std::terminate; prefer std::jthread.
  • jthread auto-joins and supports cooperative cancellation via stop_token.
  • Thread arguments are copied; use std::ref deliberately and mind lifetimes.
  • Avoid detach(); don't run more CPU-bound threads than cores.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What happens if a joinable std::thread is destroyed?

Show answer

std::terminate() is called.

Q2. Can request_stop() forcibly stop a thread?

Show answer

No — it only sets a flag; the thread must check its stop_token and return.

Q3. Why is std::thread t{f, std::ref(local)}; t.detach(); dangerous?

Show answer

The thread may still use local after the enclosing function returns — a dangling reference.

docs.title: Lesson 13.2: Data races, mutexes, and deadlock
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Two threads each add 1 to a counter a million times. Expected: 2,000,000. Actual: maybe 1,213,407 — and different every run. That's a data race: two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, and nothing orders them. In C++ a data race isn't just a wrong number — it's undefined behaviour.

docs.title: The wrong way
docs.text:
Deliberately buggy

CI runs this under -fsanitize=thread and checks the sanitizer reports the bug.

examples/week13/lesson02_race.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

int main() {
    int counter = 0;                                   // shared, unprotected
    {
        std::jthread a{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) ++counter; }};
        std::jthread b{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) ++counter; }};
    }
    std::cout << "counter = " << counter << " (expected 200000)\n";   // data race: UB
}

++counter is read-modify-write; two threads interleave and lose updates. ThreadSanitizer flags this immediately (CI runs this example under TSan and checks it's reported).

docs.title: Mutexes and RAII locks
docs.text:
std::mutex m;
{ std::lock_guard lock{m}; ++counter; }   // unlocked automatically, even on exceptions

Never call m.lock()/m.unlock() by hand. Use lock_guard (simple), unique_lock (movable, can unlock early, needed for condition variables), scoped_lock (locks several mutexes at once without deadlock).

examples/week13/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <mutex>
#include <shared_mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Account { std::mutex m; int balance; };

void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, int amount) {
    std::scoped_lock lock{from.m, to.m};       // locks both, deadlock-free regardless of order
    from.balance -= amount;
    to.balance += amount;
}

class Settings {
public:
    std::string get(const std::string& k) const {
        std::shared_lock lock{m_};             // many readers at once
        auto it = values_.find(k);
        return it == values_.end() ? "" : it->second;
    }
    void set(const std::string& k, std::string v) {
        std::unique_lock lock{m_};             // exclusive writer
        values_[k] = std::move(v);
    }
private:
    mutable std::shared_mutex m_;
    std::map<std::string, std::string> values_;
};

int main() {
    int counter = 0;
    std::mutex m;
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> ts;
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
            ts.emplace_back([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) { std::lock_guard lock{m}; ++counter; } });
    }
    std::cout << "counter = " << counter << '\n';

    Account a{{}, 1000}, b{{}, 1000};
    {
        std::jthread t1{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) transfer(a, b, 1); }};
        std::jthread t2{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) transfer(b, a, 1); }};   // opposite order: no deadlock
    }
    std::cout << "balances " << a.balance << ' ' << b.balance << '\n';

    Settings s;
    s.set("rate", "48000");
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> readers;
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) readers.emplace_back([&] { for (int j = 0; j < 1000; ++j) (void)s.get("rate"); });
        s.set("bits", "24");
    }
    std::cout << "rate=" << s.get("rate") << " bits=" << s.get("bits") << '\n';

    std::once_flag once;
    int inits = 0;
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> ts;
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) ts.emplace_back([&] { std::call_once(once, [&] { ++inits; }); });
    }
    std::cout << "initialized " << inits << " time(s)\n";
}

Output:

counter = 400000
balances 1000 1000
rate=48000 bits=24
initialized 1 time(s)

docs.title: Deadlock
docs.text: Thread A locks m1 then waits for m2; thread B locks m2 then waits for m1. Forever. Fixes: always lock in a consistent global order, or lock both at once with std::scoped_lock{m1, m2}, and never call unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock.

docs.title: Readers–writer locks and one-time init
docs.text:
std::shared_mutex lets many readers hold shared_lock at once while writers take unique_lock. Useful for read-mostly data (but measure — it's heavier than a plain mutex). std::call_once and function-local static variables give thread-safe lazy initialization.

Pitfall

Keep critical sections short. Holding a lock while doing I/O or calling a callback serializes your program and invites deadlock.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A data race (unsynchronized access with at least one write) is undefined behaviour.
  • Protect shared data with a mutex and RAII locks; never lock/unlock by hand.
  • Use std::scoped_lock for multiple mutexes, or a consistent lock order, to avoid deadlock.
  • shared_mutex for read-mostly data; call_once/static locals for one-time init.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Is ++counter on a shared int from two threads safe?

Show answer

No — it's a data race (UB); use a mutex or std::atomic<int>.
