Q2. How does std::scoped_lock{m1, m2} avoid deadlock?

Show answer

It uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (like std::lock) to acquire both without holding one while blocking forever on the other.

Q3. Why avoid calling user callbacks while holding a lock?

Show answer

The callback might take another lock (deadlock risk) or be slow, serializing other threads.

docs.title: Lesson 13.3: Condition variables and a thread-safe queue
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A decoder thread produces audio blocks; a player thread consumes them. When the queue is empty the player should sleep, not spin burning a core, and wake the moment a block arrives. That's what condition variables do — and they have two famous traps.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
std::unique_lock lock{m};
cv.wait(lock, [&] { return !queue.empty(); });   // ALWAYS wait with a predicate

wait atomically unlocks the mutex and sleeps; on wake-up it re-locks and re-checks the predicate.

docs.title: The two traps
docs.text:
1. Spurious wakeups: wait may return without a notify. The predicate form loops for you.
  2. Lost wakeups: if you change the condition without holding the mutex, a notify can slip between the waiter's check and its sleep. Always modify the shared state under the lock.
examples/week13/lesson03.cpp
#include <condition_variable>
#include <deque>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <optional>
#include <stop_token>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
class BlockingQueue {
public:
    void push(T v) {
        { std::lock_guard lock{m_}; q_.push_back(std::move(v)); }   // modify under the lock
        cv_.notify_one();
    }
    std::optional<T> pop() {                                       // nullopt once closed and drained
        std::unique_lock lock{m_};
        cv_.wait(lock, [&] { return !q_.empty() || closed_; });    // predicate handles spurious wakeups
        if (q_.empty()) return std::nullopt;
        T v = std::move(q_.front()); q_.pop_front();
        return v;
    }
    void close() {
        { std::lock_guard lock{m_}; closed_ = true; }
        cv_.notify_all();
    }
private:
    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable cv_;
    std::deque<T> q_;
    bool closed_ = false;
};

int main() {
    BlockingQueue<int> q;
    long long total = 0;
    int consumed = 0;
    std::mutex result_m;
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> consumers;
        for (int c = 0; c < 3; ++c)
            consumers.emplace_back([&] {
                while (auto block = q.pop()) {
                    std::lock_guard lock{result_m};
                    total += *block; ++consumed;
                }
            });
        std::jthread producer{[&] { for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; ++i) q.push(i); q.close(); }};
    }
    std::cout << "consumed " << consumed << " blocks, total " << total << '\n';

    std::mutex m;
    std::condition_variable_any cv;
    std::jthread waiter{[&](std::stop_token st) {
        std::unique_lock lock{m};
        bool ready = cv.wait(lock, st, [] { return false; });       // wakes on stop request
        std::cout << "waiter woke by stop, predicate=" << std::boolalpha << ready << '\n';
    }};
    waiter.request_stop();
}

Output:

consumed 1000 blocks, total 500500
waiter woke by stop, predicate=false

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
A blocking queue needs a way to say "no more items". The example uses a closed flag; C++20's condition_variable_any::wait(lock, stop_token, pred) also wakes on stop requests.

notify_one wakes one waiter (one item added); notify_all wakes everyone (state change like shutdown).

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Always wait with a predicate — it handles spurious wakeups.
  • Change the shared condition while holding the mutex to avoid lost wakeups.
  • Blocking queues need an explicit close/shutdown path.
  • condition_variable_any can wait on a stop_token (C++20).

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why must wait take a unique_lock and not a lock_guard?

Show answer

wait needs to unlock and re-lock the mutex, which lock_guard can't do.

Q2. What's a lost wakeup?

Show answer

A notify that happens after the waiter checked the condition but before it went to sleep, so it sleeps forever; prevented by changing state under the mutex.

Q3. When is notify_all the right choice?

Show answer

When a change matters to all waiters, e.g. shutdown/close.

docs.title: Lesson 13.4: Futures, promises, async, and packaged_task
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Threads and mutexes are low-level. Often you just want "compute this in the background and give me the answer later". A std::future is a one-shot channel for a result — or an exception — from another thread.

docs.title: std::async
docs.text:
auto f = std::async(std::launch::async, analyze, file);   // runs on another thread
Report r = f.get();                                        // waits; rethrows if analyze threw

Always pass std::launch::async: the default policy may run the task lazily on get() in the calling thread. And beware: the destructor of a future returned by std::async blocks until the task finishes — std::async(...) whose result you ignore runs synchronously.

docs.title: promise and packaged_task
docs.text:
A promise is the writing end of a future: someone calls set_value or set_exception. A packaged_task wraps a callable so that calling it fulfils a future — the building block of thread pools (Week 14).

examples/week13/lesson04.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <future>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

double analyze(const std::vector<double>& samples) {
    if (samples.empty()) throw std::invalid_argument{"no samples"};
    return std::accumulate(samples.begin(), samples.end(), 0.0) / static_cast<double>(samples.size());
}

int main() {
    std::vector<double> a{1, 2, 3, 4}, b{10, 20};
    auto fa = std::async(std::launch::async, analyze, std::cref(a));
    auto fb = std::async(std::launch::async, analyze, std::cref(b));
    std::cout << "means: " << fa.get() << ' ' << fb.get() << '\n';

    auto bad = std::async(std::launch::async, analyze, std::vector<double>{});
    try { (void)bad.get(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::cout << "exception crossed threads: " << e.what() << '\n'; }

    std::promise<int> p;
    std::future<int> f = p.get_future();
    std::jthread producer{[pr = std::move(p)]() mutable {
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds{10});
        pr.set_value(42);
    }};
    if (f.wait_for(std::chrono::seconds{0}) == std::future_status::timeout) std::cout << "not ready yet\n";
    std::cout << "promise delivered " << f.get() << '\n';

    std::packaged_task<int(int, int)> task{[](int x, int y) { return x * y; }};
    std::future<int> tf = task.get_future();
    std::jthread runner{std::move(task), 6, 7};
    std::shared_future<int> shared = tf.share();
    std::cout << "packaged_task: " << shared.get() << " (read twice: " << shared.get() << ")\n";
}

Output:

means: 2.5 15
exception crossed threads: no samples
not ready yet
promise delivered 42
packaged_task: 42 (read twice: 42)

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: std::future has no continuations (.then), no composition (when_all), and get() can only be called once (use shared_future for many readers). For larger async systems look at std::execution (C++26, Week 14) or libraries.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A future is a one-shot result channel that also carries exceptions.
  • Use std::launch::async explicitly; an ignored std::async future blocks in its destructor.
  • promise sets a future manually; packaged_task ties a callable to a future.
  • std::future lacks continuations and composition — bigger systems need more.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What happens to an exception thrown inside a std::async task?

Show answer

It's stored in the shared state and rethrown by get().

Q2. Why might std::async(f); (result ignored) not run concurrently?

Show answer

The temporary future's destructor blocks until the task finishes, so the statement waits right there.

Q3. How do several threads read the same result?

Show answer

Convert to std::shared_future (share()); its get() can be called multiple times.

docs.title: Lesson 13.5: Latches, barriers, semaphores, and thread_local
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Some coordination patterns are so common C++20 gave them names: "wait until all N workers are ready" (latch), "everyone finish phase 1 before anyone starts phase 2" (barrier), "at most 3 downloads at once" (semaphore). Using the named tool is clearer and less bug-prone than building it from a mutex and condition variable.

docs.title: The tools
thread_local
docs.text: A thread_local variable has one instance per thread — e.g. a per-thread scratch buffer or random engine, with no locking. It's constructed on first use in each thread and destroyed when the thread exits.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: Start with the highest-level tool that fits: a future for one result, a queue for streams of work, latch/ barrier for phases, a mutex for shared state. Atomics (next week) are the lowest level — reach for them last.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • latch = one-shot countdown; barrier = reusable phases with a completion step.
  • Semaphores bound concurrency; binary_semaphore is a cheap signal.
  • thread_local gives each thread its own instance — no locking needed.
  • Prefer the highest-level primitive that fits the pattern.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Can a std::latch be reused after it reaches zero?

Show answer

No — it's single-use; use std::barrier for repeated phases.

Q2. What does a barrier's completion function do?

Show answer

Runs once per phase, after all threads arrive and before they're released.

Q3. How many instances of a thread_local variable exist with 5 threads?

Show answer

One per thread that uses it (up to 5, plus main if it uses it).

docs.title: Week 13 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 13.1) What happens if a joinable std::thread is destroyed?

Show answer

std::terminate() is called.

Q2. (from 13.1) Can request_stop() forcibly stop a thread?

Show answer

No — it only sets a flag; the thread must check its stop_token and return.

Q3. (from 13.2) Is ++counter on a shared int from two threads safe?

Show answer

No — it's a data race (UB); use a mutex or std::atomic<int>.

Q4. (from 13.2) How does std::scoped_lock{m1, m2} avoid deadlock?

Show answer

It uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (like std::lock) to acquire both without holding one while blocking forever on the other.

Q5. (from 13.3) Why must wait take a unique_lock and not a lock_guard?

Show answer

wait needs to unlock and re-lock the mutex, which lock_guard can't do.

Q6. (from 13.3) What's a lost wakeup?

Show answer

A notify that happens after the waiter checked the condition but before it went to sleep, so it sleeps forever; prevented by changing state under the mutex.

Q7. (from 13.4) What happens to an exception thrown inside a std::async task?

Show answer

It's stored in the shared state and rethrown by get().

Q8. (from 13.4) Why might std::async(f); (result ignored) not run concurrently?

Show answer

The temporary future's destructor blocks until the task finishes, so the statement waits right there.

Q9. (from 13.5) Can a std::latch be reused after it reaches zero?

Show answer

No — it's single-use; use std::barrier for repeated phases.

Q10. (from 13.5) What does a barrier's completion function do?

Show answer

Runs once per phase, after all threads arrive and before they're released.

docs.title: Week 14: Concurrency II: atomics, lock-free code, thread pools, and coroutines
docs.text:
Last week used locks. This week goes underneath them — atomics and the C++ memory model — then builds two real components (a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue and a thread pool, both feeding the capstones), and finishes with coroutines, C++20's machinery for writing asynchronous code that reads like sequential code. This is the hardest week of the course. Go slowly, and lean on ThreadSanitizer.

# Lesson Standard Length 14.1 Atomics and the memory model C++20 15 min 14.2 A lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer C++20 14 min 14.3 Building a thread pool C++20 14 min 14.4 Parallel algorithms and a preview of std::execution C++20 10 min 14.5 Coroutines I: the machinery, and writing a generator C++20 15 min 14.6 Coroutines II: awaitables and async tasks C++20 14 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 14 programming assignment: Parallel pipeline with a pool and an SPSC ring
docs.text:
Combine this week's pieces: a producer thread generates 10,000 "audio blocks" (integers) into an SpscRing; a dispatcher thread pops them and submits a processing job (e.g. square modulo 1000) for each to a ThreadPool; gather futures and print the count and checksum, verifying against a sequential computation. Must be ThreadSanitizer-clean.

Reference solution examples/week14/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <array>
#include <atomic>
#include <condition_variable>
#include <cstddef>
#include <deque>
#include <functional>
#include <future>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <optional>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class SpscRing {
public:
    bool try_push(const T& v) {
        auto t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed), next = (t + 1) & (N - 1);
        if (next == head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return false;
        buf_[t] = v; tail_.store(next, std::memory_order_release); return true;
    }
    std::optional<T> try_pop() {
        auto h = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        if (h == tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return std::nullopt;
        T v = buf_[h]; head_.store((h + 1) & (N - 1), std::memory_order_release); return v;
    }
private:
    std::array<T, N> buf_{};
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> head_{0};
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> tail_{0};
};

class ThreadPool {
public:
    explicit ThreadPool(unsigned n) { for (unsigned i = 0; i < n; ++i) w_.emplace_back([this] { run(); }); }
    ~ThreadPool() { { std::lock_guard l{m_}; stop_ = true; } cv_.notify_all(); }
    std::future<int> submit(std::function<int()> f) {
        auto t = std::make_shared<std::packaged_task<int()>>(std::move(f));
        auto fut = t->get_future();
        { std::lock_guard l{m_}; q_.emplace_back([t] { (*t)(); }); }
        cv_.notify_one();
        return fut;
    }
private:
    void run() {
        for (;;) {
            std::function<void()> j;
            { std::unique_lock l{m_}; cv_.wait(l, [&] { return stop_ || !q_.empty(); });
              if (q_.empty()) { return; }
              j = std::move(q_.front()); q_.pop_front(); }
            j();
        }
    }
    std::mutex m_; std::condition_variable cv_; std::deque<std::function<void()>> q_; bool stop_ = false;
    std::vector<std::jthread> w_;
};

int process(int block) { return (block * block) % 1000; }

int main() {
    constexpr int blocks = 10000;
    SpscRing<int, 256> ring;
    std::vector<std::future<int>> futures;
    futures.reserve(blocks);
    {
        ThreadPool pool{4};
        std::jthread producer{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < blocks; ++i) while (!ring.try_push(i)) std::this_thread::yield(); }};
        std::jthread dispatcher{[&] {
            for (int got = 0; got < blocks;) {
                if (auto b = ring.try_pop()) { int v = *b; futures.push_back(pool.submit([v] { return process(v); })); ++got; }
                else std::this_thread::yield();
            }
        }};
        dispatcher.join();
        long long sum = 0;
        for (auto& f : futures) sum += f.get();
        long long expected = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < blocks; ++i) expected += process(i);
        std::cout << "processed " << futures.size() << " blocks, checksum " << sum
                  << (sum == expected ? " (matches sequential)" : " (MISMATCH)") << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

processed 10000 blocks, checksum 4615000 (matches sequential)

docs.title: Lesson 14.1: Atomics and the memory model
docs.text: C++20 · about 15 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Modern CPUs and compilers reorder memory operations aggressively for speed. On one thread you never notice. Across threads, it means writing data = 42; ready = true; doesn't guarantee another thread that sees ready == true also sees data == 42. The memory model tells you exactly what's guaranteed — and atomics with the right memory order give you those guarantees without a mutex.

docs.title: Atomics: indivisible operations
docs.text: std::atomic<int> n; ++n; is a single indivisible read-modify-write — no lost updates, no data race. compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired) is the building block of lock-free algorithms: "if the value is still expected, set it to desired; otherwise tell me the current value".

docs.title: Memory order, intuitively
docs.text:
• seq_cst (default): all threads agree on one global order of all seq_cst operations. Easiest to reason about. Use it unless you've measured a need.
  • release store + acquire load: the publishing pattern. Everything written before the release store is visible to a thread whose acquire load reads that store. This is "message passing".
  • relaxed: atomic, but no ordering of other memory. Fine for counters and statistics.
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant C as Consumer
    P->>P: data = 42 (plain write)
    P->>C: ready.store(true, release)
    C->>C: ready.load(acquire) == true
    C->>C: read data -> guaranteed 42
examples/week14/lesson01.cpp
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::atomic<long> hits{0};
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> ts;
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
            ts.emplace_back([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) hits.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); });
    }
    std::cout << "relaxed counter: " << hits.load() << '\n';

    int data = 0;                                     // plain, non-atomic payload
    std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
    {
        std::jthread producer{[&] { data = 42; ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release); }};
        std::jthread consumer{[&] {
            while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}       // spin (fine for a demo)
            std::cout << "consumer sees data = " << data << '\n';   // guaranteed 42
        }};
    }

    std::atomic<int> maximum{0};
    auto update_max = [&](int v) {
        int cur = maximum.load();
        while (v > cur && !maximum.compare_exchange_weak(cur, v)) {}   // cur refreshed on failure
    };
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> ts;
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t) ts.emplace_back([&, t] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) update_max(t * 1000 + i); });
    }
    std::cout << "CAS max: " << maximum.load() << '\n';

    std::atomic<int> state{0};
    std::jthread waiter{[&] { state.wait(0); std::cout << "woken with state " << state.load() << '\n'; }};
    state.store(1);
    state.notify_one();
    waiter.join();

    int plain[3] = {0, 0, 0};
    {
        std::jthread a{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) std::atomic_ref{plain[1]}.fetch_add(1); }};
        std::jthread b{[&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) std::atomic_ref{plain[1]}.fetch_add(1); }};
    }
    std::cout << "atomic_ref on array element: " << plain[1] << '\n';
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << "atomic<long> always lock-free: " << std::atomic<long>::is_always_lock_free << '\n';
}

Output:

relaxed counter: 400000
consumer sees data = 42
CAS max: 3999
woken with state 1
atomic_ref on array element: 2000
atomic<long> always lock-free: true

docs.title: volatile is not a synchronization tool
docs.text: volatile stops the compiler from optimizing away accesses (for memory-mapped hardware registers — Week 16) but provides no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering. Using it for flags between threads is a data race.

docs.title: C++20 additions
docs.text:
atomic::wait(old) blocks until the value changes (efficient, futex-based), notify_one/all wakes waiters. std::atomic_ref performs atomic operations on a plain object you don't own (e.g. inside an array).

Honest advice

Weaker orders than seq_cst are an expert tool. A wrong relaxed can pass all tests on x86 (strongly ordered hardware) and fail on ARM. If you use them, document why each one is correct.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Atomics make single operations indivisible; compare_exchange is the lock-free building block.
  • Release/acquire pairs publish data from one thread to another.
  • relaxed is fine for independent counters; default to seq_cst otherwise.
  • volatile is not for threading; C++20 adds wait/notify and atomic_ref.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why might ready.store(true, relaxed) be insufficient for publishing data?

Show answer

Relaxed provides no ordering of other memory, so the consumer may see ready == true but a stale data.

Q2. Why does compare_exchange_weak sit in a loop?

Show answer

It can fail spuriously and fails when another thread changed the value; on failure it updates expected, so you retry.

Q3. Is volatile bool flag a correct way to signal between threads?

Show answer

No — it's still a data race (UB) with no ordering guarantees; use std::atomic<bool>.

docs.title: Lesson 14.2: A lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer
docs.text: C++20 · about 14 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: The audio callback (real-time, can't block) receives samples from the decoder thread. A mutex could block the callback if the decoder holds it while being descheduled — an audible glitch. The standard answer is a single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) lock-free ring buffer: fixed capacity, no allocation, no locks, and only acquire/release atomics. It's also the heart of the embedded capstone.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
A fixed array plus two indices: head (written only by the consumer) and tail (written only by the producer). Because each index has a single writer, we don't need CAS — just loads and stores with the right ordering:

  • Producer: write the slot, then tail.store(next, release) — publishes the element.
  • Consumer: tail.load(acquire) to see published elements, read the slot, then head.store(next, release) to hand the slot back.

We keep one slot empty to distinguish "full" from "empty", and use a power-of-two capacity so wrap-around is a cheap mask.

examples/week14/lesson02.cpp
#include <array>
#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <optional>
#include <thread>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class SpscRing {
    static_assert(N >= 2 && (N & (N - 1)) == 0, "capacity must be a power of two");
public:
    bool try_push(const T& v) {                               // producer thread only
        auto t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        auto next = (t + 1) & (N - 1);
        if (next == head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return false;   // full
        buf_[t] = v;
        tail_.store(next, std::memory_order_release);          // publish
        return true;
    }
    std::optional<T> try_pop() {                              // consumer thread only
        auto h = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        if (h == tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return std::nullopt;   // empty
        T v = buf_[h];
        head_.store((h + 1) & (N - 1), std::memory_order_release);  // hand slot back
        return v;
    }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N - 1; }
private:
    std::array<T, N> buf_{};
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> head_{0};            // separate cache lines: no false sharing
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> tail_{0};
};

int main() {
    SpscRing<int, 1024> ring;
    constexpr int count = 200000;
    long long sum = 0;
    bool in_order = true;
    {
        std::jthread producer{[&] {
            for (int i = 1; i <= count; ++i) while (!ring.try_push(i)) std::this_thread::yield();
        }};
        std::jthread consumer{[&] {
            int expected = 1;
            while (expected <= count) {
                if (auto v = ring.try_pop()) { in_order = in_order && *v == expected; sum += *v; ++expected; }
                else std::this_thread::yield();
            }
        }};
    }
    std::cout << "received " << count << " items in order: " << std::boolalpha << in_order << ", sum " << sum << '\n';
    std::cout << "usable capacity " << SpscRing<int, 1024>::capacity() << '\n';
}

Output:

received 200000 items in order: true, sum 20000100000
usable capacity 1023

docs.title: False sharing
docs.text: If head and tail share a cache line, every write by one core invalidates the other core's copy, even though they touch different variables. Put them on separate cache lines with alignas(64) (or std::hardware_destructive_interference_size where available).

docs.title: Beyond SPSC
docs.text: Multi-producer/multi-consumer lock-free queues need CAS and run into the ABA problem (a value changes A→B→A and CAS wrongly succeeds) and safe memory reclamation (hazard pointers, RCU — std::hazard_pointer and std::rcu are coming in C++26). Use a well-tested library (e.g. moodycamel, Folly, Boost.Lockfree) rather than rolling your own.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Single-writer indices + acquire/release make an SPSC ring buffer lock-free without CAS.
  • Keep one slot empty to tell full from empty; power-of-two sizes make wrap-around a mask.
  • Separate hot atomics onto different cache lines to avoid false sharing.
  • MPMC lock-free structures face ABA and reclamation problems — use proven libraries.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why doesn't the SPSC queue need compare-exchange?

Show answer

Each index has exactly one writer thread, so plain atomic stores suffice.

Q2. What would happen if the producer stored tail before writing the slot?

Show answer

The consumer could see the new tail and read a slot that hasn't been written yet.

Q3. What is false sharing?

Show answer

Independent variables on the same cache line causing cache-line ping-pong between cores when written.

docs.title: Lesson 14.3: Building a thread pool
docs.text: C++20 · about 14 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Creating a thread per task costs tens of microseconds and unbounded threads thrash the machine. A thread pool creates N workers once and feeds them tasks through a queue. It's the most-used concurrency component in real systems — and the core of the first capstone. Let's build a small, correct one.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• A std::deque of tasks guarded by a mutex + condition variable (Week 13).
  • N std::jthread workers loop: wait for a task or stop, run it.
  • submit(f, args...) wraps the call in a std::packaged_task, pushes it, and returns a std::future.
  • The destructor stops accepting work, drains the queue, and joins.

Because packaged_task is move-only and std::function requires copyable callables, we hold it via std::shared_ptr (portable everywhere); with C++23 std::move_only_function you can store it directly.

Why CI doesn't run this one under ThreadSanitizer

GCC 14's TSan reports a false "data race" in std::exception_ptr's reference count when an exception travels through a future: the count is updated inside the prebuilt (uninstrumented) libstdc++.so, so TSan can't see its atomics. It's a tooling limitation, not a bug in the pool. The capstone's tests run under TSan with Clang.

examples/week14/lesson03.cpp
#include <condition_variable>
#include <deque>
#include <functional>
#include <future>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <thread>
#include <type_traits>
#include <vector>

class ThreadPool {
public:
    explicit ThreadPool(unsigned n) {
        for (unsigned i = 0; i < n; ++i) workers_.emplace_back([this] { run(); });
    }
    ~ThreadPool() {
        { std::lock_guard lock{m_}; stopping_ = true; }
        cv_.notify_all();
    }                                                       // jthreads join after draining
    template <typename F, typename... Args>
    auto submit(F&& f, Args&&... args) -> std::future<std::invoke_result_t<F, Args...>> {
        using R = std::invoke_result_t<F, Args...>;
        auto task = std::make_shared<std::packaged_task<R()>>(
            [f = std::forward<F>(f), ... a = std::forward<Args>(args)]() mutable { return std::invoke(f, a...); });
        auto fut = task->get_future();
        {
            std::lock_guard lock{m_};
            if (stopping_) throw std::runtime_error{"pool is stopping"};
            q_.emplace_back([task] { (*task)(); });
        }
        cv_.notify_one();
        return fut;
    }
private:
    void run() {
        for (;;) {
            std::function<void()> job;
            {
                std::unique_lock lock{m_};
                cv_.wait(lock, [&] { return stopping_ || !q_.empty(); });
                if (q_.empty()) return;                     // stopping and drained
                job = std::move(q_.front()); q_.pop_front();
            }
            job();                                          // run outside the lock
        }
    }
    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable cv_;
    std::deque<std::function<void()>> q_;
    bool stopping_ = false;
    std::vector<std::jthread> workers_;                     // declared last: destroyed (joined) first
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::future<long long>> results;
    {
        ThreadPool pool{4};
        for (int i = 1; i <= 8; ++i)
            results.push_back(pool.submit([](int n) { long long s = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n * 1000; ++k) s += k; return s; }, i));
        auto failing = pool.submit([] { throw std::runtime_error{"bad input"}; return 0; });
        try { (void)failing.get(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::cout << "task failed: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
        auto hello = pool.submit([](const std::string& who) { return "hello " + who; }, std::string{"pool"});
        std::cout << hello.get() << '\n';
    }
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < results.size(); ++i) std::cout << "sum(1.." << (i + 1) * 1000 << ") = " << results[i].get() << '\n';
}

Output:

task failed: bad input
hello pool
sum(1..1000) = 500500
sum(1..2000) = 2001000
sum(1..3000) = 4501500
sum(1..4000) = 8002000
sum(1..5000) = 12502500
sum(1..6000) = 18003000
sum(1..7000) = 24503500
sum(1..8000) = 32004000

docs.title: Things the simple pool doesn't do
docs.text:
• Work stealing: per-worker deques where idle workers steal from busy ones (reduces contention).
  • Priorities, cancellation, back-pressure (bounded queue).
  • Tasks waiting on other tasks inside the pool can deadlock if all workers block — a classic trap.

The capstone extends this pool with a bounded queue, statistics, and tests.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A thread pool reuses N workers fed by a mutex/condvar queue.
  • packaged_task + future returns values and exceptions from tasks.
  • Run tasks outside the lock; drain and join on shutdown (member order matters!).
  • Watch for tasks that block on other tasks in the same pool — deadlock.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is workers_ declared last in the class?

Show answer

Members are destroyed in reverse order, so the jthreads join first, while the mutex, condvar and queue they use still exist.

Q2. Why wrap packaged_task in a shared_ptr?

Show answer

std::function requires a copyable callable and packaged_task is move-only.

Q3. How can a pool with 4 workers deadlock?

Show answer

If 4 tasks each wait on futures of tasks still in the queue, no worker is free to run those tasks.

docs.title: Lesson 14.4: Parallel algorithms and a preview of std::execution
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Often you don't need threads at all: you need "sort this faster" or "sum this faster". C++17 lets you add a single argument — an execution policy — to most algorithms and let the library parallelize. It's the cheapest speedup in the language, when it works.

docs.title: Execution policies
docs.text:
std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end());
double total = std::reduce(std::execution::par_unseq, xs.begin(), xs.end(), 0.0);
Policy Meaning seq sequential par may run on multiple threads par_unseq multiple threads and vectorized — no locks or allocation inside your function! unseq (C++20) vectorized on one thread

Your element functions must not race. std::reduce (unlike accumulate) may reorder operations, so the operation must be associative and commutative — floating-point sums may differ slightly between runs.

examples/week14/lesson04.cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <execution>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v(1'000'000);
    std::iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);
    std::reverse(v.begin(), v.end());

    std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end());
    std::cout << "sorted: " << std::boolalpha << std::is_sorted(v.begin(), v.end()) << '\n';

    long long total = std::reduce(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);
    std::cout << "reduce: " << total << '\n';

    long long sq = std::transform_reduce(std::execution::par_unseq, v.begin(), v.begin() + 1000, 0LL,
                                         std::plus<>{}, [](int x) { return static_cast<long long>(x) * x; });
    std::cout << "sum of squares 0..999: " << sq << '\n';

    std::vector<double> out(v.size());
    std::transform(std::execution::par_unseq, v.begin(), v.end(), out.begin(), [](int x) { return x * 0.5; });
    std::cout << "out[10] = " << out[10] << '\n';
}

Output:

sorted: true
reduce: 499999500000
sum of squares 0..999: 332833500
out[10] = 5

Library support

GCC's libstdc++ implements the parallel policies on top of Intel TBB (link -ltbb; without TBB they may run sequentially). MSVC supports them natively. libc++'s support is still experimental, which is why this example is marked "may be unsupported" locally.

docs.title: Preview: std::execution (C++26)
docs.text: C++26 adds senders/receivers (P2300): a composable model for async work — schedule(sched) | then(f) | let_value(g), when_all, structured cancellation. It fixes std::future's lack of composition. Compilers are only starting to ship it (NVIDIA's stdexec is the reference implementation), so we don't compile it here; see the C++26 preview lesson in Week 16.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Adding an execution policy is the cheapest way to parallelize standard algorithms.
  • Element functions must be race-free; par_unseq forbids locks and allocation.
  • std::reduce may reorder operations — use associative, commutative ops.
  • std::execution (C++26) brings composable senders/receivers.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why might std::reduce give a slightly different floating-point sum than std::accumulate?

Show answer

It may group and reorder additions, and FP addition isn't associative.

Q2. Can you lock a mutex inside a par_unseq lambda?

Show answer

No — vectorized execution may interleave iterations on one thread, so locking can deadlock; it's disallowed.

Q3. What does libstdc++ need for real parallel execution?

Show answer

Intel TBB (link with -ltbb).

docs.title: Lesson 14.5: Coroutines I: the machinery, and writing a generator
docs.text: C++20 · about 15 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A coroutine is a function that can pause in the middle and resume later, keeping its local variables. That lets you write a lazy sequence ("yield the next sample") or an async operation ("wait for the network, then continue") as straight-line code instead of callbacks and state machines. C++20 gives you the raw machinery; libraries (and C++23's std::generator) give you friendly types. Let's see the machinery once.

docs.title: What makes a function a coroutine
docs.text:
Any function whose body uses co_yield, co_await or co_return. The compiler then:

  1. allocates a coroutine frame (locals + state), usually on the heap;
  2. creates a promise object of type ReturnType::promise_type;
  3. calls promise.get_return_object() to make the value returned to the caller;
  4. inserts suspension points at initial_suspend, each co_yield/co_await, and final_suspend.
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller
    participant Coro as Coroutine
    Caller->>Coro: call fib()
    Coro-->>Caller: returns Generator (suspended at initial_suspend)
    Caller->>Coro: handle.resume()
    Coro-->>Caller: co_yield 0 (suspends)
    Caller->>Coro: handle.resume()
    Coro-->>Caller: co_yield 1 (suspends)

docs.title: A minimal generator
In practice
docs.text: Use std::generator (C++23, Week 11) when available; write your own types only when you need special behaviour. The point of this lesson is that you can now read coroutine library code.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A coroutine is a function that can suspend and resume, keeping its state in a coroutine frame.
  • The return type's promise_type controls behaviour; coroutine_handle resumes and destroys it.
  • Wrap the handle in an RAII type that calls destroy().
  • Take coroutine parameters by value to avoid dangling references.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What makes a function a coroutine?

Show answer

Using co_await, co_yield or co_return in its body.

Q2. Why does our generator use suspend_always for initial_suspend?

Show answer

So the body doesn't run until the caller asks for the first value (lazy).

Q3. Why is Generator<std::string> tokens(const std::string& s) risky?

Show answer

The coroutine may run after the caller's argument (e.g. a temporary) is destroyed, leaving a dangling reference.

docs.title: Lesson 14.6: Coroutines II: awaitables and async tasks
docs.text: C++20 · about 14 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Generators produce values. The bigger win of coroutines is async I/O: "read from the socket, then parse, then write" without callback pyramids. The key is co_await, which suspends the coroutine until some operation finishes and then resumes it with the result. Let's build a tiny single-threaded event loop and a Task type to see how async frameworks work under the hood.

docs.title: The awaitable protocol
docs.text:
co_await x calls three functions on the awaiter:

Function Question it answers await_ready() Is the result already available? If true, don't suspend. await_suspend(handle) We're suspending — who will resume us? (store the handle somewhere) await_resume() Resumed — what's the value of the co_await expression?

docs.title: A lazy Task and an event loop
docs.text:
In the example, sleep_ticks(n) is an awaitable that schedules the current coroutine on a simple event loop n ticks later. Task<T> is lazy: it starts when awaited, and when it finishes, its final_suspend resumes the awaiting coroutine via symmetric transfer (returning the continuation's handle), which avoids stack growth in long chains.

examples/week14/lesson06.cpp
#include <coroutine>
#include <exception>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct EventLoop {
    std::multimap<int, std::coroutine_handle<>> timers;   // tick -> who to resume
    int now = 0;
    void run() {
        while (!timers.empty()) {
            auto it = timers.begin();
            now = it->first;
            auto h = it->second;
            timers.erase(it);
            h.resume();
        }
    }
};
EventLoop loop;

struct SleepTicks {
    int ticks;
    bool await_ready() const noexcept { return ticks <= 0; }
    void await_suspend(std::coroutine_handle<> h) const { loop.timers.emplace(loop.now + ticks, h); }
    void await_resume() const noexcept {}
};
SleepTicks sleep_ticks(int n) { return {n}; }

template <typename T>
class Task {
public:
    struct promise_type {
        T value{};
        std::coroutine_handle<> continuation = std::noop_coroutine();
        Task get_return_object() { return Task{std::coroutine_handle<promise_type>::from_promise(*this)}; }
        std::suspend_always initial_suspend() noexcept { return {}; }            // lazy
        struct Final {
            bool await_ready() noexcept { return false; }
            std::coroutine_handle<> await_suspend(std::coroutine_handle<promise_type> h) noexcept {
                return h.promise().continuation;                                  // symmetric transfer
            }
            void await_resume() noexcept {}
        };
        Final final_suspend() noexcept { return {}; }
        void return_value(T v) { value = std::move(v); }
        void unhandled_exception() { std::terminate(); }
    };
    explicit Task(std::coroutine_handle<promise_type> h) : h_{h} {}
    Task(Task&& o) noexcept : h_{std::exchange(o.h_, {})} {}
    ~Task() { if (h_) h_.destroy(); }

    bool await_ready() const noexcept { return false; }
    std::coroutine_handle<> await_suspend(std::coroutine_handle<> awaiting) {
        h_.promise().continuation = awaiting;
        return h_;                                                               // start the child
    }
    T await_resume() { return std::move(h_.promise().value); }
    void start() { h_.resume(); }                                                // for top-level tasks
    bool done() const { return h_.done(); }
private:
    std::coroutine_handle<promise_type> h_;
};

Task<std::string> fetch(std::string name, int latency) {
    std::cout << "[t=" << loop.now << "] fetch " << name << " started\n";
    co_await sleep_ticks(latency);
    std::cout << "[t=" << loop.now << "] fetch " << name << " done\n";
    co_return name + "-data";
}

Task<int> handle_request(std::string id, int latency) {
    std::string a = co_await fetch(id + "/meta", latency);
    std::string b = co_await fetch(id + "/body", latency);
    std::cout << "[t=" << loop.now << "] request " << id << " got " << a << " + " << b << '\n';
    co_return static_cast<int>(a.size() + b.size());
}

int main() {
    auto r1 = handle_request("A", 3);
    auto r2 = handle_request("B", 2);
    r1.start();
    r2.start();
    loop.run();                                   // single thread, interleaved requests
    std::cout << "both done: " << std::boolalpha << (r1.done() && r2.done()) << '\n';
}

Output:

[t=0] fetch A/meta started
[t=0] fetch B/meta started
[t=2] fetch B/meta done
[t=2] fetch B/body started
[t=3] fetch A/meta done
[t=3] fetch A/body started
[t=4] fetch B/body done
[t=4] request B got B/meta-data + B/body-data
[t=6] fetch A/body done
[t=6] request A got A/meta-data + A/body-data
both done: true

Notice the output: two "requests" interleave on a single thread — that's concurrency without threads.

docs.title: Use a library
docs.text: Production code should use a proven library (Asio's coroutines, Folly, cppcoro-style libraries, or std::execution in C++26). Writing your own task type is educational but has many subtle lifetime corners.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • co_await uses await_ready / await_suspend / await_resume.
  • A lazy Task starts when awaited and resumes its awaiter at final_suspend.
  • Symmetric transfer (returning a handle) avoids stack growth in chains of coroutines.
  • Coroutines give concurrency without threads; use a proven library in production.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does await_suspend typically do?

Show answer

Arranges for the suspended coroutine's handle to be resumed later (e.g. registers it with an event loop or I/O completion).

Q2. Why is the Task lazy (suspend at start)?

Show answer

So the awaiting coroutine can register itself as the continuation before the child runs, avoiding races and wasted work.

Q3. In the example, why do requests A and B interleave on one thread?

Show answer

Each suspends at co_await sleep_ticks, returning control to the event loop, which resumes whichever timer is due next.

docs.title: Week 14 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 14.1) Why might ready.store(true, relaxed) be insufficient for publishing data?

Show answer

Relaxed provides no ordering of other memory, so the consumer may see ready == true but a stale data.

Q2. (from 14.1) Why does compare_exchange_weak sit in a loop?

Show answer

It can fail spuriously and fails when another thread changed the value; on failure it updates expected, so you retry.

Q3. (from 14.2) Why doesn't the SPSC queue need compare-exchange?

Show answer

Each index has exactly one writer thread, so plain atomic stores suffice.

Q4. (from 14.2) What would happen if the producer stored tail before writing the slot?

Show answer

The consumer could see the new tail and read a slot that hasn't been written yet.

Q5. (from 14.3) Why is workers_ declared last in the class?

Show answer

Members are destroyed in reverse order, so the jthreads join first, while the mutex, condvar and queue they use still exist.

Q6. (from 14.3) Why wrap packaged_task in a shared_ptr?

Show answer

std::function requires a copyable callable and packaged_task is move-only.

Q7. (from 14.4) Why might std::reduce give a slightly different floating-point sum than std::accumulate?

Show answer

It may group and reorder additions, and FP addition isn't associative.

Q8. (from 14.4) Can you lock a mutex inside a par_unseq lambda?

Show answer

No — vectorized execution may interleave iterations on one thread, so locking can deadlock; it's disallowed.

Q9. (from 14.5) What makes a function a coroutine?

Show answer

Using co_await, co_yield or co_return in its body.

Q10. (from 14.5) Why does our generator use suspend_always for initial_suspend?

Show answer

So the body doesn't run until the caller asks for the first value (lazy).

Q11. (from 14.6) What does await_suspend typically do?

Show answer

Arranges for the suspended coroutine's handle to be resumed later (e.g. registers it with an event loop or I/O completion).

Q12. (from 14.6) Why is the Task lazy (suspend at start)?

Show answer

So the awaiting coroutine can register itself as the continuation before the child runs, avoiding races and wasted work.

docs.title: Week 15: Building, testing, and performance engineering
docs.text:
Writing correct C++ is half the job. The other half is building it reliably, proving it works, finding out why it's slow, and keeping it secure. This week is about the tools and habits that professional C++ teams rely on: CMake and modules, linking and ABI, tests and sanitizers, profilers, cache-aware design, and hardening.

# Lesson Standard Length 15.1 Build systems: CMake, packages, and C++20 modules C++20 13 min 15.2 Linking, the ODR, ABI, and extern "C" C++20 12 min 15.3 Testing, sanitizers, and static analysis C++20 13 min 15.4 Debugging, profiling, and compiler optimization C++20 12 min 15.5 Performance: caches, memory layout, and data-oriented design C++20 13 min 15.6 Security hardening and the C++ Core Guidelines C++20 12 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 15 programming assignment: Harden and test a parser
docs.text:
Take a small key=value packet parser that reads lengths from untrusted bytes, write table-driven tests including malicious inputs (truncated, oversized lengths, negative values), and make it safe using std::span, std::in_range and std::expected. Run under ASan+UBSan. Bonus: write a libFuzzer entry point (LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput) for it.

Reference solution examples/week15/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <expected>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

enum class ParseError { truncated, too_long, empty_key };
std::string_view to_string(ParseError e) {
    switch (e) {
        case ParseError::truncated: return "truncated";
        case ParseError::too_long: return "too_long";
        case ParseError::empty_key: return "empty_key";
    }
    return "?";
}

using Field = std::pair<std::string, std::string>;

// Format: repeated [klen:u8][key bytes][vlen:u8][value bytes]
std::expected<std::vector<Field>, ParseError> parse(std::span<const std::uint8_t> in) {
    std::vector<Field> out;
    auto take = [&](std::size_t n) -> std::expected<std::span<const std::uint8_t>, ParseError> {
        if (n > in.size()) return std::unexpected{ParseError::truncated};
        auto s = in.first(n);
        in = in.subspan(n);
        return s;
    };
    while (!in.empty()) {
        auto klen = take(1); if (!klen) return std::unexpected{klen.error()};
        if ((*klen)[0] == 0) return std::unexpected{ParseError::empty_key};
        if ((*klen)[0] > 64) return std::unexpected{ParseError::too_long};
        auto key = take((*klen)[0]); if (!key) return std::unexpected{key.error()};
        auto vlen = take(1); if (!vlen) return std::unexpected{vlen.error()};
        auto val = take((*vlen)[0]); if (!val) return std::unexpected{val.error()};
        out.emplace_back(std::string(key->begin(), key->end()), std::string(val->begin(), val->end()));
    }
    return out;
}

extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const std::uint8_t* data, std::size_t size) {
    (void)parse({data, size});                     // must never crash, whatever the bytes
    return 0;
}

int main() {
    struct Case { const char* name; std::vector<std::uint8_t> bytes; };
    std::vector<Case> cases{
        {"valid", {4, 'r', 'a', 't', 'e', 5, '4', '8', '0', '0', '0', 2, 'c', 'h', 1, '2'}},
        {"empty input", {}},
        {"truncated key", {10, 'a', 'b'}},
        {"value length past end", {1, 'k', 200, 'v'}},
        {"zero-length key", {0, 1, 'x'}},
        {"oversized key", {200}},
    };
    for (const auto& c : cases) {
        auto r = parse(c.bytes);
        std::cout << c.name << ": ";
        if (r) { std::cout << r->size() << " field(s)"; for (auto& [k, v] : *r) std::cout << ' ' << k << '=' << v; }
        else std::cout << "error " << to_string(r.error());
        std::cout << '\n';
    }
    std::uint64_t state = 1;                         // mini fuzz loop: random bytes must never crash
    for (int i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) {
        std::vector<std::uint8_t> buf(state % 40);
        for (auto& b : buf) { state = state * 6364136223846793005ULL + 1442695040888963407ULL; b = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(state >> 56); }
        LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(buf.data(), buf.size());
    }
    std::cout << "2000 random inputs parsed without crashing\n";
}

Output:

valid: 2 field(s) rate=48000 ch=2
empty input: 0 field(s)
truncated key: error truncated
value length past end: error truncated
zero-length key: error empty_key
oversized key: error too_long
2000 random inputs parsed without crashing

docs.title: Lesson 15.1: Build systems: CMake, packages, and C++20 modules
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Your project grows from one file to fifty, plus three libraries. Compiling by hand stops scaling the first day. CMake is the de facto standard C++ build generator, and C++20 modules are the first real fix for C++'s 50-year-old textual #include model, which re-parses the same headers thousands of times.

docs.title: Modern CMake: think in targets
docs.text:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)
project(mixer LANGUAGES CXX)

add_library(dsp src/gain.cpp src/filter.cpp)
target_include_directories(dsp PUBLIC include)
target_compile_features(dsp PUBLIC cxx_std_20)
target_compile_options(dsp PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)

add_executable(mixer src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(mixer PRIVATE dsp)

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(Catch2 GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/catchorg/Catch2.git GIT_TAG v3.5.2)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(Catch2)
add_executable(tests tests/test_gain.cpp)
target_link_libraries(tests PRIVATE dsp Catch2::Catch2WithMain)
enable_testing()
add_test(NAME tests COMMAND tests)

PUBLIC/PRIVATE/INTERFACE say whether a usage requirement propagates to dependents. Avoid global include_directories / CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS — set properties on targets. Build out of source: cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja && cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build.

docs.title: Modules (C++20)
docs.text:
// gain.cppm
export module dsp.gain;
export double apply_gain(double x, double g) { return x * g; }
// main.cpp
import dsp.gain;
import std;            // C++23: the whole standard library as one module

Modules are compiled once into a binary interface, don't leak macros, and make the interface explicit (export). Honest status (2026): MSVC, Clang ≥ 17 and GCC ≥ 14 support them, and CMake ≥ 3.28 handles dependency scanning with Ninja — but tooling (IDEs, package managers) is still catching up, so many codebases still use headers. Our checker compiles single files, so modules are shown here, not compiled.

docs.title: Portable feature detection
docs.text:
When code must work across compilers, test feature-test macros rather than compiler versions:

examples/week15/lesson01.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <version>          // defines all __cpp_lib_* macros

#if __has_include(<expected>)
#include <expected>
#endif

int main() {
#ifdef __cpp_lib_expected
    std::cout << "std::expected available (" << __cpp_lib_expected << ")\n";
#else
    std::cout << "std::expected not available in this mode\n";
#endif
#ifdef __cpp_concepts
    std::cout << "concepts: yes\n";
#endif
    std::cout << "__cplusplus = " << (__cplusplus >= 202002L ? ">= C++20" : "< C++20") << '\n';
}

Output:

std::expected not available in this mode
concepts: yes
__cplusplus = >= C++20

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Modern CMake is target-based: set includes, features and links on targets with PUBLIC/PRIVATE.
  • Use FetchContent or a package manager (vcpkg, Conan) for dependencies.
  • Modules replace textual inclusion with compiled interfaces; tooling support is maturing.
  • Use <version> feature-test macros for portability, not compiler-version checks.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does PUBLIC mean in target_include_directories(dsp PUBLIC include)?

Show answer

The include directory is used to build dsp and propagates to targets that link dsp.

Q2. Name two advantages of modules over headers.

Show answer

Faster builds (parsed once), no macro leakage, explicit export control, less ODR fragility.

Q3. Why prefer #ifdef __cpp_lib_expected over checking GCC's version?

Show answer

It checks the actual feature, works across compilers and standard libraries, and handles -std modes.

docs.title: Lesson 15.2: Linking, the ODR, ABI, and extern "C"
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: "undefined reference to mixer::Gain::apply(double)" — every C++ programmer meets the linker the hard way. Understanding what the compiler hands to the linker explains these errors, the One Definition Rule, why C libraries need extern "C", and why changing a private member can break binaries that use your library.

docs.title: The two phases
docs.text: The compiler turns each .cpp (translation unit) into an object file with symbols — defined and referenced names. The linker matches references to definitions. "Undefined reference" = nobody defined it (missing .cpp or library in the link); "multiple definition" = two TUs defined it.

docs.title: The One Definition Rule
docs.text:
Each non-inline function or variable must be defined exactly once in the program. Things defined in headers (classes, templates, inline functions, C++17 inline variables) may appear in many TUs but must be token-identical. Two different struct Config definitions with the same name in two TUs is an ODR violation — undefined behaviour, often silent.

Give helpers internal linkage (anonymous namespace or static) so they can't collide.

docs.title: Name mangling and extern "C"
docs.text:
C++ encodes parameter types into symbol names (_ZN5mixer4Gain5applyEd) to support overloading. C doesn't. To call C code from C++, or expose a C API from C++, use extern "C" — no overloading, no mangling.

examples/week15/lesson02.cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <iostream>

// What a C header would declare; extern "C" disables mangling so C code can link to it
extern "C" {
    int mixer_version(void);
    double mixer_apply_gain(double sample, double gain);
}

namespace {                                    // internal linkage: invisible to other TUs
int helper_calls = 0;
double clamp1(double x) { ++helper_calls; return x > 1.0 ? 1.0 : (x < -1.0 ? -1.0 : x); }
}

extern "C" int mixer_version(void) { return 3; }
extern "C" double mixer_apply_gain(double sample, double gain) { return clamp1(sample * gain); }

inline constexpr int kMaxChannels = 32;        // C++17 inline variable: safe to define in a header

int compare_ints(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *static_cast<const int*>(a), y = *static_cast<const int*>(b);
    return (x > y) - (x < y);
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "C API version " << mixer_version() << ", gain(0.8, 2) = " << mixer_apply_gain(0.8, 2.0) << '\n';
    int v[] = {5, 2, 9, 1};
    std::qsort(v, 4, sizeof(int), compare_ints);  // a C library calling back into C++
    for (int x : v) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << "\nhelper calls: " << helper_calls << ", max channels " << kMaxChannels << '\n';
}

Output:

C API version 3, gain(0.8, 2) = 1
1 2 5 9 
helper calls: 1, max channels 32

docs.title: ABI
docs.text: The ABI is the binary contract: object layout, calling conventions, mangling, vtable layout. Adding a private data member changes sizeof and breaks every binary compiled against the old header. Libraries that need stability use the pimpl idiom (Week 5) or a C API. (GCC's switch to a C++11-conforming std::string in 2015 required a dual ABI — that's how costly ABI breaks are.)

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Undefined reference = missing definition in the link; multiple definition = defined twice.
  • The ODR requires identical definitions across TUs; violations are silent UB.
  • Use anonymous namespaces for TU-local helpers and inline for header definitions.
  • extern "C" disables mangling for C interop; pimpl or C APIs preserve ABI stability.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why can't C code call an overloaded C++ function directly?

Show answer

C++ mangles parameter types into symbol names; C expects plain names. Use extern "C" wrappers (which can't be overloaded).

Q2. Is adding a private member to a class in a shared library's header ABI-compatible?

Show answer

No — it changes the object's size/layout, breaking binaries compiled against the old header.

Q3. How do you define a global constant in a header without ODR problems?

Show answer

inline constexpr (C++17 inline variable) — or constexpr at namespace scope, which has internal linkage.

docs.title: Lesson 15.3: Testing, sanitizers, and static analysis
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: In C++, a bug can sit silently for months — reading freed memory "works" until a different allocator layout makes it crash in production. The defence is layered: tests prove behaviour, sanitizers catch UB while the tests run, static analysis finds bugs without running anything, and fuzzing finds inputs you didn't think of. This course's own CI does exactly this for every example.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Frameworks (GoogleTest, Catch2, doctest) give you assertions, fixtures and test discovery. The core idea fits in a few lines — here's a tiny self-contained harness so the example compiles on its own:

examples/week15/lesson03.cpp
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

// --- a tiny test harness (real projects: GoogleTest / Catch2 / doctest) ---
struct TestCase { std::string name; std::function<void()> fn; };
std::vector<TestCase>& registry() { static std::vector<TestCase> r; return r; }
int failures = 0;
#define CHECK(cond) do { if (!(cond)) { ++failures; std::cout << "  FAILED: " #cond " (line " << __LINE__ << ")\n"; } } while (0)
struct Register { Register(std::string n, std::function<void()> f) { registry().push_back({std::move(n), std::move(f)}); } };

// --- code under test ---
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Ring {
public:
    bool push(T v) { if (size_ == N) return false; data_[(head_ + size_++) % N] = v; return true; }
    bool pop(T& out) { if (size_ == 0) return false; out = data_[head_]; head_ = (head_ + 1) % N; --size_; return true; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
private:
    std::array<T, N> data_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0, size_ = 0;
};

static_assert(sizeof(Ring<char, 4>) >= 4, "compile-time tests are free");

Register t1{"empty ring pops nothing", [] { Ring<int, 3> r; int x; CHECK(!r.pop(x)); CHECK(r.size() == 0); }};
Register t2{"full ring rejects push", [] { Ring<int, 2> r; CHECK(r.push(1)); CHECK(r.push(2)); CHECK(!r.push(3)); }};
Register t3{"wrap-around keeps order", [] {
    Ring<int, 3> r; int x = 0;
    r.push(1); r.push(2); r.pop(x); r.push(3); r.push(4);
    r.pop(x); CHECK(x == 2); r.pop(x); CHECK(x == 3); r.pop(x); CHECK(x == 4);
}};
Register t4{"property: FIFO for random sequences", [] {
    std::mt19937 rng{7};
    for (int trial = 0; trial < 200; ++trial) {
        Ring<int, 8> r; std::vector<int> model; int next = 0;
        for (int step = 0; step < 50; ++step) {
            if (rng() % 2) { if (r.push(next)) model.push_back(next); ++next; }
            else { int x; bool ok = r.pop(x); CHECK(ok == !model.empty()); if (ok) { CHECK(x == model.front()); model.erase(model.begin()); } }
        }
        CHECK(r.size() == model.size());
    }
}};

int main() {
    for (auto& t : registry()) { std::cout << "[ RUN ] " << t.name << '\n'; t.fn(); }
    std::cout << registry().size() << " tests, " << failures << " failures\n";
    return failures == 0 ? 0 : 1;
}

Output:

[ RUN ] empty ring pops nothing
[ RUN ] full ring rejects push
[ RUN ] wrap-around keeps order
[ RUN ] property: FIFO for random sequences
4 tests, 0 failures

With Catch2 the same test is TEST_CASE("ring wraps") { ... REQUIRE(r.size() == 2); }.

Test edge cases (empty, one element, full, wrap-around, max values), not just the happy path. A property test checks an invariant over many random inputs (e.g. "pushing then popping N items returns them in order").

docs.title: Sanitizers: run your tests under them
docs.text:
Sanitizer Flag Finds AddressSanitizer -fsanitize=address out-of-bounds, use-after-free, leaks (with LSan) UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer -fsanitize=undefined signed overflow, bad shifts, misaligned access, null deref ThreadSanitizer -fsanitize=thread data races, some deadlocks MemorySanitizer (Clang) -fsanitize=memory reads of uninitialized memory

Cost: roughly 2× (ASan) to 5–15× (TSan) slowdown. Run them in CI on every commit, not just when hunting.

docs.title: Static analysis and formatting
docs.text:
• Compile with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror (and -Wconversion -Wshadow for new code).
  • clang-tidy with cppcoreguidelines-*, bugprone-*, modernize-* checks.
  • cppcheck as a second opinion.
  • clang-format with a committed .clang-format ends style debates.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text: libFuzzer calls extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t*, size_t) millions of times with mutated inputs, under ASan/UBSan. Any parser that reads untrusted data should be fuzzed.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Test edge cases and invariants (property tests), not only happy paths.
  • Run tests under ASan+UBSan and TSan in CI on every commit.
  • Warnings-as-errors, clang-tidy and cppcheck catch bugs before running.
  • Fuzz any code that parses untrusted input.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Which sanitizer finds a data race?

Show answer

ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread).

Q2. Can ASan and TSan be combined in one build?

Show answer

No — they're incompatible; use separate builds.

Q3. What's a property-based test?

Show answer

A test that checks an invariant holds across many generated inputs, often against a simple reference model.

docs.title: Lesson 15.4: Debugging, profiling, and compiler optimization
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: "It's slow" is not a diagnosis. Professionals measure first: profile to find the 5% of code that takes 90% of the time, then optimize that, then measure again. And when it crashes, a debugger beats a hundred std::cout lines. This lesson is a field guide to the tools.

docs.title: Debugging essentials
docs.text: Build with -g -O0 (or -Og) for debugging. In gdb/lldb: break file.cpp:42, run, bt (backtrace), frame 2, print x, watch buffer[3] (stop when memory changes), catch throw. Enable core dumps (ulimit -c unlimited) to inspect crashes after the fact.

docs.title: Optimization flags
docs.text: -O2 is the usual release level; -O3 adds aggressive inlining/vectorization (measure — not always faster). -march=native uses your CPU's instructions (don't ship it to unknown machines). LTO (-flto) optimizes across translation units; PGO (-fprofile-generate → run → -fprofile-use) lets the compiler optimize for real workloads — often 10–20% for branchy code.

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text: Sampling profilers (perf record -g ./app && perf report, VTune, Instruments) show where time goes with low overhead. Frame profilers like Tracy are great for games and real-time code.

docs.title: Micro-benchmarks lie unless you're careful
docs.text:
The compiler deletes work whose result is unused; caches are warm on the second run; timers have resolution limits. Use Google Benchmark (benchmark::DoNotOptimize), repeat runs, and report medians.

examples/week15/lesson04.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

template <typename F>
double time_ms(F&& f, int reps) {
    auto best = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>::max();
    for (int r = 0; r < reps; ++r) {                    // take the best of several runs
        auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        f();
        auto dt = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0);
        if (dt < best) best = dt;
    }
    return best.count();
}

int classify(int x) {
    if (x < 0) [[unlikely]] return -1;
    return x % 3;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<std::int32_t> data(2'000'000);
    std::iota(data.begin(), data.end(), 0);
    volatile std::int64_t sink = 0;                     // keep results observable so work isn't deleted

    double loop_ms = time_ms([&] {
        std::int64_t s = 0;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < data.size(); ++i) s += data[i];
        sink = s;
    }, 5);
    double accum_ms = time_ms([&] { sink = std::accumulate(data.begin(), data.end(), std::int64_t{0}); }, 5);

    std::cout << "checksum " << sink << '\n';
    std::cout << "classify(-5)=" << classify(-5) << " classify(7)=" << classify(7) << '\n';
    std::cerr << "loop " << loop_ms << " ms, accumulate " << accum_ms << " ms (machine-dependent)\n";
}

Output:

checksum 1999999000000
classify(-5)=-1 classify(7)=1

The example measures a summation two ways and is careful to use the result. Timings are machine-dependent, so only the checksum is verified.

docs.title: Hints to the compiler
docs.text: [[likely]]/[[unlikely]] (C++20) mark branch probabilities; [[assume(expr)]] (C++23) promises a condition (UB if false!). C++26 adds std::simd for portable data-parallel types. Use hints only after profiling shows they help.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Measure before optimizing: sampling profilers find the hot spots.
  • -O2 for release; LTO and PGO give cross-TU and workload-driven gains.
  • Benchmarks must defeat dead-code elimination, warm caches deliberately and repeat runs.
  • Use [[likely]]/[[assume]] sparingly and only with evidence.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why might a benchmark of for (...) s += x; report 0 ns?

Show answer

If s is unused the optimizer removes the loop entirely.

Q2. What does PGO do?

Show answer

Uses profiles from representative runs to guide inlining, layout and branch decisions.

Q3. What happens if an [[assume(x > 0)]] is false at run time?

Show answer

Undefined behaviour — the compiler may have optimized based on it.

docs.title: Lesson 15.5: Performance: caches, memory layout, and data-oriented design
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A main-memory access costs ~100 ns; an L1 cache hit ~1 ns. On modern hardware, how your data is laid out often matters more than the algorithm's big-O constant. Data-oriented design — organizing data for the way it's accessed — routinely gives 2–10× speedups in games, audio and simulation code.

docs.title: The rules of thumb
docs.text:
1. Contiguous beats linked: std::vector iterates at memory bandwidth; std::list chases pointers and misses cache on every node.
  2. Only load what you use: if a loop touches one field of a 64-byte struct, you load 64 bytes to use 4.
  3. Avoid allocations in hot loops: reserve, reuse buffers, use arenas (Week 12).
  4. Predictable branches are cheap; unpredictable ones cost ~15 cycles each.

docs.title: AoS vs SoA
docs.text:
struct Particle { float x, y, z, vx, vy, vz; std::uint32_t color; bool alive; };   // AoS
struct Particles { std::vector<float> x, y, z, vx, vy, vz; ... };                  // SoA

Updating positions in SoA streams through tightly packed arrays (and vectorizes); AoS drags the unused fields through the cache.

examples/week15/lesson05.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <list>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

struct Padded { char a; double b; char c; };          // 1 + 7 pad + 8 + 1 + 7 pad = 24
struct Reordered { double b; char a; char c; };        // 8 + 1 + 1 + 6 pad = 16

struct ParticleAoS { float x, y, z, vx, vy, vz; std::uint32_t color; bool alive; float mass, age; };
struct ParticlesSoA { std::vector<float> x, vx; };

template <typename F> double ms(F f) {
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); f();
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - t0).count();
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "sizeof Padded=" << sizeof(Padded) << " Reordered=" << sizeof(Reordered) << '\n';

    constexpr std::size_t n = 1'000'000;
    std::vector<ParticleAoS> aos(n, ParticleAoS{0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, true, 1, 0});
    ParticlesSoA soa{std::vector<float>(n, 0.0f), std::vector<float>(n, 1.0f)};

    double t_aos = ms([&] { for (auto& p : aos) p.x += p.vx * 0.5f; });
    double t_soa = ms([&] { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) soa.x[i] += soa.vx[i] * 0.5f; });
    std::cout << "positions equal: " << std::boolalpha << (aos[n / 2].x == soa.x[n / 2]) << '\n';

    std::vector<int> v(n, 1);
    std::list<int> l(n, 1);
    long long sv = 0, sl = 0;
    double t_vec = ms([&] { sv = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL); });
    double t_list = ms([&] { sl = std::accumulate(l.begin(), l.end(), 0LL); });
    std::cout << "sums " << sv << ' ' << sl << '\n';
    std::cerr << "AoS " << t_aos << " ms, SoA " << t_soa << " ms; vector " << t_vec << " ms, list " << t_list << " ms\n";
}

Output:

sizeof Padded=24 Reordered=16
positions equal: true
sums 1000000 1000000

The example also shows padding: member order changes sizeof. Timings print to stderr since they're machine-dependent; on typical hardware SoA and vector traversal are several times faster.

Pro tip

Don't restructure everything into SoA. Do it for the hot data that profiling identifies. Clear code first, then optimize with evidence.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Memory access patterns often dominate performance; keep hot data contiguous.
  • SoA layouts stream only the fields a loop uses and vectorize well.
  • Order members largest-to-smallest to reduce padding.
  • Optimize the hot path identified by profiling, not everything.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is iterating a std::list slower than a std::vector of the same size?

Show answer

List nodes are scattered in memory, so each step is a likely cache miss; vector elements are contiguous and prefetched.

Q2. What is sizeof(struct { char a; double b; char c; }) on a typical 64-bit ABI?

Show answer

24 bytes due to padding for 8-byte alignment of double.

Q3. When does SoA beat AoS?

Show answer

When hot loops access only a few fields of many objects.

docs.title: Lesson 15.6: Security hardening and the C++ Core Guidelines
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Roughly 70% of serious security bugs in large C and C++ codebases are memory-safety bugs. Governments and companies now ask hard questions about C++. The honest answer: modern C++ with good habits and hardened builds eliminates most of these bugs — but only if you actually use them. This lesson collects the habits.

docs.title: Habits that eliminate whole bug classes
docs.text: Bug class Modern C++ habit Buffer overflow containers + std::span, range-for, hardened library checks Use-after-free / leaks RAII, smart pointers, no raw owning pointers Dangling references don't return references to locals; watch string_view/span lifetimes Integer overflow / sign bugs std::cmp_less, std::in_range, checked narrowing Uninitialized memory always initialize; -ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero; C++26 makes it erroneous behaviour Type confusion no C casts; std::variant over unions; dynamic_cast when downcasting

docs.title: Hardened builds
docs.text:
• -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS (libstdc++) or -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_FAST (libc++) turns operator[] out-of-bounds and similar precondition violations into a trap. Cost is usually low single-digit percent; many vendors ship with it enabled.
  • -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -O2, -fstack-protector-strong, -fstack-clash-protection, -fPIE -pie, -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now — see the OpenSSF compiler hardening guide.
examples/week15/lesson06.cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>
#include <span>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename To, typename From>
To narrow_checked(From v) {                            // like gsl::narrow
    if (!std::in_range<To>(v)) throw std::range_error{"narrowing would lose data"};
    return static_cast<To>(v);
}

double average(std::span<const double> xs) {          // pointer+length travel together
    if (xs.empty()) return 0.0;
    double s = 0;
    for (double x : xs) s += x;                        // no index arithmetic to get wrong
    return s / static_cast<double>(xs.size());
}

int main() {
    std::vector<double> levels{0.5, 0.25, 0.75};
    std::cout << "average " << average(levels) << '\n';
    try { (void)levels.at(10); } catch (const std::out_of_range&) { std::cout << "at() caught out-of-bounds\n"; }

    int count = -1;
    std::size_t size = 3;
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << "-1 < 3u with raw compare: " << (static_cast<unsigned>(count) < size)
              << ", with cmp_less: " << std::cmp_less(count, size) << '\n';
    try { (void)narrow_checked<std::uint8_t>(300); } catch (const std::range_error& e) { std::cout << e.what() << '\n'; }
    std::cout << "narrow 200 -> " << int{narrow_checked<std::uint8_t>(200)} << '\n';

    int initialized{};                                 // always initialize
    std::cout << "initialized = " << initialized << '\n';
}

Output:

average 0.5
at() caught out-of-bounds
-1 < 3u with raw compare: false, with cmp_less: true
narrowing would lose data
narrow 200 -> 200
initialized = 0

docs.title: The C++ Core Guidelines
docs.text: The C++ Core Guidelines (Stroustrup & Sutter) are the community's style and safety rulebook: R.* for resources, F.* for functions, ES.* for expressions, CP.* for concurrency. The GSL library provides helpers like gsl::not_null<T*> and gsl::narrow<T> (throws on lossy conversion). clang-tidy can enforce many rules automatically.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Most memory-safety bugs are prevented by RAII, containers, spans and no raw owning pointers.
  • Ship hardened builds: library assertions, FORTIFY_SOURCE, stack protector, PIE/RELRO.
  • Use std::cmp_less/std::in_range and checked narrowing for integer safety.
  • Follow the C++ Core Guidelines and enforce them with clang-tidy.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS do?

Show answer

Enables libstdc++ precondition checks, e.g. trapping on out-of-bounds vector::operator[].

Q2. Why is -1 < 3u false?

Show answer

-1 converts to a huge unsigned value; use std::cmp_less(-1, 3u) which compares mathematically.

Q3. Name three Core Guidelines-backed habits that prevent use-after-free.

Show answer

RAII ownership, smart pointers instead of raw owning pointers, not storing references/views that outlive their owner.

docs.title: Week 15 quiz
docs.text:
Mixed review of the whole week. Try answering before you peek.

Q1. (from 15.1) What does PUBLIC mean in target_include_directories(dsp PUBLIC include)?

Show answer

The include directory is used to build dsp and propagates to targets that link dsp.

Q2. (from 15.1) Name two advantages of modules over headers.

Show answer

Faster builds (parsed once), no macro leakage, explicit export control, less ODR fragility.

Q3. (from 15.2) Why can't C code call an overloaded C++ function directly?

Show answer

C++ mangles parameter types into symbol names; C expects plain names. Use extern "C" wrappers (which can't be overloaded).

Q4. (from 15.2) Is adding a private member to a class in a shared library's header ABI-compatible?

Show answer

No — it changes the object's size/layout, breaking binaries compiled against the old header.

Q5. (from 15.3) Which sanitizer finds a data race?

Show answer

ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread).

Q6. (from 15.3) Can ASan and TSan be combined in one build?

Show answer

No — they're incompatible; use separate builds.

Q7. (from 15.4) Why might a benchmark of for (...) s += x; report 0 ns?

Show answer

If s is unused the optimizer removes the loop entirely.

Q8. (from 15.4) What does PGO do?

Show answer

Uses profiles from representative runs to guide inlining, layout and branch decisions.

Q9. (from 15.5) Why is iterating a std::list slower than a std::vector of the same size?

Show answer

List nodes are scattered in memory, so each step is a likely cache miss; vector elements are contiguous and prefetched.

Q10. (from 15.5) What is sizeof(struct { char a; double b; char c; }) on a typical 64-bit ABI?

Show answer

24 bytes due to padding for 8-byte alignment of double.

Q11. (from 15.6) What does -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS do?

Show answer

Enables libstdc++ precondition checks, e.g. trapping on out-of-bounds vector::operator[].

Q12. (from 15.6) Why is -1 < 3u false?

Show answer

-1 converts to a huge unsigned value; use std::cmp_less(-1, 3u) which compares mathematically.

docs.title: Week 16: C++ in the real world: interop, embedded, design, and what's next
docs.text:
The final week zooms out. C++ rarely lives alone: it talks to C, Python, Java/Android and hardware. We look at embedded constraints, the design patterns and API design principles that make large C++ codebases maintainable, and finish with a tour of C++26. Then it's capstone time.
