# Lesson Standard Length 16.1 Interoperability: C, Python (pybind11), and Java/Android (JNI) C++20 13 min 16.2 Embedded and real-time C++ C++20 13 min 16.3 Design patterns in modern C++ C++20 13 min 16.4 API and library design C++23 12 min 16.5 C++26 preview: reflection, contracts, std::execution, and more C++26 14 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 16 programming assignment: Ship a library
docs.text:
Package one of your earlier assignments (e.g. the LRU cache or the config parser) as a library: a namespaced public header with strong types and [[nodiscard]], a C API wrapper with opaque handles and error codes, tests, and a CMakeLists.txt with PUBLIC/PRIVATE usage requirements. The reference solution shows the C API wrapper over the LRU cache, exercised from "C-style" client code.

Reference solution examples/week16/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

namespace cache {
class Lru {
public:
    explicit Lru(std::size_t cap) : cap_{cap} {}
    [[nodiscard]] const std::string* get(const std::string& k) {
        auto it = index_.find(k);
        if (it == index_.end()) return nullptr;
        order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, it->second);
        return &it->second->second;
    }
    void put(std::string k, std::string v) {
        if (auto it = index_.find(k); it != index_.end()) { it->second->second = std::move(v); order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, it->second); return; }
        if (order_.size() == cap_) { index_.erase(order_.back().first); order_.pop_back(); }
        order_.emplace_front(k, std::move(v));
        index_[std::move(k)] = order_.begin();
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return order_.size(); }
private:
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::list<std::pair<std::string, std::string>> order_;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::list<std::pair<std::string, std::string>>::iterator> index_;
};
}  // namespace cache

extern "C" {
typedef struct lru_cache lru_cache;
enum { LRU_OK = 0, LRU_MISS = 1, LRU_ERR = 2, LRU_TOO_SMALL = 3 };
lru_cache* lru_create(size_t capacity);
void lru_destroy(lru_cache* c);
int lru_put(lru_cache* c, const char* key, const char* value);
int lru_get(lru_cache* c, const char* key, char* out, size_t out_size);
}

struct lru_cache { cache::Lru impl; };

extern "C" lru_cache* lru_create(size_t capacity) {
    if (capacity == 0) return nullptr;
    try { return new lru_cache{cache::Lru{capacity}}; } catch (...) { return nullptr; }
}
extern "C" void lru_destroy(lru_cache* c) { delete c; }
extern "C" int lru_put(lru_cache* c, const char* key, const char* value) {
    if (!c || !key || !value) return LRU_ERR;
    try { c->impl.put(key, value); return LRU_OK; } catch (...) { return LRU_ERR; }
}
extern "C" int lru_get(lru_cache* c, const char* key, char* out, size_t out_size) {
    if (!c || !key || !out || out_size == 0) return LRU_ERR;
    try {
        const std::string* v = c->impl.get(key);
        if (!v) return LRU_MISS;
        if (v->size() + 1 > out_size) return LRU_TOO_SMALL;
        std::memcpy(out, v->c_str(), v->size() + 1);
        return LRU_OK;
    } catch (...) { return LRU_ERR; }
}

int main() {                                           // written like C client code
    lru_cache* c = lru_create(2);
    lru_put(c, "kick", "kick.wav");
    lru_put(c, "snare", "snare.wav");
    char buf[32];
    if (lru_get(c, "kick", buf, sizeof buf) == LRU_OK) std::printf("kick -> %s\n", buf);
    lru_put(c, "hat", "hat.wav");                       // evicts snare (least recently used)
    std::printf("snare -> %s\n", lru_get(c, "snare", buf, sizeof buf) == LRU_MISS ? "(evicted)" : buf);
    char tiny[4];
    std::printf("small buffer -> rc=%d\n", lru_get(c, "hat", tiny, sizeof tiny));
    std::printf("create(0) -> %s\n", lru_create(0) ? "handle" : "NULL");
    lru_destroy(c);
}

Output:

kick -> kick.wav
snare -> (evicted)
small buffer -> rc=3
create(0) -> NULL

docs.title: Lesson 16.1: Interoperability: C, Python (pybind11), and Java/Android (JNI)
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Your C++ DSP engine is great — now the Python data team, the Android app and a legacy C codebase all want it. The universal adapter is a C API: every language can call C. On top of it (or directly), tools like pybind11 and JNI make C++ feel native in Python and Java.

docs.title: The opaque-handle pattern
docs.text:
Expose a C API with an incomplete type and create/destroy functions; never let C++ exceptions or types cross the boundary:

examples/week16/lesson01.cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

// ===== dsp.h — what C (and every FFI) sees =====
extern "C" {
typedef struct dsp_mixer dsp_mixer;                       // opaque handle
typedef void (*dsp_level_cb)(double level, void* user);
enum { DSP_OK = 0, DSP_ERR_ARG = 1, DSP_ERR_INTERNAL = 2 };
dsp_mixer* dsp_mixer_create(int channels);
void dsp_mixer_destroy(dsp_mixer* m);
int dsp_mixer_process(dsp_mixer* m, const float* samples, int n, dsp_level_cb cb, void* user);
}

// ===== dsp.cpp — the C++ implementation =====
struct dsp_mixer {
    int channels;
    std::vector<float> scratch;
    double process(const float* s, int n) {
        if (n < 0) throw std::invalid_argument{"negative length"};
        scratch.assign(s, s + n);
        double sum = 0; for (float x : scratch) sum += static_cast<double>(x) * x;
        return n ? std::sqrt(sum / n) : 0.0;
    }
};

extern "C" dsp_mixer* dsp_mixer_create(int channels) {
    try { return new dsp_mixer{channels, {}}; } catch (...) { return nullptr; }
}
extern "C" void dsp_mixer_destroy(dsp_mixer* m) { delete m; }
extern "C" int dsp_mixer_process(dsp_mixer* m, const float* s, int n, dsp_level_cb cb, void* user) {
    if (!m || (!s && n > 0)) return DSP_ERR_ARG;
    try {                                                 // no exception may escape into C
        double level = m->process(s, n);
        if (cb) cb(level, user);
        return DSP_OK;
    } catch (const std::invalid_argument&) { return DSP_ERR_ARG; }
    catch (...) { return DSP_ERR_INTERNAL; }
}

// ===== a "C client" =====
static void on_level(double level, void* user) {
    *static_cast<double*>(user) = level;
}

int main() {
    dsp_mixer* m = dsp_mixer_create(2);
    float samples[] = {0.5f, -0.5f, 0.5f, -0.5f};
    double level = 0;
    int rc = dsp_mixer_process(m, samples, 4, on_level, &level);
    std::printf("rc=%d level=%.3f\n", rc, level);
    rc = dsp_mixer_process(m, samples, -1, on_level, &level);
    std::printf("negative length -> rc=%d (exception stayed inside C++)\n", rc);
    std::printf("null handle -> rc=%d\n", dsp_mixer_process(nullptr, samples, 4, nullptr, nullptr));
    dsp_mixer_destroy(m);
}

Output:

rc=0 level=0.500
negative length -> rc=1 (exception stayed inside C++)
null handle -> rc=1

Rules: catch everything at the boundary (try { ... } catch (...) { return error_code; }) — an exception unwinding into C is undefined behaviour. Pass callbacks as a function pointer plus void* user_data. Document who frees what.

docs.title: Python with pybind11
docs.text:
#include <pybind11/pybind11.h>
#include <pybind11/stl.h>
namespace py = pybind11;
PYBIND11_MODULE(dsp, m) {
    py::class_<Gain>(m, "Gain")
        .def(py::init<double>())
        .def("apply", &Gain::apply)
        .def_property_readonly("db", &Gain::db);
    m.def("rms", &rms, "Root mean square of a list of samples");
}

Build with CMake + pybind11_add_module, then import dsp in Python. pybind11 converts STL types and translates exceptions to Python exceptions. nanobind is a lighter, faster successor. Release the GIL (py::gil_scoped_release) around long C++ computations.

docs.title: Java/Android with JNI
docs.text:
extern "C" JNIEXPORT jdouble JNICALL
Java_com_example_dsp_Native_rms(JNIEnv* env, jclass, jfloatArray samples) {
    jsize n = env->GetArrayLength(samples);
    jfloat* p = env->GetFloatArrayElements(samples, nullptr);
    double r = rms({p, static_cast<std::size_t>(n)});
    env->ReleaseFloatArrayElements(samples, p, JNI_ABORT);   // always release!
    return r;
}

On Android, the NDK builds C++ with CMake (externalNativeBuild) and you load it with System.loadLibrary("dsp"). JNI local references, array pinning and thread attachment (AttachCurrentThread) are the common traps.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A C API with opaque handles is the universal interop layer.
  • Never let exceptions cross a C boundary; convert them to error codes.
  • pybind11/nanobind bind C++ to Python; JNI/NDK bind it to Java/Android.
  • Make ownership explicit across language boundaries.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why must dsp_mixer_process catch all exceptions?

Show answer

Unwinding through C frames (or into another language's runtime) is undefined behaviour.

Q2. How does a C callback get access to the caller's state?

Show answer

Through a void* user_data parameter passed back to the callback.

Q3. What does JNI_ABORT in ReleaseFloatArrayElements mean?

Show answer

Free the buffer without copying changes back to the Java array (we only read it).

docs.title: Lesson 16.2: Embedded and real-time C++
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A microcontroller might have 64 KB of flash, 16 KB of RAM, no OS, and an interrupt that must be serviced in 2 µs. C++ is excellent here — templates and constexpr cost nothing at run time — but you have to choose the right subset: no heap after startup, often no exceptions or RTTI, and very deliberate access to hardware.

docs.title: The embedded subset
docs.text:
• No heap after init: fragmentation and non-deterministic timing. Use static storage, fixed-capacity containers (std::array, the ring buffer capstone, C++26 std::inplace_vector), and pools.
  • Exceptions/RTTI are often disabled (-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti) for code size and determinism; use error codes / std::expected.
  • Compute at compile time: constexpr tables live in flash, not RAM.

docs.title: Hardware registers
docs.text:
struct Uart { volatile std::uint32_t data, status, ctrl; };
inline Uart& uart0 = *reinterpret_cast<Uart*>(0x4000'1000);   // on real hardware

volatile tells the compiler every access matters (it can't cache or remove them). C++20 deprecated compound operations like reg |= bit on volatile because they suggest atomicity that doesn't exist; write reg = reg | bit. Below we simulate a register block in RAM so the example runs anywhere.

examples/week16/lesson02.cpp
#include <array>
#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

// ---- simulated memory-mapped peripheral ----
struct GpioRegs {
    volatile std::uint32_t mode;
    volatile std::uint32_t out;
    volatile std::uint32_t in;
};
GpioRegs fake_gpio{};                                    // on hardware: *reinterpret_cast<GpioRegs*>(0x48000000)

constexpr std::uint32_t pin(unsigned n) { return 1u << n; }
void led_on(GpioRegs& g, unsigned n) { g.out = g.out | pin(n); }      // not `|=`: deprecated on volatile
void led_off(GpioRegs& g, unsigned n) { g.out = g.out & ~pin(n); }

// ---- Q15 fixed point ----
using q15 = std::int16_t;
constexpr q15 to_q15(double x) { return static_cast<q15>(x * 32768.0 >= 32767.0 ? 32767 : x * 32768.0); }
constexpr q15 q15_mul(q15 a, q15 b) {
    std::int32_t p = (static_cast<std::int32_t>(a) * b) >> 15;
    return static_cast<q15>(p > 32767 ? 32767 : (p < -32768 ? -32768 : p));
}

// ---- compile-time lookup table (lives in flash on an MCU) ----
constexpr auto make_square_table() {
    std::array<std::uint16_t, 16> t{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < t.size(); ++i) t[i] = static_cast<std::uint16_t>(i * i);
    return t;
}
constexpr auto kSquares = make_square_table();
static_assert(kSquares[15] == 225);

// ---- a static pool: fixed number of objects, no heap ----
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class StaticPool {
public:
    T* acquire() { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) if (!used_[i]) { used_[i] = true; return &items_[i]; } return nullptr; }
    void release(T* p) { used_[static_cast<std::size_t>(p - items_.data())] = false; }
private:
    std::array<T, N> items_{};
    std::array<bool, N> used_{};
};

int main() {
    led_on(fake_gpio, 5);
    led_on(fake_gpio, 0);
    led_off(fake_gpio, 5);
    std::cout << "GPIO out = 0x" << std::hex << fake_gpio.out << std::dec << '\n';

    q15 half = to_q15(0.5), gain = to_q15(0.25);
    std::cout << "0.5 * 0.25 in Q15 = " << q15_mul(half, gain) << " (" << q15_mul(half, gain) / 32768.0 << ")\n";
    std::cout << "saturating -1 * -1 = " << q15_mul(-32768, -32768) << '\n';

    std::cout << "kSquares[12] = " << kSquares[12] << '\n';
    std::cout << "popcount(0xF0F0) = " << std::popcount(0xF0F0u) << ", bit_width(1000) = " << std::bit_width(1000u)
              << ", float bits = 0x" << std::hex << std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(1.0f) << std::dec << '\n';

    StaticPool<int, 2> pool;
    int* a = pool.acquire(); int* b = pool.acquire(); int* c = pool.acquire();
    std::cout << "pool: a " << (a ? "ok" : "null") << ", b " << (b ? "ok" : "null") << ", c " << (c ? "ok" : "null") << '\n';
    pool.release(a);
    std::cout << "after release: " << (pool.acquire() ? "ok" : "null") << '\n';
}

Output:

GPIO out = 0x1
0.5 * 0.25 in Q15 = 4096 (0.125)
saturating -1 * -1 = 32767
kSquares[12] = 144
popcount(0xF0F0) = 8, bit_width(1000) = 10, float bits = 0x3f800000
pool: a ok, b ok, c null
after release: ok

docs.title: Fixed-point
docs.text: Many MCUs lack an FPU. Q15 fixed-point stores values in [-1, 1) as int16_t scaled by 2^15; multiplication is (a * b) >> 15 in 32-bit. The example implements a Q15 gain with saturation.

docs.title: Sharing with interrupts
docs.text: An ISR and the main loop share data like threads do. Use std::atomic (if lock-free on the target) or a critical section (disable interrupts briefly). The SPSC ring buffer from Week 14 is the classic ISR→main channel — see Capstone B.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Embedded C++ avoids the heap after init and often disables exceptions/RTTI.
  • volatile is for hardware registers; avoid compound ops on volatile (deprecated in C++20).
  • constexpr tables, fixed-point math and static pools give deterministic, small code.
  • Share data with ISRs via lock-free atomics or brief critical sections (SPSC ring buffer).

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why avoid dynamic allocation after startup on an MCU?

Show answer

Fragmentation and non-deterministic timing can cause failures or missed deadlines.

Q2. Why did C++20 deprecate reg |= bit on a volatile?

Show answer

It looks atomic but is a separate read and write; writing it out makes the two accesses explicit.

Q3. What is 0.5 × 0.25 in Q15 as an integer?

Show answer

4096 (0.125 × 32768).

docs.title: Lesson 16.3: Design patterns in modern C++
docs.text: C++20 · about 13 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Classic design patterns were described for 1990s Java and C++. Modern C++ often expresses them more simply: a strategy can be a lambda, a visitor can be std::visit over a variant, and an observer must care about lifetimes (who unsubscribes when an object dies?). Knowing the modern form keeps designs small.

docs.title: Modern forms of classic patterns
When not to use a pattern
docs.text: Patterns are vocabulary, not goals. If a plain function solves it, write a plain function. Every indirection (virtual call, std::function, registry) costs readability; add it when you need the flexibility, not before.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Many patterns shrink in modern C++: strategy = callable, visitor = std::visit.
  • Observers must handle listener lifetime; weak_ptr or tokens avoid dangling callbacks.
  • Registries of creator functions make extensible factories.
  • Use a pattern when you need its flexibility, not by default.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. When is std::variant + std::visit better than a virtual-function hierarchy?

Show answer

When the set of types is closed and known, and you want to add operations easily without touching the types.

Q2. What bug does weak_ptr prevent in the observer?

Show answer

Calling a listener that has been destroyed (dangling callback).

Q3. What's the cost of using std::function for a strategy?

Show answer

Type erasure: possible heap allocation and an indirect call that's hard to inline; a template parameter avoids it.

docs.title: Lesson 16.4: API and library design
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: set_volume(0.8, 1) — is that 80% on channel 1, or volume 1 with 0.8 seconds fade? Good APIs make correct use easy and incorrect use hard at compile time. A library's interface outlives its implementation by years; this lesson is about getting it right.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Make illegal states unrepresentable: strong types (Gain, Channel, Milliseconds) instead of naked double/int; enums instead of bool flags.
  2. Mark results that must be used: [[nodiscard("check the error")]].
  3. Pick one error policy per library (Week 9) and document it.
  4. Value semantics and const-correctness: take const T&/std::string_view/std::span for inputs, return values, avoid out-parameters.
  5. Evolve without breaking: [[deprecated("use X")]], inline namespaces for versioning, keep ABI policies explicit (pimpl, Week 15).
examples/week16/lesson04.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <expected>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace mixer {
inline namespace v2 {                                   // default version; v1 kept for old clients

struct Channel { int index; explicit constexpr Channel(int i) : index{i} {} };
struct Gain {
    double linear;
    static constexpr Gain from_percent(double p) { return Gain{p / 100.0}; }
};
using Fade = std::chrono::milliseconds;

enum class Error { bad_channel, out_of_range };
constexpr std::string_view describe(Error e) { return e == Error::bad_channel ? "bad channel" : "gain out of range"; }

class Console {
public:
    [[nodiscard("check whether the change was applied")]]
    std::expected<void, Error> set_volume(Channel ch, Gain g, Fade fade = Fade{0}) {
        if (ch.index < 0 || ch.index >= 8) return std::unexpected{Error::bad_channel};
        if (g.linear < 0 || g.linear > 2) return std::unexpected{Error::out_of_range};
        std::cout << "ch" << ch.index << " -> " << g.linear << " over " << fade.count() << "ms\n";
        return {};
    }
    [[deprecated("use set_volume(Channel, Gain, Fade)")]]
    bool setVol(int ch, double v) { return set_volume(Channel{ch}, Gain{v}).has_value(); }
};

}  // namespace v2
namespace v1 { inline int api_version() { return 1; } }
inline int api_version() { return 2; }
}  // namespace mixer

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono_literals;
    mixer::Console c;
    // c.set_volume(0.8, 1);                            // won't compile: arguments can't be mixed up
    if (auto r = c.set_volume(mixer::Channel{1}, mixer::Gain::from_percent(80), 250ms); !r)
        std::cout << "error: " << describe(r.error()) << '\n';
    if (auto r = c.set_volume(mixer::Channel{9}, mixer::Gain{0.5}); !r)
        std::cout << "error: " << describe(r.error()) << '\n';
    std::cout << "api v" << mixer::api_version() << " (old clients can call v1: " << mixer::v1::api_version() << ")\n";
}

Output:

ch1 -> 0.8 over 250ms
error: bad channel
api v2 (old clients can call v1: 1)

docs.title: Checklist for a public header
docs.text:
• Includes only what it needs (consider forward declarations).
  • No using namespace at header scope.
  • Everything in a project namespace.
  • Every function documents preconditions, errors, and ownership.
  • Tests use only the public API.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Strong types and enums turn argument mix-ups into compile errors.
  • [[nodiscard]] and std::expected make errors hard to ignore.
  • Use [[deprecated]] and inline namespaces to evolve APIs without breaking users.
  • Keep public headers minimal, namespaced and fully documented.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Why is void f(bool fast, bool safe) a weak signature?

Show answer

Call sites like f(true, false) are unreadable and easy to swap; use enums or strong types.

Q2. What does an inline namespace give you for versioning?

Show answer

Its contents are accessible from the enclosing namespace by default, while older versions remain addressable explicitly (and mangled names differ per version).

Q3. What happens when a caller ignores a [[nodiscard]] result?

Show answer

The compiler warns (an error with -Werror).

docs.title: Lesson 16.5: C++26 preview: reflection, contracts, std::execution, and more
docs.text: C++26 · about 14 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: C++26 is the biggest release since C++11. Static reflection alone will change how we write serialization, bindings and logging. Compilers are implementing it now, so this lesson is honest about status: the C++26 code below is not compiled by our checker (marked preview); the runnable example shows the C++23 code you write today for the same problems, so you can see what C++26 will replace.

docs.title: Static reflection (P2996)
docs.text:
// C++26 (preview): print any aggregate's fields with no macros
template <typename T>
void print_fields(const T& obj) {
    template for (constexpr auto m : std::define_static_array(std::meta::nonstatic_data_members_of(^^T, std::meta::access_context::current())))
        std::println("{} = {}", std::meta::identifier_of(m), obj.[:m:]);
}

^^T reflects a type into a std::meta::info value; [: m :] splices it back into code. Serialization, enum-to-string, ORM mappings and Python bindings become library code instead of macros or code generators. (Experimental implementations: Bloomberg's clang-p2996 fork and EDG; GCC 16 has initial support.)

docs.title: Contracts (P2900)
docs.text:
double rms(std::span<const float> xs)
    pre(!xs.empty())
    post(r: r >= 0.0);

Preconditions and postconditions become part of the declaration, checked according to a build-selected evaluation semantic (ignore, observe, enforce, quick-enforce). contract_assert(expr) replaces assert.

docs.title: std::execution (P2300)
docs.text:
auto work = stdexec::schedule(pool.get_scheduler())
          | stdexec::then([] { return decode(); })
          | stdexec::then([](Audio a) { return analyze(a); });
auto [report] = stdexec::sync_wait(std::move(work)).value();

Composable, cancellable async work with explicit schedulers — usable today via NVIDIA's stdexec.

docs.title: Smaller but welcome
docs.text:
• std::inplace_vector<T, N>: a vector with fixed capacity and no heap — perfect for embedded (Week 16.2).
  • Pack indexing: Ts...[0] is the first type in a pack.
  • void f(int) = delete("use f(Channel)"); — deletion with a reason.
  • auto [_, value] = pair; — _ placeholders you can reuse.
  • #embed "logo.png" — include binary data at compile time.
  • std::simd, std::hazard_pointer, std::rcu, std::linalg, saturating arithmetic (std::add_sat).
  • Erroneous behaviour: reading an uninitialized variable is no longer UB but "erroneous" (a defined, diagnosable value); hardened library preconditions are standardized.

docs.title: What you write today
Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Static reflection (C++26) turns macros and code generators into ordinary library code.
  • Contracts make preconditions/postconditions part of declarations with selectable checking.
  • std::execution provides composable, cancellable async work; usable today via stdexec.
  • Many smaller features (inplace_vector, pack indexing, _, #embed, saturating math) remove workarounds.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What does ^^T produce in C++26?

Show answer

A std::meta::info value representing the type T at compile time.

Q2. How do C++26 contracts differ from assert?

Show answer

They're part of the function declaration (visible to callers and tools) and have standardized evaluation semantics selectable at build time.

Q3. Which C++26 container replaces a hand-written fixed-capacity vector?

Show answer

std::inplace_vector<T, N>.
